When interviewing suspects on audio visual recording, summarising should be used regularly to lock the suspect into their account and emphasise important aspects of their account to the suspect and anyone watching the interview. Use summarising with witness interviews to ensure you understand correctly what they have told you and can prepare an accurate written statement. Summarise back to them using their own words using a clarification seeking approach. Explain to the witness that they need to correct you if any part of your summary is inaccurate. Careful accurate summarising is vital as inaccurate summarising can contaminate the person's memory. QUESTIONING Introduction All members of the public have a duty to help investigators to prevent crime and identify offenders. This is a civic rather than a legal duty. When you are trying to discover whether, or by whom, an offence has been committed, you are entitled to question any person from whom you think useful information can be obtained. Most people will assist your investigations readily, but if a witness is unwilling to answer questions about a particular offence or incident, no action can normally be taken. The exception to this rule is when there is a legal obligation to provide information. (E.g. Road Traffic Act). Basic Rules of Questioning The type of questioning you use in an investigative interview is vital. An outline of the basic rules are as follows: • Vocabulary - The language used should be simple, unambiguous and jargon free so all parties understand what is meant; • Relevance - Each question must have a purpose and not be used to fill time. A well prepared interview plan accompanied by listening carefully to everything that is said should eliminate repetitive questioning. • Pace - The interviewee must be allowed time to understand the question, think what knowledge they have of the matter, formulate their answer and deliver it. • Interruptions - Interviewers must learn to curb any tendency to interrupt the interviewee as this will break the person's train of thought and stop the flow of information, potentially preventing important facts from emerging; and • Control - If a suspect interviewee strays from the point, direct him or her back firmly but tactfully e.g. ‘That's very interesting, but before you continue, can you tell me what happened when you first saw the person acting suspiciously in the street?’ Suspects often try to take interviewers off track to avoid difficult or evidential topics in the hope you will be side tracked and not go back. However this 'redirection' back to topics by the interviewer should be used sparingly with witnesses as they will often move to information that is readily available i.e. what comes to mind and therefore what they are thinking about. In those circumstances we need to ask questions that are compatible with what they are thinking about. Once we have done that, we can move back to the unfinished issue or topic. Appropriate Questions There are a variety of different types of questions you can use as an investigative interviewer. The types you use should be those that will elicit the most accurate, complete and reliable information. How the first question of the interview is worded is vital to the usefulness or otherwise of any subsequent information provided by the interviewee. Open Questions An open question is the best type of question and is framed to encourage the interviewee to provide a detailed answer. Advantages of asking open questions include: • Allowing interviewees to give a detailed full account; • Encouraging the interviewee to control the information flow; and • Minimising the risk of the interviewer influencing what the interviewee says. The resulting account will have better quality and quantity of information than if other types of questions were used. Open questions should be used as much as possible during the interview and your full attention is required to observe and listen to everything. TEDS Style Questions Learning to ask open questions is a skill that will take practice. Asking questions using the words represented by the mnemonic TEDS will assist with this process: • Tell:……………..Tell me. • Explain:…………Explain to me. • Describe:……….Describe to me. • Show:…………...Show me. TEDS act as instructions rather than questions and encourages the interviewee to provide a full and detailed account of what they know. For example: • Tell me everything that happened... • Explain what you mean… • Describe the man in as much detail as possible... • Show me what happened... Probing Questions Probing or closed questions are ones that allow only a relatively small range of responses, usually a word or short phrase. They should only be used when an attempt to use an open question failed. They can be used to get specific detail or to probe information given from an open question. 5W&H Who, what, when, where, why and how (5W&H) can often be framed as open questions but are also used to elicit short answers. These are appropriate probing questions that can be used: • 'Who said that?' • 'What did they say?' • 'When was that?' • 'Where were you standing?' • 'Why did you go there?' • 'How long were you there?' As investigators, we want to know the answers to these types of questions and the temptation is to use them to control the interview and minimise irrelevant information. This should be avoided as it causes the interviewee to be passive, interrupts their concentration and affects memory recall. Closed questions are also more likely to provide incorrect responses than they would with open questions. Instead, you should always start the interview using TEDS questions giving the interviewee an opportunity to provide a full account. When open questions are no longer fruitful the 5W&H questions can be used to probe their account for any details omitted. An example of the appropriate use of a probing question: While interviewing a witness who has already given you a detailed description of the offender but not mentioned the offender’s height, it would be proper in this situation to ask the witness, ‘You said the man was 6 feet tall, what makes you think that?' Be careful when repeating questions to witnesses because they might infer their initial response was incorrect (it might be better to ask the same question in a different way). Questions beginning with ‘why’ should be limited or avoided in interviews with victims and to an extent, witnesses, because of the possibility they might think you are judging or blaming them. Inappropriate Questions There are a number of types of questions that should be avoided as they may affect the quality and quantity of the information given. The ultimate closed questions seek to elicit a 'yes' or 'no' answer, these may start with 'Did you…?', 'Can you…?', 'Would you…?', etc. This type of question will encourage very short answers. Repeated requests for short answers will quickly train the witness to respond with short answers and can reduce the responses to following open questions. These types of questions are generally used as a last resort when all else fails. Leading and Misleading Questions Leading and misleading questions imply the answer or assume facts that are likely to be in dispute. Leading questions imply the correct response whereas misleading questions imply an incorrect response. These types of questions may provide the interviewee’s with knowledge or ideas they have not previously formulated. An example of a leading or misleading question: The interviewee has not mentioned the type of car but the interviewer says: ‘Was the car you saw driving off, a station wagon?' If the car was a station wagon this is a leading question, if it was a van this is a misleading question. Interviewees may give the expected answer for a variety of reasons including: • They are trying to be helpful because they are confused or frightened. • They may see you as a person in authority and believe you know more about a subject than they do and will often defer to what you appear to know. • They may be susceptible to suggestion and incorporate your suggestion into their own memory. This is especially true for young children and people of a limited mental capability, though is not limited to these groups. When this happens, the integrity of the information obtained during an interview might be challenged in court on the basis the interviewer influenced the interviewee’s recall. The information you provide may also be incorrect and reduce the quality of the investigation and the evidence. Forced-Choice Questions These types of questions leave the interviewee with a small number of alternatives to choose from. There is no guarantee any of the alternatives are the correct option. The interviewee may guess the answer by selecting one of the options given, even if they know the correct option is not provided. You should never use these types of questions. An examples of forced-choice questions: Interviewer states, ‘Was the car dark blue or black?’ 'Did it happen on Monday or Tuesday?’ By giving the interviewee only two alternatives, both of which could be wrong, they may pick one in an attempt to assist the interviewer. Multiple Questions Asking more than one question at once is a multiple question and can lead to confusion. Firstly, the interviewee does not know which part of the question to answer and must choose between them. This results in either part of the sub-question being unanswered or additional cognitive loading on the interviewee who is trying to remember the sub-questions at the same time as retrieving information to answer each sub-question. Secondly, when an answer is given, the interviewer does not know which question was answered. Make sure you ask only one question at a time. An example of a multiple question: Interviewer states, ‘Did you see him? What was he wearing? Did he have a jacket on?’ If the interviewee answers ‘Yes’ what question are they answering? Complex Questions Avoid using grammatically complex questions. They are confusing and reduce the confidence of the interviewee. Where possible, keep your language simple and at the level used by the interviewee. An example of a complex question: Interviewer states, ‘You said you’ve never been there before but I think you did go there, and you said you’ve never been there before because you know you would get in trouble for being there because you know the place was burgled. What do you say to that?’ Negative Phrasing Avoid using negative phrasing as it is confusing for the interviewee. This is especially true for people with English as a second language. An example of negative phrasing: Interviewer states, ‘You’re not employed are you?’ In this situation if the interviewee was unemployed they could answer ‘Yes’ or ‘No’ and be quite correct. Opinion Type Questions Avoid asking questions that include a personal statement or opinion. An example of an opinion type question: Interviewer states ‘We know you did it, so why don't you just admit it?' Jargon Avoid using jargon of any sorts. Police jargon such as "decamped" is not understood by everyone. Use everyday language that is unlikely to make someone feel inferior or be misunderstood.
docint|inve-inte-phil-THE-PEACE-MODEL: Introduction This section is an introduction to the PEACE model, which has been adopted by the WA Police Force. Investigators are to conduct all interviews using the PEACE model. This involves the following phases:
docint|inve-inte-phil-PHASE-ACTION: 1. Planning and Preparation: Review available information and establish interview aims and objectives. 2. Engage and Explain: Develop rapport and explain interview processes and procedures. 3. Account, Clarify and Challenge: Using the Free Recall, Cognitive Interviewing or Conversation Management Model to gain an account of events, clarify and challenge any inconsistencies. Account for new information. 4. Closure: Conclude the interview and address any concerns and future ground i.e. Court process, giving evidence. 5. Evaluation: Evaluate how the information obtained impacts on the investigation and also evaluate the performance of the interviewer. Time should be spent on each phase but no rigid boundaries exist between the phases. The amount of time on each phase should be determined by the seriousness of the offence. The PEACE model18 of investigative interviewing: The PEACE model provides the structure for all investigative interviews whether with witnesses or suspects. The term model recognises the interview is something we build or create. As the interviewer, you are responsible for the planning and conduct of the interview. A well planned and carefully conducted interview has a good chance of obtaining complete, accurate and reliable information. The PEACE model helps you do that. Movement Between Phases in the Interview The ‘PEACE model’ diagram shows lines linking the phases of the interview. Some lines are solid, indicating there is a natural forward movement from one phase to the next. For example, explaining the purpose of an interview is a task that may require repetition and redefinition throughout the interview. Similarly, Closure is linked back to Account, Clarifying and Challenge with a dotted line. This indicates you might need to re-open discussion of the interviewee’s account during the Closure phase. The interviewee may recall some new information or may wish to test your memory of what they previously said. When this happens you will naturally return to the Account, Clarifying & Challenge stage. It is important to remember there are no rigid boundaries between the phases and flexibility is required throughout. Time should be spent on each phase but no rigid boundaries exist between the phases. The PEACE Model for Every Interview For every interaction requiring you to obtain information, whether conducting a vehicle stop or interviewing a suspect for a homicide, the PEACE model can be applied. Time must always be spent on each of the phases and the type of interaction will determine how much time you spend. 18 Adopted from ‘Practical Guide to Investigative Interviewing’, Central Police Training and Development Authority (Centrex) 2004. Interview Models Within the PEACE model you can apply different interview models to elicit information. The models are known as 'Free Recall', 'Cognitive Interviewing' and 'Conversation Management’. These models are used during the actual interview process so affect the Engage and Explain, Account and Closure stages of PEACE. The individual interviewing models, The Free Recall, Cognitive Interviewing and Conversation Management Models will be discussed fully in the Witness Investigative Interview Manual and the Suspect Investigative Interview Manual. Time Taken To Conduct Interviews Learning to use the PEACE model with the Free Recall, Cognitive Interview or Conversation Management Models will take practice. Initially you may find your interviews take longer as you are still learning the skills. Once your skills develop, you will become more efficient at interviewing and find any extra time you do spend interviewing will be due to the increased quantity and quality of information you generate. You will find by asking the right questions and allowing the interviewee to give their recall of events without interrupting is a more efficient way of producing a complete and accurate account than continuous questioning. In addition, higher quality interviews will save you time later during the prosecution process. The PEACE model is flexible and you will develop the ability to tailor the interview so the amount of time spent matches the investigation needs. ADVICE For advice on investigative interviewing related matters, contact the Detective Training School or the Investigative Standards Unit.
docinv|commissioners-message: COMMISSIONER’S MESSAGE I am proud to present to you the revised WA Police Force Investigation Doctrine (the Doctrine). The original version was created to address criticism regarding the manner in which we conduct investigations. Since then we have further learnt and evolved; and whilst we are at the ten-year mark, we still face the challenge of ensuring our Force’s practices are flexible and responsive to a changing policing and investigative environment. The original version of the Doctrine fostered effective communication and collaboration between generalist and specialist police by providing a common investigative language. The common usage of the terms The5KIS and the CRIME model are evidence of its success. We now find ourselves in an ever evolving environment with competing demands on police resources and a need to find efficiency gains and better ways of doing our business. This version of the Doctrine builds on the successes of the original and balances the key fundamentals of effectiveness and efficiency, without relaxing our key goal of improving the quality of investigations whilst maintaining and building on our standards of practice. There is a duty for supervisors to make quality decisions based on prioritisation, categorisation and allocation to ensure matters are investigated in a timely and efficient manner. Investigation permeates every aspect of policing within Western Australia. It is the responsibility of all members of the WA Police Force to know, understand and apply the principles of the Doctrine without fear, favour or prejudice to ensure all investigations are conducted appropriately and in an honest and accountable manner. The need to embrace the Doctrine is binding on all WA Police officers, consistent with our mission to provide trusted and valued policing for Western Australia. CHRIS DAWSON APM COMMISSIONER OF POLICE
docinv|introduction: INTRODUCTION Purpose of Doctrine Doctrine is the codification of beliefs, instructions or taught principles in a given branch of knowledge or a belief system. Doctrine provides philosophical guidance on the way an organisation conducts business. Purpose of the WA Police Force Investigation Doctrine The Doctrine is the cornerstone of the Western Australia Police Force’s (WA Police Force) commitment to quality investigations. The Doctrine is based on proven investigative and resource management principles. It is firm in its intent but requires judgement in its application. The Doctrine applies to all situations where a systematic approach and careful examination is required. It is equally applicable to criminal and non-criminal investigations. It promotes and standardises good investigative practice by providing a framework of investigation ownership and accountability. The Doctrine outlines the CRIME Model and The Five Key Investigative Strategies (The5KIS) both of which guide investigators in making logical, structured and accountable decisions. Scope of the Document The Doctrine applies to all WA Police Force investigators involved in the conduct of investigations. It provides a narrative on: • The investigative environment • The attributes which promote good investigative practice • The key principles of a good investigation • Overall investigation management. The WA Police Force publishes numerous documents to support the Doctrine; however, the Doctrine underpins all investigative practices for the WA Police Force. This is a public document and may become disclosable in judicial proceedings. Doctrine Management The intent of the Doctrine should not be hampered due to organisational or terminology changes, any reference to a specific term includes the current equivalent. The Doctrine is a corporately endorsed document and any significant amendments or modifications must have the approval of the Commissioner of Police or his delegate. Any minor amendments or modifications must have the approval of the Divisional Detective Inspector, governing the agency’s Investigative Standards Unit.
docinv|investigation-principles: INVESTIGATION PRINCIPLES The Investigative Environment The WA Police Force is the public face of law enforcement in Western Australia. Quality investigations contribute significantly to the community’s expectations and our mission: To provide trusted and valued policing for Western Australia. It is the responsibility of the WA Police Force to investigate matters in an impartial manner. Investigators will not have a vested interest in one party over another; and will always maintain a neutral position, remaining objective at all times. The WA Police Force encourages a collegiate approach to investigations. Investigators will be called upon to conduct investigations into a variety of crime types each with individual complexity. Investigators must be astute to the dynamic nature of each investigation and apply judgement and innovation with a goal of successful resolution. Successful resolution includes the completion of an investigation which has been undertaken thoroughly, efficiently and ethically. Success should not solely be measured on arrest rates or charges preferred. The investigative environment does not cease at resolution. Investigative information is held in perpetuity and may be the subject of internal and external reviews. In these instances, the investigative standards may be held to account years later. Adherence to the Legal Framework WA Police Force investigations must be conducted in accordance with statute law, common law and established legal principles. Investigators must be conversant with relevant law to ensure the conduct of the investigation is legally defensible and evidentially sound. Adherence to Values Underpinning all WA policing are our values of Duty, Teamwork, Integrity and Care. To further enhance our values there are two additional principles specific to investigations, commitment and transparency. In abiding by these principles, investigators ensure investigations are completed with the highest integrity and in accordance with community expectations. Investigative Attributes Good investigators combine the attributes of tenacity and objectivity within well-established legal and ethical parameters to conduct a thorough, professional and impartial search for the truth. They apply critical thinking and innovation in the development of investigative strategies which are adaptable and scalable in application. They are always current with relevant laws, governance and investigative techniques. A good investigator is logical, intuitive and accountable. Their decisions are reasonable, proportionate and necessary. Critical Thinking Critical thinking is an investigator’s ability to look inward and understand how and why a particular decision was made. It requires an ability to identify personal experiences and unintended biases which may impact on the decision making process. Good investigators must be able to take their thinking apart systematically, to analyse each part, assess it for quality and improve it. This will result in an investigation that is innovative, balanced and focussed towards a successful outcome. Recording Decisions By applying critical thinking, investigators will ultimately make balanced and justified decisions. All decisions associated with an investigation must be recorded on a recognised WA Police Force system. Investigator Levels (iLevels) Crucial to the successful resolution of an investigation is the deployment of suitably trained and experienced officers. The WA Police Force uses the iLevels to ensure the management of an investigation is conducted by an appropriately qualified individual.
docinv|investigation-ownership: INVESTIGATION OWNERSHIP Offences Outside of Western Australia Where an offence has occurred outside of Western Australia, ownership of the investigation rests with the jurisdiction where the offence occurred. When the WA Police Force is requested to assist or required to respond, the response should be the same as if the offence occurred within Western Australia. Multi-Agency or Multi-Jurisdictional Investigations If the WA Police Force engages in a multi-agency or multi-jurisdictional investigation the investigative standards are the responsibility of the lead agency. Where the WA Police Force is the lead agency, the Doctrine will apply. Offences within Western Australia Responsibility for investigations typically rests with the district superintendent where the offence occurred. Agency standards or circumstances may require allocation of the investigation to another district or division. Where an investigation is reallocated, the relevant superintendent assumes responsibility. Reallocation of serious offences may require a formal handover. The WA Police Force will ensure timely and professional investigations are conducted, by clearly determining and communicating ownership. The business unit assigned the investigation retains ownership of the offence and must appoint an Investigating Officer (IO).
docinv|crime-model-overview: THE ‘CRIME’ MODEL Good practice is achieved by distilling a process into its critical elements and designing a framework based on expertise and experience. The investigative framework used by the WA Police Force is the CRIME model which assists practitioners, supervisors and the agency conduct quality investigations. The CRIME model reflects the steps of a typical investigation by highlighting the five critical elements namely Contact, Respond, Investigate, Manage and Evaluate.
docinv|crime-contact: Contact Contact is the initial step of an investigation. It is the first opportunity to engage with the reporting person and instil confidence and trust in the WA Police Force. The Initial Contact Officer (ICO) whether sworn or police staff, must demonstrate good communication and empathy to maximise rapport and disclosure. Crucial to the Contact step is the ICO’s ability to swiftly and accurately elicit information, to ascertain the exact nature of the allegation, identify appropriate police response and maximise the early collection of evidential material. All of the ICO’s skills share equal importance in setting the professional tone for the subsequent investigation.
docinv|crime-respond: Respond Respond in the CRIME model represents the reaction to the initial contact. It has a wide application ranging from telephone response to scene attendance. Police will manage response in accordance with policy, agency standards and statutory requirements. The protection of life and property will always override evidentiary collection. The Respond step of the investigation aims to determine what offence has been committed and whether further investigation is required or if it may be finalised at that point. The role of responding officers is not simply to attend an incident. They must be inquisitive, organised and apply an investigative mindset to identify potential avenues of inquiry.
docinv|crime-investigate-overview: Investigate ‘Investigate’ is typically the major component of the CRIME model but should not be considered more important than the other stages. It promotes an objective search for evidentiary material in order to establish the truth. Police investigations must be organised, systematic and scaled to the offence. To encourage and prompt a thorough search for evidence, the WA Police Force has The5KIS. The5KIS create a common investigative language which standardises planning, briefings, and the management of investigations. Each of the key investigative strategies represents an area or discipline in which evidence may be located namely; Witnesses, Suspects, Physical Material, Intelligence and Public Awareness. The5KIS maximise investigative opportunities and prompt investigators to look broadly when identifying lines of inquiry. The strategies must all be considered, but not all will yield lines of inquiry at a given time. The5KIS need to be continually re-assessed in an attempt to fill information gaps. They can be applied in any order, concurrently or in isolation.
docinv|crime-investigate-witnesses: Witnesses This strategy is used to identify, locate and interview witnesses to an incident in order to elicit information. Witnesses are categorised dependant on their knowledge of the offence and interviewed in accordance with fairness, legislation and WA Police Force policies and procedures. The WA Police Force categorises witnesses as victim, eye witness, other significant witness, police witness, expert witness and general witness. There is always potential for a witness to become a suspect, at which point they must be afforded their rights. Witnesses will be interviewed in accordance with the Investigative Interviewing model. Investigators must be mindful of potential vulnerabilities which may induce suggestibility or result in a flawed account from the witness. When required the witness strategy should encompass security and wellbeing.
docinv|crime-investigate-suspects: Suspects The suspect strategy involves the development of lines of inquiry to identify, locate, and interview suspects. Suspect categorisation assists investigators to prioritise investigative focus. The WA Police Force aligns categorisation to the legal framework. Suspects are categorised in the following way: • Suspect: A person suspected of having committed an offence, albeit the threshold of reasonable suspicion has not been reached • Arrestable Suspect: A person reasonably suspected of committing an offence within the meaning of s4 Criminal Investigation Act, 2006 (CIA). This person is arrestable but has not been arrested • Arrested Suspect: A person arrested pursuant to s128 CIA. Categorisation is based on the circumstances at the time and is equally applicable to single and multiple suspects. If the circumstances change the category of a suspect may change. Suspects will be interviewed using the Investigative Interviewing, Conversation Management model. The principles of fairness and voluntariness must always be applied. Investigators must be mindful of potential vulnerabilities which may induce suggestibility or result in a flawed account from the suspect. (Refer to Investigative Interviewing on the Investigative Standards intranet page at Investigative Standards.)
docinv|crime-investigate-interviewing: Investigative Interviewing Witnesses and suspects can provide valuable information which assists in establishing the truth of the matter under investigation. Fundamental to the ‘Witness’ and ‘Suspect’ strategies is interviewing. Well planned interviews can significantly progress an investigation. Planning includes the early identification of the interviewee’s legal status to ensure they are well informed about their rights. The WA Police Force uses the Investigative Interviewing Model (IIM) when conducting interviews.
docinv|crime-investigate-physical-materi: Physical Material The Physical Material strategy relates to the development of lines of inquiry to identify items potentially related to the offence. It encompasses all real and documentary evidence. Physical Material strategies can be considered from two perspectives: • The identification and collection of physical material • The analysis, treatment or management of the physical material to link it to an incident or person.
docinv|crime-investigate-intelligence: Intelligence The Intelligence strategy aims to identify information or sources that add value to investigations. In context, intelligence may be based on information, supposition or reasoning supported by facts. Intelligence can help link multiple offences or link an offender to an offence.
docinv|crime-investigate-public-awarenes: Public Awareness The Public Awareness strategy is used to promote public support and reassurance, elicit information and ensure public safety. Great care must be taken to ensure the Public Awareness strategy does not compromise the investigation; prosecution; contaminate potential witness and suspect accounts; jeopardise community confidence or safety; or expose the WA Police Force or the State to civil liability. Caution should be applied when discussing the status of a particular person. Unless it forms a specific strategy, police should avoid any term that could be construed by the community as a descriptor for offender.
docinv|crime-manage: Manage ‘Manage’ within the CRIME Model has its own specific requirements, it applies to all stages within the model and ensures overall good governance of the investigation. Manage is applied at three distinct levels: • Agency: Responsible for establishing investigative practices • Supervisor: Responsible for compliance with investigative practice • Individual: Responsible for the application of investigative practice. Agency The WA Police Force will provide infrastructure and resources to meet investigative demands. It is responsible for establishing good practice and communicating the need for standardised professional investigations. The agency will implement and maintain a management structure which quality assures investigations and identifies training relevant to the needs of the investigator, community expectations and disclosure. The agency evaluates investigative performance to ensure continuous improvement. Supervision District or Divisional Officers will actively promote and ensure compliance with the Doctrine. Officers in Charge (OIC) and supervisors will implement procedures and practice to ensure compliance with the Doctrine. The OIC and supervisors commit to: • maintaining investigative skills and knowledge commensurate with their role • mentoring staff by identifying training needs • reviewing investigations for compliance with the Doctrine. Individual The Investigating Officer (IO) and/or Senior Investigating Officer (SIO) will: • conduct investigations in adherence with the Doctrine • identify and prioritise potential investigative actions by using The5KIS • apply investigative practices in accordance with relevant legislation • comply with agency policy and guidelines • commit to their own professional development • consider disclosure obligations from the commencement of the investigation.
docinv|dimensions-of-investigation: Dimensions of an Investigation Every investigation can be characterised in terms of priority, category and allocation. Prioritisation Prioritisation applies to all aspects of the investigation. Investigation prioritisation is based on: • risk to victim or community safety • potential for the loss of evidence • potential for significant undermining of agency reputation and public confidence. Categorisation The WA Police Force has three investigation categories; confined, compound and complex. Investigations are categorised to ensure allocation to appropriately resourced business units and to assist supervisors assess the investigation’s impact on a business unit’s capacity. Categorisation is not static and as an investigation evolves, it may be necessary to recategorise it. Categorisation is the responsibility of the OIC or Supervisor. In the event an investigation category needs to be arbitrated, it will be referred to the Assistant District or Divisional Officer or the District/Divisional Officer. Confined investigations involve a limited number of investigative actions and minimal human resources. Compound investigations involve a significant number of investigative actions but limited human resources; or a limited number of investigative actions but significant human resources. Complex investigations involve a significant number of investigative actions and a significant number of human resources. Allocation Generally The allocation of an investigation is not to be delayed for administrative purposes. Allocation of investigations is based on the following criteria: • the category of the investigation • the business unit resource capacity • the required skill and knowledge of the investigator or investigation team. Investigation allocation will be based on investigator iLevels. Uniformed Police (i1 to i3) Generally, uniformed police should be allocated simple and ‘either way’ offences that are confined or compound. In all instances officers must have the contemporary skills to conduct the investigation and have access to adequate guidance. This does not preclude uniformed officers from undertaking investigative actions for any investigation. District Detective Office (i4 to i7) District detectives are generally allocated complex ‘either way’ offences and purely indictable offences. The district must have the resources to undertake the investigation. The IO must have contemporary skills and knowledge to conduct the investigation or have access to adequate guidance. Specialist Investigation Units/Squads (i4 to i7) Specialist investigation units will be allocated offences which fall within their charter. In general, this includes purely indictable offences and ‘either way’ offences which are compound or complex. The SIO/IO must have the contemporary skills and knowledge to conduct the investigation. Allocation to an Investigating Officer The Doctrine does not limit investigators of any iLevel being the initial responder to an incident, neither does it restrict any investigator from completing subsequent investigative actions. Rather, the focus is on the ongoing management of an investigation to ensure it is allocated to suitable business units and managed by appropriately qualified investigators. An IO will be appointed in all instances. Consideration must be given to their accredited investigation level (iLevel), skills, knowledge, experience and availability. Indictable offences that cannot be heard summarily will be investigated by a current serving detective (minimum i4). Where this is not possible, another officer with sufficient investigative skills may be appointed the IO under the management of a substantive Detective Sergeant. Responsibility for an investigation is always retained by the business unit. Where an IO is transferred or absent for a significant period of time, the investigation will be re-allocated to another IO to ensure victim support and investigative continuity. Where an IO has intimate knowledge of an investigation, responsibility may be transferred with the IO to another business unit. The Investigating Officer The IO is responsible for conducting the investigation in compliance with the Doctrine and legal framework. The IO will identify and communicate any issues which may impact the quality of the investigation to their supervisor. In the majority of cases, an IO will be responsible for management of all investigative actions. However, in some instances the complexity of the investigation may require additional specialist investigation roles. Senior Investigating Officer (SIO) Divisional or district superintendents may appoint a SIO when an investigation requires senior leadership. The SIO will be a Detective Senior Sergeant or above, i7 qualified and have the requisite skills and experience in the specific crime type. The SIO should be given relief from their normal duties to meet the demands of the investigation.
docinv|crime-file-management: CRIME File Management The WA Police Force has a legislative requirement to retain documents associated with investigations. It is the ethos of WA Police Force to adopt a centralist approach to retention. CRIME File The WA Police Force utilises the CRIME file as the individual investigation collation source for documents or items which cannot be retained in a recognised WA Police Force system. CRIME File Repository Maintaining a central location for investigative documentation is essential to the efficient and effective management of investigative records, ensuring ready access and accountability. To supplement agile retrieval of both hardcopy and electronic documents a logical and intuitive approach should be adopted.
docinv|crime-evaluate: Evaluate Evaluate is the final stage of the CRIME model and completes the investigative cycle by seeking to identify best practice and measuring current performance against that standard. The WA Police Force aims to achieve investigative validation through evaluation at three levels: • Agency • Supervisor • Individual. The Endorsement to Charge (ETC) Process Within the context of an investigation, the WA Police Force uses the ETC process to comply with the legal framework. The ETC acts as a validation process to ensure prima facie evidence exists prior to a charge being preferred. Investigation Review The WA Police Force is committed to conducting investigative reviews using a formal process with clear ‘Terms of Reference’. Investigative reviews will be conducted utilising the CRIME model and ‘The5KIS’ standards.
docinv|commitment: COMMITMENT The role of an investigator is a crucial part of policing within Western Australia. All members of the WA Police Force have a professional responsibility to know, understand and apply the principles of the Doctrine. The need to embrace the Doctrine is binding on all WA Police Force personnel as we move forward to provide trusted and valued policing for Western Australia.

docrom|rwa-oic-repo-OFFENDER-REGISTRY: All Australian police authorities register, manage and monitor convicted child sex offenders who are not in custody by utilising and sharing information via NCOS. SOMS is responsible for the registration, ongoing management and monitoring of all reportable offenders within the metropolitan area. Regional WA OIC’S are delegated case managers and manage and maintain reportable offenders and dangerous sex offenders within regional districts of Western Australia. SOMS supports the Department of Corrective Services in the management of Dangerous Sexual Offenders (DSOs) who breach their obligations pursuant to the Dangerous Sex Offenders Act 2006. SOMS provide support to case managers and each regional district also has a Local District Manager (LDM) as a point of contact for advice and guidance regarding case management and NCOS. All case managers are encouraged to pro-actively target high risk offenders and liaise with other agencies such as the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and the Department of Communities to assist in the effective case management of RO’s. The Registry coordinates NCOS access, case file access and intrastate or interstate transfers. The Registry also facilitates the governance, audit and risk assessment of all case files. The Registry will provide administrative assistance and guidance when requested and also facilitates the Community Protection website for offenders who are published on the website.
docrom|rwa-oic-repo-RELEVANT-FORMS-SUPPO: All forms, SOPs and case management guidelines associated with the management of RO’s are located on the WA Police Intranet site. This can be found under State Crime/Sex Crime Division/Sex Offender Registry webpage and includes the application form (refer page 45 of Appendices) to gain access to NCOS on the completion of the required blackboard training. Send your completed access form to the Registry email sex.offender.registry@police.wa.gov.au You can contact the Registry directly to obtain forms or advice on 1800 300 400. A copy of the most commonly used forms is attached to the back of this document. Also located on the webpage is a Quick Link to the Community Protection (Offender Reporting) Act 2004 and Dangerous Sexual Offenders Act 2006. Page | 7
docrom|rwa-oic-repo-HOW-TO-ACCESS-LOG-IN: NCOS is a system owned and managed by Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC). To navigate to the ACIC log on page for NCOS utilise the WA Police Intranet site. Select Internet Links/Useful Links Directory; choose CrimTrac Portal (authorised users only). From the resulting list displayed - National Systems - select NCOS – National Child Offender System (refer to page 43 of the Appendices for further guidance). Your User ID will be the letter W followed by your PD number (e.g. W12345) then enter your password. Once successfully logged in, the system will take you to the homepage of NCOS. After you have utilised the system, if you require a password reset, there is an option for a Self-service Password Reset. This allows you to reset you own password without the need to request one from your authorised contact. A valid email address is required and must be associated with your ACIC online account. A copy of this process is included in the Appendices on page 44 of this document. Section 81 of the CPOR Act states the Register (NCOS) must only be accessed by a person who is authorised by the Commissioner of police. Authorised person means a police officer or a person who falls within a class as prescribed in the regulations. Information release regarding the personal details of ROs held in the register are only to be disclosed by an authorised police officer of or above the rank of Inspector unless to a police officer or law enforcement agency. Section 82 of the CPOR Act states a person must not directly, or indirectly, record, disclose or make use of any personal information in the Register except;  In the course of an officers duty  As required or authorised by or under the CPOR Act or another written law  For the purpose of proceedings relating to a protection order  With the written authority of the minister or the person to whom the information relates  In other circumstances prescribed by Regulations Section 82 MUST be read in conjunction with Section 81.
