docstyle|introduction: INTRODUCTION The Western Australia Police Force Corporate Writing Style Guide has been prepared to help WA Police Force employees prepare a range of written communication. The material in this document is based on information from the following publications: • The Style Manual for Authors, Editors and Printers, Sixth Edition, 2002, John Wiley & Sons Australia, Ltd • The Western Australia Police Service Communication Manual, 1998, Western Australia Police Academy • The Macquarie Dictionary Revised, Third Edition, 2003. This document should be treated as a basic guide and is by no means exhaustive. Further information or clarification can be obtained from the Corporate Communications Branch by emailing Corporate.Communications.Branch@police.wa.gov.au
docstyle|writing-style: WRITING STYLE Many types of written documents need to be prepared by the WA Police Force. For example: • briefing notes • reports • letters • memorandums • research papers • business proposals • planning submissions • operational orders • stories for publications • emails To help you prepare these documents, this Style Guide provides the basic skills to ensure your correspondence is professional, consistent, neat and accurate. When preparing documents, remember the following: • Use language that readers will understand and avoid using jargon. Never assume people know what you are talking about. • Be precise, avoid unnecessary words and stick to the point you are trying to make. • Vary sentence lengths and try to use an average of about 22 words a sentence. • Avoid euphemisms, clichés and overused words/phrases. • Be consistent with how you format the document and the style/words you use. This ensures the document looks “clean,” is easy to understand and is presented in a precise fashion. • Always proof-read your document at least twice and, if appropriate, ask someone else to read it for you. Mistakes can be easily missed when you work on a document for many hours, so a second or third proof-reader will help alleviate this problem. • Try not to rush yourself on a document. It is always safest to spend extra time having something proof-read and thoroughly checked, than to rush it, not have it read and find something is wrong with it once published. Remember that what you are writing is not only a reflection of you, but the agency as a whole and the Commissioner of Police.
docstyle|abbreviations: Abbreviations An abbreviation is a shortened or contracted form of a word or phrase. It is usually the first letter of a word, a few other letters but not the last, and is followed by a full stop. For example: • approx. (approximately) • vol. (volume) • enc. (enclosed) • att. (attached) • Hon. (Honourable) • sic (thus) is used to draw attention to an error in quoted material/text • cc. (carbon copy) is to be placed under the signature block • etc. (et cetera) is preceded or followed by a comma only when the sentence structure demands it • i.e. (that is) and e.g. (for example) are both preceded by a comma but there is no comma after them • c/- (care of) is used in addresses
docstyle|acronyms: Acronyms An acronym is the formation of the initial letters of words (and sometimes other words), pronounced as a single word. The full spelling must be used in the first reference, followed by the acronym. For example: • Department of Fire and Emergency Services (DFES) • State Emergency Service (SES) • Queensland Police Service (QPS)
docstyle|ampersands: Ampersands (&) Ampersands should not be used except in very specific circumstances such as where it is used as part of an organisation’s name. For example: • Cobb & Co. • P & N Bank • P & C Association
docstyle|apostrophes: Apostrophes (’) There are two main uses of apostrophes: 1. To show the omission of letters. For example: • I couldn’t (could not) attend the meeting. 2. To indicate possession. For example: • The student’s chair is red. • The students’ chairs are red. • His father’s car is red. Do not use apostrophes for: 1. Simple plurals. For example: • Full-time employees (FTEs NOT FTE’s) • Non-commissioned officers (NCOs NOT NCO’s) • Explosive detection dogs (EDDs NOT EDD’s) 2. Referring to a number of years. For example: • During the 1980s, police officers wore khaki uniforms. (NOT During the 1980’s, police officers wore khaki uniforms).
docstyle|attachments-and-enclosures: Attachments and enclosures Attachments (att.) Where correspondence says other documents are attached, ensure the hardcopy version is stapled or included with the reply. If an attachment is a previous letter it must be a copy of the original signed document. Ensure ‘att.’ appears after the date in the correspondence. Enclosures (enc.) Enclosures are generally too large to attach but are in the same envelope as the correspondence. Where correspondence states there are enclosures, ensure they are enclosed and that ‘enc.’ appears after the date at the bottom of the correspondence.
docstyle|brackets: Brackets ( ) [ ] Brackets are generally used to enclose material that is not essential to the meaning of a sentence. The two common types of brackets used are: • parentheses (round brackets) • square brackets. Parentheses ( ) The main function of parentheses is to enclose definitions, acronyms, comments, clarifications, additional information, etc. For example: • Whenever police (often detectives) have attended the scene, the offenders have run away. Square brackets [ ] These are used in material to show editorial insertions made by someone other than the author, to clarify something or highlight an error in the text. For example: • Police often need to attend the High Court [which is in Canberra] which is the most senior court in Australia. • When Deputy Commissioner [sic] Col Blanch attended the graduation parade, he spoke to all the new constables. NOTE: The italicised word sic (which means thus) is used to draw attention to an error in the text that has been quoted by someone.
docstyle|capital-letters: Capital letters Sentences should always start with a capital letter. Initial capitals should also be used for proper nouns and the names of specific people, places and organisations. For example: • Commissioner Col Blanch • Sergeant John Smith • Australian Federal Police • Perth Police Station • Newman Police Station When referring to a specific position but without the name, you should capitalise it. For example: • The meeting comprised the Director, Corporate Communications Branch and the Director, Human Resources. When referring to non-specific names/nouns, etc you do not need to capitalise. For example: • The meeting comprised many agency directors, managers and police officers. • One sergeant and three constables attended the meeting. When referring to nationalities, races, tribes and inhabitants of a particular area of a country, adherents of particular religions, languages and language groups, you must use initial capitals. For example: • Australian • Aboriginal • Indigenous • Torres Strait Islanders • American • Chinese When referring to a specific government, capital letters must be used for the title. For example: • Government of Western Australia • Commonwealth Government However, when the words are used in a non-specific way, lower case must be used. For example: • The role of any government is to provide the people with what they want. • Many staff in government departments do not receive training. • The new headquarters is at the corner of Roe and Fitzgerald streets.
docstyle|colons-and-semicolons: Colons (:) and semicolons (;) Colons (:) Colons are most commonly used to introduce lists. If the list is the continuation of a sentence, a colon should be used. For example: • Officers will be sent to the following locations: Perth o Mandurah o Broome o Colons can also be used in the following instances: • To separate subtitles from main titles. For example: Joe Bloggs: The true story. • To formally introduce a quotation of reported speech. For example: In his address, the Commissioner of Police made the following statement: “We must be vigilant.” Semicolons (;) A semicolon is used to link two clauses that could be treated as separate sentences but have a close link. Another use for the semicolon is to separate a series of phrases or clauses that also contain commas. For example: • We expect ministerial approval next week; they can then start immediately. Alternatively, to make things simpler, these statements can be joined by ‘and’ or be made into two shorter sentences.
docstyle|contractions: Contractions A contraction is a shortened form of a word (or words) using the first and last letters of the word. Contractions are not followed by a full stop unless they end a sentence. For example: • Mr • Dr • Pty Ltd
docstyle|dash: Dash The purpose of the dash (-) is to indicate an abrupt or dramatic break in the text. For example: • Now she knew who the culprit was – her son.
docstyle|dates-and-times: Dates and times Dates For internal and external publications such as memorandums, formats, briefing notes, publications, media releases, etc, dates must be consistent throughout the document. For example: • 1 January 2023 Expressions of time The usual way to write references of time, using the 12-hour system, is with am (ante meridiem, before noon) and pm (post meridiem, after noon). For example: • 10.30am or 12.01pm • 10 o’clock • 7 hours (7 hrs) • 45 minutes (45 min) • 36 seconds (36 secs) When using the 24-hour system, the hours are written from 0000 hours (midnight) to 2359 hours (a full 24 hours). For example: • 0630 hours • 1201 hours • 2347 hours Shortened forms such as BC (before Christ), AD (anno Domini, in the year of our Lord), CE (of the common era) and BP (before present) should be written without full stops and with a space separating them from the year. There should always be a space between the year and the era indicator. For example: • 125 BC • 1788 AD • the third century AD NOTE: As Western Australia is in a different time zone than the rest of the country, it may be necessary to specify which time zone you are referring to. For example: • 4.50am WST (Western Standard Time) • 6.50am AEST (Australian Eastern Standard Time) • 1650 WST (Western Standard Time) • 1850 AEST (Australian Eastern Standard Time)
docstyle|dot-points: Dot points If all of the dot points are full sentences, each must start with a capital letter and end with a full stop. For example: Reasons for attending the course would be: • Officers from the WA Police Force could investigate the feasibility of developing legislated guidelines for future investigations. • Applications for research funding could be supported in the main areas of investigation. • Liaising with officers from other jurisdictions to allow WA Police Force members the chance to gain knowledge and share information. If the dot points are arranged more like a short list, no initial capital letter is used. Leave each point without closure. For example: The four types of assistance available are: • monetary assistance • equipment or environmental modifications • resources • advisory services
docstyle|exclamation-marks: Exclamation marks (!) Exclamation marks/points are used at the end of a sentence to indicate surprise, emphasis, strong emotion or a command. For example: • How dare you yell at me like that! • Stop! Police. Try to avoid using exclamation marks, especially in headlines.
docstyle|hyphens: Hyphens (-) Hyphens are mostly used to connect words to better explain following nouns or a position. For example: • The new school-based officers were enjoying helping students • An 18-year-old man was charged with arson • Officers undertake a 10-day course • Sergeant John Smith, Officer-in-Charge, Perth Police Station When the last letter of a single-syllable prefix (e.g. de-) is a vowel, and the word that follows begins with the same vowel, a hyphen is inserted to prevent any misunderstanding. For example: • de-emphasise • re-enter • co-operate • co-ordinate However, many words nowadays have become common place so the hyphens are dropped. When deciding to use hyphens, remember why the words are hyphenated, i.e. to show the joining of words that have been shortened, or to join two or more words to give them one meaning. Remember to be consistent with whatever method you choose. For example: • officer-in-charge • up-to-date • well-known
docstyle|inquire-or-enquire: Inquire or enquire Inquire/inquiry and enquire/enquiry can be used interchangeably, but inquire/inquiry are the forms used by the WA Police Force.
docstyle|ise-or-ize: ‘ise’ or ‘ize’? Often people get confused as to whether to use ‘ise’ or ‘ize’ in certain words. The Australian version is to use ‘ise’. For example: • modernise • organise • recognise As ‘ize’ is an international version (mainly American) and the only time you should use this version is when it appears in official titles/names of groups, countries, people, organisations, etc. For example: • National Association of Police Organizations • Polizei Berlin NOTE: Check or update your Microsoft Word dictionary so it uses the Australian English version.
docstyle|italics: Italics Italics must be used for the titles of: • Books and periodicals e.g. From the Line, The Power of One, The West Australian • Plays and long poems e.g. The Man From Snowy River, The Mousetrap • Musical compositions/songs e.g. The Phantom of the Opera • Films, videos, and television and radio programs e.g. Gone With The Wind, Four Corners • Works of art e.g. Mona Lisa, Blue Poles • Legislation and legal cases e.g. Police Powers and Responsibilities Act 2000 • Names of ships, aircraft and vehicles e.g. Titanic, Cygnet V • Scientific names of plants and animals NOTE: For animals, scientific names at the genus, species and subspecies levels are italicised. With botanical names, italics are used for the genus, species, subspecies, variety, form and subform levels, e.g. such as the Cassia nemophila var. coriacea. • Technical terms and technical terms being defined e.g. Gouache (a method of painting) • Letters, words and phrases being cited e.g. Guerrilla (comes from the Spanish word meaning ‘little war’)
docstyle|measurements: Measurements Measurements are written in metric (Australian standard). For example: • 12 kilometres (km) = 12 km • 52 metres (m) = 52 m • 29 centimetres (cm) = 29 cm • 9 millimetres (mm) = 9 mm • 2 tonne (t) = 2 t • 458 kilograms (kg) = 458 kg • 145 litres (L) = 145 L • 897 millilitres (ml) = 897 ml
docstyle|monetary-amounts: Monetary amounts Currency is to be expressed as a combination of numerals and symbols. For example: • $10,000 • $150.32 • 10c • $10,567.25 Millions of dollars can be written as $3,500,000 or $3.5 million or $3.5m (no space is used in $3.5m). It is only necessary to distinguish Australian currency if multiple currencies are being referred to in the one document, and for reasons of consistency, the preferred style within the WA Police Force is one recommended by the International Organisation of Standardisation (currency codes). For example: • AUD10,000 (i.e. Aussie dollar) • NZD2,055 (i.e. New Zealand dollar) • EUR5,000 (i.e. Euro) • USD25.90 (i.e. US dollar) • SGD5.94 (i.e. Singapore dollar) • GBP17.50 (i.e. British pound) NOTE: European countries use a comma as a decimal point, e.g. EU 145,50 whereas in Australian documents the same amount would be shown as $145.50.
docstyle|numbers: Numbers Numbers from zero to nine are written in full, while numbers from 10 and above must be written as numerals – unless they are written at the start of a sentence. For example: • There are nine police stations awaiting refurbishment, while 35 have been completed. • Staff from the Corporate Communications Branch raised more than $12,000 for Police Legacy. • Thirty police officers attended the crime scene. Hyphens are used to connect numbers (up to ninety-nine) that have been written in full. For example: • Fifty-five students attended the meeting. • Seventy-three constables graduated today. Hyphens should be retained when part of a larger number but the large round number does not require a hyphen. For example: • One hundred and ninety-five officers attended the ceremony. • Three thousand and seventy-two people marched in the rally. A number expressed in numerals can use hyphens to join to other hyphenated words, but hyphenated numbers expressed in words should not be used as it will cause confusion. For example: • The 35-year-old car was used in an armed robbery. (NOT…The thirty-five-year-old car was used in an armed robbery). Mathematical relationships Numerals should always be used to express precise mathematical relationships, such as an equation or ratio. For example: • 43 + 65 = 108 • 5:1 In general text, words can be used when the mathematical relationship is not exact. For example: • Many officers – about one in five – will be promoted within three years. Percentages Percentages can be written in various ways. When using the percentage symbol, it should only be used with numerals, whereas ‘per cent’ can be written with both numerals AND words. For example: • 12% • 12 per cent • two per cent (NOT percent) Roman numerals Traditionally used for the numbering of preliminary pages in books, research papers, documents, etc. or in the titles of monarchs and popes. Try to limit the use of Roman numerals, as they can be confusing. In government publications, they also can be used to signify certificate level qualifications. For example: • Certificate I in Policing • Certificate II in Policing Using a space or a comma in a number For reasons of clarity, in the WA Police Force it is preferable to use a comma (rather than a space) when writing large numbers of four digits or more. For example: • 1,785 (not 1 785 or 1785) • 200,000 (not 200 000 or 200000) • $4,015.25 (not $4 015.25 or $4015.25) Years When referring to years in decades, do not use an apostrophe. For example: • 1970s NOT 1970’s • During the 80s, people started buying mobile telephones. (NOT 80’s)
docstyle|question-marks: Question marks (?) A question mark signals a query or can be used to express doubt. For example: • Did the officers follow the appropriate procedures for such a situation? • Why were the youths attacking police officers?
docstyle|quotation-marks: Quotation marks (“ ”) Quotation marks (otherwise known as inverted commas) are used to show direct speech and the quoted work of another author. If there are several consecutive sentences quoted, quotation marks are used at the beginning of each paragraph with a full stop at the end and no closing quotation mark. Only close the final quote/paragraph in the quoted text, with a full stop and closing quotation mark. To attribute many consecutive quotes to an author, you can, after the very first paragraph/quote, write “he said”. This introduces the person and also ensures there is no confusion or wrong attribution. For example: Inspector Tony Hill, Officer-in-Charge of the Regional Operations Group (ROG) said the group was dedicated to supporting police across the Metropolitan Region. “Formed on 19 January 2004, ROG is a highly visible, highly mobile police presence that provides tasking support; a trained response to antisocial behaviour, and provides operational support, on a priority basis, to the metropolitan area and regional WA,” he said. “Its primary role is to be available throughout the region to provide tasking support to assist the districts to improve response times, reduce tasking loads during peak periods and improve service delivery. “The group’s secondary role is to develop and maintain a suitable standard of preparedness to respond to antisocial behaviour and civil disorder incidents. This involves regular structured training, incorporating other units such as Mounted Section and Dog Squad, to ensure all ROG officers have the necessary skills and capability to respond. “We have recently up-skilled all the ROG supervisors to Civil Disorder Commander level, to enable them to confidently lead our people in the field and ensure a professional and coordinated police response to these types of incidents,” Inspector Hill said. Double or single quotation marks? It is often debated whether to use double or single quotation marks for quotes, etc. Either style can be used, as long as they are used consistently. NOTE: Do not chop and change between the styles within a single document. Therefore, if you use double quotations for direct speech, then you would use single quotations for quotes within quotes. For example: • “There were many people at the riot yelling out, ‘give peace a chance’, and no damage was done,” Commissioner Blanch said.
docstyle|singular-or-plural: Singular or plural? When deciding whether a statement is singular or plural, you need to closely examine the sentence and how the nouns are used. Singular If the noun refers to a body or organisation, then it is singular. For example: • The WA Police Force is going to change its policy on uniforms. Plural If you are referring to the noun as a group of more than one thing, then it is plural. For example: • WA Police Force officers are going to endorse the uniform change.
docstyle|spelling: Spelling Always be careful when spelling words, such as names, places, buildings, etc. Never assume that what you have been given is accurate, especially if it is an unusual word. It is highly recommended that you always try to check the spelling with the source so you know you have clarified it correctly. Also, be mindful that some words are spelt differently in other countries. Sometimes the simplest words can be misinterpreted, so try to be as thorough as possible with checking spelling in your document. In addition, be consistent – make sure that if one name is mentioned throughout a document, that it is spelt properly each time. Sometimes there can be many variations on a word, so be careful. For example: • Pearl Harbor (NOT Pearl Harbour) • World Health Organization • Mr Whyte/White • Jennifer/Gennifer • Kasey/Casey/Kasee/Casie • John/Jon
docstyle|proffer-or-prefer: Proffer or prefer It is incorrect to say that the WA Police Force has ‘proffered’ a charge. The correct verb is ‘preferred’ which when legally applied, means to put (charges) before a court, judge, magistrate etc, for consideration and judgement.
docstyle|titles-and-ranks: Titles and ranks Titles Titles such as Mr, Mrs, Ms and Miss are used when referring to people or attributing direct or indirect speech. For example: • Mr Neil Smith will be attending the police concert. Do not use a person’s title and honorific in the same phrase. For example: • Corporate Communications Branch Director, John Smith • NOT…Corporate Communications Branch Director, Mr John Smith Ranks For ranks of police officers, always spell them out in full in when used initially in written correspondence, as abbreviations can look messy and unprofessional. It is also a mark of respect for officers. For example: • Commissioner John Smith • Deputy Commissioner John Smith • Assistant Commissioner John Smith • Commander John Smith • Superintendent John Smith • Inspector John Smith • Senior Sergeant John Smith • Sergeant John Smith • Senior Constable John Smith • First Class Constable John Smith • Constable John Smith • Probationary Constable John Smith However, sometimes using abbreviations is unavoidable, for instance, when making reference to an officer more than once in a written document, or when completing police forms where space is limited. The following abbreviations are preferred: • DC John Smith • AC John Smith • Cdr John Smith • Supt John Smith • S/Sgt John Smith • Sgt John Smith • S/C John Smith • 1/C John Smith • Const. John Smith • P/C John Smith
docstyle|format: When preparing correspondence in the WA Police Force, some basic rules need to be followed. Format Correspondence should be: • Arial font • 12-point type • fully justified • printed on approved WA Police Force letterhead (where applicable). The tone of the correspondence from the WA Police Force must reflect the premise that the writer has a right to the information sought and a right to think and feel the way he or she does. Replies must not be defensive.
docstyle|references-to-wa-police-force: References to the Western Australia Police Force When the WA Police Force is referred to in externally-facing written communication, the ‘Western Australia Police Force’ is to be used in the first instance and written out in full. It is not necessary to then put brackets immediately following and abbreviate our name as (WA Police Force). For multiple references to our name in the one piece of communication, use the ‘Western Australia Police Force’ in the first instance, and the ‘WA Police Force’ or ‘the agency’ in instances thereafter. For internal communication, either the ‘Western Australia Police Force,’ ‘WA Police Force’ or the ‘agency’ may be used. Never refer to our agency as the ‘Western Australian Police Force,’ ‘Western Australia Police Service,’ ‘WA Police Service,’ ‘Police Service,’ ‘WA Police,’ ‘WAPF,’ ‘WAPS,’ ‘WAPOL’ or any variations thereof in any communication, whether it be external or internal.
docstyle|preparation-of-correspondence-f: Preparation of correspondence for signature The content of all correspondence must: • be written in plain language • be clear, concise, direct, helpful and polite • respond to all issues raised in the letter received • where appropriate, provide a specific officer’s name, position and contact details Drafts of official correspondence must have the approval of the portfolio head or authorised officer before being sent.
docstyle|preparation-of-internal-memoran: Preparation of internal memoranda and reports Internal memoranda and reports must be prepared as follows: • be printed on plain paper • the address block should be in upper case and bold and include the title of the person or group to whom it is addressed and also the title of the author (using Arial font, 12-point type) • subject headings are to be in lower case and bold (using Arial font, 12-point type) • there is no closing salutation but the name and title of the responsible officer (in full capitals) and date (day/month/year) are included at the end of the document • when referring to names of people in the body of the memo or report, the surname of the person should be shown in upper case. This is to limit confusion about the person’s surname (e.g. Brian JOHN).
docstyle|page-numbering: Page numbering Documents of more than one page in length must have the pages numbered. Place the number at the bottom of the page, and centre it. In documents of more than one page, the page number should not appear on the first page.
docstyle|spacing-after-punctuation: Spacing after punctuation In typewritten (as distinct from typeset) material, it used to be customary to place two spaces after a colon, semicolon, full stop or other sentence-closing punctuation. Today however, programs for word processing and desktop publishing offer more sophisticated, variable spacing, so this practice of double spacing is now avoided as it can create distracting gaps on a page.
docstyle|reference-block: Reference block The reference block provides details so a document can be tracked, or it can identify other relevant documents and must: • include the relevant reference file number (e.g. Ministerial file number, Objective file number or Records file number) • be written in 8-point Arial font.
docstyle|address-block: Address block The full name of the addressee and his/her address is always in capital and lower case letters. For example: Mr George and Mrs Joan Smith Smith and Smith Associates GPO Box 6622 PERTH WA 6001 If a letter has been signed jointly by a couple, e.g. ‘John and Susan Brown’, the format of address in the reply is: Mr John and Ms Susan Brown NOT Mr and Ms J Brown Addresses must not be abbreviated or contracted. The suburb and town must be in capitals in the address block. For example: 2 Adelaide Terrace EAST PERTH WA 6004 In the address block on addressed letters, insert two spaces between the suburb and state, and the state and postcode. For example: CARINE WA 6020 (note that this line is all in capitals)
docstyle|name-of-police-station: Name of police station Police station names must be spelt in full in any correspondence. For example: • Albany Police Station • Mandurah Police Station
docstyle|opening-salutation: Opening salutation Use the appropriate title in the address and opening salutation. For example: • Mr • Mrs • Ms • Dr • Professor Always use the title used by the writer in the original correspondence. If it is not possible to identify the title, use Mr or Ms.
docstyle|opening-paragraph: Opening paragraph The opening paragraph refers to the correspondence that is being responded to. When replying, the date of the correspondence and the subject matter are identified. For example: • Thank you for your letter dated (date) regarding… If there is no date on the correspondence, date it from when it was received at your office. For example: • Thank you for your letter received in this office on (date).
docstyle|closing-paragraph: Closing paragraph Try to end on a positive note. The closing paragraph should thank the writer for bringing the issues to the attention of the signatory. For example: • Thank you for bringing this matter to my attention. • Thank you for raising your concerns with me. • I trust that this information clarifies the situation for you
docstyle|closing-salutation: Closing salutation When a letter is addressed to a person by name, such as ‘Dear Mr Jones’, the letter is signed: Yours sincerely (without a comma) When the addressee is not known and the letter is addressed as ‘Dear Sir’ or ’Dear Madam’ (or an impersonal approach is warranted) the usual closing salutation is: Yours faithfully (without a comma)
docstyle|signature-block: Signature block Should read: RANK / NAME POSITION STATION / BUSINESS UNIT Date For example: SERGEANT JOHN SMITH or JOHN CITIZEN OFFICER-IN-CHARGE EXECUTIVE MANAGER WEMBLEY POLICE STATION BUSINESS SERVICES 1 March 2023 1 March 2023
docstyle|telephone-and-facsimile-numbers: Telephone and facsimile numbers If telephone and facsimile numbers are to be part of a signature block they should be on one line to keep the length of the signature block to a reasonable size. Telephone and facsimile numbers should be separated by five spaces. For example: SERGEANT JOHN SMITH or JOHN CITIZEN OFFICER-IN-CHARGE EXECUTIVE MANAGER WEMBLEY POLICE STATION BUSINESS SERVICES Ph: 9387 6777 Fax: 9383 9063 Ph: 9222 8989 Fax: 9222 8999 1 March 2023 1 March 2023 A number of versions may be used when putting telephone and facsimile numbers in signature blocks. Local or intrastate As telephone calls within WA no longer need the area code (08) included for WA telephone numbers, it does not need to be used in the signature block. For example: Ph: 9222 1404 Fax: 9222 1060 Mob: 0413 701 357 Interstate If you send a lot of emails interstate to other police jurisdictions or contacts, use the (08) area code in your signature block. For example: Ph: (08) 9222 1404 Fax: (08) 9222 1060 Mob: 0413 701 357 International If you are sending information overseas via email and you may need people to contact you, make sure you use the area code and international dial code in your signature block. For example: Ph: +61 8 9222 1404 Fax: +61 8 9222 1060 Mob: +61 0413 701 357
docstyle|referring-to-acts: Referring to acts The title of an act of parliament should be referred to exactly. For example, an act or a section of an act is referred to as follows: • Police Act 1892 • The Workplace Relations Act 1996 (Cth) s 33 details the powers of… The title and year of the act is in italics. Only add the state/jurisdiction in brackets after the title if it is not a WA act.
docstyle|using-referencing-or-citations: Using referencing or citations Using referencing in written communication (such as certain types of reports), enables an acknowledgement to be made of the contribution of other writers or researchers in preparing your written work. Referencing respects the intellectual property rights of other writers, and avoids plagiarism. Referencing also provides supportive evidence to strengthen the claims or arguments you are presenting in your written work. A simple example of when a reference is not required is: “White is a popular colour for a car in Australia.” Reasoning: This is generally widely known and accepted in Australia. As compared with a simple example of when a reference is required: “White is the most popular colour for a car in Australia.” Reasoning: This is a quantifiable statement and a reference should be made to the source from which it was obtained. References should always be accurate to allow readers the ability to trace the source of information referred to. The Harvard Referencing System is the preferred standard to be used when referencing source material in reports. This means the author and date/year of publication (as a minimum) should be shown in brackets following the statement in the body of the report (as shown in this sentence). You can also correlate the reference to a piece of footnoted information that supports the statement, as shown at1 and2 below. 1 A referencing footnote may be inserted numerically via the References Tab in Word. 2 The author and date/year of publication should be detailed in brackets within the body of the report, or it can be shown as a footnote.
docstyle|preparation-of-ministerial-and-: Preparation of Ministerial and Parliamentary documents The Office of the Commissioner coordinates the preparation and quality assurance of: • Ministerial correspondence • Advice to the Minister for Police • Ministerial briefing notes and submissions • Parliamentary Questions on Notice • Parliamentary Questions Without Notice • Requests for comments on Cabinet Submissions For help with any Ministerial or Parliamentary matters, call 9222 1965. You may also refer to the Office of the Commissioner Intranet site.
docstyle|format-of-emails: Emails are a major method of communication throughout the WA Police Force. The following guidelines outline the professional use of email by agency personnel. Format of emails Email messages should be formatted as plain black text on a white background using a standard font such as Arial. Personalisation of work emails is not professional. Do not include: • Quotations from famous people • Animated GIFS • Photographs or images • Different background colours, creative fonts and text colours as they are often distracting, cause difficulties for people with visual impairment, and can be incorrectly displayed in different email applications At times, other details may be approved for inclusion for corporate reasons (such as promotion of a corporate event), but approval is required from the Corporate Communications Branch. Email Corporate.Communications.Branch@police.wa.gov.au
docstyle|corporate-email-signature-block: Corporate email signature block All email applications can be set to automatically insert a corporate signature block that identifies the sender’s name and work details at the end of every email sent, i.e. sender’s full name, rank (if a police officer), PD number (digit number only, not the letters ‘PD’), job title, business unit, work address, telephone number, fax number and email address. It is good practice to include these details on every email sent. In the case of employees who do not wish to have their full details stated in emails, sensitive information (such as location of work) may be omitted. Supervisors and OICs are encouraged to monitor and attend to variations of the corporate email signature block for staff within their control. For examples and instructions on how to set up your corporate email signature block, refer to the Western Australia Police Force Corporate Branding Style Guide, page 6. All WA Police Force emails have the following disclaimer automatically attached: This email message and any attached files may contain information that is confidential and subject of legal privilege intended only for use by the individual or entity to whom they are addressed. If you are not the intended recipient or the person responsible for delivering the message to the intended recipient be advised that you have received this message in error and that any use, copying, circulation, forwarding, printing or publication of this message or attached files is strictly forbidden, as is the disclosure of the information contained therein. If you have received this message in error, please notify the sender immediately and delete it from your Inbox. If you send a lot of emails, you may be responsible for a large amount of unnecessary printing. A common element of a signature block that is recommended is: Please consider the environment before printing this email.
docstyle|professional-use-of-emails: Professional use of emails It is essential to use appropriate language, correct spelling and punctuation in all emails sent. Do not use profanities or other socially-unacceptable language. The tone should be sincere and neutral. Be concise - if more than a few paragraphs are required it may be better to use a memo or pick up the telephone. Do not add unnecessary attachments. Do not use an email when dealing with conflict situations or sensitive, difficult, complex or emotional matters, as these can be misinterpreted and may lead to unnecessary friction. Pick up the telephone, or better still, meet with the person. Take care when forwarding emails. Email trails (copies of previous email communications) can be very long and may contain comments that were not intended for widespread viewing. Where a response is required, aim to respond within two working days. This is particularly important when dealing with people outside the agency. Use the ‘Automatic Replies (Out of Office)’ function for absences from the office and to advise the sender of an alternative contact or when his/her email will be read or actioned.
docstyle|respect-for-others-when-using-e: Respect for others when using emails Never send an email when angry - the tone of the message often reflects the sender’s mood, even if unintentionally. If a matter is urgent it is best dealt with face-to-face or by telephone. Setting unrealistic timelines or using inappropriate language in an email may be considered bullying. Circulate copies of emails (cc) only when necessary and appropriate. If in doubt, don’t. It is good practice when sending emails to more than one person, to ensure that everyone knows to whom the email has been distributed. Normally recipients should see the email addresses of each other. With large groups, it is a useful strategy to create a group email list, so that the name of the group shows as the recipient e.g. Project Team X, rather than 50 email addresses of the individual members. Whenever a person is referred to by name in an email, it is polite to include them in the recipient list so they are aware of the communication and what is being said. If the intention is that the person should not see the email it is wise to mark the email ‘confidential’ so that it is treated as such.
docstyle|out-of-office-messaging: Out of Office messaging It is considered good practice for all WA Police Force personnel to place an appropriate Out of Office message on their personal email accounts – something professional, concise and polite that alerts enquirers (both within and external to the agency) that they are unavailable and who they should contact instead. Messages can be tailored to suit each particular situation, but some simple examples are: • Thank you for your message but I’m out of the office until Monday 16 July. Please contact Constable Bill Brown on 9399 3399 or by email. • Thank you for your message but I’m out of the office until Monday 11 June. If your enquiry is urgent, please contact Sergeant Wanda White on 9488 4488 or by email. • Thank you for your message but I’m out of the office until Monday 13 August and will get back to you then. However, if your enquiry is urgent, please contact Inspector John Smith on 9577 5577 or by email.
docstyle|legal-aspects-of-emails: Legal aspects of emails Emails are not secure. Give consideration to how confidential information is transferred. Exercise caution when sending emails with third party information (e.g. email addresses and personal details). This could be a breach of privacy if there is no consent to share the information. The content of emails should be treated with the same care as letters printed on letterhead as they are a record of written correspondence. Be aware that emails may be accessed, even after they are deleted from a computer, and copies may need to be provided as part of legal disclosure processes. Emails can be considered contractual agreements when a staff member sends an email and it indicates they are representing the WA Police Force.

Arrested suspects, rights of ................................................................................ 40 ANNEXURE SIX ............................................................................................................... 42 Section 29 Criminal Code (WA) Fact Sheet: Criminal Responsibility of Children (doli incapax) ............................................................................................................................ 42 ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS The Western Australia Police Force (WA Police Force) acknowledges and greatly appreciates the material and assistance provided by the New Zealand Police Service and National Policing Improvement Agency, United Kingdom in the development of this manual. Majority of the material utilised has been adapted from: Investigative Interviewing Doctrine Investigative Interviewing Suspect Guide Investigative Interviewing Witness Guide New Zealand Police 'Practical Guide to Investigative Interviewing' Central Police Training & Development Authority (Centrex) 2004 ‘Investigative Interviewing: psychology and practice’ (Milne & Bull, 1999) INTRODUCTION Investigating officers should, whenever possible, follow the mandate, investigate then interview rather than interview then investigate. This manual provides information on the Conversation Management Model. It is designed to develop knowledge and understanding of the model to assist officers to conduct effective suspect interviews. Some researchers consider there is no difference between the style of interview required for a witness and that required for a suspect. There are many similarities, particularly in relation to structure, but an interview with a suspect is usually conducted in an entirely different atmosphere and within a vastly different legal framework. For this reason, the two are dealt with separately. The success or otherwise of an interview with a suspect should not be measured by proof of a suspect’s guilt or whether the suspect makes some form of admission. The aim of the interview is to discover whether the suspect was involved in the matter for which they are being interviewed and to obtain accurate and reliable information. It is essential that every effort be made to obtain an account from the suspect. The purpose of an interview with a suspect is no different to that with a witness: to ascertain the truth of the matter under investigation. Interviewers must always enter an interview with an open mind and remain that way throughout the interview. At the same time, interviewers must not accept the account at face value, but rather must listen carefully and objectively to what is said. The account must be probed at the appropriate time and subsequently compared to what is already known at that time, to help determine truth and accuracy. Interviewers should be constantly aware of the dangers of not listening to the suspect and only hearing what the interviewer expects or wants to hear. A good interviewer listens to all that is said, disregarding information only when the interviewer is satisfied it is irrelevant, but still keeping it at the back of the mind in case it later becomes relevant1. This resource will either refresh your understanding of investigative interviewing, or provide you with the foundations if the concepts are new to you. Related Information More information on investigative interviewing can be found on the Investigative Standards Unit Intranet Site (Investigative Interviewing page). 1 Investigative Interviewing Explained 4th edition LexisNexis Butterworths. DEFINITIONS To assist officers, a definition of terms used in this manual is shown below. Audiovisual Record of Interview (AVROI): Recording of an interview by means of DVD or video or other electronic method. Automated Interview Plan (AIP): Electronic interview plan used for suspects and witnesses. Located on the WA Police Force Intranet here . Challenge: Seeking an explanation from the interviewee for inconsistencies between facts known by police and the interviewees account. Confession: An admission or part admission, or any inculpatory statement, whether communicated verbally, in writing, or any other form. Conversation Management Model: A structured interview model used to interview a suspect. Culturally and Linguistically Diverse (CaLD): A person who is vulnerable due to their culture or whose second language is English. Interviewee: The person who is being interviewed. Investigating Officer (IO): The officer who is investigating the incident. Investigative interviewing: The questioning of witnesses and suspects to obtain accurate and reliable information about matters under investigation. Investigatively important topics: Of value to the investigation because it helps to establish the nature and elements of the offence, possible defences, the identity of the offender or further lines of enquiry. PEACE Model: An interviewing framework that provides a structure to planning and conducting effective investigative interviews. Physical Material (PM): Items which include DNA, fingerprints, impressions, photographs, clothing, weapons, documents, computer generated data, trace evidence, Closed Circuit Television (CCTV) footage, ballistics, crash reports and all other forensic samples. Suspect: A person suspected of having committed an offence, whether or not he or she has been charged with the offence. TEDS: A mnemonic that is helpful when constructing open questions. It stands for: Tell, Explain, Describe, Show. The Five Key Investigative Strategies (The5KIS): The5KIS are strategies designed to capture, categorise, manage and evaluate all potential evidence relevant to an investigation. The5KIS are categorised into Physical Material, Witnesses, Intelligence, Public Awareness and Suspects. Vulnerable Person: For the purpose of a police interview, be that suspect or witness, is defined as someone who falls within one or more of the following categories: • A child is always a vulnerable person. • People with impaired intellectual function are always vulnerable. Or people who: • Have impaired physical functioning. • Are Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islanders. • Are from non-English speaking backgrounds. • Have suffered an emotional or traumatic incident. Which as a result, may: • Predispose them to suggestibility. • Impact on voluntariness. • Complicate communications between the police and the interviewee. Any of the above circumstances may result in flawed information being captured during the interview. Persons fitting this definition must be afforded enhanced services to ensure fairness to the person and accuracy of the information obtained during an interview. 5W&H: A mnemonic that is helpful when constructing open questions. It stands for Who, What, When, Where, Why and How.
docsus|inve-inte-susp-SUSPECT-INTERVIEWI: Definition of a Suspect A person suspected of having committed an offence, whether or not he or she has been charged with the offence2. PEACE Model for Suspects The PEACE Model is the framework utilised by WA Police Force to conduct suspect interviews. Planning and Preparation Prepare and plan for the interview using the Five Key Investigative Strategies (The5KIS). Identify if the suspect is vulnerable and prepare prior to interview. For example, during the planning phase the need to consider Anunga Guidelines or a responsible adult is identified. Engage and Explain Build rapport, explain the interview process, and cover legislative, policy and case law obligations. Account, Clarify and Challenge Using the Conversation Management Model gain an account of events, clarify and challenge any inconsistencies. Account for new information. Closure Conclude the interview as per the Audiovisual Record of Interview (AVROI) guide. Discuss future state with the suspect. For example, procedures to be undertaken if the suspect is charged, future court appearances etc. Evaluate Evaluate how the information obtained impacts on the investigation and also evaluate the performance of the interviewer. 2 Section 115 Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA). The Conversation Management Model is the model utilised to interview suspects. The steps to conduct a Conversation Management interview are outlined below. The Conversation Management Model will be covered fully in this manual.
docsus|inve-inte-susp-SUSPECT-ACCOUNT: • What is your involvement in (enter the offence under investigation)? • Obtain an account by use of an open question. • Note down topics for further questioning. • Summarise the suspect’s initial account. • Question the suspect on each topic using TEDS and 5W&H questions. • Pass over to the corroborator at the end of each topic. • When the corroborator finishes asking questions on the identified topic summarise what has been said by the suspect. • Move on to next topic.
docsus|inve-inte-susp-POLICE-AGENDA: • Identify topics from your plan (investigatively important topics) that have not been explored during the suspect account. • Question the suspect on each investigatively important topic using TEDS and 5W&H questions. • Pass over to the corroborator at the end of each topic. • When the corroborator finishes asking questions on the identified topic summarise • what has been said by the suspect. • Ensure you have questioned the suspect on all investigatively important topics before you move to the challenge phase. CHALLENGE • Must be after all topics are exhausted. • Must have previously questioned on the topic of the challenge. • Order your challenges from weakest to strongest. • Adopt a clarifying approach. • Ask for an explanation.
docsus|inve-inte-susp-SUSPECTS-ACCOUNT: Lead interviewer ask open TEDS 5W&H questions on the topic. Once all questions asked pass topic to corroborating officer. TOPIC Lead interviewer ask further Corroborating officer ask questions on the topic and then Questions on topic using summarise OR Summarise the TEDS & 5W&H questions topic and move onto next topic
docsus|inve-inte-susp-POLICE-AGENDA-2: Lead interviewer ask open TEDS 5W&H questions on the topic. Once all questions asked pass topic to corroborating officer. docsus|inve-inte-susp-CHALLENGE-PHASE: Only one interviewer to challenge. Start with weakest challenge working up to the strongest challenge. docsus|inve-inte-susp-PLANNING-AND-PREPA: Planning is an essential element of a good interview. At the earliest stage of planning, any vulnerabilities of a suspect must be identified and accommodated. (Refer Vulnerable Suspect section). The detail of an interview plan may vary depending upon the overall circumstances. The successful outcome of an interview is often determined by the level of thought and preparation applied before the interview. The interview plan is a documented record of the objectives to be covered during the interview, incorporating The5KIS and all factual, legal and procedural matters that need to be addressed. Topics to be covered should be listed. An interview plan is not a thought, it is a written plan to assist you throughout the interview. An interview plan can be located at Investigative Standards intranet site. The essence is to investigate then interview – not interview then investigate.3 Consider these areas in your planning and preparation for interviewing a suspect: Interview objectives (The5KIS). Investigatively important topics (Police Agenda). Production of Physical Material (PM) during AVROI (include any documentation, i.e. maps, photographs etc, or any PM to be shown to the suspect). Suspect profile: includes criminal history, associations, family circumstances, employment, etc. Legal requirements (Legislative, policy or case law obligations). Practical arrangements (Security of suspect, interview location etc) Consider breaks during the interview. During a suspect interview it also may be beneficial to break up the interview into multiple interviews. For example, after completely exhausting the suspects account of an alleged offence, before commencing the Police Agenda. Interview Objectives Examine all available information, witness statements, scene examination, PM, Closed Circuit Television (CCTV) footage and other supporting documents. Review witness statements/reports to assist in your written plan. Set the objectives for the interview (include covering identified investigatively important topics using The5KIS, For example, elements of offence, suspect's movements at relevant times, forensic material linking the suspect to the crime scene, For example, blood, DNA material, fingerprints, clothes). Written Interview Plans Police Agenda – Investigatively important topics 3 Investigative Interviewing Explained 4th Edition Brian Ord, Gary Shaw, Tracey Green A written interview plan: Summarises the interviewer's objective(s) and provides a framework on which to base questioning; Assists you to: • Keep track of what's been covered and what remains to be dealt with; • Identify areas where the suspect’s account conflicts with what is already known or has been suggested in other accounts; and • Identify new information while keeping track of the interview's objectives. Gives you confidence and flexibility to conduct a professional and effective interview. Should include: • Your opening question. “What was your involvement in……………….” • What is known and what needs to be established; and • The investigatively important topics (Police Agenda) you plan to cover; evidence, element/s of the offence/s and probable defences. Decide how to cover these during the interview. Identify the geographical area of the offence. It is an advantage to physically examine the scene. Introduce PM. Identify possible challenges and in what order they are to be delivered. Decide what allegations, if any, to outline to the suspect if they adopt their right to silence. Demonstrate that police considered legal, policy and case law obligations before and during an AVROI. Contain any other relevant points. You may need to change or add to these points during the interview as the suspect introduces new information requiring clarification or challenging. Officers are encouraged to use the Automated Interview Plan (AIP) when interviewing suspects even when not mandatory to do so. It allows the interviewer to produce an interview plan tailored to the suspects vulnerabilities that need to be addressed during interview. The completed AIP will include legislative, policy and procedural requirements that need to be met to ensure a legally defensible interview is conducted. The AIP is located here. Determine the Roles of the Interviewers Unless exceptional circumstances exist, a suspect will be interviewed by two police officers; the lead interviewer and the corroborating interviewer. It should be decided during the planning stage as to who the lead is and who the corroborator is. It is vitally important that interviewers understand their respective roles and maintain the required discipline to keep to their designated role4. Status of a Person to be Interviewed Prior to interview, it is important to establish the status of person, to ensure they are afforded the correct rights. Interviewees are defined as: • Arrested suspect. • Suspect / accompanying person. Arrested Suspect Definition: There is a reasonable suspicion the person has committed the offence under investigation and been arrested on suspicion for that offence. Consideration must be given at this stage to the manner in which you are going to effect the arrest. The way in which the suspect is arrested will impact on their demeanour, cooperation and willingness to speak. An arrested suspect must be given Section 137 & 138 Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA) (CIA) rights. Record the time, date and the suspect’s responses when the rights are given. During this process, you will be able to identify if the arrested suspect is vulnerable and requires further considerations. Investigators need to be aware that to comply with Section 118 CIA any admissions or confessions made by an adult suspect for an indictable offence that cannot be dealt with by a court of summary jurisdiction, or any admissions made by a child for an indictable offence, irrespective of whether, if an adult were charged with it, it could be dealt with by a court of summary jurisdiction must be audiovisually recorded5 to be admissible in court. Investigators will keep accurate records of all interactions with the suspect. If the suspect makes an immediate denial or admission ensure the denial or admission is covered during your planning phase and addressed during the subsequent AVROI. Investigators need to develop rapport with the suspect (continue talking to them about unrelated topics prior to the AVROI). Ensure that you keep a brief record outlining what was discussed. It is important to consider any circumstances that may make the suspect vulnerable and ensure the suspect’s vulnerability is catered for during your planning. Ensure the interview is conducted accordingly. For example; Juvenile, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, interpreter required, Anunga Guidelines, responsible adult etc. 4 Investigative Interviewing Explained 4th Edition. 5 Exceptions to this requirement can be found at Section 118(4) CIA. Accompanying Person / Suspect If an Investigating Officer (IO) identifies a suspect during an investigation where the level of suspicion has not reached the burden of reasonable suspicion, the IO can interview the person as a suspect. Give the suspect Section 28 CIA rights and with the exception of advising the suspect they are under arrest, give Section 137 & 138 CIA rights. During this time, assess if the person is a vulnerable person. If at any time you reach a reasonable suspicion of the suspect you must immediately arrest the person on suspicion for the offence and confirm that they understand their rights under Section 137 & 138 CIA. Allow them the opportunity to exercise the rights if they wish to do so. Vulnerable Suspects It is vital that all officers understand the different characteristics that may lead to a suspect being classified as a vulnerable suspect and understand the steps that need to be undertaken to ensure the vulnerable suspect is interviewed appropriately. Use of the AIP will assist in identifying and addressing the suspects vulnerabilities, ensuring the interview is conducted appropriately. Definition of a Vulnerable Person Vulnerable Person: For the purpose of a police interview, be that suspect or witness, is defined as someone who falls within one or more of the following categories: • A child is always a vulnerable person. • People with impaired intellectual function are always vulnerable. Or people who: • Have impaired physical functioning. • Are Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islanders. • Are from non-English speaking backgrounds. • Have suffered an emotional or traumatic incident. Which as a result, may: • Predispose them to suggestibility. • Impact on voluntariness. • Complicate communications between the police and the interviewee. Any of the above circumstances may result in flawed information being captured during the interview. Persons fitting this definition must be afforded enhanced services to ensure fairness to the person and accuracy of the information obtained during an interview. The following are important considerations that will impact on what provisions need to be made relating to suspects. Decisions on who will conduct the interview, the structure, style, duration, and pace of the interview will be made based on information relevant to these issues. As the investigating officer (IO) it is paramount any factors effecting the vulnerability of a suspect are identified and dealt with in line with legislation, policy and case law. If suspects are not interviewed appropriately, vital information may be missed, contaminated or not accepted by the court. While it is not possible to supply an exhaustive list of people who may be vulnerable in the criminal justice system, the following list will assist in identifying vulnerability factors: Child / juvenile. Aboriginal people and Torres Strait Islanders Immaturity, either in terms of age or development. Any infirmity, including early dementia or disease. Mental illness. Intellectual disability Illiteracy or limited education which may impair a person’s capacity to understand police questions. People who are of non-English speaking background. Alcoholism. Physical disabilities including deafness or loss of sight. Drug dependence. Cultural, ethnic or religious factors including those relating to gender attitudes. Trauma. It must be understood that a person’s vulnerability does not have to be permanent. Suspects need to be assessed in accordance with how they present to police at the time of contact and should be dealt with appropriately. Any suspect identified as vulnerable must be dealt with in a manner that ensures fairness. Whilst it is widely thought that the Anunga Guidelines relate specifically to Aboriginal or Torres Strait Island people, the principles contained in the guidelines should be considered when dealing with any person identified as vulnerable. Juvenile / Child Suspects Prior to interviewing a juvenile there are a number of legislative, policy and case law obligations to be met. As a minimum, and before interviewing a juvenile, police should be familiar with the below references: Police Manual JV-01.01.17 Procedure for Interview of Juveniles JWRL (a child) –v- The State of WA Case Law citing considerations for the interview [2009] WASC 285 of a Juvenile Section 20 Young Offenders Act 1994 Legislation citing obligations when interviewing a (WA) Juvenile Offender Section 29 Criminal Code A person under the age of 14 years is not criminally responsible for an act or omission, unless it is proved that at the time of doing the act or making the omission he had capacity to know that he ought not to do the act or make the omission. Rebutting the presumption: IO’s may use the following indicators to rebut the presumption with the following: • Electronic Record of Interview (EROI); • Home background and school life; • The ‘more obviously heinous’ the offence, • the easier to rebut the presumption; • Circumstances surrounding the offence • which can prove capacity; • Evidence of normality; • Previous record; • Statements by the child to police; or • Statement made by the child during or after the offence AVROI evidence is the most preferable form of evidence as it comes directly from the child and refers directly to the child’s appreciation of the act. A child must be cautioned and afforded their rights under the Criminal Investigation Act 2006 prior to being questioned in relation to their capacity in connection with a suspected offence IO’s avoid leading questions and yes/no answers. A child should be encouraged to provide reasons for their answers and explore the dimension of moral reasoning. There is a 3-Stage general approach in AVROI’s to cover capacity. The case of R v El (2009) QCA 177 sets out a line of hypothetical questioning which can be used in AVROI’s to prove capacity. Stage 1 – involves family level questions in order to establish the child knows right or wrong in a moral sense. IO’s may choose the use the following questions (or similar) as a guideline: • If you get into trouble at home – if you bully your little sister/brother and yell at them. Is that the right thing or wrong thing? Why? What would your mum/dad do? • If you don’t clean your room and make your room messy. Is that right or wrong? Why? What would your mum/dad do? Stage 2 – involves asking school level questions to determine that the child knows right or wrong in a moral sense at a higher level. IO's may choose the use the following questions (or similar) as a guideline: • If you get into trouble in school – so if you do something naughty at school like push/hit your classmate for no reason. Is that right or wrong? Why? What would your teacher do? Stage 3 – involves real world questions to determine if the child knows what is lawful and unlawful. IOs may choose the use the following questions (or similar) as a guideline: • Do you know what is stealing / stealing a motor vehicle / robbery / burglary? Is it right or wrong to steal other people’s things? • Is it right or wrong to break into someone’s home? Why? Would Police be involved? • What will be the punishment or consequence if Police get involved? If the Prosecution can successfully establish all 3 stages of questioning – they have the evidence to prove the child not only has the capacity to know what is right or wrong, but also know what is lawful and unlawful– this can help to establish the burden of proof, beyond reasonable doubt. Australian Courts appear to be more open to receiving evidence of a previous finding of guilt by a child.6 It has been held that it is admissible to establish capacity, even though it is not allowed under similar circumstances for an adult offender. There is no set formula for evidence sufficient to rebut the presumption, it will depend on the circumstances of each case. The best approach for IO’s is to collect as much evidence as possible, to assess whether the Prosecution can prove capacity beyond reasonable doubt. Who can be an Independent Person • An adult, other than a member of the police, who is present with the consent of the person responsible for the young person (if the responsible person can be found). • In the case of a young person who is of or above the age of 16 years, an adult who was present at the consent of the young person. • A legal practitioner of the young person's own choosing (if the young person is over 16 years of age). • A person who has not been involved in the investigation of the offence and has no interest in the outcome of the investigation and who is present during the interview and who is approved by the child. Police officers should endeavour to identify responsible persons within their district who may be used as independent persons when required. Where practicable, persons of the same sex and similar ethnic, cultural and/or religious background to the young person should be utilised. Juvenile Aboriginal or Torres Strait Island Descent Suspect Police interviewing juvenile Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island people, will comply with the following policy and procedures: • Anunga Guidelines. • Advise Aboriginal Legal Service of juvenile arrest (Police Manual JV-01.01.04 & LP- 02.02) – via Custody Notification System (CNS). • Put the child in contact with the Aboriginal Visitors Scheme. Adult Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander Suspect To interview an adult who is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Island descent, in addition to legislative considerations (sections 10, 28, 137 & 138 CIA) the interviewing officer must comply with the Anunga Guidelines. Suspect Who is Culturally and Linguistically Diverse (CaLD) or English is Their Second Language To interview an adult who does not understand, speak or communicate in English as a first language the interviewing officer must comply with Sections 10, 137 and 138 CIA. The interviewing officer shall utilise an approved interpreter or translator as outlined in the Police Manual. Practical Arrangements Decide: • Whether the suspect is a vulnerable suspect. • Who should conduct the interview and who should corroborate. • Who should be present during the interview (For example, interpreter, responsible adult, interview friend; etc). • Where and when the interview should take place. (For example, is the suspect in prison)? Examine the interview room and arrange seating to ensure all people in the interview room are visible. (Usually in the ten to two position if only the suspect and interviewing officers present). Check equipment. Make sure the equipment is functional. Have communication aids ready including pens and paper. Prepare PM to be presented during the interview. Decide whether you want the interview monitored by a supervisor, colleague etc. and make necessary arrangements. Consider what is likely to happen after the interview. For example; arrest, medical examination, photographs, fingerprints, DNA, returned home. Safety Considerations Suspects being interviewed may pose a danger to your safety and others in the office, as well as to the security of police property and information. Ensure that: The suspect is always searched prior to the interview. If the suspect has a history of violence or displays violent or unstable behaviour, a plan must be put in place to ensure officer safety during the interview. A designated and secure interview room is used wherever available and is searched prior to the start of the interview to remove any items that could be used as a weapon. A second officer is present or nearby to ensure security of the suspect. If an officer feels it is unsafe to interview an arrested suspect do not conduct the interview, officer safety is paramount. The suspect is not left unattended and is accompanied at all times. Visitors, including legal advisers, are not left unattended while on police premises, other than when in private consultation with their client. If Suspect Elects to Speak to a Legal Practitioner On advising the suspect that they can communicate with a legal practitioner, you must provide them with appropriate means to facilitate this. If there is a genuine belief that by allowing the suspect to communicate with a legal practitioner (or another person) an ongoing investigation may be jeopardised you may suspend this right see Section 138(4) CIA. Ensure this decision is recorded and outline the reasons. If they do not have a legal practitioner or their legal practitioner is unavailable, the suspect should not be interviewed until they have an opportunity to communicate with a legal practitioner. (The legal practitioner does not need to be “their” legal practitioner or a legal practitioner nominated by the suspect). Allow the suspect to speak to the legal practitioner and receive instruction. Allow the suspect to speak to the legal practitioner in private. If the suspect chooses not to communicate with a legal practitioner proceed with the AVROI after completing your interview plan. If a person cannot contact their legal practitioner and does not wish to participate in an AVROI until they speak to a legal practitioner, they can be lawfully detained pursuant to Section 141(g) CIA until they speak to a legal practitioner. No Pre-Interview Interviews9 Do not conduct interviews off-record. Start AVROI as MCKINNEY DIRECTION: soon as practicable. Ensure that you have planned Officers are reminded of the McKinney and are prepared to conduct the AVROI with the warning which can be issued to a jury in suspect. Never engage in pre-interview interviews the case of uncorroborated and disputed confessions: “It is inherently dangerous (engaging the suspect in an interview off camera in to convict on the uncorroborated an attempt to gain admissions before the AVROI). disputed confessions of the accused to Judges view these interviews as highly inappropriate police as police are considered and there is a high likelihood of your pre-interview professional witnesses”. interview and subsequent AVROI being ruled inadmissible. Note Taking It is important to remember that the suspect’s interview is going to be recorded. It is not necessary to take comprehensive notes. Limited notes should be taken by the lead interviewing officer to identify topics raised by the suspect and to assist their memory when summarising the information obtained from the suspect. The lead interviewer should 9 McKinney v The Queen (1991) 171 CLR 468 maintain good interaction with the suspect including body language and actively listening. More comprehensive notes should be taken by the corroborating interviewer to assist their recollection of information obtained to assist them in identifying questions possibly missed by the interviewing officer on each topic. Notes made of the suspect’s answers to investigatively important topics will be used to assist in formulating effective challenges. ‘Notes made at the time’ by police comprise documentary evidence. Authorship is always important when presenting documentary evidence in court. Notes made at the time should be signed and dated by the officer making the notes and countersigned and dated by the corroborating officer. Any notes made are disclosable and will be retained in the CRIME file.
docsus|inve-inte-susp-ENGAGE-AND-EXPLAIN: The Engage and Explain phase starts when you commence the AVROI. Ask the suspect the questions from the AVROI guide and record their responses. Explain the reason for the interview as outlined in the AVROI guide. Provide the suspect with their appropriate CIA rights including the caution. Ensure the suspect fully understands the rights and has been given the opportunity to exercise them. A simple yes they understand is not sufficient, you must be satisfied (and be able to satisfy a court) the suspect fully understands their rights. Break the rights and caution down into sections and ask the suspect to explain their understanding of each part. Importance of Listening During the interview you must actively listen to the suspect and consider how their account relates to the evidence.
docsus|inve-inte-susp-ACCOUNT-CLARIFY-AN: Suspect Account At the completion of Engage and Explain, the Interviewers first question should be: • “What is your involvement in………………..…….... (the offence under investigation)?” Do not ask the suspect, “What do you know about the offence?” The subtle difference between asking a person to describe their involvement as opposed to what they know about an offence is important. Police seek to determine the suspect’s involvement in the offence. The suspect may know about the offence from having been told something or read something in the media. The question, “What is your involvement in…?” is specific and designed for this purpose. Questions to be asked at the commencement of the interview: • If the suspect admits the offence………………………… “Tell me what happened” • If the suspect denies the offence………………………“Tell me what you were doing between [the relevant time span, day and date of the offence under investigation.]” For example; “Tell me what you were doing between 10am and 12pm last Tuesday 16 September 2016 in as much detail as you can.” If the offence you are interviewing in relation to is a historic offence, (For example, the suspect does not remember the day of the offence), you may wish to proceed straight to the Police Agenda (your interview plan) and ask questions relevant to investigatively important topics. If the suspect is willing to give an account then police will use the Conversation Management Model and ask for a suspect account. Use the following guidelines to obtain the suspect account: Obtain an account by use of an open question. Note down topics for further questioning. Summarise the suspect’s initial account. Identify topics from suspects initial account. Question the suspect on each topic using TEDS and 5W&H questions. Pass to the corroborator at the end of each topic. When the corroborator finishes asking questions on the identified topic, you can either summarise what has been said by the suspect or ask more questions on the topic and then summarise. Move on to the next topic. The below diagram summarises the method of questioning when obtaining the suspect account.

TOPIC Lead interviewer ask further Corroborating officer ask questions on the topic and then Questions on topic using summarise OR Summarise TEDS & 5W&H questions the topic and move onto next topic Production of Physical Material During AVROI All PM to be used during an interview should be taken into the interview room. If the PM is too large or dangerous, photographs of the PM should be taken and produced at the relevant point during the interview. If possible do not allow the suspect to view the PM / photographs prior to questioning them on the relevant topic. All PM to be shown to the suspect during the interview should be produced during the Police Agenda phase of the AVROI. The exception to this is if the suspect discusses the topic during the suspects account. If this occurs produce the PM as below. Ask all relevant questions relating to the PM as you would have during the Police Agenda. There are a number of ways PM can be produced during an AVROI: • The PM can be shown to the suspect before any questions relating to it are asked. Show the PM to the camera, describe the PM and any relevant reference numbers. Ask relevant questions pertaining to the PM. Remember to cross to the corroborator to ascertain if they have any relevant questions to ask. Ensure the security of the PM is maintained at all times. • The second method is to commence asking the suspect questions relating to the PM. When several questions have been asked, produce the PM as described in example one. Continue to ask relevant questions relating to the PM until all questions are exhausted. Remember to cross to the corroborator to ascertain if they have any relevant questions to ask. Ensure the security of the PM is maintained at all times. • The third method is to question the suspect prior to showing them the PM. When the interviewer is satisfied the suspect has been asked all relevant questions cross to the corroborator to ascertain if they have any questions to ask. Show the PM to the suspect as described in example one. Ensure the security of the PM is maintained at all times. Prior to the challenge phase all questions relevant to the PM should be asked of the suspect either during the Suspects Account or the Police Agenda. For example; if the suspects DNA is recovered from 1 Smith Street, Joondalup, the suspect must be questioned as to whether he/she has ever been to 1 Smith Street, Joondalup before the challenge phase. Cover all aspects of the suspect’s involvement, if any, with 1 Smith Street, Joondalup. This will limit their ability to change their story when the challenge of their DNA being at the address is given. You do not have to accept the first answer given. Avoid excessive repetitive questioning on the same point. However, re-phrasing the question and being robust at times in demanding an explanation is acceptable. There is no prescriptive number of times a question can be asked. Remember a magistrate or judge will decide whether your questioning is oppressive or unfair. Check your plan and ensure you have covered the relevant 5KIS, elements of the offence, probable defences, mitigating circumstances and motives. If the interview is being monitored take a break and check with the monitor whether there are any more questions that need to be asked.
