Challenge The challenge phase of the interview should never be made prematurely. Ensure you have clarified the suspect account and police agenda before challenging the account provided. The challenge phase of the interview is used when police have reason to believe the suspect is withholding relevant information or is knowingly giving a false account. The purpose of this phase is to compare what police know against the suspect’s account. Use the following guide to obtain responses during the Challenge phase of the interview: Must be after all topics are exhausted. Must have previously been questioned on the topic of the challenge. Order of challenges - weakest to strongest. Adopt a clarifying approach. Ask for an explanation. Inconsistencies between the suspect's account and the evidence should always be challenged. Follow these steps to challenge evidence: • If there are inconsistencies between what the suspect said and the evidence, you should challenge them by seeking an explanation. • Before challenging the suspect consider having a short break in the interview to review your challenges to ensure they are still relevant and in the correct order. Let the suspect know what you are doing, for example: • "I just need to consider what you have said to me and look over the information I have." Structure the challenges so each is dealt with individually and you present the challenges from weakest to strongest. For example: • Challenge 1: inconsistencies within the suspect's account and known information. • Challenge 2: inconsistencies between the suspect's account and witness information. • Challenge 3: inconsistencies between the suspect's account and forensic material. Introduce each challenge by seeking an explanation following this process: • You said............... state the suspect's version of what he/she said. • We have………... state the evidence that contradicts their version of events. • Explain that …….. ask them to explain inconsistencies between what they have said and the evidence. For example: • "You said you know nothing about the burglary at 1 Smith Street, Joondalup on the 13 September 2016 and that you have never been to that address. We have your fingerprints inside the house. Explain that to me..." Challenge evidence in a clear and focused way. Present each challenge in a way the suspect can understand. Do not express opinions. Your opinion is irrelevant, it is the evidence itself that is important. Avoid putting suggestions to the suspect about what happened. If there is no reply, use silence (pause for a while) and then move to the next challenge.
docsus|inve-inte-susp-CHALLENGE-PHASE-2: Only one interviewer to challenge. Start with weakest challenge working up to the strongest challenge. Ensure you have spoken about the topic of challenge before challenging on it. THE CHALLENGE Listen to response You said …………………. Move on to next challenge We have or know ……….. Explain that to me? If the suspect declines to answer a question then there is no account which can be compared against what police know. An investigative advantage may be gained by asking questions in relation to facts known with a view to elicit a response from the suspect. For example; police are investigating a burglary and possess a Forensic Analysis Report identifying the suspect’s fingerprint inside 1 Smith Street, Joondalup. Police ask, “Have you ever been to 1 Smith Street, Joondalup” and the suspect replies, “No comment”. Because the suspect has not offered any explanation, there is no inconsistency between what is known and the suspect account. Interviewers should not be put off by this response. Police should be prepared to ask a limited number of questions supported by the available potential evidence. These questions should be put to the suspect during the challenge phase of the interview. Remain Professional Always act professionally when challenging the suspect. Being too overbearing may render the interview inadmissible. What might seem an acceptable risk to take in the heat of the moment may be viewed as unacceptable by the court. Think of the challenge phase as presenting evidence that is inconsistent with or contradicts what the suspect said. Do not be frightened to challenge but remember you do not have to call somebody a liar to make them realise you do not believe them. Never call a suspect a liar or say you don't believe them as this is opinion evidence and irrelevant. It may affect the admissibility of your interview if it is deemed to be oppressive or overbearing. Put challenges calmly and clearly allowing the suspect every opportunity to understand what is being suggested and to provide an explanation. There is no need for raised voices, offensive language or demeaning behaviour. Admissions Admissions can be partial or full (a confession). If a suspect confesses to the offence, ask the suspect “Tell me your involvement in the….….. (The offence)” If the suspect gives you a full and honest account of their involvement, you will not need to challenge the suspect. Ensure all the topics in the Police Agenda phase are covered and clarification of the incident obtained in full. (The challenges become corroboration of the suspect’s honest account). If the suspect partially admits the offence, ask the suspect “Tell me your involvement in the…………….. (The offence)” If the suspect does not give an honest account the challenges will need to be put to the suspect following the Conversation Management Model. When Suspects Exercise Their Right to Silence Always plan and prepare for the possibility of a suspect who exercises their right to silence. Ensure that you plan to address elements of the offence, other investigatively important topics and any defences that may be offered. While it is your duty as an investigator to ask questions in relation to allegations made against the suspect it must be remembered that all suspects have the right to silence. This means that if they decide not to talk to you, you cannot compel them to answer questions. Remember that if the court deems that the suspect’s right to silence was overborn any admissions made or information gained may be deemed inadmissible10 . 10 See ARTHURS -v- THE STATE OF WESTERN AUSTRALIA [2007] WASC 209 – Whether admissions made voluntarily or as a result of persistent importunity, insistence or pressure. Despite an initial refusal, unless the suspect is rigorously opposed to answering questions, it is your professional responsibility to attempt to interview the suspect in line with the AVROI guide and the Conversation Management Model. It is the responsibility of the interviewing officers to ensure their questioning of the suspect is reasonable and any answers given by the suspect are voluntary. Never tell the suspect that participating in an AVROI is in fairness to them. The above principles apply unless you are interviewing a suspect to whom the Anunga Guidelines relate. Specifically, rule number eight as outlined below: ‘Should an Aboriginal seek legal assistance reasonable steps should be taken to obtain such assistance. If an Aboriginal states he does not wish to answer further questions or any questions the interrogation should not continue’. For instance, if the suspect indicates they do not want to answer any questions the interview should be stopped immediately, however, the interviewer needs to be mindful of whether the interviewee is merely uncomfortable with that particular topic or whether they are declining to answer any questions. Suspect Sketch If it is relevant and the suspect agrees, ask them to draw a sketch during the interview. This could include a sketch of the location of the offence, weapon/s, route/s taken etc. Remember, a picture speaks a thousand words. Any sketch that is produced should be signed, dated and given a title by the suspect. The interviewing officer is to countersign and date the document as it is most likely to be produced as an exhibit. Keep the sketch available for review and reference as required throughout the interview. Any sketches made during an interview by the interviewer or the suspect are disclosable and will be retained in the CRIME file. Breaks During the Interview It is not compulsory to take breaks during an interview, however, it is acceptable to take breaks if required by police or the suspect. If you have a short break during an AVROI (one officer leaves the room to get a glass of water or box of tissues for the suspect), you may leave the recording device running. If the break will be protracted, state the time of the break and request the corroborator to pause the recording on the AVROI recording device. On completion of the break, ask the corroborator to press the record button on the AVROI recorder when the interviewer and the suspect are seated in the AVROI room. State the time the interview is recommencing and confirm with the suspect that there was no discussion relating to the matter for which he/she is being interviewed off camera. Confirm there have been no threats or promises made to the suspect during the break and remind the suspect they are still under caution. NB: The suspect should not be left unsupervised. Documents Used During an Interview If documents, maps, sketches are used during an interview, ensure that the suspect signs, dates and titles the document if they are willing. The interviewing officer must also sign, date and time the documents. These documents become exhibits and will be retained in the CRIME file. Suspect Admits Offence Part Way Through the Challenge If the suspect admits the offence part way through the challenges, return to the suspect account and ask. “Tell me what happened?” Conduct the interview using the Conversation Management Model. Unrelated Information If a suspect volunteers information unrelated to the offence for which they are being interviewed, continue with the interview and advise them their information will be discussed later. Take care not to imply or infer that the information they have given, or may give, could have a bearing on the present interview. There must be no suggestion, implied or otherwise, that any promise or inducement has been held out to the suspect. Once the interview is complete, the suspect is free to give any information they wish. You do not need to conduct an AVROI about information unrelated to the offence in respect of which they have been interviewed unless you are going to arrest them on suspicion for an offence for which the unrelated information relates. Allegations of Misconduct If during the interview, the suspect makes any allegation against you or your corroborator, do not stop the recording. Either the interviewer or corroborator will leave the AVROI room and speak to a supervisor. The supervisor will enter the AVROI room and clarify the complaint and advise the suspect the matter will be investigated. The supervisor will also ensure the suspect understands their right to speak or be silent and the suspect does not feel compelled to speak to police before the AVROI continues. If the suspect’s complaint relates to a police officer not directly related to the AVROI, advise the suspect their complaint will be brought to the attention of your supervisor and will be investigated. Ensure the suspect understands their right to speak or be silent and they do not feel compelled to continue with the AVROI. CLOSURE It is important to plan the closure of an interview. This should be done in a courteous and professional manner. When the interview is clearly drawing to its close, your aim should be to: • Review information obtained and confirm all topics have been covered by referring to your interview plan. • Ensure there is mutual understanding about what has taken place. • Explain what will happen in the future. • Facilitate a positive attitude towards providing accurate and reliable information in the future. • The interview should be concluded according to the AVROI guide on the Investigative Standards Intranet site. Once you have closed the interview you should continue to adopt an approachable and professional style. Remember this may be one of a series of interviews. You should continue to maintain a working relationship with the suspect throughout. EVALUATE As soon as practical after the interview, consider: • What information has been obtained. • How the account given fits in with other available evidence. • Whether any action needs to be taken. • What further enquiries need to be made? Self- Evaluation Self-evaluation is an important part of professional development. Through critical review of your performance you can identify areas of improvement that may lead to a more professional collection of evidence. When practical, review your AVROI. Self-evaluate your own performance: What did you do well? What could you have done better? What areas can you develop? How will you acquire these skills? ADVICE For advice on investigative interviewing related matters, contact the Detective Training School or the Investigative Standards Unit.
docsus|inve-inte-susp-ANNEXURE-ONE: Anunga Rules AD-01.00 Attachment B - Anunga Rules Judgement Delivered By Chief Justice Forster On 30 April, 1979, Mr. Justice FORSTER handed down his reasons for rejecting typewritten records of conversations in the matter of QUEEN v Angus ANUNGA, Sandy AJAX, Clancy AJAX, TJINGUNYA, Nari WHEELER and Frankie Miller JAGAMARA in the Northern Territory Supreme Court in August, 1975. (R v Anunga (1976) 11 ALR 412) Inter alia Mr. Justice FORSTER said: "It seems to me now, however, to be important that the Court should put on record general guidelines for the conduct of Police Officers when interrogating Aboriginal persons. I preface this statement of guidelines by pointing out that Aboriginal people often do not understand English very well and that, even if they do understand the words, they may not understand the concepts which English phrases and sentences express. Even with the use of interpreters this problem is by no means solved. Police and legal English sometimes is not translatable into the Aboriginal language at all and there are no separate Aboriginal words for some simple words like "in", "at", "on", "by", "with", or "over'', these being suffixes added to the word they qualify. Some words may translate literally into Aboriginal language but mean something different. "Did you go into his house?" means to an English-speaking person, "did you go into the building?", but to an Aboriginal it may also mean, "Did you go within the fence surrounding the house?" English concepts of time, number and distance are imperfectly understood if at all by Aboriginal people, many of the more primitive of whom cannot tell the time by a clock. One frequently hears the answer "long time", which depending on the context may be minutes, hours, days, weeks, or years. In case I may be misunderstood, I should also emphasise that I am not expressing the view that Aboriginal people are any less intelligent than white people but simply that their concepts of certain things and the terms in which they are expressed may be wholly different to those of white people. Another matter which needs to be understood is that most Aboriginal people are basically courteous and polite and will answer questions by white people in the way in which they think the questioner wants. Even if they are not courteous and polite there is the same reaction when they are dealing with an authority figure such as a policeman. Indeed their action is probably a combination of natural politeness and their attitude to someone in authority. Some Aboriginal people find the standard caution quite bewildering, even if they understand that they do not have to answer questions, because if they do not have to answer questions, then why are the questions being asked? Guidelines to be Followed when Interviewing Aboriginals Bearing in mind these preliminary observations which are based partly upon my own knowledge and partly by evidence I have heard in numerous cases I lay down the following guidelines. They apply, of course, to persons who are being questioned as suspects. 1. When an Aboriginal person is being interrogated as a suspect, unless he is as fluent in English as the average white man of English descent, an interpreter able to interpret in and from the Aboriginal person's language should be present, and his assistance should be utilised whenever necessary to ensure complete and mutual understanding. 2. When an Aboriginal is being interrogated it is desirable where practicable that a "prisoner's friend" (who may also be the interpreter) be present. The "prisoner's friend', should be someone in whom the Aboriginal has apparent confidence. He may be a mission or settlement superintendent or a member of the staff of one of these institutions who knows and is known to the Aboriginal. He may be a station owner, manager or overseer or an officer from the Department of Aboriginal Affairs. The combinations of persons and situations are variable and the categories of persons I have mentioned are not exclusive. The important thing is that the "prisoner's friend', be someone in whom the Aboriginal has confidence, by whom he will feel supported. 3. Great care should be taken in administering the caution when it is appropriate to do so. It is simply not adequate to administer it in the usual terms and say, "Do you understand that?" or "Do you understand you do not have to answer questions?" Interrogating Police Officers, having explained the caution in simple terms, should ask the Aboriginal to tell them what is meant by the caution, phrase by phrase, and should not proceed with the interrogation until it is clear the Aboriginal has apparent understanding of his right to remain silent. Most experienced police officers in the Territory already do this. The problem of the caution is a difficult one but the presence of a "prisoner's friend" or interpreter and adequate and simple questioning about the caution should go a long way towards solving it. 4. Great care should be taken in formulating questions so that so far as possible the answer which is wanted or expected is not suggested in any way. Anything in the nature of cross-examination should be scrupulously avoided as answers to it have no probative value. It should be borne in mind that it is not only the wording of the question, which may suggest the answer, but also the manner and tone of voice which are used. 5. Even when an apparent frank and free confession has been obtained relating to the commission of an offence, police should continue to investigate the matter in an endeavour to obtain proof of the commission of the offence from other sources. Failure to do this, among other things, led to the rejection of confessional records of interview in the cases of Nari WHEELER and Frank JAGAMARA. 6. Because Aboriginal people are often nervous and ill at ease in the presence of white authority figures like policemen, it is particularly important that they be offered a meal, if they are being interviewed in a Police Station, or in the company of Police or in custody when a meal time arrives. They should always be offered a drink of water. They should be asked if they wish to use the lavatory if they are in the company of Police or under arrest. 7. It is particularly important that Aboriginal and other people are not interrogated when they are disabled by illness or drunkenness or tiredness. Admissions so gained will probably be rejected by a Court. Interrogation should not continue for an unreasonably long time. 8. Should an Aboriginal seek legal assistance reasonable steps should be taken to obtain such assistance. If an Aboriginal states he does not wish to answer further questions or any questions the interrogation should not continue. 9. When it is necessary to remove clothing for forensic examination or for the purposes of medical examination, steps must be taken forthwith to supply substitute clothing."
docsus|inve-inte-susp-ANNEXURE-TWO: Section 10 Criminal Investigation Act 2006 Interpreters Criminal Investigation Act 2006 Section 10 - Informing people who do not understand English. If under this Act [CIA] an officer is required to inform a person about any matter and the person is for any reason unable to understand or communicate in spoken English sufficiently, the officer must, if it is practical to do so in the circumstances, use an interpreter or other qualified person or other means to inform the person about the matter. Identify the country they come from and the exact language they speak (For example, a Chinese person may speak Mandarin or Cantonese). Arrange for an interpreter using the contracted interpreting service. Provide the interpreter with an outline of the incident and the reason for the interview. Ascertain whether the interpreter is an appropriate person to assist. They must be: • Able to write and speak the suspect’s language fluently. • Impartial and independent (has no prior knowledge of the suspect or witnesses involved in the investigation). If they know any of the parties involved in the investigation (including the suspect), they should only be used in exceptional circumstances, i.e. no one else is available and the interview cannot be delayed. The extent of the connection should also be taken into account when making this decision. If you use an interpreter who knows the parties involved make sure you keep a record of your rationale. Record the interpreter’s qualifications and contact details or those of their organisation. Prepare for the interview in the usual manner. When the interpreter arrives: • Allow the interpreter the opportunity to brief both you and the suspect on their professional role and how they will conduct themselves. • If necessary, inform the interpreter their role is to interpret your questions and the suspect's answers back to you. • Their interpretation should be as direct as possible in 'first person'. They should not enter into general discussion with the suspect. Make sure the interpreter understands the caution/ rights. Instruct them to clearly explain these to the suspect to ensure the suspect understands. Consider seeking advice from the interpreter about any communication issues that may arise. Consider the interpreter's needs for breaks during the interview. Using the interpreter, complete the usual Engage and Explain process as you would for any other suspect. Where appropriate inform the suspect of their caution/ rights with the aid of the interpreter. While video recording the interview: • Ask the interpreter to introduce themselves, explain their role, experience and qualifications. (They may later be required to give evidence in respect of their knowledge and experience). • Explain the interpreter's role as detailed above. • Ensure the interpreter is clearly visible during the interview. Do not speak in segments. Let the interpreter control the length of each segment and signal to you when to stop. Complete the account phase using an appropriate interview model. Your questions are interpreted to the suspect in their language and their answers interpreted back to you. For safety and impartiality reasons make sure the interpreter leaves the room with you if you take any interview breaks. Complete the closure process as usual. Before the interpreter leaves, ensure you have their full contact details (or that of their agency). Conduct an interview evaluation in the usual manner. Ensure the appropriate forms are completed to initiate payment of the interpreter.
docsus|inve-inte-susp-ANNEXURE-THREE: Section 28 Criminal Investigation Act 2006 28. Persons accompanying officers to be informed of rights 1. An officer who requests a person who is not in lawful custody to accompany the officer or another officer for the purposes of assisting in the investigation of an offence must inform the person and be satisfied that the person understands — a. that he or she is not under arrest; and b. that he or she does not have to accompany the officer concerned; and c. that if he or she accompanies the officer concerned, he or she is free to leave at any time unless he or she is then under arrest. 2. Subsection (1) does not apply to or in respect of a person to whom a requirement has been made by a police officer under the Road Traffic Act 1974 Section 66.
docsus|inve-inte-susp-ANNEXURE-FOUR: Section 118 Criminal Investigation Act 2006 118. Admission in serious case inadmissible unless recorded 1. In this section — admission means an admission made by a suspect to a police officer or a CCC officer, whether the admission is by spoken words or by acts or otherwise; adult means a person who has reached 18 years of age; child means a person who is under 18 years of age; reasonable excuse, for the absence of an audiovisual recording of an admission, includes — a) the admission was made when it was not practicable to make an audiovisual recording of it; b) equipment to make an audiovisual recording of the admission could not be obtained while it was reasonable to detain the suspect; c) the suspect did not consent to an audiovisual recording being made of the admission; d) the equipment used to make an audiovisual recording of the admission malfunctioned. 2. This section applies in respect of a suspect who is — a) a child charged with an indictable offence, irrespective of whether, if an adult were charged with it, it could be dealt with by a court of summary jurisdiction; or b) an adult charged with an indictable offence that cannot be dealt with by a court of summary jurisdiction. 3. On the trial of the suspect for the offence, evidence of any admission by the suspect is not admissible unless — a) the evidence is an audiovisual recording of the admission; or b) in the absence of an audiovisual recording of the admission — i. the prosecution proves, on the balance of probabilities, that there is a reasonable excuse for the absence; or ii. the court decides otherwise under Section 155. 4. Subsection (3) does not apply to an admission by a person made before there were reasonable grounds to suspect that he or she had committed the offence.
docsus|inve-inte-susp-ANNEXURE-FIVE: Section 137 & 138 Criminal Investigation Act 2006 137. Arrested people, rights of 1. In this section — officer means a police officer, a public officer, or any person who holds an office with power to arrest people. 2. This section applies to a person who has been arrested by an officer, no matter under what authority or written law. 3. The arrested person is entitled — a) to any necessary medical treatment; and b) to a reasonable degree of privacy from the mass media; and c) to a reasonable opportunity to communicate or to attempt to communicate with a relative or friend to inform that person of his or her whereabouts; and d) if he or she is for any reason unable to understand or communicate in spoken English sufficiently, to be assisted in doing so by an interpreter or other qualified person. 138. Arrested suspects, rights of 1. In this section — arrested suspect means a person who is under arrest having been arrested — a) under Section 128, under an arrest warrant, or under another written law, on suspicion of having committed an offence; or b) under the Criminal Investigation (Extra-territorial Offences) Act 1987; officer means a police officer, a public officer, or any person who holds an office with power to arrest people. 2. In addition to the rights in Section 137 an arrested suspect is entitled — a) to be informed of the offence for which he or she has been arrested and any other offences that he or she is suspected of having committed; b) to be cautioned before being interviewed as a suspect; c) to a reasonable opportunity to communicate or to attempt to communicate with a legal practitioner; d) if he or she is for any reason unable to understand or communicate in spoken English sufficiently, not to be interviewed until the services of an interpreter or other qualified person are available. 3. The officer in charge of the investigation must, as soon as practicable after the arrest of an arrested suspect — a) inform the suspect of his or her rights under Section 137(3)(c) and subsection (2)(c); and b) afford the suspect his or her other rights under Section 137 and subsection (2). 4. An officer may refuse an arrested suspect his or her right to communicate or to attempt to communicate with a person if the officer reasonably suspects that the communication would result in — a) an accomplice taking steps to avoid being charged; or b) evidence being concealed, disturbed or fabricated; or c) a person’s safety being endangered. [Section 138 amended by No. 21 of 2008 Section 656(8).]
docsus|inve-inte-susp-INFORMATION-FOR-PO: Section 29 Criminal Code (WA) Fact Sheet: Criminal Responsibility of Children (doli incapax)
docsus|inve-inte-susp-LEGALLY-PRIVILEGED: This factsheet is intended for the internal use of the Western Australia Police Force only and is confidential and privileged. It must not be copied and/or provided externally without consulting Legal Services. Scope This factsheet addresses the age of criminal responsibility under section 29 of the Criminal Code (WA) (Code), the presumption of doli incapax (latin, meaning incapable of crime) and how this presumption can be rebutted. This factsheet provides information and examples of various ways for Investigating Officers (IOs) to rebut the presumption. Summary It is presumed that a child between the ages of 10 and 14 cannot be criminally responsible. However, this presumption can be rebutted if the Prosecution leads admissible evidence to persuade the court that the child had the capacity to know that their acts/omissions were morally wrong by the standards of a reasonable adult. Further, evidence led by the Prosecution must be unequivocal and unambiguous. The rebuttal of the presumption should be considered an element of the offence during the investigative stage and form part of the Evidence Matrix. Section 29 of the Code states: ‘A person under the age of 10 years is not criminally responsible for any act or omission. A person under the age of 14 years is not criminally responsible for an act or omission, unless it is proved that at the time of doing the act or making the omission he had capacity to know that he ought not to do the act or make the omission.’ The Prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had the ‘capacity to know’ that they ‘ought not to do’ the act they did.11 The Prosecution does not have to prove that the child actually knew it was seriously wrong to do the act/omission.12 To rebut the presumption of incapacity the Prosecution is required to prove that the child had the capacity to know what they were doing was wrong at the time of the offence, instead of proving that they knew this generally. 11 RYE v State of WA [2021] WASCA 43 [44]. 12 Ibid. Seriously wrong or just naughty? The requirement for the Prosecution to establish ‘capacity to know’ exists to prevent merely naughty children from being convicted of crimes and protect them from the subsequent consequences of convictions. The Prosecution is to establish that the child knows their act is not just ‘naughty’ for which they would be punished at home or school, but rather something that is ‘seriously wrong’ which requires punishment by a Court.3 Rebutting the presumption IO's may use the following indicators to rebut the presumption with the following: • Electronic Record of Interview (EROI); • Home background and school life; • The ‘more obviously heinous’ the offence, the easier to rebut the presumption; • Circumstances surrounding the offence which can prove capacity; • Evidence of normality; • Previous record; • Statements by the child to police; or 3 KNL v State of WA [2023] WASCA 72[76]. • Statement made by the child during or after the offence.13 EROI EROI evidence is the most preferable form of evidence as it comes directly from the child and refers directly to the child’s appreciation of the act. A child must be cautioned and afforded their rights under the Criminal Investigation Act 2006 prior to being questioned in relation to their capacity in connection with a suspected offence. IOs need to avoid leading questions and yes/no answers. A child should be encouraged to provide reasons for their answers and explore the dimension of moral reasoning. There is a 3-Stage general approach in EROIs to cover capacity. The case of R v El (2009) QCA 177 sets out a line of hypothetical questioning which can be used in EROI’s to prove capacity. Stage 1 – involves family level questions in order to establish the child knows right or wrong in a moral sense. IO’s may choose the use the following questions (or similar) as a guideline: • If you get into trouble at home – if you bully your little sister/brother and yell at them. Is that the right thing or wrong thing? Why? What would your mum/dad do? • If you don’t clean your room and make your room messy. Is that right or wrong? Why? What would your mum/dad do? 13 Thomas, Croft ‘Prosecuting Child Offenders: Factors Relevant to Rebutting the Presumption of Doli Incapax’ (2018) 40(3) Sydney Law Review 339. Stage 2 – involves asking school level questions to determine that the child knows right or wrong in a moral sense at a higher level. IOs may choose the use the following questions (or similar) as a guideline: • If you get into trouble in school – so if you do something naughty at school like push/hit your classmate for no reason. Is that right or wrong? Why? What would your teacher do? Stage 3 – involves real world questions to determine if the child knows what is lawful and unlawful. IO’s may choose the use the following questions (or similar) as a guideline: • Do you know what is stealing / stealing a motor vehicle / robbery / burglary? Is it right or wrong to steal other people’s things? • Is it right or wrong to break into someone’s home? Why? Would Police be involved? • What will be the punishment or consequence if Police get involved? If the Prosecution can successfully establish all 3 stages of questioning – they have the evidence to prove the child not only has the capacity to know what is right or wrong, but also know what is lawful and unlawful – this can help to establish the burden of proof, beyond reasonable doubt. If an EROI is not sufficient to prove capacity, consider whether the forms of evidence listed below are sufficient to meet the requirements. Home background and school life The home and school background that a child experiences has a significant effect on the child’s ability understand the wrongfulness of their behaviour. In these environments children learn what is right and wrong, what is acceptable and unacceptable. IO’s can obtain statements from a teacher, social worker or a family member who know the child well and can give good evidence of capacity. When statements are obtained from the above individuals, it is important to cover whether when they told the child of a wrongdoing, did the child acknowledge this? Even a child with low literacy/numeracy skills or a child who is unengaged at school has the capacity to understand a wrongdoing. In RP v The Queen14, the High Court held that a child accused has the requisite understanding that performing sexual acts on his younger sibling was ‘seriously wrong’ due to observing his brother’s distress. This finding does not mean that it can be assumed that the infliction of hurt and distress means that a child accused understands that an action is seriously wrong in a direct sense, however it may point to a requisite understanding. The ‘more obviously heinous’ the crime, the easier to rebut It was held on appeal by the House of Lords in C (A Minor) v DPP (1996) AC 1, 33 that the ‘more obviously heinous’ the offence, the easier it is to rebut the presumption. Courts must be satisfied that the act was so evidently wrong that every child should know the 14 [2016] HCA 53 [35]. wrongfulness of the act and therefore there should be no, or little need for further evidence to establish capacity. For example, some acts such as causing damage or mischief that has turned into vandalism can be more easily aligned with naughtiness. Whereas acts of dishonesty such as stealing is more likely to be understood as seriously wrong. However, the presumption cannot be rebutted merely as an inference from doing the act/omission, no matter how obviously wrong the act/omission may be. Therefore, IOs must seek other evidence to prove capacity remembering the burden of proof. Circumstances surrounding act proving capacity The established circumstances which support a finding that the child understood the wrongfulness of their actions are: • evidence of careful planning of the crime, particularly sophisticated or devious methods of carrying out the act – for example – whether a child had a tool on them to assist them to steal an object can establish pre-meditation of the crime; • assertion of a false alibi; • making effort to conceal the act or divert blame; or • running away from police – running away can be proof of an appreciation that an act was seriously wrong, however children may run away from police because they think they have done something naughty or because they are afraid of the police – therefore it is important to ascertain the context of running away. Inferences drawn in from the circumstances surrounding the act alone need to be placed in the context of other evidence about the child’s mental capacity. The best approach is to obtain further forms of evidence to confirm any conclusion to be drawn from the evidence available. Evidence of normality For some offences, it may be argued that it was inevitable that every child of normal intelligence (between the ages of 10-14) would be expected to have the capacity to know that the act is so obviously wrong and they should not behave in that way.15 However, this expectation does not mean that the Prosecution can simply disregard the presumption and not lead any evidence. The expectation of a child to have the capacity to understand that certain acts are wrong doesn’t affect the existence of the presumption of doli incapax. It only affects the strength of the evidence likely to be necessary to rebut it.16 To prove that a child is a normal and ordinary child, IOs can obtain: • evidence from the child’s parents/guardians concerning their performance at school or behaviour generally. 15 R v LAH [2016] QCA 82 [50]. 16 R v B [1997] QCA 486 (Pincus JA). • evidence from school teachers and school reports – evidence establishing that a child is ‘normal’ can come from statements from teachers and school reports but can also include an analysis of their handwriting. • an expert report or call an expert witness (psychiatrist or psychologist) to give evidence on the child’s developmental state. This is possible but may not always be necessary. Previous record Australian Courts appear to be more open to receiving evidence of a previous finding of guilt by a child.17 It has been held that it is admissible to establish capacity, even though it is not allowed under similar circumstances for an adult offender. This evidence is seen to be acceptable only for the purpose of ascertaining whether the child knew the act was wrong and not to establish the commission of the crime. IO’s need to be aware that previous convictions say little for certain offences. For example, a conviction for assault does not show that the child understands the wrongfulness of forgery. The exceptions that IO’s need to be aware of are: • Section 22(4) of the Young Offenders Act 1994 (WA) states that where “a caution is given any admission made by the person cautioned at or about the time the caution is given is not admissible in civil or other proceedings as evidence of any matter to which the caution refers.” • An acceptance of responsibility under a court referred juvenile justice diversion cannot be used in evidence against the child. Statements by the child to the police The presumption has been rebutted where there has been an admission by the child to police that they knew the wrongfulness of the act.18 Such an admission refers directly to a child’s appreciation of the act. It not drawn from a general analysis of the personality and behaviour of the child or generalised expectations of children. However, the use of statements by children must be approached with caution. It may be found that the child knew the consequences of the act, but did not have an appreciation that the act was seriously wrong. The possibility must be considered that a child may not appreciate the wrongfulness of the act at the time of commission, but came to the realisation it was seriously wrong as a direct result of being questioned by the police or other adults. At this point the usefulness of statements made at a much later date is doubtful. Statement by child during or after offence Statements made during the commission of the offence can point to a child’s capacity. The language used by the child must be examined closely. The WA Supreme Court in R v JA19 found that the language used by the child offender to induce the child’s victim to comply with the child offender’s demands revealed that the child 17 R v GW [2015] NSWDC 52 [17]-[22]; R v F; Ex parte A-G (Qld) [1998] QCA 97. 18 JM (a minor) v Runeckles (1984) 79 Cr App R 255. 19 [2007] ACTSC 51 [83]; KNL v State of WA [2023] WASCA 72 [127]. offender was acting out of a fantasy, rather than knowing they were engaging in serious criminal activity. Utterances made to others, not in the context of police questioning, but after the commission of the offence can be a useful form of evidence. Particularly, if the child was boasting to others about the commission of the offence, as this can make clear that they had the capacity to understand the wrongfulness of the act. These statements may be more reliable as they are not made in direct response to questioning by a person in a position of authority. Therefore, a child is less likely to be led to give an answer. Nevertheless, there is a danger that such statements can amount to boasting to peers but does not truly reflect an understanding of the wrongfulness of the act. Conclusion There is no set formula for evidence sufficient to rebut the presumption, it will depend on the circumstances of each case. The best approach for IOs is to collect as much evidence as possible, to assess whether the Prosecution can prove capacity beyond reasonable doubt. The more indicators that are assessed by IOs, the clearer the picture is of a child’s capacity to commit a crime. Approached this way, the presumption of doli incapax provides appropriate protection for children. It allows a child to be prosecuted when the Prosecution adduces evidence that the child understood the act to be seriously wrong as opposed to mischievous or naughty. Where such evidence is not forthcoming, the child must not be prosecuted.
docswp|introduction: INTRODUCTION This manual contains the overarching principles relating to the execution of search warrants by the WA Police Force. Any police officer can execute a search warrant, whether it was applied for by them or another officer1. Every member in charge of a warrant and every member involved in a warrant is individually responsible for their actions. This manual is an informing document that provides guidance for members in charge of a search warrant, supervisors and staff at all stages of development who seek to learn about search warrants. Reference material relating to WA Police Force search warrants is located in the following areas: • Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA) (CIA) s.41-45. • Misuse of Drugs Act 1981 (WA) - (MDA) s.24. • Firearms Act 1973 (WA) - (FA) s. 26. • Weapons Act 1999 (WA) – (W/Act) s.14. • Police Manual SZ-01.03 Search Warrants. • Body Worn Camera (BWC) SOPs 8.2 Use of BWC During Search Warrants. This document principally refers to the procedures required to comply with the CIA. Where specific legislation relates to MDA, FA or W/Act warrants, reference is made to the different procedures and relevant statute. Although many similarities exist when executing all types of warrants, members must know the legislative differences that apply in the relevant acts. Warrant templates can be located: • The WA Police Force CIA Forms intranet page, located here. • The Investigative Standards intranet page under the heading, Search Warrants. • Relevant legislation. CONSIDERATIONS PRIOR TO EXECUTING A SEARCH WARRANT
docswp|obtaining-the-warrant: Obtaining the Warrant Application for search warrants must meet legal requirements for the valid issue of the warrant. The Search Warrant Drafting Guide provides instructions that align with the legal requirements. For approval relating to warrants for unoccupied premises and conditions for an independent person, refer to the unoccupied premises section, within this document. 1 s.43(5) CIAFor approval relating to planned covert execution under the provisions of the MDA refer to undisclosed search warrants within this document.
docswp|planning-and-responsibilities: Planning and Responsibilities Operational Order In every case where members execute a search warrant, the member in charge shall ensure that an investigative operational order is prepared. The order will contain: • A risk assessment of the premises and occupants. • A statement of the roles and responsibilities for the: ▪ Member-in-charge of search ▪ Interviewing officer ▪ Physical material officer ▪ Video camera operator ▪ Searching officer ▪ Security officer • A record of the briefing provided by the member in charge of the warrant or senior investigating officer. Member in Charge of Search The member in charge of the search will ensure: • The warrant is reviewed for correctness and is signed by a Justice of the Peace (JP). • They are in possession of the warrant at the time of execution, unless the warrant is obtained by remote communication. • All members of the search warrant have reviewed the operational order, are aware of their responsibilities and are aware of potential risks. Physical Material Officer The physical material officer will ensure a forensic exhibits kit2is provided at each warrant. Video Camera Officer The video camera operator will ensure an approved electronic device used to audio-visually record the planned search warrant is charged and in working order. Minimum Number of Officers Six officers is the recommended minimum to conduct a safe, efficient and effective search.3 2 Refer to Forensic exhibit handling and packaging guidelines. 3 This does not preclude an officer in charge of a search from deploying fewer officers; for example, when executing a low risk search warrant to seize CCTV footage etc. The member in charge of the warrant will continually assess the risk, ensuring sufficient staff are provided to mitigate the risk.
docswp|planned-time-of-execution: Planned Time of Execution The warrant is to be executed at a time appropriate to the legislation. Under s.43(6) CIA, a search warrant is to be executed between 6:00am and 9:00pm, unless the officer executing it reasonably suspects that if it were, the safety of any person, including the officer, may be endangered or the effectiveness of the proposed search may be jeopardised. Under s.24(1) MDA, a search warrant can be executed at any time, however it is recommended all search warrants are executed between 6:00am and 9:00pm unless for the reasons above. ENTRY PROCEDURE The execution of all search warrants and searches will be audio visually recorded4. All members are to ensure searches are conducted in a thorough and professional manner and the integrity of the search is maintained at all times. In general, search warrants may be executed by: • Knocking and announcing. Planned lower risk warrant where it is planned to approach the target place, and seek occupiers consent to enter by knocking on the door and talking to an occupant5. • Tactical forced entry. Planned higher risk warrant where rapid tactical entry is reasonably believed to be necessary, and occupiers rights are given to the occupant after an initial security search of the target place is complete. The policy for tactical forced entry is located at FR-01.08 Forced Entry to Premises. A third type of warrant, a covert entry warrant is discussed later in this manual.
docswp|entry-bwc: Body Worn Cameras - Entry BWCs are to be turned on and recording prior to entering a target place6, until after occupier’s rights7 are given and the target place is secured. After police enter and secure the target place, the member in charge of the search will coordinate the turning on of the audiovisual recording device and switching BWC to buffering mode.8 4 s.45(2) CIA and Police Manual SZ-01.03.2. 5 s.31 CIA 6 SOP 8.2 Use of BWC in Search Warrants 7 S.31 CIA 8 SOP 8.2 Use of BWC in Search Warrants
docswp|entry-occupiers-rights: Occupier’s Rights s.31(2) CIA CIA occupier’s rights are an essential consideration of any warrant. The officer in charge must consider the requirements of the legislation under which the warrant was issued. For example: • ‘Occupier’s Rights’, s.31 CIA are to be provided to all occupants in CIA search warrants. Rights will generally be given before entry unless the member in charge of the search reasonably suspects that to do so will endanger any person, including the officer, or jeopardise the purpose of the proposed entry and or the effectiveness of any search of the place9. • In MDA Warrants there is no legislative requirement to provide occupiers rights found at s.31 CIA. It is recommended that where practicable, the same rights outlined in s.31 CIA are given to occupiers where an MDA warrant is executed. This recommendation does not apply to MDA warrants where covert entry is made. The decision and rationale to provide or not to provide occupier’s rights rests with the member in charge of the MDA warrant.
docswp|entry-knock-and-announce: Knock and Announce Entry BWC is to remain activated until occupier’s consent is obtained and the premises is secured10. Officers will11: • Identify themselves to the occupier. If in plain clothes, produce police identification. • Inform the occupier that it is intended to enter the place. • If the place is to be entered under a search warrant, give the occupier a copy of the warrant. • If the place is to be entered under some other statutory authority, inform the occupier of the reason, and the statutory authority, for the entry • Give the occupier an opportunity to give informed consent to the place being entered. Occupier’s consent only extends to allowing police to enter the premises. The CIA search warrant gives police the power to both enter and search the premises. Regardless of occupier’s consent, police will execute the search warrant.
docswp|entry-use-of-force: Use of Force If entry is refused, reasonable force may be used to gain entry12.
docswp|entry-security: Security Once entry is made, secure the target premises and assemble those present in a suitable area. Safety and security of police, suspects, witnesses and members of the public is to be a primary consideration at all times. 9 s.31(2) CIA 10 SOP 8.2 Use of BWC in Search Warrants 11 s.31 CIA 12 s.16 CIA
docswp|entry-tactical-forced: Tactical Forced Entry A tactical forced entry may be necessary when an officer reasonably suspects that if they were to enter in compliance with s.31(2) CIA (Occupier's Rights), such entry will endanger any person and or may jeopardise the proposed entry or effectiveness of the search. Where an officer intends to conduct a tactical entry, they must be justified in doing so. For all search warrants, officers are encouraged to consult their supervisor or an independent senior officer prior to executing a tactical entry. A “Forced Entry Risk Assessment” form must be completed where it is known a forced entry will occur. Before consideration of forced entry is made to premises, the member in charge shall ensure: • The correct target address is confirmed. • The necessity to use force is considered. • The amount of planned force is reasonable. • The vulnerabilities and age (especially children) of all occupants is considered. • All members are dressed in contemporary personal protective equipment as prescribed by Operational Safety & Tactics Training Unit (OSTTU). • Damage is kept to the minimum required to affect the entry. • The necessity for Senior Officer Orders for adjacent premises is considered. In cases of high risk, officers may request the Tactical Response Group (TRG) to assist in the entry. Refer to High Risk Entry and SS-7.2.2 TRG Call-Out and Deployment Procedures. • Upon arrival operate BWC in accordance with BWC SOP 8.2. • Enter the premises in accordance with Method of Entry procedures available from OSTTU, using approved method of entry equipment available on RMIS. • Once entry is made, secure the premises and assemble those present in a suitable area. • As soon as possible after police have entered and secured the target place, provide occupiers rights to the occupant. ARRESTED SUSPECT AND ACCOMPANYING PERSONS RIGHTS After entry is made and the target place is secured, occupier’s rights are given and occupants are secured in a suitable area, the legal status of all occupants must now be considered. Obtain personal details from each occupant and decide their status.
docswp|arrested-suspect-rights: Arrested Suspect – s.128 CIA Ensure the Arrested Suspect is provided their CIA s.137 and s.138 rights. Record the time and place the rights were given. Ensure the arrested suspect is cautioned and has a full understanding of each section of the police caution and their rights.
docswp|accompanying-person-rights: Accompanying Person – s.28 CIA People accompanying officers to be informed of their rights – s.28 CIA. This applies to all search warrants regardless of the legislative power. Record the time and place the rights were given. Ensure the accompanying person is cautioned and has a full understanding of each section of the police caution and their rights. If there is any uncertainty whether the accompanying person may become a suspect, provide all of their rights at s.137 and s.138 CIA, with the exception of telling them they are under arrest. This will safeguard any subsequent confessional evidence.
docswp|detain-and-search-persons-present: Detain and Search Persons Present s.43(8)(b)(ii) CIA authorises an officer to conduct a basic or strip search of a person who is in the target place when the warrant is being executed for the target thing. s.24(1) MDA specifies that any person present can be detained and searched during a search warrant, using such force as necessary. If necessary to search an occupant of the premises the video camera is to remain on during the course of the body search. In the case of a strip search the camera is to be pointed away so as not to visually record the body search. The officer conducting the search is to provide an audio commentary of what is occurring so as to allow the audio to be recorded. If any items of interest are located they may be photographed in the position they are found on the body. 13 SEARCHING PROCEDURES AND GUIDELINES
docswp|searching-mic: Member in Charge of Search The member in charge of the warrant is expected to have sufficient experience or supervision to lead a search warrant. The member in charge of the search should oversee the search and not involve themselves in physically searching the target place. They will exercise overarching control of the search, delegating tasks where appropriate and ensuring the lawful collection of evidence. The member in charge of the search will take all necessary steps to minimise the risk of harm to all people present. After entry the member in charge will consider: • Inviting the occupant to declare any prohibited or dangerous items, or those items prescribed in the warrant. • Ensure where possible that the occupant views the search14. 13 s.65(4) CIA 14 s.31 CIA• If the occupant is not present or declines to accompany police, the member in charge of the search will stop the search and comply with the process outlined in the unoccupied premises and independent person section. • Do not place the occupant or independent person in a position where they must observe police search more than one room (or area) at a time15. • Conduct a systematic (room to room, one room at a time) search of the target place. • Where a room or area is locked, or access is made difficult because the occupant has secured a room, request the occupier’s assistance to access the room (keys, code) before using force to gain entry. • Prior to stopping an audiovisual recording ensure a time and date is announced. • When an audiovisual recording is recommenced, ensure a time and date is announced, and provide a short commentary on what occurred whilst the camera was switched off. Invite the occupier to comment. Remind the occupier of their rights and the police caution. • Sign and date the execution of the search warrant on both the occupiers copy and the original. • File the endorsed warrant with the application on the CRIME file. • Ensure you retain possession of the original warrant so it can be produced in court if required. • Ensure that forced entry repairs or damage to any property is dealt with appropriately.
docswp|searching-audiovisual-recording: Audiovisual Recording of Search Warrants s.45(2) CIA states that if reasonably practicable, an audiovisual recording must be made of the execution of the search warrant. Officers will audio visually record all search warrants, unless exceptional circumstances exist. Where a recording is not made, officers must be prepared to justify the absence of that recording to the court. Generally, it is not practical to video record an entire search warrant, therefore intermittent recording should be adopted. Where intermittent video recording is utilised, on each occasion recording is re-commenced, the officer in charge will give a short commentary on what occurred whilst the camera was switched off and invite the occupier to comment. Where a search is not audio visually recorded, the officer entering the execution of a search warrant on IMS will briefly outline the reasons for the absence of any audiovisual recording of the search in the free form text area of that system. All members participating in the search are to be mindful of inappropriate language or comments made during search warrants. Poor language, comments or behaviour by police can unnecessarily prejudice the admissibility of evidence. Officers are to take great care and remain professional at all times. All search warrant recordings are copied to disc and placed onto IMS property as a Search Warrant Recording, including search warrants recorded on One Force mobile phones. This 15 If there is more than one occupant, this would not preclude arranging for sufficient staff to conduct more than one room search simultaneously, observed by individual occupants. disc is sent to the Video Interview Suspects Unit as a master for storage, in the same manner as a suspect interview16.
docswp|searching-video-camera-operator: Video Camera Operator The nominated camera operator will record the warrant. The camera operator's duties include: • Ensuring the audiovisual equipment is functional before deploying to the search location. • Ensuring the time and date showing on the video camera is correct. • Ensuring the time and date is recorded. If the time and date is not correct or is not functioning, consider changing the video camera. If this is not a viable option explanation of the incorrect date and time should be stated on the recording at the earliest opportunity. • The camera operator will record the current condition of the target premises by conducting a pan of the premises before searching commences, and at the conclusion of the search, in company with the occupier and security officer. These procedures outline the minimum requirement for the recording of searches. Where deemed appropriate and practicable, additional parts of the search or the entire search may be recorded. The audiovisual recording of the search shall include: • An introduction of all members assisting during the search warrant to the occupier. • A commentary of all occupier’s rights and introductions provided. • The police caution and check of understanding. • The production of the search warrant. • A request to declare any prohibited items such as prohibited drugs. • A request to declare any dangerous items secured or unsecured that pose a potential occupational health and safety risk to occupiers or police involved such as hypodermic syringes. • A request to declare any weapons secured or unsecured such as firearms. • A request to declare any large sums of money or items of value such as jewellery or gold. • A request to declare any items particularised in the warrant. • An explanation to the occupier of the procedure to be adopted during the search. • Any items located during the search, which are to be seized. • The counting of any money located during the search. • The sealing into Security Movement Envelopes (SMEs) of any money, items of value or drugs. • Any comment made by the occupier relating to items located during the search. • The process where the physical material officer identifies and shows the items seized to the occupant, providing them with an Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log (Copy), including the return of any items to the occupier. • Any damage caused during the entry to the premises or the subsequent search. • Any complaint made by the occupier. • While recording, if a recording is interrupted for any technical reason (battery, fault), upon resumption of recording an explanation is to be recorded. 16 Police Manual SZ-01.03 and ER-01.01
docswp|searching-officer: Searching Officer Great care is to be taken when searching for evidence. Experience has shown when searches are rushed or not systematic, evidence can be overlooked. Personal safety is to be exercised when searching and members should take every opportunity to use appropriate personal protective equipment. Searchers will employ a mindset that considers the protection of all forensic evidence in accordance with forensic exhibit handling procedures. If physical material is located and a video recording device is not on, if the officer is wearing BWC they should immediately activate their BWC, back capturing the previous 30 seconds, including the moments when they discovered the item. The member in charge of the search will coordinate the switching of BWC to buffering mode once the video camera operator recommences recording.
docswp|searching-pmo: Physical Material Officer • Direct the video camera operator to video or photograph seized property in situ prior to moving the item. This is particularly important if the weight or nature of an exhibit is likely to make production in court impractical. • Packaging of seized items will comply with Forensic Exhibit Handling and Packaging Guidelines. • Every item seized is to be recorded on the Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log, noting the location of where it was found. Where possible use the description of the room as specified by the occupant in the initial pan of the premises. • Where no property or drugs are seized the Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log shall be endorsed “Nil Seized”. • Ensure that seized money, items of value or drugs are recorded. • SMEs are used to secure seized money, items of value or drugs. • At completion of the search, the physical material officer will: ▪ Review the Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log. ▪ Identify items located during the search which are to be seized. ▪ Return any items not to be seized to the occupier. • A copy of the Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log is to be provided to the occupier. Invite the occupier to sign the log as a true and accurate record of the items seized.
docswp|securing-premises-after-search: Securing the Premises After the Search At the completion of a search, where no person is to remain at the premises, the member in charge shall ensure the premises are left secure. If the premises are unable to be secured, arrangements shall be made for a contractor to attend and affect the necessary repairs prior to police departure. Where damage has occurred effecting entry or during the search, such damage shall be photographed or audio visually recorded.
docswp|forced-entry-repairs: Forced Entry Repairs At the completion of a forced entry search, where no person remains at the premises, the member in charge of the search must ensure that the premises are left secured. The following procedure will assist officers when securing premises: • If the premises are unable to be secured, arrangements should be made in the metropolitan area through the District Operational Supervisor (DOS) or in Regional WA (RWA), the relevant District Office for a service provider to attend and affect the necessary repairs prior to police departure. • Upon receiving the following information, DOS or RWA equivalent will arrange for the service provider to attend. The requesting officer will provide: ▪ Name, rank and regimental number. ▪ Station/unit. ▪ CAD incident job number. ▪ Nature of the damage. • Payment by WA Police for forced entry repairs shall only be authorised where: ▪ Temporary repairs are required in order to secure premises. ▪ Unnecessary or unreasonable force was used to gain entry. ▪ No offender or evidence was found and no charges result from the search. ▪ An innocent third party is financially disadvantaged as result of damage caused on entry or during the search. PROPERTY GENERALLY
docswp|seizure-of-property: Seizure of Property • All seized property is to be recorded onto an Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log. • The original Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log (white copy) is to be retained with the CRIME file/brief, the duplicate copy (pink) is to be given to the occupier and the triplicate copy (yellow) is to remain in the book for Good Governance. • Property details recorded on the Property Receipt/Physical Material Log are to be entered onto IMS as soon as practicable17. • All seized property shall be correctly labelled and include the IMS number and IMS barcode. • All seized property shall be stored securely and correctly prior to transfer to the Exhibit Management Unit (EMU). Seized property is not to be stored in desks, filing cabinets or the general office areas of your working area. • All movements of seized property shall be recorded on IMS. • At the completion of the court hearing, all seized property shall be dealt with in accordance with the court order. • All receipts for the return of property shall be filed with the officer-in-charge. 17 PR-1.1.3 Recording and Entering Property in Police Possession
docswp|seizure-of-drugs: Seizure of Drugs • All drug seizures shall be sealed in SMEs or a vented bag and secured with a security tag. • The securing of the prohibited drugs into the SME is to be audio visually recorded. • The SME shall be marked with a description of the seizure and the signature and regimental number of the exhibit officer and correctly recorded onto the Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log. • The occupier or an independent person shall be requested to sign the SME. • Subsequent weighing of drugs at a police station will be done in accordance PR-01.02. All seized drug (and paraphernalia) property shall be correctly entered on IMS. ‘Clan Lab’ responses are located in the Clandestine Drug Laboratories section of this document.
docswp|seizure-of-money: Seizure of Money • Audio visually record and photograph in situ any money located. • In the presence of the occupier, count the money and place it into an SME. • If the volume of money is substantial, package the money into an SME and use the ‘money serial recorder’ located at the Drug & Firearm Squad. • If the volume of money presents a handling problem, additional envelopes shall be obtained or a commissioned officer may arrange for another secure method of transport. • The occupier shall be requested to read aloud the envelope numbers. • All seized money shall be correctly entered onto IMS. • All SMEs containing money shall be stored in a safe or another secure location designated for that purpose. • All seized money shall be banked in the Police Suspense Account unless it is required for some legitimate forensic purpose. The receipt shall be filed with the officer-in-charge. • Prior to banking any seized money or dealing with it in any way it shall be photographed in a manner to record type, denominations and consideration should be given to recording individual serial numbers. • When any money is banked, IMS shall be updated.
docswp|opening-smes: Opening Security Movement Envelopes (SMEs) • When SMEs containing drugs or other items seized are opened for any reason, the whole procedure shall be audiovisually recorded in the presence of two officers. • The SME shall be cut open at the bottom, so that the seals are left intact. The member cutting open the SME shall endorse the time, date and location of opening the envelope and sign it. A witnessing member shall also sign the envelope. The reason for the opening the envelope should be audio visually recorded. • Upon re-sealing the contents into a new SME, the opened envelope shall also be sealed in the new envelope in a manner so that the serial number is clearly visible. • Both officers are to sign the new SME.• Record the number of the second SME on the item record within the IMS, together with the date and time of opening, the reasons for opening, and the names of the authorising supervisor, the officer opening the SME, and the witnessing officer. • Audiovisual recordings used to record the opening of SMEs and the processing of physical material shall be stored at the recording office/station. • For further information, refer PR-01.02.1.1. OTHER SEARCH WARRANT CONSIDERATIONS
docswp|unoccupied-premises-independent-p: Unoccupied Premises and Independent Person Considerations When entry is affected and the premises are found to be unoccupied, the member in charge shall: • Immediately withdraw all staff from the premises. • Advise a commissioned officer who may nominate an independent person (sergeant or above) to be present during the search. • Ensure no search is conducted until the arrival the nominated independent person. • No approval shall be granted unless it is shown that it is necessary to conduct the search in the absence of the occupier or owner. • Where the premises are unoccupied the member in charge must leave the following in a prominent position: ▪ A notice stating the officer’s official details and that the place has been entered. ▪ If entry was gained by search warrant, a copy of that warrant. ▪ A copy of the Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log. ▪ If entry was obtained by the use of another statutory authority, the reason, and the statutory authority, for the entry. Independent Person Guide Independent persons are appointed to ensure and observe compliance with search warrant procedures. They are to ensure impartiality. They will not make operational decisions or have specific involvement in the search or seizure. Should a situation arise that requires intervention from the independent person, they shall bring this matter to the attention of the member in charge of the search. Independent persons must: • Be nominated by an authorising commissioned officer. • Hold the rank of sergeant or above (includes a member officially acting in that position or rank). • Where practicable, not be from the case officer’s organisational unit. • Ensure the search warrant is sighted and correct. • Be present throughout the entirety of the search. • Monitor compliance and ensure the search is conducted in a professional manner.Upon arrival, and at commencement of their role, the following statements should be used as a guide, and is to be audiovisually recorded before recommencement of the search: “I am a nominated Supervisor, from [business unit], appointed by [Name of Authorised Commissioned Officer], as the independent person for the execution of this search warrant. My role is to monitor compliance with regards to Legislation, WA Police Force Policy and Standard Operating Procedures. I have sighted the search warrant which has been approved by a Justice of the Peace, and will ensure any physical material seized during the execution of the search warrant is recorded onto an Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log.”
docswp|other-investigative-interviewing: Investigative Interviewing All interviews, whether recorded at the search warrant location, police station or other location are to be conducted in accordance with the WA Police Force investigative interviewing model. A preliminary interview of a suspect at the location does not negate the need for an audiovisual record of interview upon return to the police station.
docswp|other-clan-labs: Clandestine Drug Laboratories In the event of discovery of a clandestine drug laboratory, the member in charge of the warrant will cease all activity and withdraw all personnel to a safe distance18. Initial action includes: • All Police personnel and suspects depart the site and remain at a safe distance in case of fire, explosion and/or chemical contamination. • No ignition sources are taken into the site. • The scene will be preserved and Drug & Firearm Squad are to be notified immediately. • No attempt is made to shut down any on-going chemical process or remove a power source to the premises without the advice of a Forensic Chemist. • Where possible provide the Forensic Chemist with a description of the laboratory set-up, including whether the laboratory appears to be operating at the time. • Do not re-enter a laboratory for any of the above purposes. • After the Forensic Chemist has rendered the site safe, photographs and audiovisual recordings of the scene may be made, where appropriate.
docswp|other-proceeds-of-crime: Proceeds of Crime Considerations The Proceeds of Crime Squad (PCS) conduct investigations into matters pursuant to the Criminal Property Confiscation Act 2000 (WA) (CPCA) and may commence confiscation proceedings where: 18 CR-07.05 Clandestine Drug Laboratories• A person has been charged with a serious drug offence and has the potential to be declared a drug trafficker pursuant to s.32A(1) of the MDA. • A person has property directly or indirectly used in or derived from a confiscable offence (i.e. punishable by two or more years imprisonment) including being in possession of large amounts of unexplained cash. • The apparent wealth of individuals or criminal organisations cannot be adequately explained. PCS can assist during the planning stage of a search warrant by compiling or providing financial / asset profiles of the target and should be contacted in all instances at the earliest opportunity if there is any potential the target person may be charged with: • A serious drug offence likely to render them a drug trafficker under the MDA; or • In any other Act, where property is crime used (i.e. a house used for cannabis cultivation or a vehicle used in a sex assault) or crime derived (i.e. paid for with the proceeds of crime). If, during a search warrant, large amounts of cash or assets reasonably suspected to be crime used or crime derived are located, contact PCS. PCS will provide advice and may attend the location. The powers under the CPCA are “here and now” powers and must be executed while the target is in possession of the property, during the search warrant. Charging the suspect prior to PCS conducting a compulsive interview will likely prevent a compulsive interview being conducted and result in potential loss of evidence. For more information on PCS guidelines refer to the Proceeds of Crime Investigation Manual located on the Investigative Standards intranet site.
docswp|other-high-risk-terrorist: High Risk/Terrorist Incident The deployment of TRG for all other incidents should fall within the roles and responsibilities of the TRG as outlined in SS-07.02 and will be at the discretion of the OIC TRG or the Police Tactical Group (PTG) Commander. All personnel requesting the TRG for planned operations shall submit a Tasking Request Form and Investigators Target Summary as located in the WAPOL Intranet under the SID T&CG Process. Requests must be approved at District Inspector or Divisional Inspector level prior to being forwarded to the TRG. The TRG will respond to all incidents classified high-risk as determined by the provisions of SS-07.02 Tactical Response Group (TRG).
docswp|other-undisclosed-mda: Undisclosed Search Warrant – s.24 Misuse of Drugs Act s.24 MDA Undisclosed Search Warrants should only be considered under exceptional circumstances and where operationally necessary. Where it is necessary to conduct a planned search covertly on a premises pursuant to s.24 MDA, the Drug & Firearm Squad is to be notified.
docswp|other-detection-dogs: Use of Detection Dogs • The Canine Section is able to provide the following specialist resources: ▪ Narcotic detection dogs (NDDs) for the searching of premises, vehicles, vessels etc. ▪ Passive alert drug detection dogs (PADs) for the mass screening of passengers on public transport, patrons in entertainment districts and at special events. • Where practical, a Tasking Request Form (TRF) is to be submitted to the Canine Operations Deployment Supervisor. Dynamic requests will be accepted by telephone or by Station Mail email. • The Canine Section can be contacted 24/7 via 9370 7368 and all out of hours requests must be submitted to SOCC. • Under no circumstances are WA Police Force members to approach other agencies such as the Australian Border Force (ABF), Australian Federal Police (AFP) or the Department of Justice (DOJ). Protocols have been established between these external agencies to utilise all resources appropriately. These agencies will only consider the use of their dog resources at the request of the OIC Canine Section. • After entry has been effected, and before searching commences, the dog handler shall instruct the occupier of the procedure to be adopted during the search. • Before searching commences the handler and the dog may examine the premises in the presence of the occupier or independent person and a nominated member of the search team. • Any positive reaction shown by the dog shall be brought to the attention of the member in charge of the search before the actual search is conducted. • The area or object of positive reaction shall be searched in the presence of the occupier or an independent person in accordance with these procedures.
docswp|cia-ancillary-powers: CIA Search Warrant Ancillary Powers A search warrant issued under the provisions of the CIA also authorises the officer executing it to exercise any or all of the ancillary powers found at s.44 CIA. Officers are required to be fully conversant with the powers conferred under a search warrant within the relevant Act prior to executing the search warrant.
