I currently hold an Advanced Diploma in Public Safety (Police Investigations).
docwsr|sp-marginal-notes: MARGINAL NOTES Throughout many statements there will be a need to include marginal notes to notify the prosecutor of the introduction of an exhibit or the identification of the accused. Exhibit If the witness makes reference to any 'real evidence' in their statement the word 'EXHIBIT' is to be placed on the left-hand side of the page opposite the place or places in the statement where a reference is made to the exhibit. This does not only occur when the witness is tendering an exhibit but should occur at any point the first time an exhibit is referred to, for each individual item. This will prompt the prosecutor to show the exhibit to the witness and have it either tendered or marked for identification. Marked for identification is a process where an exhibit is shown to witnesses involved in the trial and the witness indicates that is the exhibit to which they are referring, the exhibit is not tendered in evidence until the chain of custody is complete and the witness that had last possession of the exhibit gives evidence. The statement should include a detailed description of the exhibit including, if applicable serial numbers and model numbers. A minimal description of the exhibit could lead to confusion or legal challenge during the trial. The most detailed description a witness can give for every exhibit is important. The statement must also address what interaction the witness had with the exhibit, such as how the witness came to be in possession of the exhibit and what was done with it at the completion of dealing with it. This information will assist in constructing the chain of custody. A document that is to be tendered through a witness should be explained by reference to the personal experience of the witness. The relevance of the document needs to be explained to ensure that's it importance is conveyed to the jury. Identify Insert 'IDENTIFY' on the left-hand side of the page opposite the place or places in the statement where a reference is made to an offender that has been categorically identified by name. This does not include when a witness that sees an offender and the offender is subsequently identified. In a police statement the 'IDENTIFY' marginal note should again be when the offender is categorically identified by name and not by description. This does not include the first instance the police associate the name with an offence. Once the suspect has been identified by name in the police statement he/she is to then be referred to as the accused thereafter.

docwsr|sp-statement-conclusion: Statement Conclusion The conclusion of the statement should outline the final piece of information that witness has to offer the court. A witness statement may include the circumstances that caused the witness to supply a statement i.e. I then attend at the Wanneroo Police Station and gave this statement. A Police Statement in which the investigator prefers a charge may need to state the final dealings they had with the accused i.e. At the conclusion of the interview, the present charge was preferred and whether the accused was arrested, charged and bailed, or was charged by summons. It is not necessary to state that the accused was lodged at the lock-up. Investigators should be cautious as to how they conclude the statement and avoid terminology such as 'the accused refused to participate in a video record of interview'. This type of statement has been deemed to be prejudicial to the accused as the jury may infer some guilt as to why an innocent person would refuse to talk to police.
docwsr|sp-declarations: DECLARATIONS ON WITNESS STATEMENTS The Criminal Procedures Act mandates that a declaration must be placed at the end of every statement that is made by a person who is twelve years of age or over. The Criminal Procedures Act outlines that the declaration complies with the act if it contains words to the effect of: This statement is true to the best of my knowledge and belief. I have made this statement knowing that, if it is tendered in evidence, I will be guilty of a crime if I have wilfully included in the statement anything that I know to be false or that I do not believe is true. To comply with this schedule of the act the WA Police have adopted the following as the standard jurat to be contained within a witness statement: This statement is true to the best of my knowledge and belief. I have made this statement knowing that, if it is tendered in evidence, I will be guilty of a crime if I have wilfully included in the statement anything that I know to be false or that I do not believe is true. Where the maker of a statement is a child of less than twelve years of age then the following declaration should be contained within the statement: I know what the truth is and what lies are. Everything I have said today is the truth and is what happened to me. I have not told any lies. I know it is wrong to tell lies. Where the statement is made by a person who cannot read, it should be read aloud to them by a person whom the witness nominates (not the interviewing officer), before they sign it. It is accompanied by a declaration of the person who read the statement to the effect that it was so read. The following declaration should be included after the official declaration: I declare that this statement was read aloud to me whereupon I agree that its contents are true and correct and that the statement is in compliance with the above mentioned declaration. It is the accepted practice in Western Australia that the declaration forms the last paragraph of the statement. Ensure the declaration is presented in its entirety and not as a split paragraph. Immediately following the declaration the maker of the statement and a witness must adopt the statement.
docwsr|sp-adoption: Adoption Adoption is crucial for the legal admissibility of the statement and care in this area will ensure that the witness statement is not the subject of legal argument during the court case. The investigator must ensure that the person making the statement adopts it as being a true and accurate record of events. Prior to the statement being adopted, the witness must be given the opportunity to read the statement and cause any amendment they wish to be made. Every witness statement must be adopted by the maker and witnessed: • For handwritten and typed hard copy statements the maker must sign and date the bottom of every page observed by the witness, who then signs and dates the bottom of every page. On the last page further witness details such as where, time, date and who need to be completed. • An electronic statement via the Statement Generator App can be completed with electronic signatures appearing on the last page only. Both comply with the Schedule 3 provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act 2004. The difference in adoption is due to the electronic statement initial pages are subject to PDF and cannot be changed whereas the hand written or typed hard copy initial pages can be amended and substituted if unsigned. The final page of all statements must also include the suburb the statement was taken. If the witnessing officer's name is not clearly evident from their signature, then they should legibly write their name along with their signature. It is most important that the officer taking a witness statement can identify the statement in court using their signature as a verification method. It is important an officer can demonstrate the witness was fully aware of the requirement to tell the truth during the interview and that the statement accurately represents their knowledge of the event(s). The correct adoption procedure and inclusion of the jurat are key methods of demonstrating the above. Police statements are adopted in the same way as other witness statements and reinforce that a police witness is treated equally before the law. At the completion of the statement the witness should be offered a copy of the statement as a matter of courtesy and professional conduct. All copies of the statement including handwritten statements shall reflect the above mentioned adoption process.

docwsr|sp-handwritten: Handwritten Statements It is acceptable to take a handwritten statement from a witness. Handwritten statements are commonly taken at scenes of incidents. One common example is a victim's statement at the scene of an assault. The statement must be clearly legible. Handwritten statements must comply with the Criminal Procedures Act to be considered acceptable in court and compliance with the details stated earlier in this subject will accomplish that. Do not use any type of correction fluid on handwritten statements, any mistakes or changes should have a neat line ruled through mistakes and initialed by the witness. Where circumstances are such that only a handwritten statement can be obtained it should be retyped at the earliest possible opportunity and signed by the witness, remembering at all times retain the original handwritten statement, as it will form part of your case file and will be subject to disclosure. All handwritten statements must also be copied onto the statement template for inclusion on a trial brief. The typed copy is to be attached to the handwritten statement. Even though there is no legal need to have the typed copy signed by the witness, as a matter of professionalism it is recommended that investigators get all handwritten statements typed and signed, this will enhance the professionalism of the brief. The typed copy must be an exact copy of the handwritten statement in every detail, including any grammatical errors. The details of the countersigning officer are also to be endorsed on the last page of the typed copy. It is of utmost importance that witness statements are obtained as soon after the event as possible, the human memory is fallible and erodes with the passage of time. The timely taking of a statement will aid in capturing the best evidence.
docwsr|sp-versions: Versions of Statements Planning an interview and gathering all the evidence a witness has to offer at the earliest opportunity is imperative. Poorly written first statements which omit salient points will necessitate additional work to capture the required information. This will then inevitably become a point of cross examination as to why such important information was not included in the first statement. Where a witness makes a new statement, the original statement is to be attached to the rear of the new one. In most cases the contents of the first statement is generally repeated in the new one. However, by attaching the original statement to the new statement, the original statement date is still effective in relation to that evidence. Where a witness is re-interviewed to clarify a matter, or provide further information relating to an event, the second statement should commence with: 'Further to my statement made on (Date) I wish to provide further information that was not detailed in my previous statement'. The statement should then detail what the additional information (observation) is and also explain why this was not included in the original statement. Where additional information is supplied by a witness i.e. something they have done post the arrest, such as convey an item to Pathwest, then the additional or addendum statement is to be attached to the rear of the original statement. Every subsequent or new statement is to be signed and dated when it was done, do not back date to the original statement date. Where the subsequent or new statement conflicts with the original, the reason why should be stated by the witness in the subsequent or new statement. Witnesses are also on occasion known to change their recollection of events, there can be a number of reasons for this to occur, but there is always the possibility that a witness may become hostile.
docwsr|sp-hostile-witnesses: Hostile Witnesses The Evidence Act deals with hostile witnesses and stipulates that the party producing the witness is not be allowed to impeach his credit by general evidence of bad character, but may contradict him by other evidence, if in the opinion of the judge he is hostile to the party producing him. The Judge may allow a previous inconsistent statement to be produced to the witness under certain circumstances. A detailed statement taken at the time of the event can assist the prosecution in discrediting a hostile witness.
docwsr|sp-negative-statements: Negative Witness Statements Occasions arise from time to time where the police interview a person who claims to have seen and heard nothing, knows nothing and will say nothing about an event , even though other evidence at hand may indicate otherwise. There are various reasons why the witness may adopt this attitude. It may be because the witness entertains prejudices against the police generally, or it may be because the witness is aligned towards the suspect under investigation. A statement should be obtained from the witness under these circumstances to the effect that the witness saw nothing, heard nothing, etc. Statements of this nature are referred to as 'negative statements', however this is a police term only and a negative statement should only ever be referred to as a statement. In the event that the witness is called by defence counsel at a subsequent hearing, and offers evidence which is favourable to the accused, or in any way inconsistent with the previous statements made to the police investigator, the negative statement can be used by the prosecution to negate the credibility of the witness. The taking of negative statements can be an integral part of the investigative process and should be considered at all times when a witness claims to know nothing but evidence suggests otherwise.
docwsr|sp-summary: SUMMARY Investigators should remember that witnesses are individuals, each may entertain a specific point of view, perception, bias or prejudice and from time to time a witness may even try to influence the course of an investigation by providing misleading information. Some witnesses may be cooperative and others reluctant, some may be experts in a given field and others not, some witnesses may require special considerations to be afforded them either by law, established procedure or by circumstance e.g.: children, victims of sexual assaults, people who cannot speak or understand the English language. The compilation of a witness statement is a crucial part of any investigation as it commences building a picture of what has happened. Attention to detail and thoroughness is essential when obtaining a witness statement, they should not be seen as mundane or insignificant, and a detailed witness statement has the potential to direct the investigation to its desired conclusion. Witness statements also form an important part of the court process and a quality witness statement will reflect the professionalism of the investigator taking it and the professionalism of the investigation as a whole.

Page 11 Child Exploitation Material (CEM) Investigation and Prosecution Guide V1.3 OVERVIEW This document serves as a guide to the Western Australia Police Force (WA Police) Prosecuting Division, the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP) and the Commonwealth Director for Public Prosecutions (CDPP) in regards to the way WA Police will prepare evidentiary material for court use where Child Exploitation Material (CEM) is located and analysed. This has been implemented following the decision by WA Police to align with other Australian Law Enforcement Agencies by adopting the Australian Child Abuse Categorisation Schema or ACACS in place of the current 9-point ANVIL (otherwise known as Oliver) Scale. The ACACS is modelled on the INTERPOL Baseline for classifying CEM. This decision has been made after consideration of a report prepared by the Queensland Sentencing Advisory Council (QSAC)1 and acknowledges the clear occupational health and safety risk to investigators and members of the criminal justice system posed by the onerous current requirements to view, classify and then provide detailed descriptions of CEM for prosecution purposes. The change to the ACACS will allow a transition from the current time consuming manual CEM examination processes to using purpose designed computer programs to automatically analyse seized images which are then compared with known international CEM databases. In addition, WA Police have introduced limits to the quantity of images and video files that will be classified (per device) in order to limit the exposure of staff (wherever possible) to harmful CEM examinations. The new standardised CEM evidence package will provide information as to the nature of the suspect’s involvement in the alleged offending and the potential risk they pose to the public. It will also provide a condensed examination report regarding the nature of the seized CEM however, it will not break down the seized images into distinct detailed categories, as has previously been the case. This evidence package will include: • Court Brief • Field Triage Reports • Arresting Officers Statement – including a CEM Analysis Report and Annexure • Classification of CEM report (ACACS – 4 category scale)
rcav|cem-inve-and-COURT-BRIEF: The Court Brief will summarise the investigation and include: • How the suspect came to the attention of police • How police identified the suspect • The nature of the relationship between the suspect and the victim (if known) 1 Classification of child exploitation material for sentencing purposes: Final report Published by Queensland Sentencing Advisory Council, July 2017. Child Exploitation Material (CEM) Investigation and Prosecution Guide V1.3 • The nature of the suspect’s involvement in the matter (including overt acts) • Any admissions made by the suspect • Any other charges laid (such as contact sexual offending) • Details of any co-accused (where possible) • The nature of any ongoing investigations (where possible to disclose) • The conduct of any search warrants • Details of any relevant internet searches made by the suspect • Details of any relevant file paths, file types or file names linked to seized CEM • The level of compliance of the suspect in relation to the provision of passwords or compliance with Data Access Orders. • Results of any field triage of CEM • General investigator observations (where relevant) regarding any CEM located • Any use of anonymising or encryption software (designed to prevent detection) • Perceived risk to the community (or themselves) • Detailed bail submissions • Any other relevant information or supporting documents for the prosecutor This is intended to provide prosecutors with sufficient accurate information to properly progress matters through the court system, with a particular emphasis on describing the nature and context of the alleged offending, any risk to the community and relevant bail submissions.
rcav|cem-inve-and-FIELD-TRIAGE-REPORT: Wherever possible, an automated triage process will be undertaken in the field to examine electronic devices and any interaction with these devices by the suspect. The Field Triage Reports will provide supporting evidence when an investigator has observed that CEM exists on a seized device. The types of reports will be as follows: • Advanced Digital Forensics (ADF Triage) This system is primarily used for the automated field examination of electronic storage devices to identify CEM on devices that are powered ‘on’ or capable of accepting power (such as USB’s or external hard drives). There is also some capacity to remove and examine devices that are not powered, such as internal hard drives, although this cannot be undertaken in the field. Further in-depth examination of any information extracted can be undertaken in an examination suite, however this may cause some delays for prosecutors (especially around first court appearances) as this information may not yet be available. At the completion of the analysis, the investigator can provide an electronic .html report that is provided on USB, disc or by email. These reports are provided as a separate document for each device. Typically, the ADF Triage system will be used in the field to simply identify the presence of CEM on devices, which are then seized for further analysis. This reduces the unnecessary seizure of devices where no CEM is detected. This also means that the Field Triage Report is typically completed sometime after the initial examination, as opposed to during the initial search in the field. Child Exploitation Material (CEM) Investigation and Prosecution Guide V1.3 • Universal Forensic Extraction Device (UFED) otherwise known as Cellebrite This is typically used for mobile phones or tablet/hand held devices and can also be used for some portable storage devices. At the completion of the analysis, the investigator can provide an electronic .html report that is provided on USB, disc or by email. These reports are provided as a separate document for each device. Utilising these forensic tools, investigators can ‘tag’ and comment on any relevant material to substantiate charges (i.e. the possession of CEM) and can be used to quickly identify CEM and suspicious items located in the field. It also enables located devices to be excluded from further time-consuming examinations when no CEM is located. Each report can provide the investigator with the opportunity to summarised electronic .html report of any offending located in the field. Field Triage Reports can be provided to prosecutors at a much earlier stage of the investigation to substantiate a prima-facie case. Exactly when a Field Triage Report can be provided depends on: • Whether the software was successful in the field • Whether additional (more detailed) examination is necessary (or possible) • Whether a specialist examination or expert assistance is required (for whatever reason) • The number and type of devices seized Field Triage Reports will contain CEM, so they can only be made available for viewing by defence counsel (and not served as part of disclosure).
rcav|cem-inve-and-ANNEXURE-AND-CAVEAT-TO: This document is provided to demonstrate the presumptive presence of CEM on each exhibit identified during the field triage process. It is not intended as a forensic evidentiary report, but an evidentiary guide to help understand the evidence identified during the investigation. This will be provided with the Investigating Officer’s (IO’s) statement and will form part of the brief of evidence.
rcav|cem-inve-and-INVESTIGATOR-STATEMENT: The primary investigating officer’s statement will include information concerning the investigation and how the defendant came to police attention (as per the Court Brief section above). It will address the investigative actions of the police including references to the in- field triage of devices and references to any CEM. It will address the level of co-operation by the accused through the provision (or not) of passwords and compliance with any Data Access Orders. To assist with any sentencing considerations, the statement will include information to address the: • Nature of the Offending – including a general summary of the evidence, any relationship between the suspect and the victim, the circumstances surrounding the possession, distribution, accessing or producing of CEM as well as the alleged source of the CEM and whether it has been transmitted or shared with others. Child Exploitation Material (CEM) Investigation and Prosecution Guide V1.3 • Nature of the CEM – providing an overall description of the nature and content of the material including (but not limited to) the estimated number of unique victims and their apparent age, the general type (or types) of activity depicted and the extent of cruelty or physical harm. A detailed description of a small number of representative images or videos is required, but it is not necessary to provide a fully detailed or itemised description of all seized CEM. The Investigator Statement must follow the template attached as Appendix 2. CLASSIFICATION of CEM REPORT The “Griffeye” software also used by WA Police is a categorisation tool used by law enforcement agencies around the world and offers a purpose-built forensic tool that allows categorisation under the new (4 tier) ACACS. The ACACS has been adopted across Australia to ensure consistency, to allow integration with international law enforcement CEM databases and to better assist with victim identification. Two of the four categorises are illegal in WA.
rcav|cem-inve-and-INTERPRETATION-GUIDE: Category Child Exploitation Material Guide (CEM) Category Description 1 CEM – Baseline • Must depict a pre-pubescent child (or one very early into puberty) who is perceived to be under 13 years of age. • Must be a “real child”. • Must show sexual activity involving a child (including having a child watch sexual activity) or; la • Have a clear focus on either the genitals or anus. g e llI 2 CEM – Any Other CEM Any other CEM that meets the Western Australian or Australian Commonwealth legislative definitions of CEM that is not category 1, including; • Animated or written CEM • Children over the age of 13 years, including Commonwealth Child Abuse Material (CAM) with children under the age of 18 years. 3 Related Investigative Non-illegal related child material which is; Interest – Not Illegal but • Believed to form part of a series containing CEM Connected • Of investigative interest la g e L 4 Ignorable Anything else, including; • Adult pornography • Windows artefacts • Files unable to be determined At the completion of the analysis, the investigator can provide an electronic .html report that is provided on USB, disc or by email. One significant advantage is that Griffeye reports can be provided as one combined document for all seized devices. A user guide (such as above) will be included in the brief of evidence to assist with the interpretation of any CEM examination reports. Child Exploitation Material (CEM) Investigation and Prosecution Guide V1.3 PROCESS Seized devices subject to a Field Triage Report can still be subject to further specialist examination by qualified technical experts in a manner and location endorsed by WA Police Technology Crime Services (TCS). Typically, devices will be uploaded using Griffeye software, which will allow investigators to commence a more in-depth analysis to identify additional evidence including; locating CEM files possessed and accessed, timeframes of offending, frequency and method of CEM distribution and frequency of access to material, as well as the task of classifying the material seized. Whether any seized device examinations are limited to Field Triage Reports or further in-depth expert analysis will be determined on a case by case basis. When evidence has been classified by the investigator against the (4 tier) ACACS, a categorisation report is requested by the investigator from TCS. Once that report is made available, the investigator can provide the report which sets out the total number of images or videos in each category that have been categorised. This report can then be provided to the prosecuting authority. Importantly, the TCS Report is not a witness statement or evidentiary certificate, but is an aid to the court (particularly for sentencing) to assist with providing an understanding of the CEM possessed or created by the accused person.
rcav|cem-inve-and-LIMITING-ANALYSIS: Unless there is: • Clear concerns for contact offending • A reasonable possibility of victim identification • An opportunity to use automated CEM categorisation software WA Police have adopted a policy of only manually categorising 1000 CEM images or 50 CEM video files per device. The per device policy will ensure there is sufficient grounds to obtain an order for destruction for each of the seized devices where CEM is located. Where this policy is followed, police will only allege the quantity of CEM that is categorised, as under current legislative provisions, the court cannot draw an inference regarding how many additional CEM images may exist within material that has not been classified. This policy has been implemented to ensure WA Police comply with their Occupational Safety and Health obligations by limiting harmful CEM exposure to staff both internally and across the broader criminal justice system. As detailed earlier in this document, the brief of evidence should provide a detailed account of all relevant factors in the case to assist the court for sentencing purposes. TIMEFRAMES Examinations of devices will be prioritised based on levels of perceived community risk. Timeframes to complete examinations may also vary considerably, and often depend on a number of factors which include the volume of information to be reviewed, the number of distinct devices seized, any technical difficulties which may be associated with encryption or password protections and the availability of suitably qualified staff to attend to each of the specific tasks. Should Commonwealth “accessing” charges be preferred, this will also require a longer examination time due to extra processes that are required for these types of offences. All inquiries as to timeframes should be directed to the Investigating Officer in Child Exploitation Material (CEM) Investigation and Prosecution Guide V1.3 the first instance, or otherwise through his or her supervisor. Inquiries are not to be made directly to TCS. Field Triage Reports may, or may not be available for inclusion on the prosecution brief at first appearance. This will depend on a variety of factors, including the complexity of the matter. This report (once available) may however be disclosed by the investigating officer at any time, or when requested. More detailed examination reports are available for disclosure once received, however timelines for these reports are subject to many variables, making a defined time period impossible to comply with. In regards to full trial reports being provided by TCS, unless there are significant extenuating circumstances associated with a particular matter, these reports will only be prepared when a trial date is set. These reports will be provided in sufficient time to ensure WA Police comply with disclosure obligations under the Criminal Procedure Act. CONTACT All queries in relation to the adoption of these guidelines should be directed to the Detective Senior Supervisor – Taskforce Odessa, through the following email address: ChildAbuseSquadSMAIL@police.wa.gov.au Child Exploitation Material (CEM) Investigation and Prosecution Guide V1.3 MEMORANDUM

rcav|talk-poin-chil-SEXUAL-ABUSE: Sexual abuse occurs when a child is exposed to, or involved in, sexual activity that is inappropriate to the child’s age and developmental level. It also includes situations where the child is exploited or where the child has been bribed, threatened, or coerced. Such as:- • letting a child watch or read pornography; • allowing a child to watch sexual acts; • fondling the child’s genitals; • having oral sex with a child; • vaginal or anal penetration; • using the internet to find a child for sexual exploitation. Possible signs of sexual abuse include when a child: • acts in a sexualised way that is inappropriate to his/her age; • has pain, bleeding or swelling in his/her genital area; • starts doing things they have grown out of such as crying a lot, bed wetting or soiling, clinging to caregiver; • has nightmares or sudden unexplained fears ; • has a sexually transmitted infection or is pregnant. If you are a victim of child abuse or paedophilia, or if you have information about someone else being abused, contact police on 131 444. rcl|anun-rule-v-content: Anunga Rules Judgement Delivered By Chief Justice Forster On 30 April, 1979, Mr. Justice FORSTER handed down his reasons for rejecting typewritten records of conversations in the matter of QUEEN v Angus ANUNGA, Sandy AJAX, Clancy AJAX, TJINGUNYA, Nari WHEELER and Frankie Miller JAGAMARA in the Northern Territory Supreme Court in August, 1975. (R v Anunga (1976) 11 ALR 412) Inter alia Mr. Justice FORSTER said: "It seems to me now, however, to be important that the Court should put on record general guidelines for the conduct of Police Officers when interrogating Aboriginal persons. I preface this statement of guidelines by pointing out that Aboriginal people often do not understand English very well and that, even if they do understand the words, they may not understand the concepts which English phrases and sentences express. Even with the use of interpreters this problem is by no means solved. Police and legal English sometimes is not translatable into the Aboriginal language at all and there are no separate Aboriginal words for some simple words like "in", "at", "on", "by", "with", or "over'', these being suffixes added to the word they qualify. Some words may translate literally into Aboriginal language but mean something different. "Did you go into his house?" means to an English-speaking person, "did you go into the building?", but to an Aboriginal it may also mean, "Did you go within the fence surrounding the house?" English concepts of time, number and distance are imperfectly understood if at all by Aboriginal people, many of the more primitive of whom cannot tell the time by a clock. One frequently hears the answer "long time", which depending on the context may be minutes, hours, days, weeks, or years. In case I may be misunderstood, I should also emphasise that I am not expressing the view that Aboriginal people are any less intelligent than white people but simply that their concepts of certain things and the terms in which they are expressed may be wholly different to those of white people. Another matter which needs to be understood is that most Aboriginal people are basically courteous and polite and will answer questions by white people in the way in which they think the questioner wants. Even if they are not courteous and polite there is the same reaction when they are dealing with an authority figure such as a policeman. Indeed their action is probably a combination of natural politeness and their attitude to someone in authority. Some Aboriginal people find the standard caution quite bewildering, even if they understand that they do not have to answer questions, because if they do not have to answer questions, then why are the questions being asked? Guidelines to be Followed when Interviewing Aboriginals Bearing in mind these preliminary observations which are based partly upon my own knowledge and partly by evidence I have heard in numerous cases I lay down the following guidelines. They apply, of course, to persons who are being questioned as suspects. 1. When an Aboriginal person is being interrogated as a suspect, unless he is as fluent in English as the average white man of English descent, an interpreter able to interpret in and from the Aboriginal person's language should be present, and his assistance should be utilised whenever necessary to ensure complete and mutual understanding. 2. When an Aboriginal is being interrogated it is desirable where practicable that a "prisoner's friend" (who may also be the interpreter) be present. The "prisoner's friend', should be someone in whom the Aboriginal has apparent confidence. He may be a mission or settlement superintendent or a member of the staff of one of these institutions who knows and is known to the Aboriginal. He may be a station owner, manager or overseer or an officer from the Department of Aboriginal Affairs. The combinations of persons and situations are variable and the categories of persons I have mentioned are not exclusive. The important thing is that the "prisoner's friend', be someone in whom the Aboriginal has confidence, by whom he will feel supported. 3. Great care should be taken in administering the caution when it is appropriate to do so. It is simply not adequate to administer it in the usual terms and say, "Do you understand that?" or "Do you understand you do not have to answer questions?" Interrogating Police Officers, having explained the caution in simple terms, should ask the Aboriginal to tell them what is meant by the caution, phrase by phrase, and should not proceed with the interrogation until it is clear the Aboriginal has apparent understanding of his right to remain silent. Most experienced police officers in the Territory already do this. The problem of the caution is a difficult one but the presence of a "prisoner's friend" or interpreter and adequate and simple questioning about the caution should go a long way towards solving it. 4. Great care should be taken in formulating questions so that so far as possible the answer which is wanted or expected is not suggested in any way. Anything in the nature of cross-examination should be scrupulously avoided as answers to it have no probative value. It should be borne in mind that it is not only the wording of the question, which may suggest the answer, but also the manner and tone of voice which are used. 5. Even when an apparent frank and free confession has been obtained relating to the commission of an offence, police should continue to investigate the matter in an endeavour to obtain proof of the commission of the offence from other sources. Failure to do this, among other things, led to the rejection of confessional records of interview in the cases of Nari WHEELER and Frank JAGAMARA. 6. Because Aboriginal people are often nervous and ill at ease in the presence of white authority figures like policemen, it is particularly important that they be offered a meal, if they are being interviewed in a Police Station, or in the company of Police or in custody when a meal time arrives. They should always be offered a drink of water. They should be asked if they wish to use the lavatory if they are in the company of Police or under arrest. 7. It is particularly important that Aboriginal and other people are not interrogated when they are disabled by illness or drunkenness or tiredness. Admissions so gained will probably be rejected by a Court. Interrogation should not continue for an unreasonably long time. 8. Should an Aboriginal seek legal assistance reasonable steps should be taken to obtain such assistance. If an Aboriginal states he does not wish to answer further questions or any questions the interrogation should not continue. 9. When it is necessary to remove clothing for forensic examination or for the purposes of medical examination, steps must be taken forthwith to supply substitute clothing."

rcl|cc-v-rayn-COMMISSIONER-SLEIGHT: COMMISSIONER SLEIGHT: The accused Mr Rayney is charged with the wilful murder of his wife, Mrs Corryn Veronica Anne Rayney. This decision concerns appeals by the police from orders made by his Honour Magistrate G Calder pertaining to items of property seized by the police from the motor vehicle of Mr Rayney at the time of his arrest and which his Honour ordered be returned to Mr Rayney. The appeals fall into two parts: 1. an appeal against a decision of the magistrate declining to adjudicate on a claim of legal professional privilege by Mr Rayney under the procedure contained in s 151 of the Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA) (the CI Act); and 2. an appeal against an order made by the magistrate pursuant to Criminal and Found Property Disposal Act 2006 (WA) (the C & FPD Act) that items seized by the police at the time of Mr Rayney's arrest be returned to Mr Rayney. The determinative issue in this appeal is whether the magistrate should have declined to make an order to release to Mr Rayney the seized items, notwithstanding: (i) the unchallenged findings by the magistrate that the police who seized the items did not reasonably suspect that the items were things relevant to an offence; and (ii) there was no evidence presented to the magistrate that could establish there were objectively reasonable grounds for suspecting the items were things relevant to an offence. Background On 8 December 2010, Mr Rayney's motor vehicle was intercepted in Perth and Mr Rayney was arrested. On the same day, the police executed a search warrant at Mr Rayney's place of residence. On the day of the arrest, the police seized a number of items which included the following: Item A: two files of documents Item B: an envelope marked with the name Corryn Rayney Item C: a mobile phone Item D: a mobile SIM card Document Name: WASC\SJA\2012WASC0056.doc (SM) Page 5 [2012] WASC 56
rcl|cc-v-rayn-COMMISSIONER-SLEIGHT-2: Item E: a $10 Telstra phonecard Items A, C, D and E were seized from Mr Rayney's motor vehicle. Item B was seized from Mr Rayney's residence, which was being searched pursuant to a search warrant. A claim was made by Mr Rayney that each of the items seized were subject to legal professional privilege. Pursuant to the provisions of s 151(4) of the CI Act, the items seized were delivered into the custody of the Magistrates Court, and the officer in charge of the investigation made an application to the Magistrates Court to decide whether the information contained in the seized items was privileged. Mr Rayney made an application to the court under s 11 of the C & FPD Act for an order that the Commissioner of Police release the seized items and that the items be returned to Mr Rayney. This application was based upon a preliminary issue that the court could not retain custody of the items under s 151 of the CI Act, as the items were not lawfully seized pursuant to the CI Act and therefore s 151 had no application. The magistrate ruled that item B was lawfully seized. In relation to this item there remains the issue of whether the item or any part of the item is privileged, pursuant to s 151 of the CI Act. This issue has been adjourned. In relation to items A, C, D and E, the magistrate found that the items had not been seized in accordance with the provisions of the CI Act and that accordingly s 151 of the CI Act had no application. He ordered, pursuant to the C & FPD Act, the items be returned to Mr Rayney. Jurisdiction issues of the appeal. The first of the appeals relates to the decision of the magistrate that s 151 of the CI Act had no application in relation to items A, C, D and E. Pursuant to s 151(14) and (15) of the CI Act, proceedings under s 151 are a part of the court's criminal jurisdiction and any appeal against a decision pursuant to s 151 lies to the Supreme Court of Western Australia under the Criminal Appeals Act 2004 (WA) (the CA Act). Based upon these provisions, the Commissioner of Police initially lodged an appeal (SJA 1119 of 2011) under the provisions of the CA Act. On 15 December 2011, I made an order that the application for leave to appeal be heard at the time of the appeal. Subsequently, solicitors for the Commissioner of Police formed the view (in my view, correctly) that, as the magistrate had ruled that s 151 had no application, the procedures under the CA Act had Document Name: WASC\SJA\2012WASC0056.doc (SM) Page 6 [2012] WASC 56
rcl|cc-v-rayn-COMMISSIONER-SLEIGHT-3: no application. Accordingly, on the hearing of the appeal a draft application under s 36 of the Magistrates Court Act 2004 (WA) (the MC Act) was presented and, without objection from the respondent, the appeal proceeded on the basis that the appeal be heard on its merits either under the CA Act or the MC Act. Since the hearing of the appeal, an application under s 36 of the MC Act has been filed. In the matter of Rayney v AW [2009] WASCA 203, McLure JA, as she then was, considered the construction of s 36 of the MC Act. The power to review only arises on one of the grounds set out in s 36(1)(a), (b) or (c) of the MC Act. Under s 36(1)(a), a ground of review is the failure of the court officer to do any act the officer was under a duty to do: Rayney v AW [34]. In this matter, the appellant complains the magistrate failed to consider an application under s 151 of the CI Act when he was under a duty to determine the application. Accordingly, the appeal comes under the powers of review under s 36 of the MC Act. The second appeal is against the magistrate's decision made pursuant to the C & FPD Act. A decision of a magistrate under the C & FPD Act is within the civil jurisdiction of the Magistrates Court and, accordingly, any appeal is to the District Court. The appeal comes for hearing before the Supreme Court as result of an order by his Honour Judge McCann that the hearing of the appeal be remitted to the Supreme Court under s 77 of the District Court of Western Australia Act 1969 (WA). Legislative Framework The legislative framework regarding the issues raised in this appeal concern provisions in the CI Act and the C & FPD Act for seizing and dealing with seized property as part of criminal investigations. The CI Act and C & FPD Act were part of a package of reform legislation to replace the provisions of the Police Act 1892 (WA) and to implement recommendations of the Law Reform Commission of Western Australia's 'Report on Police Act Offences'. During the second reading speech of the Criminal Investigation Bill, it was stated the legislation represented 'a balance between the needs of law enforcement officers to effectively investigate crime and the rights of individuals'. There was particular emphasis upon the rights of the individual. The bill was said to 'introduce significant controls on these powers (the powers of the police) to ensure that individual's human rights are protected and to minimise the opportunity for the misuse of the powers'. rcl|cc-v-rayn-COMMISSIONER-SLEIGHT-4: (a) Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA) The CI Act was not meant to be a complete codification of the law in relation to criminal investigation. The legislation specifically retains common law powers insofar as they are not inconsistent with the legislation. Section 7 of the CI Act provides as follows: (1) Subject to this section, a police officer has the powers, duties and responsibilities that a constable has under the common law. (2) If this Act confers a power, duty or responsibility on a police officer that the officer also has by reason of subsection (1), the power must be exercised and the duty or responsibility must be performed in accordance with this Act. (3) If there is an inconsistency between a provision of this Act and a power, duty or responsibility that a police officer has by reason of subsection (1), the provision of this Act prevails. The seizure of the items by the police from the vehicle of Mr Rayney at the time of his arrest was purportedly pursuant to s 133 of the CI Act. Section 133(7) provides: (7) If an officer doing a search under subsection (2) or (3) finds a thing relevant to an offence, whether the serious offence or another offence, the officer - (a) may, subject to section 146, seize the thing; and (b) whether or not the officer seizes the thing, may do a forensic examination on it. (emphasis added) The meaning of the words 'thing relevant to an offence' is contained in s 5 of the CI Act, which provides as follows: (1) For the purposes of this Act, a thing is a thing relevant to an offence if it is reasonably suspected that - (a) the thing has been, is being, or is intended to be used for the purpose of committing an offence; (b) the thing has been obtained by the commission of an offence; (c) an offence has been, is being, or may be committed in respect of the thing; (d) the thing is or may afford - Document Name: WASC\SJA\2012WASC0056.doc (SM) Page 8 [2012] WASC 56
rcl|cc-v-rayn-COMMISSIONER-SLEIGHT-5: (i) evidence relevant to proving the commission of an offence or who committed an offence; or (ii) evidence that tends to rebut an alibi. (2) For the purposes of this Act, a thing relevant to an offence may be material or non-material, animate (other than human) or inanimate. Section 146 relevantly provides: If this Act provides that an officer may seize a thing that is relevant to an offence the officer may do so only if the officer reasonably suspects one or more of the following - … (e) that it is necessary to seize the thing for one or more of the following purposes - (i) to prevent it from being concealed, disturbed or lost; (ii) to preserve its evidentiary value; (iii) to do a forensic examination on it; (iv) to prevent it from being used in the commission of another offence. Section 4 of the CI Act provides the meaning of the words 'reasonably suspects' as follows: For the purposes of this Act, a person reasonably suspects something at a relevant time if he or she personally has grounds at the time for suspecting the thing and those grounds (even if they are subsequently found to be false or non-existent), when judged objectively, are reasonable. The net effect of these provisions (relevant to this case) is that for a seizure to be authorised, under the circumstances where items are found in a motor vehicle at the time of the arrest of a person, it must fulfil the following conditions: 1. The item must be a 'thing relevant to an offence' (s 133(7)); that is, it is reasonably suspected that the thing is or may afford: (i) evidence relevant to proving the commission of an offence or who committed the offence, or (ii) evidence that tends to rebut an alibi (s 5). rcl|cc-v-rayn-COMMISSIONER-SLEIGHT-6: 2. The officer who seizes the item must reasonably suspect that it is necessary to seize the item for one or more of the following purposes: (i) to prevent it from being concealed, disturbed or lost; (ii) to preserve its evidentiary value; (iii) to do a forensic examination on it; or (iv) to prevent it from being used in the commission of another offence (s 146). 3. There must be grounds for reasonably suspecting the thing and the grounds must be, when judged objectively, reasonable (s 4). The test of whether an item is 'a thing relevant to an offence' and whether the officer 'reasonably suspected', the matters referred to in s 146, involve both a subjective and objective assessment of the items to be seized. Section 151 of the CI Act sets out a procedure to be followed if an item seized is the subject of a claim of privilege. This section relevantly provides as follows: (1) In this section - court means the Magistrates Court; privileged means privileged because of either or both - (a) legal professional privilege; (b) public interest privilege. (2) If a record is seized or, under an order to produce a business record issued under section 53, a business record is produced and - (a) a person entitled to possession of the record claims that all or some of the information in it is privileged; or (b) the officer seizing the record or to whom it is produced reasonably suspects that all or some of the information in it is privileged, the record must be dealt with in accordance with this section. (3) The record must be secured in a manner - Document Name: WASC\SJA\2012WASC0056.doc (SM) Page 10 [2012] WASC 56
rcl|cc-v-rayn-COMMISSIONER-SLEIGHT-7: (a) that prevents it from being concealed, disturbed or lost; and (b) that preserves its evidentiary value; and (c) that prevents access to the information in it by any person who would not be entitled to access to the information if it were privileged. (4) The officer in charge of the investigation must apply to the court to decide whether the information is privileged and must deliver the record into the custody of the court. … (9) If the court decides that all of the information is not privileged, the court must make the record available to be collected by the applicant. (10) If the court decides that all of the information is privileged, the court must make the record available to be collected by the person from whom it was seized. (11) If the court decides that some of the information is privileged, the court must make orders to enable the applicant to have access to the information in the record that is not privileged. (12) If - (a) the court decides that all or some of the information is privileged; and (b) the applicant has applied to be permitted to do a forensic examination on the record, the court must make orders that enable the forensic examination to be done on the record and to ensure that any information in it that is privileged remains privileged. Section 152 provides that if under the CI Act 'anything is seized', the C & FPD Act applies to and in relation to it. Section 154 to s 155 of the CI Act deal with the admissibility of items seized contrary to the Act. Section 154 provides: 154. Evidence obtained improperly (1) In this section - authorisation includes a warrant and an order. Document Name: WASC\SJA\2012WASC0056.doc (SM) Page 11 [2012] WASC 56
rcl|cc-v-rayn-COMMISSIONER-SLEIGHT-8: (2) If in the purported exercise of a power conferred by this Act or by an authorisation issued or purportedly issued under this Act - (a) a thing relevant to an offence is seized or obtained; and (b) a requirement of this Act in relation to exercising the power or issuing the authorisation, including a requirement that arises before or after the exercise of the power or the issue of the authorisation, is contravened, any evidence derived from the thing referred to in paragraph (a) or from the exercise of the power is not admissible in any criminal proceedings against a person in a court unless - (c) the person does not object to the admission of the evidence; or (d) the court decides otherwise under section 155; or (e) if the power exercised was exercised in relation to a protected person (as that term is defined in section 73), the court is of the opinion that the contravention arose out of a mistaken but reasonable belief as to whether the person was a protected person. (b) Criminal and Found Property Disposal Act 2006 (WA) Section 3 of the C & FPD Act defines 'seized property' as meaning: property that has been seized in the course of a criminal investigation other than - (a) any sample taken or seized under the Criminal Investigation Act 2006 or any other written law; and (b) any thing used in obtaining an identifying particular of a person under the Criminal Investigation (Identifying People) Act 2002; A 'criminal investigation' is defined in s 3 as meaning 'an investigation into whether an offence has been committed or into who committed an offence'. The definition makes no reference to the CI Act. Section 9 of the C & FPD Act deals with the authority of the chief officer (who is the Commissioner of Police - see s 3) to retain property. It provides: 9. Authority to retain seized property (1) A chief officer's authority to retain any property that is seized property is subject to any order made under section 13 in relation to the property. (2) A chief officer's authority to retain seized property as seized property ceases if - (a) the property is not property that may be forfeited to the State; (b) the property is property that may be forfeited to the State but a court has refused to order its forfeiture; (c) the property is not the subject of proceedings under the Criminal Property Confiscation Act 2000; Document Name: WASC\SJA\2012WASC0056.doc (SM) Page 13 [2012] WASC 56
rcl|cc-v-rayn-COMMISSIONER-SLEIGHT-10: (d) seizure and retention of the property is not authorised by another written law; and (e) it is no longer necessary for the property to be retained for one or more of these purposes - (i) to do a forensic examination (as that term is defined by the Criminal Investigation Act 2006) on it; (ii) to preserve its evidentiary value; (iii) to prevent it from being used in the commission of an offence. (3) Subject to any order made under section 13, when a chief officer's authority to retain seized property ceases under subsection (2) the property is to be taken for the purposes of this Act - (a) to have ceased to be seized property; and (b) to have become held property, and the chief officer must dispose of it under Part 5. (4) Unless the chief officer releases it to a person entitled to it, the chief officer must not dispose of seized property that has become held property under subsection (3) until at least 2 months have elapsed since it became held property. Section 11 of the C & FPD Act provides: (1) A person may apply to the appropriate court for - (a) an order that the chief officer of a prescribed agency release seized property that is in the officer's possession to the applicant; or (b) an order permitting the applicant to deal with seized property that is in the possession of the chief officer of a prescribed agency. (2) The application must be made in accordance with rules of court and must be served on the chief officer. Section 13 of the C & FPD Act provides that, on an application made under s 11, the appropriate court may make any order it thinks fit. Section 13 (2) relevantly provides: (2) The court must not order that seized property be released to a person unless satisfied that - Document Name: WASC\SJA\2012WASC0056.doc (SM) Page 14 [2012] WASC 56
rcl|cc-v-rayn-COMMISSIONER-SLEIGHT-11: (a) the person is a person entitled to the property; (b) it would be lawful for the person to possess the property; and (c) under section 9 the chief officer's authority to retain the property as seized property has ceased. The magistrate's decision The magistrate delivered a very lengthy and well reasoned written decision. The magistrate made the following critical factual findings: (a) That the police officers, who seized items A, C, D and E at the time of and at the scene of Mr Rayney's arrest, did not at any time prior to or at the time of seizure, reasonably suspect that the items were 'things relevant to an offence' as defined in s 5 of the CI Act [87]. (b) That none of the officers involved in the seizure of the items, reasonably suspected that it was necessary to seize any of the items for the purpose of preventing it from being concealed, disturbed or lost or preserving its evidentiary value or doing a forensic examination on it [87]. (c) That there was no evidence before the court which would enable the court to make an objective assessment of whether it was reasonably suspected that the items were things relevant to the offence [94]. As a consequence of these finding, the magistrate concluded that items A, C, D and E were not seized in accordance with the CI Act. This finding was not challenged on the hearing of these appeals. The magistrate made the following further rulings: (a) Only a seizure made in accordance with all of the relevant provisions of the CI Act can be the subject of an application of a claim of privilege pursuant to s 151 of the CI Act. In view of the finding that the seized items A, C, D and E were not seized in accordance with the CI Act, s 151 had no application. Accordingly the magistrate declined to proceed with consideration of the issue of legal professional privilege and concluded that the court did not have the power to retain custody of the items under s 151 [100]. rcl|cc-v-rayn-COMMISSIONER-SLEIGHT-12: (b) Unless there is some other statutory provision to the contrary, if the seizure of items A, C, D and E were not seizures in accordance with requirements of the CI Act, then the Commissioner of Police was not authorised pursuant to the CI Act to retain the items [101]. (c) The requirements of s 9(2)(a) to s 9(2)(e) of the C & FPD Act must be satisfied conjunctively. Relevantly, the conditions in s 9(2)(d) and s 9(2)(e) must be satisfied before the authority of the police to retain the items has ceased [103]. (d) It is a necessary precondition to the requirement of s 9(2)(e) that, insofar as the seizure purports to have been effected in accordance with the provisions of the CI Act, there must have been compliance with the provisions of that Act relating to the seizure. Alternatively, if there is non-compliance, there must be a non-compliance of such a nature as could properly be said of it that Parliament did not intend that such non-compliance would have the consequence that the seizure was not lawfully made and was therefore invalid under the CI Act. The absence of a stipulated objectively reasonable suspicion is not such an inconsequential non-compliance [103]. (e) The test under s 9(2)(e) of the C & FPD Act of whether it is no longer necessary for the property seized purported, pursuant to the CI Act, to be retained to do a forensic examination or to preserve its evidentiary value is tied to whether the property has the characteristic that it is a thing relevant to an offence as defined in s 5 of the CI Act [103].
