rdc|faq-crim-proc-FALSE-NAMES-ERRORS-ETC: An offender will often give police a false name in the hope of escaping justice. Quite often, this deception is discovered before any charge is laid. However, some accused are charged under the false name and some actually attend court and plead guilty under the false name or submit a written plea in the false name. In cases where the false name used is that of another actual, real, innocent person, the use of the false name can have some very inconvenient consequences for the innocent person if not corrected. The correction, however, is a relatively simple process. Section 179 was specifically included in the Criminal Procedure Act 2004 to address this problem. “179. Errors in court records due to use of wrong or false name (1) If as a result of an accused using a false name, address or date of birth, a record of a court does not record the accused’s correct name, address or date of birth, the court may correct the record and make any ancillary orders needed to give effect to the correction. (2) The powers in subsection (1) may be exercised by the court on its own initiative or on an application by a person who the court is satisfied has a proper interest in the proceedings. (3) Without limiting the power to make ancillary orders, the court may — (a) set aside a conviction or order made by the court; (b) order a new trial; (c) order that records other than the court’s records be corrected.” Prior to the Criminal Procedure Act 2004, an innocent person had to take the remedial action themselves and apply to the court to have the conviction quashed. Section 179 was enacted specifically to overcome this as stated by the Attorney General in the second reading speech: “Tenth, the Criminal Procedure Bill provides for the correction of errors caused by the use of false names. Difficulties have been experienced for many years by courts and police in trying to assist individuals who have convictions recorded against their names for offences they did not commit. These convictions have occurred as a result of other individuals using their names when apprehended, for example, for offences under the Road Traffic Act 1974. The only option available currently is an application by the innocent person to the court to have the matter re-heard and the conviction quashed. The new provision will rectify the current unsatisfactory situation, which requires the affected innocent party to rectify an error that was caused through no fault of their own.”1 When an offender is charged, they become an accused. If the accused gives a false name and a charge is laid and prosecution commenced under that false name, it is still the accused who has been charged, irrespective of the name given. If the false name is that of another, real person that actually exists, it is still the accused that has been charged, not the other person. There is no need to discontinue the charge. 1 MR J.A. McGinty (Fremantle - Attorney General) Criminal Procedure Bill 2004, 2nd Reading Speech, Assembly, 26 August 2004. A problem arises, however, where investigating police, upon finding out the accused has used a false name, charge the accused with new charges such as ‘use false name’ but then again charge the accused with the original charge. It is arguable that the fresh original charge is subject to double jeopardy, especially where a finding has been entered. Perhaps the safest solution for a prosecutor is to apply to the court to correct the original prosecution notice to reflect the correct name and then discontinue the second identical ‘fresh’ charge. However, a prosecutor needs to have both charges before the court to do this. Prosecutors also need to be mindful of the statute of limitation in regards to simple offences. Example - An accused is to be charged with DUI and gives their brother’s name. They are subsequently convicted, fined and disqualified. They get sentenced as a first offender when in actual fact this is their third time and they face a permanent disqualification. It does not come to light until some 12 months later when the brother becomes aware of it. If the charge was to be brought before the court and the conviction overturned and the charge subsequently discontinued, the accused will not be able to be recharged because of the 12 months limitation to commence a prosecution. However, if an application under section179 Criminal Procedure Act 2004 is made, the details of the conviction and disqualification will simply be amended to reflect the accused’s details. The prosecution was commenced within the 12 months limitation; indeed, it was finalised within the 12 months. It is simply the error in the recording of the matter that is being fixed or adjusted. If, as in the above example, the use of a false name has also resulted in an incorrect sentence being handed down originally, then the police prosecutor can invite the court to recall the original sentencing order and resentence correctly. So, in the above case, the court could amend the name and also recall or set aside the sentence and resentence the accused as a subsequent, third time offender. (This is addressed more fully in the module on sentencing.) Section 179(3) also allows the court to set aside the conviction, although, generally, this should not be required. Expand the above to where an accused commits multiple simple offences over a period of time and gives his brother’s name because the brother lives overseas. Again, an application under section 179 should suffice to have the matters corrected. Where an accused is sentenced under a false name and receives a period of disqualification under a road law, they still commit the offence of driving contrary to the disqualification even though the disqualification is under the false name. In 1993, an appeal decision clearly confirmed that. In that case, an offender was charged with driving with a blood alcohol in excess of 0.08% and gave his brother’s name. He attended court, pleaded guilty and was fined and disqualified for three months. It was later found that he had used his brother’s name. He was subsequently caught driving and charged with driving under suspension (under his correct name). The original 0.08 charge and findings had not been reheard or amended in any way. In the appeal decision, Scott J stated - “The more important question is whether the conviction for driving with a blood alcohol in excess of 0.08% was good as against the respondent.”2 He further found that - “…it is clear that by whatever name he was then known, it was the respondent whose motor driver's licence was suspended on 31 March 1993.”3 (Emphasis added.) This decision further enforces why the original charge in the false name should not be discontinued but simply be corrected. If the original conviction is set aside, the disqualification is deemed to have not existed so any alleged breach would consequently cease to exist. When lodging an application under s179 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2004, there is no requirement to serve the accused with a copy and the application can be made in their absence. Criminal Procedure Regulations 2005 “29. Correction of court record, application for (Act s. 179) (1) If an application made under the CPA section 179 to correct a record of a court in respect of an accused is made by or on behalf of the prosecutor in the relevant prosecution against the accused, the application — (a) need not be served on the accused; and (b) may be dealt with in the absence of the accused, unless a court orders otherwise. (2) If an application made under the CPA section 179 to correct a record of a court in a prosecution is made by a person other than the prosecutor, the application — (a) must be served on the prosecutor; and (b) must not be dealt with in the absence of the prosecutor unless a court considers it is in the interests of justice to do so.” Consequently, if a situation arises where an accused has used a false name and a subsequent conviction is adversely impacting upon another innocent person, an application can be made to correct the court records even if the accused is not present, or perhaps is avoiding police. However, the prosecutor will need to be able to satisfy the court of the reasons why the change should be made; for example, fingerprints or DNA might have revealed the deception. Usually, the investigating officer will have the information needed. 2 Keady v Bradford [1993] WASC Lib. No. 930731, Scott J at page 7. 3 Keady v Bradford [1993] WASC Lib. No. 930731, Scott J at page 8.

rdc|non-disc-orde-content: WHAT IS A NON-DISCLOSURE ORDER? Police are required under the Criminal Procedure Act 2004 (the Act) to disclose all confessional and evidentiary material in our possession to the accused. The requirements are contained within sections 35, 42, 61 and 95 of the Act. However, under section 138 of the Act, the court may make an order that dispenses with part or all of a disclosure requirement. The order will be limited to very specific evidence. “138. Disclosure requirements, orders as to (1) In this section, unless the contrary intention appears — disclosure requirement means a requirement under section 35, 42, 61, 62, 95 or 96 to disclose material, other than a requirement under section 62(4)(a) or 96(3)(a). (2) The powers in this section may be exercised by a court on its own initiative or on an application by a party to a case. (3) A court may, in respect of a disclosure requirement, make an order — (a) that dispenses with all or part of the requirement, if it is satisfied — (i) there is a good reason to do so; and (ii) no miscarriage of justice will result; or (b) that shortens or extends the time for obeying the requirement; or (c) that amends or cancels an order made previously under this section, whether by the court or some other court; or (d) as to any other matter that the court considers is just. (4) An application for an order under this section may be made by a prosecutor without notice to the accused and may be dealt with in the absence of the accused. (4a) Despite section 171, an application by a prosecutor for an order under this section that is made without notice to the accused must not be dealt with in open court and the only people who may be present when it is dealt with are the applicant and those permitted by the court. (5) If an order is made under this section in the absence of an accused, the order must not be given or disclosed to the accused without the permission of the court that made it or, if it was made by a court of summary jurisdiction and the accused is committed for trial or sentence to a superior court, of the superior court. [Section 138 amended by No. 5 of 2008 s. 46.]” A non-disclosure order does not prevent disclosure of the evidence if circumstances change. Nor does the order prevent the defence from trying to subpoena the evidence if they become aware of it. (This has been clarified and confirmed with the Chief Magistrate.) Note, however, that under subsection (5), if the application is made in the absence of the accused, the order must not be given or disclosed to the accused. There must be a good reason for making a non-disclosure application and an investigating officer must ensure that no miscarriage of justice will result. There tends to be two main reasons for seeking a non-disclosure order in the absence of the accused. One is where the police want a delay in the disclosure of the evidence until closer to the trial. This may be for the protection of a witness or to enable an operation to continue, etc. For example: a witness may have supplied a statement to police and will be required to give evidence but if the accused became aware of the witness they would be in danger. The police may be arranging witness protection but it might not be available until closer to the trial. A delay in the disclosure would enable the witness’ safety to be ensured. Another example could be where legal phone taps are still in place and disclosure would alert the accused. The second reason is where the evidence would have no bearing on the accused’s defence and the police do not want the accused to know about it at all. The evidence would not be used at trial. For example, police may have a major operation going and are sitting off the house of a target. Along comes little Billy Brownpants and buys a small amount of cannabis from the target. Billy is followed and a traffic stop conducted and, lo and behold, he is found in possession of cannabis. The observations, etc, at the house, if disclosed, could easily tip off the target. So, police would not want that specific evidence being disclosed and it would not be used in court. The order given is a standard order stating the “requirements of Section 35, 42 or 61 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2004 have been dispensed with in relation to the material” which has been clearly described in the applicant’s confidential affidavit. Indeed, the one order can cover material that the applicant will disclose later but before trial and other material that the applicant does not to intend to disclose at all. As stated before, the order does not prevent material that is to be disclosed later from being disclosed earlier than planned nor does it prevent material which was not intended to be disclosed at all from being disclosed should circumstances change. Simply disclose it. Some matters need not be disclosed under the law of public interest immunity.1 There is sometimes confusion as to when a non-disclosure order should be obtained rather than using the law of public interest immunity. Very simplistically it can be divided up as follows: • Where the defence has no idea the material exists, then get a non-disclosure order. • Where the defence does or should know of the existence of the material, use the law of public interest immunity. 1 Criminal Procedure Act 2004 section 137A. Let us use a person charged with ‘possess prohibited drug with intent to sell/supply’. An undercover police officer (UCO) speaks to the offender during an operation and conducts a controlled buy which is not intended to be used as evidence and further ascertains that the offender has a quantity of drugs at their home which they intend to sell. Investigating police take out a Misuse of Drugs Act 1981 search warrant and ‘tip’ the house. The defence would not be aware of the UCO and to disclose that information about the UCO and the controlled buy would jeopardise the operation. A non-disclosure order could be obtained for that material directly relating to the UCO and the controlled buy. When taking out the search warrant, though, police would need to complete an ‘information on oath for search warrant’ form. As this is required by law and the form is in the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 1982, defence would be aware of its existence. In this case, the law of public interest immunity would apply to not disclosing all or part of it, especially in regards to the UCO and their information. APPLICATIONS An application should be made as early as possible before the trial or disclosure/committal hearing date to enable the investigating officer to comply with their legislative disclosure requirements. Applications for matters that are appearing in the Magistrates Court are made without notice to the accused and are heard in the absence of the accused. All applications, for all matters statewide, are made in Perth* and any order that is granted will be granted by the Chief or Deputy Chief Magistrate. Any order will only relieve the requirements under sections 35, 42 or 61. These will, generally, be for summary trials and matters going to a disclosure/committal hearing. These applications are dealt with by a dedicated prosecutor from the Prosecution Standards And Capability. Once a matter has been committed up to the District or Supreme Court, the DPP will need to make another application before that court to be relieved of any requirement under section 95 of the Act. These orders are granted in the relevant superior court. Non-disclosure for Children's Court matters should be referred to the Children's Court DPP team at Perth Children's Court. The required forms for making a non-disclosure application, along with this document and an Applicant’s Checklist, are located on the Prosecution Division’s Blue Book site (Blue Book | Strategy and Legal - Non-Disclosure Documents - All Documents (sharepoint.com)). The forms can also be accessed through the Prosecution System in Forms and Printing > Additional Forms. NOTE: The confidential affidavit and Form 6 is to be signed in front of the Chief or Deputy Chief Magistrate unless the applicant is in regional WA and not able to attend. For a fuller description of non-disclosure, refer to the Disclosure Manual. *Regulation 46A Magistrates Court (General) Rules 2005 "46A. Disclosure requirements, applications relating to (CPA s. 138) An application made by a prosecutor without notice to the accused for an order under the CPA section 138 must be heardby a magistrate sitting in chambers at the Court sitting at Perth. [Rule 46A inserted in Gazette 24 Aug 2007 p. 4323; amended in Gazette 23 Nov 2007 p. 5862.]"

The procedures compliment and align with standard operating procedures for Electronic Evidence Recording, Forensic Packaging Guidelines, existing Drug Management Unit (DMU) guidelines, Detective Training School and Foundation Training procedures. Management Audit Unit (MAU) maintain responsibility for assessing the controls exercised which govern all aspects of drug management. MAU conduct reviews of procedures relating to the receival, storage, auditing, and destruction of drugs. The Drug Management Exhibit guidelines reflect recommendations made by an MAU audit and review of how our agency manages illicit drugs and drug items. An employee who seizes property is required to make a determination on the evidential value of the item. Consideration should be given for the exhibit to be reduced to an electronic recording, sample, photograph, swab or other forensic application if applicable. An exhibit is required to be disposed of as soon as practical according to policy and legislation. SCOPE These procedures specifically relate to the exhibit management and Incident Management System (IMS) submission of illicit drugs and drug items seized by Police. The document has been written to provide practical packaging guidelines in line with drug property management policy and other guidelines. This will assist employees in the correct method of how to retain and submit exhibits via manual handling procedures and electronic data entry onto IMS. Employees are reminded of their obligations under work place safety regulations. rem|drug-mana-exhi-SECURITY-MOVEMENT-ENV: Drug Management Unit will accept all SME if the item is an illicit drug, a genuine smoking implement, or an item with an approved request for analysis. Genuine smoking implements should be entered onto IMS as DRUG IMPLEMENTS/ Smoking Implements. • SME are to be correctly and securely sealed with no holes or punctures, and no gaps in the sealing strip. • The SME must be sealed all the way across without deformity. • Do not use evidence tape on the SME. • Photograph and body worn camera the exhibit prior to placing your SME into secure storage. • One exhibit per SME. • Only one drug/substance type within an SME. • Do not mix other articles with drugs inside the SME. • WA Police Force - Standard Operating Procedures - Drug Exhibits and Drug Management Each item needs to be separated – no items other than drugs or drug implements to be in the same SME. Drug Types also need to be separated i.e. separate cocaine from cannabis, meth from cocaine etc. Multiple genuine smoking implements from the same IR that are updated for destruction can be placed inside the same SME for disposal. Place only valid exhibits inside SME. Use the appropriately sized P11 for your exhibit. Do not use a large P11B or P11C for a tiny amount of drugs or a small smoking pipe. BARCODE • Must be attached to the left top side of the SME. • Must be placed underneath the seal. • Do not cover the seal with the barcode. • Do not place the barcode anywhere else on the SME. • If you make an error or change details, print off another barcode and place the correct barcode on the SME in the correct position.
rem|drug-mana-exhi-ALL-DETAILS-ARE-TO-BE: INCIDENT NUMBER and PROP REF No: - FILL IN ALL THE BOXES ➢ IR number legibly written in non-smudge ink followed by property reference item number. ➢ You must complete the property item number e.g. 0001 – even if there is only one property item at the time because other items could be later added to the Incident Report. ➢ The Incident Number section should resemble 01012512009134. ➢ Property reference once entered is four digits e.g. 0001 or 0028 or 0125. EXHIBIT log number if relevant – e.g. search warrant, front counter seizure. POLICE STATION – insert the correct business area name. DEPOSITOR / SUSPECT NAME (if relevant) DATE OF INTERVIEW OR DATE SEIZED must be completed.
rem|drug-mana-exhi-CONTENT-DETAILS: • Use correct description of the contents which match the description on IMS. • The amount on IMS description must match the amount inside SME. • For example: if you place 3 meth pipes inside SME the IMS amount must match three meth pipes as well. • For example: if you seize cannabis in three small clip seal bags and the weight is 13 grams, place the three clip seal bags inside the that SME, then you must state “three clip seal bags containing green leaf material btb cannabis weight 13 grams” on the SME and onto IMS. • If you seize a liquid which is inside a syringe or a jar/container, enter the item as the illicit drug. e.g. 2ml meth inside syringe or 2ml heroin inside small container • The SME content details must match the description on IMS. • Do not mix items inside the same SME. WA Police Force - Standard Operating Procedures - Drug Exhibits and Drug Management • Do not mix tobacco/cigarette butts with illicit drugs. • Do not place plastic bags/rubbish/containers or other foreign substances inside an SME with an illicit drug or drug implement. • Physical evidence collection must be considered, validated and completed before forwarding the item to DMU. • Tick the appropriate box for photographs, weight, DFIO and EVR. • LEGIBLY PRINT YOUR NAME, REGIMENTAL NUMBER, SIGN YOUR SME. • Seal SME ensuring there are no gaps, wrinkling, holes and binding is secure. • DO NOT STAPLE THE SME. BROKEN GLASS – BUBBLE WRAP – FRAGILE ITEMS • All glass items need to be bubble wrapped as a minimum. • Broken glass items must be bubble wrapped and secured in a sharps/knife container. • If the item is too large it may be placed inside a box for safety, then sealed inside a TAG bag. • A large glass smoking implement should be sufficiently bubble wrapped to protect the thick glass bottom of the item from damage and from injuring any person. • A FRAGILE sticker should be applied. WA Police Force - Standard Operating Procedures - Drug Exhibits and Drug Management CONTAINERS – JARS – GRINDERS - SCALES: • Containers/jars/grinders/scales are not smoking implements. • Consider if it is necessary to seize a jar or a container. • Any jar/container/grinder/scales must be emptied of the illicit drug and the prohibited substance placed inside a separate SME to the container. • Any container required as an exhibit is to be placed inside a separate SME. • Hold the exhibit at the station for 3 months as general property. • After three months the item is stored at PRESS long term. • Local OIC can destroy these items. • Reference WASC Appeal [2023] WASC 445 Rowland v DPP WA Police Force - Standard Operating Procedures - Drug Exhibits and Drug Management
rem|drug-mana-exhi-DRUG-IMPLEMENTS: Section 7B of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1981 constitutes what is a drug implement/drug paraphernalia. The Supreme Court of Western Australia appeal [2023] WASC 445 clearly outlines supplementary evidence and parliamentary interpretation required to assess what is drug paraphernalia. Section 7B (6) creates the offence of possessing drug paraphernalia on which there is a prohibited drug or a prohibited plant. Drug paraphernalia is: (a) any thing made or modified to be used in connection with manufacturing or preparing a prohibited drug or a prohibited plant — (i) for administration to a person; or (ii) for smoking, inhaling or ingesting by a person; or (iii) to be burned or heated so its smoke or fumes can be smoked or inhaled by a person; or (b) any thing made or modified to be used by a person — (i) to administer a prohibited drug or a prohibited plant to a person; or (ii) to smoke, inhale or ingest a prohibited drug or a prohibited plant; or (iii) to smoke or inhale the smoke or fumes resulting from burning or heating a prohibited drug or a prohibited plant. Items such as containers, spoons, knives, bank cards, sunglasses case, plastic bags, empty clip seal bags, pestle and mortar, scales, straws, bread boards, jars, scissors, are not smoking implements – reference [2023] WASC 445. These items are general property items. If there is evidentiary value in seizing these items they can be stored at your station for 3 months. Many items can simply be photographed and recorded in situ with only the illicit item seized. e.g. a glass meth pipe inside a sunglasses case – the sunglasses case does not need to be seized as an exhibit unless a forensic test is required – seize the meth pipe and leave the sunglasses case as it is not drug paraphernalia. Bubble Wrap all glass smoking implements sufficiently to prevent damage to the exhibit and to prevent injury to any person prior to placing inside SME. If using a sharp safe container bubble wrap the implement where possible to prevent movement and damage to exhibit inside the tube. Insert paper towel inside an implement to draw out and dry up any fluids. e.g. bong. WA Police Force - Standard Operating Procedures - Drug Exhibits and Drug Management ELECTRONIC EVIDENCE PROCESS – (Electronic Evidence Recording 1.9) • When conducting an EER/EVR and placing drug items into smaller containers, write on the lid of the new container the EER item number. • The container exhibit lid should record the weight and EER number. • The combined weight of exhibits inside a SME is restricted to 1kg per SME. • Multiple containers from the same EER item number can be placed inside a single SME – each container must be identified and labelled on the top. e.g. 19FA, 19FAA, 19FAAA containers can be placed inside the same SME. • Each item within the SME needs to be completely visible and easily identified. • IMS details must record all the EER number within SME. (EER 1.9) WA Police Force - Standard Operating Procedures - Drug Exhibits and Drug Management
rem|drug-mana-exhi-FORENSIC-PROCESS: • Any local forensic process must be completed prior to sending the exhibit to PRESS or DMU. • An officer must photograph and body worn camera their exhibit at the scene or at the station prior to long term storage. • General property will be retained at the station for three months. • DMU will accept any correctly packaged item which has been approved for analysis by FACT. • The exhibit can be accompanied by the RFA approval document and transferred to DMU on IMS. • Instructions need to be updated by the IO prior to transfer. • ALL RFA approved items must be sent to DMU at the same time. INSTRUCTIONS for COURT EXHIBITS • Every property item needs instructions. • Writing “hold for court” is insufficient. • Every instruction should contain details outlining the purpose of the item. • All property items and instructions should be reviewed bi-monthly by the IO. • Update instructions immediately when circumstances change. • Once the prosecution matter is completed – the IO is responsible for updating property instructions for RTO/Destroy/Auction etc. Court exhibits: - for court exhibits the following at a minimum is required: • Investigative Officer name and PD: • Next court date: • Prosecution number: • RFA approved Yes or No LIQUIDS: Chemicals i.e. methylated spirits, 1,4-Butanediol, etc need to be packaged in a safe way to preserve the integrity of the exhibit and minimise risk to any person. • No liquids over 500ml per SME. • Chemistry Centre WA advise the best method for storage is to use correct Chemical Bottles (i.e. Schott Jars) and to seal lid with Parafilm. • All bottles must be sealed at the top using Parafilm to prevent leakage. • Parafilm available on RMIS. • Call DMU for advice. • IMS entry type – CHEMICALS (unless prohibited in MDA Schedules). WA Police Force - Standard Operating Procedures - Drug Exhibits and Drug Management MOISTURE: • All excess moisture is to be removed from wet/damp implements. • Absorbent paper is to be inserted into the implement to prevent spillage and any further moisture. • Wet cannabis is to be laid upon moisture absorbent towels and dried out prior to placing inside an SME. PLANTS and SEEDLINGS: • WET plants and seedlings are to be dried out. • Remove all excess moisture. • Remove all soil. • Do not bag plants with soil. • If soil is required as an exhibit, the soil can be stored at the police station. • Do not send soil to DMU. • If the plants are tall, bend in half and insert into the TAG (poly vented) bag. • The TAG (poly vented) bag must have sufficient room at the top to seal tightly. • No gaps or holes at the top of TAG bag – secure your exhibits. • TAG bag not to exceed 15 kg. • TAG bag must be secured with the TAG number entered onto IMS. • TAG must be secured with the teeth rachet self-locking. • A barcode must be attached to a cardboard label then secured to the TAG itself through the strap or by using string. • DO NOT USE ELASTIC BANDS TO TIE A BARCODE TO THE TAG. • All cannabis waste must be updated for destruction prior to transport to DMU. WA Police Force - Standard Operating Procedures - Drug Exhibits and Drug Management
rem|drug-mana-exhi-PRESCRIPTION-DRUGS: • Prescription drugs or medication should be entered onto IMS as medicine – not DRUGS. • It is general property and should be stored at the police station for three months. • Can be destroyed by local OIC. • Coronial medication/drugs should be entered onto IMS as medicine – not DRUGS – and sent to PRESS for long term storage. • Coronial medication can be listed as a single IMS entry with the description panel completed and placed into one storage bag. • All instructions must be updated.
rem|drug-mana-exhi-REQUEST-FOR-ANALYSIS: • Drug requests for analysis for any drug related item will be forwarded to DMU immediately once approved. • If the property item is not listed on IMS as a DRUG or IMPLEMENT, select drug connect tick on property further info tab. e.g. scales that require analysis. • Send all approved RFA items at the same time to DMU. • The IO is responsible for every RFA application and item follow up. • Contact FACT for follow up regarding drug RFA. i.e. certificates. etc. WA Police Force - Standard Operating Procedures - Drug Exhibits and Drug Management SOIL and ROOT BALLS: • No soil to be placed inside a TAG bag or P11 for storage at DMU. • Soil will not be accepted at DMU. • Seedling growing cubes. e.g. grow wall will not be accepted at DMU. • Soil contains microbes, bacteria and insects that jeopardizes the integrity of exhibits and cannot be introduced to DMU. • Root balls are generally not seized because they contain less than 0.03% THC and once severed are not considered prohibited plant material. • Roots will not regrow once cut at ground level. • If root balls are seized at the scene they can be destroyed in situ whilst complying with legislation and policy. • If an IO decides it is necessary to seize a root ball, the decision must be articulated on the IMS instruction panel for that item. • Prior to transport to DMU - all root balls must be dried and packaged individually to avoid mould, insect activity, and for health and safety risks. • All root balls must be listed for destruction prior to transport to DMU. • All Cannabis waste must be listed for destruction prior to transport to DMU.
rem|drug-mana-exhi-ACCEPTABLE-NOT-ACCEPT: WA Police Force - Standard Operating Procedures - Drug Exhibits and Drug Management SYRINGES • All empty syringes are entered on IMS as MEDICAL ITEMS – not DRUGS. • One syringe per SME for drug exhibits. • All exhibit syringes must be packaged separately. • If a syringe is not an evidential exhibit – e.g. found property item no person charged – place syringe into a sharps disposal container – no need to enter it onto IMS – can be disposed of at local police station. • Syringes must be placed into a syringe container needle tube or sharps container before packaging. • If the syringe contains a prohibited drug – the item is to be recorded as that illicit drug. e.g. approx 4 ml meth inside a syringe. • Syringe sizes are to be accurate. A 10ml syringe cannot hold 20 ml of meth. • Take care to ensure correct measure of the liquid units and enter this correct measurement onto IMS. • Place BIOHAZARD sticker on the SME that contains fluids and needle. VAPES • Enter vapes onto IMS as TOBACCO. • VAPES ARE NOT DRUGS. • VAPES ARE NOT DRUG SMOKING IMPLEMENTS. • Contact PRESS for transport and disposal options if required. • DMU will not accept vapes. • Contact DMU for queries regarding product content and storage. rem|phys-mate-mana-INVESTIGATION-PRECIS: Physical Material Management Date: 30-May-19 Version 2.3 Investigation Precis WA Police Force Physical Material Management
rem|phys-mate-mana-OCCUPATIONAL-SAFETY-A: SUMMARY ........................................................................................................................ 18 BIBLIOGRAPHY ............................................................................................................... 19 PURPOSE This précis has been written to offer guidance and assistance to all members of the WA Police Force (WA Police Force) in relation to police investigations involving The5KIS (Physical Material) management. The précis is written to highlight the theory and methodology underpinning ‘Criminal Investigations’ and are not intended to be referenced as Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs). Should information regarding SOPs be sought then readers must refer to the ‘Forensic Division’ link located on the WA Police Force intranet website under: Home - WAPOL Business Units > Forensic1. This précis is an ‘all of agency’ resource but readers should be aware they are specifically written for the Detective Investigation Training Course. INTRODUCTION Modern investigations often rely on forensic processes in which the inculpatory or exculpatory evidence is at the cellular or even molecular level. It is here, that the importance of correct exhibits management is vital. Detectives need to be mindful of the continuity of exhibits for eventual presentation in court. A comprehensive record detailing the ‘chain of custody’ of each exhibit is fundamental to criminal investigations. There are numerous instances where prosecutions have failed due to defence counsel successfully challenging exhibit continuity. Although many incident scenes are processed by trained Scenes of Crime officers, occasions may occur when exhibits will need to be collected and managed by Investigating Officers (IOs). There are two very different but equally important concepts involved in exhibit management, the prevention of contamination and continuity of exhibits. For guidelines on how to ensure both are adequately considered refer to the ‘Forensic Exhibit Handling and Packaging Guidelines’ produced by the Forensic Training and Development Unit, located on the Forensic Division intranet site. 1 Forensic Division Homepage http://intranetportal/Home/Forensic/tabid/3784/Default.aspx as 30 May 2019. CASE STUDY # 1 - Jaidyn Leskie One of most notorious cases of contamination in Australian Criminal history is that of Jaidyn Leskie. Jaidyn Raymond Leskie was the one year old child of Bilynda Williams and Brett Leskie. Jaidyn was kidnapped and murdered in 1997. Jaidyn’s murder remains unsolved; despite leads, the arrest, and a trial of a prime suspect, who was eventually found not guilty. Jaidyn was kidnapped from the house of his mother's boyfriend, who was babysitting at the time, in Newborough, Victoria. The circumstances around his disappearance and death were never clear and were complicated by a pig's head being thrown at the house and other vandalism on the evening of the toddler's disappearance. Jaidyn's body was found on 1 January 1998 at Blue Rock Dam, 30 km north of Moe. His body had been preserved by the cold waters through the winter and the clothing he was wearing was subject to a DNA test in an effort to solve the crime. Jaidyn is believed to have died of head injuries. DNA was located on the toddlers bib and the Victorian Forensic Science Centre matched the DNA to a sample in a rape case. However the DNA was not a match to the alleged offender in the rape, but was a match to the victim. The rape victim and her family were questioned extensively by investigating officers and it was found she had no connection with the murder. During the 2002 coronial inquest of Jaidyn Leskie, the issue of the DNA result was raised. Barristers representing the coroner commissioned the assistance of William C. Thompson, a Professor in the Department of Criminology, Law & Society at the University of California, Irvine. Professor Thompson closely examined the evidence and with the assistance of several DNA experts, came to the conclusion there was one of two possibilities that explained the location of the rape victim’s DNA on the bib of Jaidyn Leskie; 1. The rape victim and Jaidyn’s murderer or some unknown person had exactly the same DNA profile; or 2. There was either intentional misconduct by laboratory personnel or an egregious laboratory error. Inter alia, Thompson found the DNA result was a case of cross contamination and the laboratory processing the exhibits caused the contamination. His detailed investigation could not identify the point of the contamination but with the absence of any other plausible scenario it was deemed the two exhibits, which were processed in close proximity in time to each other, had exchanged DNA material. This case indicates just how easily the contamination of an exhibit can occur and gives foundation to the principles of exhibit packaging and exhibit preservation. See footnote 2 for reference to the report of Professor Thompson. 2 W C Thompson, Victoria State Coroner’s Inquest into Death of Jaidyn Leskie (2003) <http://www.bioforensics.com/app/download/5286528/Kranereport.pdf > at 19 October 2017.
rem|phys-mate-mana-WHAT-IS-AN-EXHIBIT: The Butterworths Australian Legal Dictionary defines an exhibit as an object received in evidence when tendered by one of the parties to a case3. As a purely legal definition, this is accurate but this definition does not reflect what an exhibit is, from a police perspective. It may be more accurate to describe an exhibit as an item taken into police custody for possible forensic examination and or tendering in court in accordance with the rules of evidence. It is for this reason the WA Police Force has adopted the term ‘physical material’ to describe items seized during an investigation. As can be seen, the procedures applicable to exhibit packaging will not only apply to those items that will be presented in court but also those that may be presented in court. It is imperative detectives treat all seized physical material the same and there is no compromise in the quality of the packaging or the way in which the physical material is dealt with.
rem|phys-mate-mana-FORENSIC-CONSIDERATIO: The WA Police Force Forensic Division has authored a number of procedures when collecting seized physical material, in particular, that which may need to be scientifically examined4. Whenever physical material is handled, it is imperative that gloves are worn. A new pair of gloves should be worn for every item to avoid cross contamination (see inset5). Physical material should be handled as little as possible. If a forensic examination is to be conducted, the more often physical material is picked up, moved or examined, the more opportunity there is for microscopic amounts of trace evidence to be lost. Once collected the physical material should be stored in a secure place. The less accessible the physical material, the less defence counsel can argue contamination has occurred. Protect physical material from heat, light and dampness. Exposure to any of the aforementioned can cause the loss of evidence. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), although it is a very stable molecule, can be degraded by heat, light, time, humidity, fungi and bacteria6. Fungi and bacteria can flourish in damp environments. 3 Butterworths Australian Legal Dictionary, (Sydney: Butterworths, 1997) [446] 4 Forensic Division Homepage http://intranetportal/Home/StateCrime/Forensic/tabid/3784/Default.aspx as 23 October 2017. 5 Max M. Houck and Jay A. Siegel, Fundamentals of Forensic Science, (1st Ed, Oxford, Academic Press, 2006) 58. 6 M M Houck et al, as above n 3, 284.
rem|phys-mate-mana-PHYSICAL-MATERIAL-LAB: Physical material should be clearly labelled at all times. WA Police Force Forensic Division have adopted a minimum standard regarding the information contained on the label (see inset). The label should reflect the following information. JSE1 Figure 1 IR 100117 0830 12345 The exhibit number (personal identifier) is created from the initials 100117 0900 hrs of the collecting officer’s first and last names followed by either ‘E’ (exhibit) 12 Smith Street, Kewdale or ‘P’ (photograph) and the numerical sequence in which the exhibit was seized. Kitchen table near door As much detail as possible should be Red texta pen included in the description of the item and it’s specific location and must be 1/c SMITH 12345 identical to the description recorded on the IMS barcode sticker. Detectives should also include the exhibit log number on the label for ease of cross referencing later in the prosecution process. Labelling should be directly written on the packaging not onto an adhesive label as labels can fall off during storage. A biological/chemical hazard label shall be attached to any evidence package or container that contains evidence which may present a hazard. The label should be attached in a prominent position to warn any person who handles the physical material of the potential danger. Initial labelling of physical material should be completed at the time of collection. Additional information should be entered onto the label once the physical material has been recorded onto the IMS system, this information should include the IMS property item number. It is important all physical material is labelled the same way to ensure consistency and accuracy. Remember it is always better to seize physical material than it is to only take a swab. The recovery of biological material is more likely if the entire item is seized. If there is a possibility of trace evidence being lost in either the packaging process or any other process prior to examination, investigators may consider taking a swab of the physical material prior to packaging it. It is recommended this course of action be only undertaken after seeking advice from a suitably qualified scene of crime officer. Physical materials should be photographed in situ. This will ensure the context of the seizure is captured. Remember, once physical material has been moved, it should not be replaced then photographed, as the evidence offered regarding its original location may be excluded. Once physical material is packaged, the same care in handling needs to be taken. This will ensure that minute particles of evidence are not lost (see inset for example7). If there is a possibility of trace evidence being lost in either the packaging process or any other process prior to examination, investigators may consider taking a swab of the physical material prior to packaging it. It is recommended this course of action is only undertaken after seeking advice from a suitably qualified scene of crime officer. Once physical material is moved, consideration should be given to examining the area surrounding its original location. Investigators should be aware of Professor Edmond Locard’s principle of exchange. This principle should be kept in mind at all times when dealing with physical material and there may have been transference of evidence from the physical material to its surroundings.
rem|phys-mate-mana-PHYSICAL-MATERIAL-PAC: Physical material should be packaged immediately upon collection. Allowing numerous items to be placed in close proximity to each other could cause cross contamination of the physical material and allow challenges by defence counsel as to the integrity of the evidence. 7 T Jalanti, P Henchoz, A Gallusser and M S Bonfanti, ‘The persistence of gunshot residue on shooters' hands’ (1998) Science & Justice 39, Issue 1, 48-52. Packaging should be used that is appropriate to the nature of the physical material and only one item per container. The type of packaging will be dependent on the circumstances. Consideration should always be given to ensure the physical material is protected from damage, that the risk of disruption to trace evidence is minimised, elimination of possible contamination and the risk of exposure to biological or chemical hazards to persons handling the physical material is eliminated or reduced. Only approved types of packaging are to be used for items collected from an incident scene. For a comprehensive description of handling and packaging exhibits refer to ‘Forensic Exhibit Handling and Packaging Guidelines’ located on the Forensic Division intranet site. Packaging is only one component of effective physical material management. The most appropriate packaging may be selected but if it is not sealed correctly the likelihood of contamination is greatly increased. It is imperative that correct methods and devices are used to seal all types of physical material packaging. When identifying what items are to be seized, it is important to evaluate what evidentiary value they have. During this evaluation process it is better to err on the side of caution. It is a simple process to later return an item to an owner, but once you have left it, the integrity is lost. Put simply; it is better to have seized it, than wished you had. CONTINUITY Seizure is simply the beginning of the management of physical material. If physical material is to be tendered in court, then continuity and a record of that continuity is paramount.
rem|phys-mate-mana-RECEIPT-PHYSICAL-MATE: The recording of physical material onto a log is the first step in recording the ‘chain of custody’. The importance of accurate recording and completion of the log cannot be over stated. Investigators should be familiar with the WA Police Force Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log, however the knowledge of how to accurately complete it will vary. Consistency in this area will greatly benefit the investigator and the organisation as a whole. With the exception of those fields relating to the property seized, the exhibit log has a number of compulsory fields that should be completed and each will be addressed individually.  Location: This field should be completed with the actual location the search is conducted. If there is not a specific address, then it should be completed with some sort of reference point i.e. Brand Highway, two kilometres north of the Cataby roadhouse. This will ensure there is no confusion as to the place the item was seized.  Occupier/Witness: The name of a person who has responsibility for the place. They may be the resident or a person who has some tangible connection. If an independent senior officer is used, then their details should be recorded here.  Date: Record date of seizure.  Arrival Time: Record time of arrival at location.  Entry Time: The time entry was made, not the time the search commenced. This may also differ from the arrival time.  Departure Time: The time police departed the premises, not the time the search ceased. It may only be possible to have this time recorded on the police copies as the witness copy may be afforded to them during the closure of the search.  Page Numbers: It is imperative page numbers are recorded so there can be no allegation more items were seized during the search. The complete number of pages ensures finality to the seizures. After the last entry relating to the property seized, on the last page, a diagonal line should be ruled from the bottom of the last entry in the ‘Physical Material’ number cell, to the bottom right corner of the ‘Distribution’ cell. In that way, no additional entries can be made by any party.  Operation/Incident: This should be filled out if there is a specific operation name associated with the search or a brief description of the type of incident.  Investigating Officer: The Investigating Officer’s (IO) details should be recorded here.  Physical Material Officer: If an officer is specifically assigned the management of exhibits (physical material) then that officer’s details must be recorded here.  Video Camera Officer: The details of the officer designated with recording events via video and the taking of photographs.  Forensic Register Reference: Unique number generated when the forensic register is utilised. Normally applies to qualified forensic officers.  PFA Declared: Protected forensic area declared (yes/no/n/a).  Time Declared: Time the PFA was declared.  Physical Material Officer Signature: The signature of the designated Physical Material officer for the duration of the search.  Occupier/Witness Signature: This signature should be that of the occupier/witness listed previously. If the person refuses to sign, then ‘Refused to Sign’ (RTS) is acceptable.  IMS Reference: This IMS report number should be specific to the search and not a general number associated with an offence.  Property Returned: Date/time of property return.  Occupier/Owner: Name of person to whom property was returned and signature.  Witnessing Officer: Signature of officer returning property (with legible rank and PD number included). Although the completion of the above details is important, the recording of the detail of the physical material seized is more so. Do not restrict yourself to a single line if more are required.  Physical Material No: As detailed earlier, the item number should not just be a numeric list, it should comprise of the exhibit officers initials accompanied by a number sequence starting at 1 (see figure 1).  Description of Physical Material Include Photography Taken: This is possibly the area that is routinely not given its due attention. A detailed description of the item needs to be entered. Entries such as “a knife” are inadequate. A more appropriate entry may be “a black handled kitchen knife, approximately 30 centimetres in length with a serrated blade”. A detailed description will ensure there is no confusion between items.  Specific Location: Another area routinely neglected is the location of where the item was located. All too often entries such as “bedroom” are recorded. Vague entries such as this can cause difficulties during trial when the specific location of an item is in issue. Insufficient detail will allow increased opportunities for challenge by the defence. A more appropriate entry in this section may be, “Bedroom one, south east corner of house, towards rear of the second drawer of the dressing table”. Associating the location point with a sketch of the scene may also prove to be beneficial.  Item Located By: This specifies the officer who located the item, regimental number or surname are suitable however regimental numbers are unique and do not allow for any discrepancies, therefore regimental number is the preferred option.  Photography In Situ: Yes/No  Conveyance Movement Envelope: The conveyance bag is a security movement envelope is used to initially secure valuable items or drugs before processing/weighing and separating into other bags.  Security Movement Envelope: This section can be used in two ways; if a drug is seized at the scene and no other process is necessary i.e. weighing, then it should be secured in a security movement envelope and the number recorded here. Alternatively, if processing or weighing is required then the number of the final bag used should be recorded.  IMS Item No: The IMS number property reference number (a four digit number i.e. 0001) should be recorded here once the item is recorded onto IMS.  Distribution: This section relates to what has happened to the physical material at the completion of the process. Options include, but are not limited to, return to owner (RTO), sent to Chemistry Centre for analysis, forwarded to Exhibits Management Unit (EMU) or storage at office. Investigators will be well served to complete the exhibit log in its entirety and with as much detail as possible. It will serve as a valuable tool during the trial process and unequivocally establish the initial ‘chain of custody’. The detailed completion of these sections of the exhibit log will prove to be of great benefit later in the process. The passage of time can alter recollections of events, information recorded at the initial stages can serve as an aide memoir later.
rem|phys-mate-mana-INCIDENT-MANAGEMENT-S: Upon return to the office, seized physical material is to be recorded onto IMS. IMS is the primary case management system and other case management systems such as VIPER should be used in conjunction with IMS. The recording of the property onto IMS forms the next step of the recordable ‘chain of custody’. It is very important the property is recorded correctly and accurately to ensure there is limited opportunity for the loss or damage of evidence while in storage. Corporate information (Police Manual PR – Property and Drugs)8 exists on the procedures for recording of physical material within IMS; therefore detailed instruction in this area is not necessary. Investigators need to be aware that once recorded onto IMS, the property is held within a system that will form the basis of the ‘chain of custody’ for the remainder of the investigation. There are several areas that have the potential to be overlooked when recording property onto IMS, these areas can be beneficial in ‘chain of custody’ issues; these shall be touched on briefly.  Exhibit Reference: The specific exhibit number the item was given should be recorded here. As this is a unique reference it will assist in identifying the item throughout the process, thus minimising confusion and error.  Interim Receipt Number: The receipt number printed onto the Interim Property Receipt / Physical Material Log is to be recorded under the ‘further info’ tab. This will assist in cross referencing. The above areas may appear to be mundane and without great benefit, however evidence of continuity can become quite convoluted and the benefit of utilising a system where each record is complimentary of all others is self-evident. There are timeframes applicable to the recording of property onto IMS and these are detailed within the Police Manual PR-01.01.3 Recording and Entering Property in Police Possession. Those timeframes are always use:  For high risk items of jewellery, money or perishables, within 12 hours or prior to ceasing duty, whichever comes first; and  For all other items, within 24 hours or prior to ceasing duty at the end of the following shift, whichever occurs first. 8 Corporate Knowledge Database: Police Manual (PR – Property and Drugs) http://prd-knowledge/html/knowledge/cops/knowledge.htm
rem|phys-mate-mana-PHYSICAL-MATERIAL-STO: Once physical material is recorded within IMS there are initially two paths it will take, either it will be stored securely or it will be transferred to another area for examination. The requirements for each option will be dealt with separately. Storage of physical material should be in an approved secure location within a police station (inclusive of district forensic office locations) and should be for the purposes of preliminary examination or pending conveyance to the EMU or other long-term storage area. All evidence deposited in or removed from the short-term storage area for the purpose of alternative storage requirements (long or short), will be recorded in the evidence log (IMS Property report or running sheet) and the Unified Physical Material List (UPML). Such notation shall include, but not be limited to, the following details:  Date of deposit/removal.  Property tracing number (IMS Number).  Number of items deposited.  Depositing member.  Removing member. When an item is not being examined, it is to be stored in an approved secure storage location. When making an assessment regarding the storage of physical material, the assessment should be made on an individual basis. Consideration needs to be given to possible environmental factors that may affect evidence and also security factors may be instigated to ensure there is no impropriety; malicious or otherwise. Should an item require scientific examination, analysis must first be approved by the Forensic Analysis Coordination Team (FACT) via the Request for Analysis (RFA) process9. All physical material forwarded to EMU for analysis by the Chemistry Centre or PathWest are to be accompanied by a FACT approved RFA form. Physical material that requires examination by an external laboratory must be sent to EMU promptly after the RFA is approved by FACT. Failure to do so may result in unrealistic time frames for testing, and may result in evidence not being available to a court. Written requests from ODPP for further testing of physical material should be forwarded directly to FACT. EMU is responsible for delivering and collecting all physical material from laboratories. Police Officers shall not convey physical material requiring analysis directly to a laboratory without permission from the OIC FACT. When physical material submitted for an analysis subsequently becomes superfluous, it is imperative the OIC FACT is notified so the analysis can be cancelled. This ensures laboratories are not inundated with unnecessary requests. Often investigators want to send every item for analysis, however an evaluation of each item must be conducted to establish evidentiary value and what analysis is required. Further assessment of the potential for forensic value from physical material should be conducted in conjunction with FACT. These steps will have the effect of ensuring only the necessary items are sent for analysis, reducing laboratory workload, allowing for faster processing and the potential to receive results quicker. Physical material should be prioritised as to which is of greater value to the investigation; i.e. physical material that is fundamental to the identification of the offender would typically be of higher priority than those that support the events in question. This determination will be unique to each investigation and a detailed interpretation of the incident scene will assist in this area. 9 Business Information Systems . (2017, November 2). RFA Procedure. Retrieved from Self-Help HQ: https://selfhelp/Pages/How%20to%20-%20RFA%20Procedure.aspx
rem|phys-mate-mana-PHYSICAL-MATERIAL-TRA: When the physical material is required to be transported, a record must be made of when it was removed and for what purpose. Records should be in both a running sheet and on IMS and include all information enumerated in the above list. The UPML should at all times reflect the current status and location of the item. Unless exceptional circumstances exist, physical material shall not be transported unless contained in sealed evidence bags or containers. Prior to transport, an assessment shall be conducted of each item, ensuring the transport method selected is suitable to guarantee its integrity. The property movement documentation should accompany the physical material during transport. Appropriate paperwork will reduce the risk of confusion at the point of receival. When transporting physical material subject to an IMS report, it is the conveying officers’ responsibility to ensure at all times, the location of the physical material is accurately reflected on the system. Whenever physical material is moved from one location to another the actions taken are to be accurately and diligently recorded onto the IMS property movement screen. The movement should also be recorded onto the investigation running sheet and the UPML. Where large bags containing multiple physical materials are conveyed to EMU for storage, the bag must clearly display a record of each item contained therein. Following transport, an up to date copy of the IMS receipt and UPML should be added to the appropriate case file showing amended instructions and the new location of the item. An appropriate entry on IMS showing the new location of physical material should follow any transport. The recording of physical material movement, which eventually forms the ‘chain of custody’, is done for one purpose - to enable the physical material to be tendered as evidence. CONTINUITY SCENARIO (Part 5) The bedding is subsequently conveyed to PathWest for analysis. The item is received as per procedure and stored pending analysis. At a later date one of the scientists at PathWest takes the item and commences the preliminary examination in preparation for the DNA analysis. Continued later. The physical material cannot be tendered by the production of supporting documentation i.e. exhibit, IMS reports or running sheets. It must be tendered via a witness. For an exhibit to be tendered, its entire ‘chain of custody’ must be proved. Therefore all persons involved in the movement, examination and storage of the exhibit must provide a statement. All too often, a statement of this nature is just referred to as a continuity statement and little understanding of its importance is realised. CONTINUITY SCENARIO (Part 6) The bedding is subsequently conveyed to the DNA analyst. The item is tested and it is found to have the DNA of the Suspect on it. The item is subsequently returned to EMU and later returned to the office of origin. Every statement detailing the movement of an item is fundamental to prove the ‘chain of custody’. An inaccuracy in any link of the chain may ultimately affect its admissibility. Therefore, it is imperative each statement accurately details the movement dates, times, reason and officer/s involved. Only then is the successful tendering of the exhibit in court assured. Throughout this section there has been an unfolding scenario. The reason for this is to demonstrate the possible complexity of physical material continuity. How many statements are required for this physical material to be successfully tendered in court? Given what has transpired throughout the scenario and at both EMU and PathWest the person receiving the physical material is different to the person securing the physical material there are no less than 18 statements required, all for the tendering of this one exhibit. The statements required are listed in the below chart. EMU Statements  Receival Station Statements  Storage Start of ‘chain of custody’  Detective C  Conveying Scene Statements.  Forensic Officer  Victim  Property Officer  Detective A  Detective B PathWest Statements  Receival  Storage Figure 2 COURT  Examination  DNA Analysis This chart indicates  Conveyance how the ‘chain of custody’ can become complex EMU Statements just in order to Station Statements  Receival tender one exhibit  Receival  Storage  Conveyance The above ‘chain of custody’ is not dissimilar to the production of most exhibits. A record of a convoluted ‘chain of custody’ is easily established if the investigator has accurately recorded the movements of the physical material within the documentation and established systems referred to earlier. In addition to an easy reference to exhibit movements, accurate recording of these movements will serve to corroborate the witness’s testimony.
rem|phys-mate-mana-TENDERING-EXHIBITS: The number of witnesses required to tender exhibits can be extensive and will form a part of the brief of evidence. As such, they will be included on the Unified Witness List (UWL) and potentially the UPML. Often at trial, many witnesses that form part of the continuity process will be conceded by the defence. Detectives must remember this is a result of consultation between the prosecution and the defence and not a ‘fait accompli’. The investigation and resulting prosecution brief must include all continuity witnesses and not anticipate continuity witnesses will be conceded. In fact, often there is confusion as to which witness will tender an exhibit. The vast percentage of the time, the exhibit will be tendered by the police. The exception may be where the exhibit is subject to a subpoena and never in police control. There is anecdotal evidence, many officers believe exhibits must be tendered at an early stage of a trial to be referred to in evidence. This is incorrect; the entire ‘chain of custody’ needs to be proved before the exhibit can be tendered. This does not prevent it from being shown to a witness, as it may be ‘marked for identification’. This essentially means the witness is shown the exhibit; it is identified but not tendered. It is tendered once the entire ‘chain of custody’ is proved. Therefore, the standard rule applied is the exhibit is tendered by a representative of the organisation that has custody of it at the time of the trial (predominantly the police). All other witnesses are shown the exhibit and they identify it as the item relative to their testimony.
rem|phys-mate-mana-OCCUPATIONAL-SAFETY-A: OSH applies to the management of physical material from its initial seizure to its ultimate disposal. Many items seized by police are dangerous to the safety of both the seizing officer and all persons having subsequent contact with the item. Emphasis must be placed on risk minimisation. The most common OSH issues include:  Handling of physical materials;  Dirty/dangerous environments; and  Biological, chemical, structural, electrical, and postural hazards. Personal protective equipment (PPE) must be worn when handling physical material. PPE can protect you from injury or illness as a result of handling physical material, it can also prevent you from contaminating the item. PPE includes but is not limited to, disposable overalls, masks, safety goggles, boot covers or gloves. It is the responsibility of all officers involved in the physical material management processes to ensure the risk of injury and or health issues to any person involved in the handling of the physical material is minimised. This will be accomplished by correct labelling, packaging, handling, storage and the use of PPE appropriate to the risk. See footnote10 for references for the case study. SUMMARY Physical material is an integral part of the majority of investigations. The correct packaging, transport and storage procedures must be complied with in order to ensure the integrity of potential exhibits. The nature of many forensic sciences is delicate and to ensure a successful examination is conducted, investigators must be mindful of the correct procedure in order to minimise the chances of contamination. For exhibits to be tendered in court, it is imperative the ‘chain of custody’ is documented and record can be subsequently submitted to the court to ensure the exhibit can and will be accepted into evidence. 10 M M Houck et al, as above n 5, 46. rhsm|acos-sour-mana-REVIEWING-UPDATING-A: In some instances, a warning may require amending, extending or reduce the active period of the warning. The warning record may also require update when the warning is due to expire. The ability to update a warning will normally be restricted to the officer who originally added the warning, and those users set as recipients of the notification on expiry (if appropriate). Once the warning record has been reviewed, it can be modified as needed, or allowed to expire as defined if no other evidence exists to justify the retention of the warning. The following updates can be made: • Effective Start Date – if this date is set in the future, you can bring it forward to activate the warning. You cannot modify the Start Date for active or expired warnings. • Effective End Date – can be lengthened or reduced as required. • You can remove a warning by setting the ‘Effective End Date’ to the current date and setting the Action on Expiry to Remove. Once the save/select button has been pressed and the profile saved, the warning will be expired and removed. rhsm|acos-sour-mana-MANAGEMENT-OF-AUDIO-: The use of an ARD should not be disclosed to the Source and the audio recording must not be saved to any other device or hard drive unless using OneDrive for the purposes of uploading content of a OneForce phone. ARDs utilised must have the ability to be pin locked. ARDs should only have internal storage and no removable SD Card. ARDs that have the ability to digitally encrypt audio are preferred, however, are not mandated for use. The following procedures apply to the use of ARDs and recordings: • All contact with a Source must be audio recorded. • Any contact involving payment to a Source (regardless of Tier) must be audio recorded. Handlers are responsible for ensuring ARDs are ready for use, and where operationally possible used for the recording of all meetings and payments. • The Supervisor is to ensure audio recordings are uploaded to ACOS in a timely manner. • Audio file names should conform with the naming convention as provided by the CR and cross referenced with the relevant Contact Sheet; • Handlers must delete audio recordings from the ARD once upload has been completed and checked to ensure it is playable. • All audio recordings must comply with Section 5(3) of the Surveillance Devices Act 1989. • If for some reason the contact isn’t or cannot be recorded, the contact description is to fully account for the conversation had with the Source and the reason the conversation was not audio recorded. • There is no requirement to audio record meetings with a Tier 1 (Community Source) unless making a payment to that person. Handlers and Supervisors must ensure disclosure obligations are complied with. Where a legislative requirement dictates, the Supervisor should contact the Investigating Officer and ensure that a Non- Disclosure Order is considered/obtained and an appropriate record made on the Sensitive Material List. rhsm|huma-sour-mana-content: 西澳大利亚警察局 线人保密协议条款和条件 日期 ___________________ 西澳大利亚警察局工作人员解释如下： 你同意做西澳大利亚警察局的登记线人，就相关调查帮助警方并提供信息。 重要的一点是，你明白你的线人登记取决于如下条款和条件。你尽管提问题，以确保你明白如下条款和条件: (1) 任何时候你都不被认为是西澳大利亚警察局的工作人员； (2) 你不得向任何人透露你的身份。这些人包括你的家人、朋友们或其它执法机关的官员； (3) 西澳大利亚警察局可能会让你执行任务。如果你同意执行任何任务，你必须按照指示完成任务； (4) 你如果未经合法授权从事犯罪活动，你的线人登记不能保护你免于被诉讼。本协议不包含法律授权。非法活动包 括煽动、鼓励或协助任何人从事违法活动； (5) 西澳大利亚警察局将尽全力保护你的身份。但是在特定情况下，法庭可能会行使决定权，在诉讼过程中公开你的 身份； (6) 如果你在协议期间犯罪，西澳大利亚警察局可能会取消你获得任何经济利益的权利； (7) 如果你能够获得一份支持信，你的法律代表将在你被判刑前收到通知。如果你的法律代表要求，西澳大利亚警察 局将提供评估的机会（参考备忘录第二页）； (8) 就你可能提供的信息和服务，西澳大利亚警察局的工作人员没有获得授权来给你任何报酬方面（现金或其它方 式）的承诺和保证； (9) 你可能会接触到不同的西澳大利亚警察局的工作人员或其他执法机关的工作人员。这些部门可能会要求你提供帮 助； (10) 西澳大利亚警察局的工作人员对你提供的任何信息，你要严格保密，不得向任何人透露。在特定情况下，透露信 息会构成刑事犯罪；并且 (11) 违背这些条款和条件会使你的线人登记被撤销，也会影响你今后为西澳大利亚警察局提供信息的机会。 我(签名人),明白本协议的条款和条件，并同意做西澳大利亚警察局的登记线人。 特殊指示/意见 签字 X 拼写名字 警方签字 （会面之后） 警方签字 拼写名字 （组长） （会面之后） 日期 1992 年 （西澳大利亚州）信息自由法 本文件可能包含不受 1992 年(西澳大利亚州)信息自由法 (FOI Act) 制约的内容。如果您收到信息自由法允许获得本文件的请求， 您必须马上通知州犯罪调查局的局长。如果没有获得负 责州犯罪调查局助理警监的批准，您不可以发布或发放本文件以及其中任何内容。 线人保密协议 我（签名人）向西澳大利亚警察局提供了信息。为此，我获得了一 份由西澳大利亚警察局提供的支持信。该文件可以在我被判刑的时 候呈交法庭。 我知道我的律师将获悉该支持信的内容。 签字： ............................ 日期： ........ / ......... / ....... 证人： ............................ 1992 年 （西澳大利亚州）信息自由法 本文件可能包含不受 1992 年(西澳大利亚州)信息自由法 (FOI Act) 制约的内容。如果您收到信息自由法允许获得本文件的请求， 您必须马上通知州犯罪调查局的局长。如果没有获得负 责州犯罪调查局助理警监的批准，您不可以发布或发放本文件以及其中任何内容。

rhsm|huma-sour-mana-ASSISTANT-COMMISSION: MESSAGE The Western Australia Police Force (WA Police Force) recognises that professional and responsible management of human sources (sources) is an essential and valuable part of the investigative and intelligence gathering process aimed at delivering increased community safety in the form of criminal prosecutions. It is of paramount importance that safeguards, controls and assessment processes are imposed to provide safe, efficient and effective management of sources. The WA Police Force Human Source Management Manual (the Manual) provides a comprehensive management structure to identify and control risk while achieving investigative results. The tiered approach to the management of sources is designed to encourage growth in the use of community (non-criminal) source and apply a scalable risk- based governance framework. Management of sources in line with this manual will reflect the expected behaviours identified in the agency’s Code of Conduct and the agency’s principles of Honesty, Performance, Competence and Conduct.
rhsm|huma-sour-mana-STATE-CRIME: INTRODUCTION The WA Police Force uses Human Source in line with The Five Key Investigative Strategies (The5KIS), as stipulated in the WA Police Force Investigation Manual. Effective management of Human Source enhances the capability of the WA Police Force to solve crimes faster and deliver positive community safety outcomes through timely and quality investigations. This Human Source Management Manual (Manual) defines the requirements of WA Police Force employees involved in the management of sources. Contravention of the HSM Manual may be subject to criminal, civil or disciplinary measures. If a matter is not covered by the HSM Manual, clarification should be sought from the Central Registrar. The HSM Manual should be read in conjunction with the ACOS instruction manual and ‘How to Use’ guides that can be obtained from the Central Registrar. Human Source Handler Level 1 training is available on the WA Police Force ‘eforce’ Learning web site. Human Source Handler Level 1 is the minimum qualification required before involvement in any Human Source management. Human Source Handler Level 2 and Level 3 training courses are regularly conducted by the Human Source Management Unit (HSMU). Contact the Central Registrar for further information. The Officer in Charge of the HSMU is the WA Police Force Central Registrar. The Central Registrar, oversighted by the Inspector Crime Support and Services Division, has overall authority regarding the management of Human Sources by employees of the WA Police Force. The identity of a Human Source must be protected at all times: • never make oral reference to the Human Source by name. • never print the name of a Human Source on any document (Exception - Letter of Recognition and Terms & Conditions). WA Police Force employees should not rely upon Public Interest Immunity (PII) as a mechanism to restrict access to information stored within ACOS. ACOS The ACOS system must be used to document the management of Human Sources. ACOS assists in the management and deployment of Human Sources and the recording and sharing of intelligence. Unrestricted ACOS access is limited to: • the Central Registrar and HSMU staff assisting the Central Registrar; • the Inspector of the Crime Support & Services Division (oversight of the Central Registrar); and • designated positions of the Internal Affairs Unit. Unrestricted access to persons outside of the above parameters requires the approval of the Commander, State Crime. The Human Source management process is designed to: • safeguard the Human Source through the application of appropriate risk management processes and strategies; • identify High Risk Human Source, ensuring appropriate risk assessments are undertaken prior to registration; • ensure appropriate actions are undertaken to protect the identity of a Human Source whilst being aware that in certain circumstances, the court may exercise discretion and require the identity of the Human Source to be revealed; • maximise the benefits to WA Police Force and the community of information obtained; • protect WA Police Force employees from false allegations of corruption or impropriety arising out of dealings with Human Sources; • provide objective supervision and assessment of the relationship between WA Police employees and Human Source; • ensure the correct application for payments, whether monetary or otherwise, are appropriately dealt with in accordance with the Manual and other guidelines that are associated with the reward/benefit processes; • ensure management and expenditure of working expenses is in accordance with this Manual; and • prevent unwarranted duplication of Human Source registrations.
rhsm|huma-sour-mana-SUPPORTING-GUIDELINE: HSMU maintains the ACOS Source Management Guidelines containing a comprehensive system user guide and contemporary user-friendly guidelines to achieve Human Source management processes. Users are to refer to and follow these guidelines. If the Guidelines contradict the Manual, then the Manual is the prevailing authority. HSMU staff are available to assist with ACOS training. Please contact the Central Registrar for further information.
rhsm|huma-sour-mana-EXEMPTIONS-FROM-USE-: Members of the Internal Affairs Unit, Crime Stoppers and employees on secondment to other agencies that have their own Human Source management systems, are not required to register Human Sources under the procedures outlined in this Manual. HUMAN SOURCE (Source) A person who for any reward or identifiable motivation, supplies information to a police employee on matters of interest or facilitates an investigative or intelligence strategy and has an expectation that their identity will be protected. The Central Registrar will determine whether a person is a Source or a witness for the purposes of determining ongoing management utilising this manual and to assist with the issue of disclosure. If a Source is supplying intelligence/information, they will be treated as a Source and managed on ACOS.
rhsm|huma-sour-mana-HUMAN-SOURCE-VERSUS-: Should the Source also be determined to be a witness, all matters relevant to an investigation that the witness is material to, must be recorded upon normal investigative practice systems. Should the investigating officer or handler of the witness, identify information in the statement that should be disseminated, they should sanitise the information and record it on the IDM system. The investigating officer or handler should request that the details of names in sanitised IDM are withheld until full disclosure of the statement has occurred. Should it be proposed that the witness become involved as a Civilian Participant in an authorised Controlled Operation (not as a witness), or provide ongoing information, then they must be registered on the ACOS system. Any concerns as to a person’s status or potential utilisation in a Controlled Operation should be directed to the Central Registrar at the earliest opportunity. Please refer to the information provided under the heading ‘Management of Human Source’, later in the Manual. Responsibility for the preparation of Non-Disclosure Orders and/or affidavits for Public Interest Immunity claims, remain with the investigator and/or the Handler under the provision of Section 138 Criminal Procedures Act. The Central Registrar must review all affidavits prepared for non-disclosure orders prior to service. Any concerns should be directed to the Central Registrar at the earliest opportunity.
