Forensic officers know the futility of collecting hair or fiber samples after a roomful of officers have shed all over the scene7. The role of detectives in protecting incident scenes cannot be overemphasised. These individuals are ultimately responsible for the investigation. Investigators who conscientiously limit the number of visitors to an incident scene may save themselves a great deal of legwork8. The simplest and most productive way for detectives to discourage incident scene contamination is to set a good example. If a senior detective walks around an incident scene at will, opening drawers and rifling through closets, what could be the harm in other officers doing the same? If a Detective Sergeant fails to implement a running sheet to record scene visitors, what is there to limit ‘visits’ by curious officers? It is in the best interests of detectives to set a good example and to make sure others follow it9. The WA Police Force have adopted a broad context model in relation to incident scene procedures and the principles can be applied to all incidents where evidence may be found.
rop|inci-scen-mana-PRIMARY-SCENE: Incident scenes can be divided into two types. The first type is the primary scene and is defined as: ‘The location where the incident actually took place’ INCIDENT SCENE SCENARIO #1 An offender breaks into a house and stabs the occupant with a knife, the knife penetrates the subclavian artery and the victim dies immediately. The offender takes the body and places it into the rear of his vehicle. The offender then drives from the scene. At some point the offender discards his shirt because it is covered in blood. The offender drives the body to an area of bushland and places the body in a shallow grave. The offender drives to a nearby building site and throws the knife into a large bin. Next the offender drives to a local shopping centre and leaves the car in the car park. The offender is arrested a short time later.
rop|inci-scen-mana-SECONDARY-SCENE: The other type of incident scene is referred to as the secondary scene and is defined as: ‘An area other than where the incident took place where any physical material leading to establishment of the incident is located’. 7 DH Garrison, as above n 7. 8 DH Garrison, as above n 7. 9 DH Garrison, as above n 7. Given the above scenario there are no less than six incident scenes involved. The primary scene being the house where the offence was committed and secondary scenes being: • the vehicle • carpark where the vehicle was left • the site where the shirt was disposed • the body disposal site • the site the knife was disposed • the offender. Each of the identified scenes must be processed in compliance with the incident scene procedures to ensure the evidence remains uncorrupted. By employing a logical and step by step approach to an incident scene, fewer mistakes will be made and evidence will not be overlooked, which will result in more thorough investigations.
rop|inci-scen-mana-INITIAL-ATTENDANCE-RE: The responsibilities of initial responders to an incident are to preserve life and to control suspects and witnesses. Then, shifting their focus somewhat, responding officers must take steps to preserve the integrity of the scene's physical boundaries10. The above enumerates some of the roles of the attending officers upon arriving at the scene, but diligence must be displayed whilst enroute to the incident scene as the process may start well before their arrival. Some initial information will need to be ascertained prior to attendance at the incident scene to ensure that the incident scene procedures can be applied appropriately and effectively. Investigators should attempt to obtain all information available enroute and it should include but not be exclusive to: • nature of offence • exact location • when committed • any suspects or vehicles - full description • direction of travel • time report received • name, address and telephone number of the person reporting the incident. Gathering as much information as possible prior to attending the incident scene will assist in the most appropriate application of the incident scene principles. 10 DH Garrison, as above n7.
rop|inci-scen-mana-INCIDENT-SCENE-OBJECT: On attendance at the incident scene, detectives need to apply the objectives of incident scene management. The initial objectives for police attending an incident scene are: • Define • Contain • Control. Define, contain and control is the catch-cry for WA Police Force when attending an incident scene. They are simple principles and as such can be applied to all types of incidents. To be able to contain and control an incident scene, it must first be ascertained where the scene is so that boundaries can be established. The detective will need to assess the scene and make an appraisal of where evidence is or is likely to be located. Remember at most scenes the offender has had to arrive and depart, those routes may afford evidence. Do not be solely focussed on the immediate area of the offence but think laterally and give consideration to what has occurred.
rop|inci-scen-mana-THE-PRICE-OF-GREATNES: The initial attending officers at any incident scene will be faced with a myriad of situations; some scenes will be calm and others chaotic. The responsibility for the incident scene management falls squarely on the shoulders of the senior officer first attending. This responsibility is non-negotiable and will remain with the incumbent until they are relieved by a more senior officer or a detective. Sir Winston Churchill When considering the size of the scene, the general rule is to make the scene too big rather than too small. This is because once the scene is contained the integrity of any evidence outside of the scene cannot be guaranteed. It is a lot easier to scale down an incident scene than it is to increase it. Keep an open mind; incident scenes are sometimes CRIME SCENE STAGING altered by offenders in an attempt to conceal or alter the A clever murderer may very well nature of the incident (see inset)11. But a systematic and accurate investigation will reveal the it to avoid further contamination. A scene is contained homicidal intent. by removing all people from the scene, including police Arne Svensson and Otto Wendel. and using physical barriers such as scene tape, motor vehicles or other objects. 11 Arne Svensson and Otto Wendel, Techniques of Crime Scene Investigation, (1st ed, Elsevier: Chatswood, 1974) Scene guards are appointed to ensure that no unauthorised person enters the scene (scene tape or other physical barriers are not effective without guards). It may also be necessary to consider arranging protection of evidence from the weather if required. The containment of the scene will of course vary from scene to scene, however the basic principles will remain the same. Examples of the variance experienced during scene containment can be seen below. Example one: Consider a knife located in the middle of a room at the scene of a stabbing. The attending officers may wish to seal off the entire area with police and incident scene tape to ensure that any DNA or blood evidence can be preserved. Example two: Now consider a knife located in the same position at the scene of a shoplifting. An officer may decide simply to place a chair over the item and have only one officer standing guard. This may be because the officer only deems that the knife will be valuable for fingerprint evidence. As can be seen above, both examples are the same and identical principles have been applied, but due to the difference in crime type and evidential value the level of containment is different. Control of the scene is the final initial objective of incident scene management. Diligence in defining and containing a scene mean nothing if the scene is not controlled correctly. A clearly recognisable entry and exit point is designated for use by staff when entering or leaving the scene. Scene guards will have been placed in position during the containment phase. These scene guards are to ensure that non-authorised persons are denied access to the scene. The designated scene guards will also be required to maintain a comprehensive running sheet to record all persons entering and leaving the scene. The running sheet entries will include at minimum, the name, rank and regimental number of all police who enter and the name, occupation and organisation of non-police personnel. Diligent incident scene control dictates that all occurrences at the incident scene should be recorded on the running sheet for later review. If the offence committed is serious then only specially appointed officers from the investigation team and those performing a forensic function should be allowed to enter. Assembly points may be considered appropriate at some incident scenes. An assembly point is simply an area where police and other services may gather to ensure that the incident scene is not compromised and that access to the scene is not restricted. If the situation allows, the assembly point should be away from the scene. The purpose of these objectives is simple; they are to minimise contamination of evidence and maximise evidentiary value. Every person that enters and leaves the scene affects the scene. If the entry is required in the course of the investigation then a record needs to be kept to ensure that any unexpected evidence located can be explained i.e. a footprint made by a forensic officer within the scene. If there is no record of the entry then doubt can be cast upon how it got there.
rop|inci-scen-mana-PRINCIPLE-OF-EXCHANGE: Dr Edmund Locard is famous for his ‘Principle of Exchange’. Essentially the principle defines contamination and how it can occur in a forensic context. The principles of Locard’s theory are as follows: • Every contact leaves its traces. Whenever one surface comes in contact with another, part of each will be transferred to the other. • When an incident scene is vacated by an offender it is 100% pure. • Purity is eroded every time a person enters or leaves an incident scene. It is interesting to note that although Locard is credited with these principles he never actually phrased his theory in the above manner. Locard recited his theory in a much more verbose manner. It was in fact Locard’s contemporaries and students that condensed his theory into ‘every contact leaves its trace’; this phrase was seen first in 1940 in the publication Police and Crime-Detection. The bane of forensic science is contamination; it causes evidentiary discrepancies and unexplained results. However contamination is almost unavoidable in most cases; it is the reduction of contamination that is the concern of the primary incident scene procedures. No matter how strictly incident scene management is applied there will always be occasions where contamination is unavoidable. The preservation of life always takes priority over the preservation of evidence. The primary responsibilities of initial responders to an incident are to preserve life and to control suspects and witnesses. Then, shifting their focus somewhat, responding officers must take steps to preserve the integrity of the scene's physical boundaries12. The preservation of property can also be an important consideration. An incident scene essentially precludes members of the public from accessing their own property. Situations may occur where members of the public wish to access their property whist it is within the boundaries of an incident scene. The incident scene controller will need to evaluate the need for the property to be accessed against the potential loss or contamination of evidence.
rop|inci-scen-mana-INCIDENT-SCENE-POWERS: The power to control an incident scene is primarily derived from two Western Australian statutes, the Criminal Investigation Act13 (CIA) and the Coroners Act14. The CIA is the primary Act used as it provides the power to secure any incident scene where evidence may be located. The Coroners Act provides similar powers but only when the incident relates to a death and only to the location the death has occurred. Division 4 of the Criminal Investigation Act 2006 provides a legally enforceable means by which members can effectively secure, maintain and manage an incident scene through the 12 DH Garrison, as above n 7. 13 Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA). 14 Coroners Act 1996 (WA). establishment of a ‘protected forensic area’. A ‘protected forensic area’ can be established in public open areas, public places, private places and vehicles. More than one ‘protected forensic area’ can be established in respect to any one offence or suspected offence. The establishment of a protected forensic area does not authorise a search of the area to which it relates. Rather, it is a means by which an area can be protected and preserved until the authority to search is obtained via – • Informed consent from the occupier to search. • A search warrant. • A senior officer approval (for which a search warrant must ultimately be obtained). While section 46 of the Criminal Investigation Act 2006 deals with the establishment of a ‘protected forensic area’, it is the application of other provisions within the Act that give rise to the authority to do so. Some terms used within this Act have more than one definition and care should be taken to ensure that when a section of the Act is being read the appropriate definition is applied. “Authorised” in Section 47(1) Criminal Investigation Act 2006 in relation to a protected forensic area, • Means authorised by the officer in charge of the investigation at the protected forensic area; “Disturb” in Section 3 Criminal Investigation Act 2006 • includes to damage, destroy, interfere with and remove; “Place” in Section 3 Criminal Investigation Act 2006 • means any land, building, structure, tent or mobile home or a part of any land, building, structure, tent or mobile home; “Public open area” in Section 3 Criminal Investigation Act 2006 • An area that is part of a road open to and used by the public; or • An area of land • To which the public has access, whether on payment or not; and • On which there is no building, structure, tent or mobile home, and It does not matter if the area is the whole or a part of a surveyed lot or of an unsurveyed piece of land, or, if the area is part of such a lot, there is a building, structure, tent or mobile home on some other part15. Section 46 CIA provides the rules for the establishment of a protected forensic area. This section applies if another section in this act authorises an officer to establish a protected forensic area under this section. • In order to establish the protected forensic area, the officer must take reasonable steps to notify people of the existence and boundaries of the area16. • The area of the protected forensic area must not be greater than is reasonably necessary for the purposes for which it is established17. 15 Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA). 16 CIA, as above n15, s 46. 17 CIA, as above n15, s 46. • The boundaries of the protected forensic area may be altered at any time18. • Whilst a protected forensic area is established, the officer who established the area, or another officer involved in the investigation, must remain at the area. • An officer must disestablish the protected forensic area when the purposes for which it was established cease to exist. • More than one protected forensic area may be established in respect of any one offence or suspected offence or in a place or vehicle. Section 47 CIA provides the powers for police officers to take actions to protect the integrity of a protected forensic area. Section 47(2) CIA allows that an officer at an established protected forensic area may take reasonable actions or give orders to: • Prevent a thing relevant to the offence to which the area relates from being concealed or disturbed; • Protect the safety of any person who is in or may enter the area19; • Secure the area against unauthorised disturbance20; • Prevent an unauthorised person, animal or vehicle from disturbing the area21; • Restrict entry to the area to authorised people, animals, and vehicles22; • Remove an unauthorised person, animal or vehicle23. • If the area is established in or around a vehicle, to prevent the vehicle from being moved24. Section 16 allows for the use of force to protect the PFA, and section 153 creates an offence not to follow an order given. E.g. order to leave PFA. Under this section a police officer who has not been given permission by the officer in charge of the investigation to enter the protected forensic area would be an unauthorised person. Under Section 16 reasonable force can be used to facilitate any of the above. Section 47(3) provides that after police establish a protected forensic area in a place that is not a public open area and before they: • Have the informed consent of the occupier, or • before they have a search warrant, • that under certain circumstances they may with the approval of a senior officer not involved in the case exercise any power that could be exercised under a search warrant. In making the application the investigating officer will need to supply the senior officer information relating to: • What the officer needs to do at the scene. 18 CIA, as above n15, s 46. 19 CIA, as above n15, s 47. 20 CIA, as above n15, s 47. 21 CIA, as above n15, s 47. 22 CIA, as above n15, s 47. 23 CIA, as above n15, s 47. 24 CIA, as above n15, s 47. • A detailed description of the area to be protected. • The reasons why the protected forensic area needs to be established before consent or a search warrant can be obtained. Where the authorisation of a senior officer has been obtained, an officer involved in the investigation has all the powers as if a search warrant had been issued for the place.
rop|inci-scen-mana-SENIOR-OFFICER-APPROV: A person is seriously assaulted in their home, they attend the local country hospital. You attend the hospital and speak with the complainant who advises you the offence occurred at 2 Giles Street. Shortly after speaking with you the complainant lapses into a coma. You attend the address, there is no person home so you cannot get informed consent. Through the front window you can see a small amount of blood on a lounge and upturned chairs. There is blood on the open front steps leading into the back patio, where you observe a shoe print in the blood and it appears it is about to rain. In this circumstance it would be appropriate to establish a PFA and obtain Senior Officer Approval (SOA) under Section 47(3) to deal with the blood and any other thing relevant to the offence that may be disturbed by the impending rain. You deal with the evidence outside under the SOA. As you have set up a PFA you would now obtain a search warrant to deal with any other thing/s relevant to the offence inside the house. In every instance that a police officer obtains senior officer approval to exercise the powers of a search warrant within an established ‘protected forensic area’ the police officer must cause or make application for a search warrant to be made as soon as is reasonably practicable and within 6 hours of the establishment of the protected forensic area. Failure to obtain a search warrant within 6 hours will result in the disestablishment of the ‘protected forensic area’. It may also render the evidence obtained inadmissible. Investigating officers will need to make accurate notes of the times that: • The protected forensic area was established. • Consent was withdrawn. • Application for search warrant was made. • The search warrant was granted or refused. • When the protected forensic area was disestablished. These times should be corroborated and recorded by a second person. In the event that an occupier withdraws their consent to enter, search and/or establish a ‘protected forensic area’, members are to cease any search being conducted and consider the need to make application for a search warrant. This is to be done to protect the admissibility of any evidence that may be found subsequent to the withdrawal of consent. Entry to the premises can be made or maintained under section 40 if the incident is a serious offence. This instruction does not apply if an immediate threat of harm to life or serious damage to property is likely if a thing so sought is not immediately found and seized. Powers to seize things in these circumstances exists at section 35 of the CIA. Where a ‘protected forensic area’ is established without a search warrant and in absence of an occupier’s consent to enter, search and/or establish a ‘protected forensic area’, police are not to commence the search and consider the need to make application for a search warrant. This is to be done to protect the admissibility of any evidence that may be found subsequent to the withdrawal of consent. This instruction does not apply if an immediate threat of harm to life or serious damage to property is likely if a thing so sought is not immediately found and seized. Powers to seize things in these circumstances exists at section 35 of the CIA. Where applicable a member may also make application to a senior officer in accordance with section 47 of the CIA. For serious or major incident scenes, the first officer to arrive at the scene is generally appointed the role of Scene Controller. This person has the ultimate responsibility of ensuring the scene is adequately defined, contained and controlled until they are relieved by someone from the investigation team. The Scene Controller will establish a control point or command post - outside the incident scene in a safe location. If a suspect or offender is present at the scene, the Scene Controller is also responsible for detaining and managing them appropriately. They are responsible for ensuring that witnesses who are at the scene are identified, names, addresses and contact details are obtained. Witnesses should be asked to remain at the control point. Witnesses also need to be managed appropriately: • Separate to minimise corruption of evidence. • Obtain full contact details. • Brief description of evidence. • Assess welfare.
rop|inci-scen-mana-SUBSEQUENT-INCIDENT-S: Once a scene has been defined, contained and controlled the risk of contamination should be greatly reduced – the evidentiary value has been preserved. Investigators will then be required to complete the subsequent incident scene objectives. These objectives will be completed by the systematic review and examination of the scene in order to: • Establish if an offence has been committed. • Establish the identity of the offender or witnesses. • Collect physical evidence for analysis. In the event of a major incident, scenes of crime officer/s (SOCO) will be advised by the Police Operations Centre (POC) and will attend along with other specialist units if required. The scene should be defined, contained and controlled by the scene controller until they arrive. Do not enter the scene unnecessarily and do not seize exhibits unless there is an urgent need to do so. At the completion of incident scene attendance you should have photographed the scene and the exhibits in situ. Dr Hans Gross wrote the following passage and it explains in essence the rationale for photography of the scene. So long as one only looks on the scene, it is impossible, whatever the care, time, and attention bestowed, to detect all the details, and especially note the incongruities: but these strike us at once when we set ourselves to describe the picture on paper as exactly and clearly as possible25. …the ‘defects of the situation’ are just those contradictions, those improbabilities, which occur when one desires to represent the situation as something quite different from what it really is, and this with the very best intentions and the purest belief that one has worked with all of the forethought, craft, and consideration imaginable26. The construction of a scene sketch is also a valuable tool when processing the incident scene. The sketch can be used to indicate where exhibits or areas of interest were located. Should the need arise it can serve as a detailed reconstruction upon which measurements may be entered. Should this be the case then the investigator needs to be mindful of the need for a datum point. A datum point is a fixed reference point within the scene from which all measurements are taken. If no datum point suggests itself then an artificial one may be used27. All witnesses should be identified and statements obtained, if it is impractical to obtain a statement then the witnesses’ details should be recorded so that a statement can be obtained at the earliest convenience. Put simply at the completion of the processing of the scene the investigator should have gleaned all possible information that the scene has to offer. SUMMARY Incident scenes often yield forensic evidence that leads to the apprehension of dangerous criminals. Perhaps just as often, though, potentially valuable evidence is destroyed or rendered useless by careless behavior at the scene. Detailed training goes some way to removing that issue, however, the ultimate responsibility rests with managers, supervisors, and investigators to reinforce positive conduct by setting a good example for other officers to follow28. 25 H Gross et al, Criminal Psychology: A Manual for Judges, Practitioners, and Students (1st ed, California, Little, Brown, 1911) 439. 26 H Gross et al, as above n25. 27 Max M. Houck and Jay A. Siegel, as above n2, 29. 28 DH Garrison, as above n7. The incident scene is arguably the most important facet of the investigation and deserves fastidious attention. optional ............................................................................ 21 ANNEXURE ONE – HEALTH CHECK PROCEDURE FOR ISU ....................................... 22 ANNEXURE TWO – HOW TO IDENTIFY CRIME FILES FOR REVIEW ........................... 23 ANNEXURE THREE – CRIME FILE REVIEW RECORD (GOOD GOVERNANCE) ......... 29 ANNEXURE FOUR – IHC ASSESSMENT KEY ................................................................ 30 ANNEXURE FIVE – CRR OUTCOME CODES ................................................................. 32 ANNEXURE SIX – AVROI IHC ASSESSMENT KEY ........................................................ 33 ANNEXURE SEVEN – WITNESS STATEMENT IHC ASSESSMENT KEY ...................... 36 SCOPE This Investigation Health Check (IHC) Manual has been produced to assist all Western Australia Police Force (WA Police Force) personnel understand what constitutes an IHC and what its purpose is. It explains the IHC intent, the framework; officer roles/responsibilities and the procedure to assess each criterion. Supervisors and business unit managers are ultimately responsible for the efficient and effective delivery of policing services in accordance with agency standards. The WA Police Force investigative standards are governed by the Western Australia Police Force Investigation Doctrine (the Doctrine)1, Police Manual policy and relevant legislation. The Doctrine is the agency’s over-arching investigative standards document which also explains investigation ownership. The standards are further explained within: • Police Manual, Investigative Standards IN-01.00 • The Doctrine – Practical Guide2 • WA Police Force Investigative Interviewing Manuals3 • Crime Recording User Guide4 and • The Integrated Staged Brief Process5. This manual describes the minimum investigative practice standards to be employed when aligning practice with the Doctrine. It is designed to be used as a guide by Officers in Charge (OICs) and their delegates, to ensure agency IHC consistency. What is the purpose of a Health Check? Agency IHCs have been implemented to determine the investigative standard of a particular business unit by examining their performance relevant to the application of the CRIME and The5KIS investigation models. The identified outcomes are compared to agency standards. The intention of a IHC is to identify and acknowledge good practice whilst identifying and making recommendations for improvement. The term ‘Business Unit’ refers to all WA Police Force organisational areas performing an investigative function. The IHC will examine the following: • Workload analysis (Investigative Standards Unit only) • Examination of repositories (hard copy and electronic) for compliance • Investigation management including supervisor input • Investigation evaluation and supervisor review • Crime recording and reporting (CRR) • Application of The5KIS by supervisors and investigating officers (IOs) 1 Western Australia Police Force, WA Police Investigation Doctrine (v2.2, Perth, WA Police Force, 2021). 2 Western Australia Police Force, The Doctrine – Practical Guide (v2.0, Perth, WA Police Force, 2020). 3 Western Australia Police Force, Investigative Standards Unit intranet site. 4 Western Australia Police Force, Crime Recording User Guide (v2.1, Perth, WA Police, 2018). 5 Western Australia Police Force, Integrated Staged Brief Process (v4.9, Perth, WA Police, 2024). • Hard copy CRIME file (HCCF) quality, content and compilation • Investigative interviewing (suspects and witnesses) • Aspects of disclosure, in particular: - 1. The endorsement to charge process 2. Statement of Material Facts (SMF) 3. Unified Physical Material List (UPML) and 4. Unified Witness List (UWL) • Opportunities for improvement. At the conclusion of a IHC a report is produced which: • Describes the level of compliance with the WA Police Force investigative practices • Identifies instances of good practice • Provides investigative performance feedback and recommendations to improve police response and investigative practice/management to enhance investigation outcomes. Timely and Quality Investigations + Accountable Prosecutions Advancements in technology and capabilities promote innovative investigations to solve crime in a timely manner. Utilising the Doctrine will also ensure a quality investigation is conducted. Critical to this process is the quality of ongoing supervision and ownership. A brief of evidence (brief) is produced at the completion of an investigation where a charge is to be preferred. Theoretically, where a charge is preferred after a quality investigation this should cause a quality brief to be compiled. The presentation of a quality and thorough brief of evidence reflects on the professionalism of the investigating officer, supervisor and OIC, with diligent and ethical prosecutions providing a balanced presentation of all facts and evidence. During the IHC, criteria relevant to investigations and briefs are assessed for adherence to legislation and standards.
rop|inve-heal-chec-ROLES-AND-RESPONSIBIL: District/Divisional Management Teams District/Divisional Officers have a responsibility to manage investigative adherence to the agency’s standards as described within the Doctrine, policy and legislation. Compliance should be measured by intermittent internal quality investigation assessments to ensure business units within their span of control, comply. All officers within District/Divisional offices must appreciate the Doctrine is the agency’s overarching standard regarding investigative quality and is not optional in its application6. 6 Western Australia Police Force, The Doctrine – Practical Guide (v2.1, Perth: WA Police, 2021) 28. Specific District Officer roles and accountabilities include: • Promote and ensure the compliance of the Doctrine within their respective district/divisions • Engaging with Investigative Standards Unit (ISU) to assist in improving district/divisional investigation standards • Ensure compliance with relevant statutory requirements, agency policy and procedures in respect of the Doctrine • Responding to and addressing any recommendations (where applicable) • Supporting the conduct of IHC by OICs as directed within the Good Governance Practice Guide. Officer in Charge The OIC plays an integral part in the HC process. OICs and supervisors must commit to maintaining professional investigative skills and knowledge commensurate with their role in the agency. Additionally, they must promote team ownership and accountability for quality investigations and adherence to the investigative Doctrine (5KIS) including ILA principles, to conduct thorough investigations and achieve timely results. Specific OIC roles and accountabilities include: • Having a comprehensive understanding of the Doctrine and its intent • Ensure compliance with relevant statutory requirements, agency policy and procedures in respect of the Doctrine and • Comply with obligations as described in the Good Governance Practice Guide, which dictates bi-annual OIC IHCs. Investigative Standards Unit (ISU) The ISU IHC regime is intended to assist districts/divisions and local business units by: • Reviewing, evaluating and reporting on investigation practices and standards across the agency • Providing feedback and guidance to business unit managers and district/divisional management teams in a consultative manner • Identifying training needs in respect to investigation standards. In partnership with stakeholders and business units, the ISU has a shared responsibility to: • Review and evaluate workplace investigation practices and standards • Provide specialist advice and support in respect to investigation standards • Suggest appropriate remedial action to achieve continuous improvement • Engage with business units to assist with IHC recommendations • Identify business units and practices at risk of compromising investigation standards • Report to executive on compliance and agency investigation standards.
rop|inve-heal-chec-HEALTH-CHECK-PROCESS-: IHCs can be conducted by any person who has the knowledge, understanding and experience relating to investigations and how the Doctrine applies. Familiarity with the Doctrine is essential. This manual has been produced to assist the reviewer to understand the process and procedure to carry out an IHC. The IHCs conducted by ISU are more involved in relation to planning, logistics and reporting than those conducted by OICs or their delegates, however the results should be the same. The assessment criteria and standards have been clearly identified and will be explained further in this document. The IHC process, as it relates to ISU, is subject to Annexure One. Process for OIC or nominated Supervisor The OIC of an investigative business unit must conduct IHCs on a six-monthly basis7. In order to assist the OIC (or delegate) comply with that obligation, this manual will describe the process. Selection of investigation An ideal selection of investigations consists of a mixture of active, filed (including no charge or no offender detected) and those resulting in an offender being processed. Of the investigations which result in the creation of a brief, a combination of guilty and not guilty is recommended. Instructions for identifying the relevant files are detailed in Annexure Two. Investigations should be no more than one year old from the date of selection. Business units with low investigation turn over may need to expand this time frame. Record the details of the investigation on a sheet as per the format suggested in Annexure Three. This document is evidence to Management Audit Unit that the bi-annual IHC was conducted. Reviewing the investigation The Incident Management System (IMS), Prosecution System, Digital Evidence Management System (DEMS), the business unit’s electronic CRIME file management and hard copy CRIME file (HCCF) repository are the usual sources of information for an IHC. Specialist units which use other electronic repositories, such as VIPER, will need to access their particular repository for information. The chosen investigations can then be reviewed in accordance with the criteria described further in this document. A record of the review should be made with the use of the IHC documents subject to the Annexures Four, Six and Seven of this manual. 7 Western Australia Police Force, Good Governance Practice Guide 2023/24 (v1.9: Perth, WA Police Force, July 2023) 13, 39 - 40
rop|inve-heal-chec-HEALTH-CHECK-CRITERIA: This portion of the manual describes the criteria a IHC will examine. The criteria are listed as they appear in the Investigation Health Check assessment key, Annexure Four. These tools are available to assist business area managers and supervisors measure their business area’s compliance with the Doctrine. At the completion of an IHC, it is recommended that all tools used to conduct a IHC be retained (preferably scanned) in the event any observations/comments require clarification. All assessments tools are available on the Investigative Standards Unit intranet site and included as annexures to this document. IMS Management The Incident Management System (IMS) is corporately approved as the electronic platform for managing investigations. There is a community expectation and a statutory obligation for the agency to accurately record and store investigative information in perpetuity. The Police Manual sets the standards and protocols required for the use of IMS (CF – IMS Case and File Management)8. The Police Manual also places an obligation on personnel, supervisors and managers to use IMS. The formal protocols are designed to guide personnel on the requirements of an investigation. It is intended to increase efficiency, performance, accountability and service delivery. Approved exceptions are IDM and VIPER, however, an IMS report must still exist with these exceptions; the IDM or VIPER reference must appear within the IMS report. IMS management is a crucial component of a IHC and source of information concerning many of the criteria reviewed by the IHC team. The business unit demonstrates IMS management by ensuring that investigations are allocated, attended to and filed in a timely manner. Hard Copy CRIME file repository All WA Police Force investigative business areas are to maintain a central hard copy CRIME file (HCCF) repository for the retention and good management of CRIME Files9. The repository should have three categories: • Active Files: investigations which are actively being investigated • Files Awaiting Court: investigations where there is a charged suspect(s) and the matter has not been finalised in court • Files Completed: investigations that have been resolved and not yet archived. Where it is impractical to maintain a central file repository due to the nature and size of the investigations conducted by a business unit, it is incumbent upon the OIC and supervisor(s) to ensure an equivalent system exists where all files are readily accessible and accountable. Archived CRIME files should be correctly referenced within IMS to the fact they have been archived; including archive box barcode number (i.e., CASE FILE ARCHIVED PP025428).10 8 Western Australia Police Force, Police Manual CF – IMS Case and File Management (Perth: WA Police Force, 2014). 9 Western Australia Police Force, The Doctrine – Practical Guide (v2.0, Perth: WA Police Force, 2020) 34. 10 Western Australia Police Force, Police Manual CF-02.04 Recording an Operation in IMS, (Perth: WA Police Force, 2014) The IHC will assess this component to ensure that at any given time the physical location of any hard copy CRIME file can be identified. 1. Initial Allocation There is a duty for supervisors to make quality decisions based on prioritisation, categorisation and allocation to ensure matters are investigated in a timely and efficient manner. The allocation of an investigation is not to be delayed for administrative purposes. Allocation of investigations is based on the following criteria: • The category of the investigation • The business unit resource capability • The skill and knowledge of the investigator and/or investigation team required to investigate the offence (iLevel)11. The IHC will assess this component by reviewing the IMS report to ascertain the category (confined, compound or complex), establish whether the investigation is being conducted by the appropriately resourced business unit and the investigation allocated to an appropriate iLevel of investigator. An example of a good entry which covers all three components of this criteria is “P3 confined investigation, assigned to PC Smith – Team 3 Cannington Police Station” Potential Score: 3 marks (one mark each for category, business unit resource capability and correct iLevel) 2. Correct Offence/s Identified Crime Recording and Reporting responsibility is agency wide, from the creation of a crime IR in IMS, to the production of strategic, operational and tactical crime reports. ‘WA Police Force personnel who create, edit or finalise a crime IR’12 within the Incident Management System (IMS) perform the function of crime recording. It is the responsibility of supervisors and managers to review and monitor crime recording to ensure compliance with the agency standard. It is important the offence listed on the IMS report is accurate and appropriate in accordance with initial information supplied. Ensure the offence listed in the IMS report is the most appropriate based on information supplied within the CAD report and narrative of the IMS report. The IHC will compare the IMS narrative and the CAD report to identify the offence/s described. Occasionally, initially identified offences may be incorrect, the IHC will also identify whether substituted offences have been identified in IMS. Potential Score: 1 mark (for compliance) 11 Western Australia Police Force, WA Police Investigation Doctrine (v2.2, Perth: WA Police Force, 2021) 12 – 13 12 Western Australia Police Force, Police Manual CQ-01.00 Crime Recording and Reporting (Perth: WA Police Force, 2018) 3. The 5KIS The5KIS refer to the five key investigative strategies to be considered in every investigation (Physical Material, Witnesses, Intelligence, Public Awareness, and Suspects). Use of The5KIS should be inclusive of ‘Identify Locate Associate’ (ILA) principles, combining proven investigation techniques with innovation to solve crime faster. The application of The5KIS prompts investigators to identify all possible avenues of inquiry. After identifying potential lines of inquiry, investigative actions are created, at which point The5KIS can be used to collate and prioritise these actions. The5KIS can be applied in any order, concurrently or in isolation of each other. The overriding principle is all of The5KIS must be considered during every investigation.13 The IHC will assess this component by reviewing IMS reports and CRIME files to ensure The5KIS review is conducted during the investigation, along with each strategy having been considered, recorded and actioned where appropriate. The IHC assessment is based on the value of The5KIS use as a briefing tool. A summary reflecting consideration of each of The5KIS should appear within the Running Sheet or Investigation Action Register (IAR) of the IMS report. Consideration of the initial 5KIS assessment can also include any SILVA Hub (or other approved system) running sheet entries which have been extracted and uploaded to IMS as a PDF document. Potential score: 10 marks (1 mark for addressing each strategy of The5KIS and 1 mark each for quality) 4. Running Sheet The running sheet is possibly the single most important document in a CRIME file as it records a chronology of all inquiries conducted by investigators. Running sheets provide a record that can easily be audited of who did what and when and are a useful tool in the event of a handover of the investigation. They can also serve as a justification at a later stage if the methodology or conclusions become subject of a complaint or a review.14 The running sheet should include: • Times and dates of investigative actions, action outcomes, events, correspondence etc. IMS now incorporates the Investigation Action Register (IAR) which automatically populates the IMS running sheet (see criteria 5 – Investigation Action Register for information concerning the content of an IAR) • The officer’s name, regimental number and the detail of the duty they performed • Supervisor input including direction and rationale of decisions • Refer to the The5KIS as common vernacular for such purposes as briefing/status reports • Clear referencing of digital evidence and its location within another system (E.g., 10 scene photographs taken by PDXXXXX and uploaded to DEMS. Viewable via ID:
rop|inve-heal-chec-010823-0700-XXXXX: • Record decisions made during the investigation.15 13 Western Australia Police Force, The Doctrine – Practical Guide (v2.0, Perth: WA Police Force 2020) 13 - 14 Western Australia Police Force, WA Police Investigation Doctrine (v2.2, Perth: WA Police Force, 2021) 5 15 Western Australia Police Force, Police Manual CF-02.04 Recording an Operation on IMS, CF-02.09 Critical Decisions, (Perth: WA Police Force, 2014) The person conducting the IHC should assess this criterion by reviewing the IMS and/or any other documented running sheet (such as handwritten or attached SILVA Hub entries) to determine whether the reviewer can comprehensively track the course of the investigation and understand the reason/s for any decisions made along the way. With the introduction of reporting systems such as Power BI, there is often a requirement to enter specific IMS running sheet or IAR headings, including ‘Supervisor Review’ and ‘Arrest Attempt’. These entries should still include sufficient detail and not be used purely to satisfy an administrative purpose. A good running sheet should leave no doubt, in the mind of an independent reviewer, how the investigation progressed and the rationale of decisions made along the way. Where a lack of information exists in the mind of the reader, then the quality should be scored accordingly. Potential score: 10 marks (for detail and quality of the content) 5. Investigation Action Register (IAR) The IAR is a crucial component of an investigation and is recommended to be used for all investigations, however it is only mandated for investigations into purely indictable offences16 or when an incident report is to be re-allocated to another business unit17. A supervisor may also direct the investigating officer to use an IAR. Overall, the IAR is a useful supervision and self-management tool with the ability to record: • A defined workload • Clear direction • The ability to plan • Identify and define timeframes • Consideration of lines of inquiry even if subsequently not pursued. The recording of investigative actions is not intended to be a cumbersome process, rather it is used to inform investigators as what has been done and what needs to be done. Accurate and detailed recording of investigative actions assists in identifying the priority of incomplete investigative actions. A thorough list of investigative actions is also beneficial when briefing supervisors and handing over the investigation to another unit18. Although not always mandatory, the use of an IAR is recognised as best practice and recommended, where applicable. The IHC will assess this component by determining the jurisdiction of the offence under investigation and, if purely indictable or to be transferred, ensure that an IAR exists, is up to date and being used as an investigative tool. The relevant IAR can be located within the IMS report. 16 Western Australia Police Force, Crime File Compilation and Management (v2.1, Perth, WA Police, 2023) 17 Western Australia Police Force, The Doctrine – Practical Guide (v2.0, Perth, WA Police, 2020) 12 18 Western Australia Police Force, as above n30 Where mandatory and an IAR exists then quality needs to be assessed; the existence of an action item needs to be supported with a clear task and appropriate result; and the action must be written off with sufficient detail to describe all the relevant facts. Potential score: 4 marks 1 mark for compliance 3 marks for the quality and level of detail contained in IAR entries (i.e., 0 = poor, 1 = average, 2 = good, 3 = excellent) 6. Witness Statements The standard of witness statements is paramount to an investigation and should be taken in accordance with the Statement Preparation precis located on the Investigative Standards Unit intranet site19. Initial witness statements contribute to the direction of an investigation and the more detailed the statement, the clearer the direction. For additional reading, the IHC reviewer is directed towards the Witness Manual20, also located on the Investigative Standards Unit intranet site. The IHC assesses a witness statement on the basis that the investigating officer is responsible for the quality of the witness statement. On the occasion when another business unit/or officer has taken a sub-standard statement, the IHC should look for an addendum statement where it is necessary. The assessment tool, Witness Review Checklist (see Annexure Seven) has been designed to assist the reviewer with conducting an IHC of witness statements. Potential score: 10 marks (for compliance and quality) 7. Supervisor Input Supervisors are expected to review first attendance (such as CAD and BWC) and IMS to ensure officers appropriately follow the Contact and Respond steps of the CRIME model. Supervisors are also to ensure appropriate investigation ownership and resources are deployed based on incident complexity. As a minimum, it is imperative that there is a formal review by supervisors of investigations at the time of allocation to an investigating officer, during the investigation and prior to filing. These reviews should lead to the identification and implementation of procedures and practices to ensure compliance with The Doctrine.21 Compliance with legislative provisions and agency investigative standards should be maintained by supervisors monitoring and reviewing their team’s investigations and workload. An independent assessment of the investigation is crucial to determine outstanding actions and priorities to enable constructive direction, where required. Supervisors must review the investigation to ensure that all investigative actions have been addressed and any decisions not to complete actions are recorded together with the rationale.22 Whilst short comments 19 Western Australia Police Force, Statement Preparation (v1.6, Perth, WA Police Force, 2019). 20 Western Australia Police Force, Witness Manual (v2.7, Perth, WA Police Force, 2023). 21 Policing Fundamentals and Performance Agreements (Office of Commissioner Blue Book page) 22 Western Australia Police Force, The Doctrine – Practical Guide, (v2.0 Perth: WA Police Force 2020) 27 - are able to be entered in the remarks section of an IMS report, it is more appropriate to record a detailed supervisor’s review within the running sheet or IAR. It should be noted that any conversations between the IO and supervisor concerning an investigation, particularly where actions or directives are discussed, should appear on the running sheet. The supervisor may instruct the IO to make the record. The IHC will assess this component by reviewing IMS reports and assessing whether supervisors had regularly reviewed investigations to ensure that there is timely completion and appropriate investigative focus. Quality is determined through entries made by the supervisor that indicate whether the investigation has been reviewed for investigative and guidance opportunities. On many occasions the supervisor may well be satisfied with the progress of an investigation and does not consider any direction is required; an entry to reflect this thought process is required. Language used within the supervisor’s comments should be in terms of The5KIS. Potential score: 10 marks (for quality of supervisor review entries demonstrating constructive investigative input and direction) 8. Audio-Visual Record of Interview (AVROI) The IHC will review AVROIs to ensure there is compliance with WA Police Force Investigative Interviewing techniques, legislation and WA Police Force policy. The IHC will specifically look for: • interview plan • interview notes • compliance with legislation and policy • adherence to the Conversation Management Model23, by examining the introduction, understanding of the caution, application of investigative interviewing and interview conduct of the AVROI. The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP) and Corruption and Crime Commission (CCC) have identified the following themes that constantly result in the inadmissibility of AVROIs: - • Vulnerabilities not considered and/or addressed • Ensuring the interviewee does in fact understand the caution • Coverage of all the s.137 and s.138 CIA 2006 rights24 • Whether admissions are made voluntarily or as a result of persistent importunity, insistence or pressure25 • Adherence to the Anunga Guidelines, where applicable. An AVROI Assessment Key, Health Check (Annexure six) has been created and is designed to cover all the critical elements. Potential score: 10 marks (for compliance and quality) 23 WA Police Force, Investigative Interviewing, Suspect Manual 2023 (v2.8, Perth, WA Police Force). 24 Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA), s 137 and s 138. 25 Arthurs v The State of Western Australia (2007) WASC 209. 9. Body Worn Cameras (BWC) Policy and SOPs for Body Worn Cameras (BWC) apply to all personnel who use a BWC in the course of their employment and duties. A BWC must be activated by an officer when it is safe and practicable to do so at a critical incident/event (as defined within the SOPs for BWC). Officers should be satisfied that, in deciding to start or stop a recording, the risk of not capturing evidential material is minimised. Police officers activating their BWC are required to, unless it is impracticable or unsafe to do so, inform the person/s that the BWC is recording the interaction and it may be livestreamed. For this criterion the IHC only assesses the operational use of BWC within the activation framework, not the content of the incident. Where BWC footage exists for multiple attending officers at the same incident, only the BWC of officers attached to the business unit subject to the IHC need be reviewed. Note. Scoring of the associated BWC metadata occurs within Criterion 11 – Management of Digital Evidence – DEMS. Potential Score: 4 marks 1 mark for use of BWC where appropriate and 1 for timeliness of activation. 1 mark for an alert being provided and 1 for quality of this notification. 10. Electronic CRIME File Management WA Police Force has an obligation to retain and manage documents associated with the investigation of offences; this obligation includes electronic documents. The IHC will identify the business unit’s electronic CFM repository and examine whether electronic copies of investigative documentation are being managed in accordance with the Management of Electronic Documents Guide. The Doctrine mandates business areas, not individual investigating officers, have overall responsibility for the management of allocated investigations. To comply with this responsibility, the Officer in Charge of a business area is responsible for the standardised governance of electronic documents accumulated during an investigation. At the time of writing this document, the P Drive remains the agency’s primary and preferred electronic crime file repository. With advancements in digital technology, there are other electronic document storage options, such as SharePoint, Teams, DEMS and Prosecution, which will eventually make the P drive obsolete. If another agency recognised electronic storage repository is utilised, it must have OIC approval and comply with the same integrity, quality and standards found within the Management of Electronic Documents Guide. An IO shall store and manage electronic documents relating to investigations in the designated business unit electronic CRIME File management (CFM) folder whether it be within the business unit’s network P Drive or other approved equivalent. Personnel must not save any documentation relating to an investigation on personal ‘H’ drives, as this restricts the ability for others to access the required information. Cross-referencing of the detail and location of all material should occur in IMS. An exception to the electronic CFM rule is an investigation into a confined simple offence where there are a limited number of related documents. In these circumstances documents can be uploaded to the Incident Management System (IMS) without creating an electronic CFM folder. Where the requirement to maintain a P Drive does not exist, the business area will not be marked adversely. Potential score: 5 marks (1 for compliance, 1 for 5KIS structure and 3 for quality) 11. Management of Digital Evidence - Digital Evidence Management System (DEMS) The Digital Evidence Management System (DEMS) is the only repository for the storage and management of purely digital evidence captured using BWC, Axon Capture, or uploaded via a Community Request link. There is no requirement to additionally store these evidence files in any other location. Any other purely digital content captured as part of the investigation and uploaded to DEMS (such as CCTV or digital photographs provided via other means) is required to be managed in the same manner. Evidence files require the following three fields to be completed;26 • ID (CAD or IMS IR) • Title (a description of the evidence file) • Category (as chosen from the list of available categories) The existence and location of evidence files should be appropriately cross-referenced in the IMS Incident Report, or other agency approved case management system (such as VIPER). It is imperative evidence files stored in DEMS are not only accessible, but searchable also. Integration with CAD and IMS systems may automate the population of some of these fields in certain circumstances, however evidence files must be manually checked and all required fields updated.27 The ID and Title must be relevant to the incident and comply with WA Police Force data entry standards, to assist in evidence retrieval.28 As with hard copy records/documents, the WA Police Force has an obligation to retain and manage electronic material associated with the investigation of offences. Material stored in DEMS are state records and must be managed in accordance with the State Records Act 2000. Retention periods in DEMS are defined by the category assigned and to prevent accidental deletion and loss of evidence officers must ensure the appropriate category is applied. (Note. Once footage has been deleted it is not retrievable.) The IHC report may include comments on statistics relating to the percentage of evidence files correctly updated as well as the overall quality of digital evidence management (such as whether all evidence files have been uploaded and can be located, tagging of material, 26 Body Worn Cameras Policy (ER-02.01); Standard Operating Procedures for Body Worn Cameras (V4.2) 27 Standard Operating Procedures for Body Worn Cameras - Management of Digital Evidence (v4.3, Section 6.3 Integration) 28 Information and Data Management (IDM) National Intelligence Protocols IR Writing Guide whether a Case has been created, and whether the evidence has been transferred to the IO.). Potential Score: 8 1 mark for ID and 1 mark for correct entry format 1 mark for Title and 1 mark for entry format 1 mark for Category applied and 1 mark for correct category selected 1 mark for cross-referencing in case management system and 1 mark for quality of entry 12. Victim Engagement Best practice suggests that victims should be contacted a minimum of three times; at the beginning, in the middle and at the end of any investigation. The beginning is no issue, the middle may be more difficult to judge but at the end is obvious. Victims of Crime Act 1994, Schedule 1, s. 629 A victim who has so requested should be kept informed about — a) the progress of the investigation into the offence (except where to do so may jeopardize the investigation); and b) charges laid; and c) any bail application made by the offender; and d) variations to the charges and the reasons for variations. There is an obligation on supervisor’s and IOs to manage the investigation of an incident by ensuring ‘the IO acts in the best interests of the victim throughout the investigation process’.30 Further obligations surrounding the treatment of victims exist within the WA Police Force Strategic Framework (Policing Fundamentals)31 and The WA Police Force Customer Service Charter.32 The IHC will review when and if the victim has been given updates as a matter of professional service and courtesy. The IHC will also assess, where it is relevant, a victim has been advised of the outcome of an investigation. This information should be recorded in either the running sheet or investigative action register of the IR. Potential score: 3 marks (1 for maintaining timely contact during the investigation, 1 for notification of the outcome upon completion and 1 for the quality of recording this contact) 13. Investigation Outcome (CRR) The outcome of an offence is of extreme importance as it will determine if the offence against which it is applied will ultimately be counted as a reported crime statistic at both a state and national level.33 Where the investigation identifies an offence different to that originally nominated in IMS, the incorrect offence must be corrected and a substituted offence entered. The IHC should 29 Victims of Crime Act 1994, (WA) Schedule 1, s. 6. 30 Western Australia Police Force, The Doctrine – Practical Guide (v2.0, Perth, WA Police, 2020) 29. 31 WA Police Force Strategic Framework – Values, Functions, Priorities, Policing Fundamentals. 32 WA Police Force Customer Service Charter (v1.0, WA Police, 2023). 33 Western Australia Police Force, Crime Recording User Guide, (v2.1, Perth: WA Police Force, 2018) 3. compare the offence/s described within the investigative material or subsequent brief (if applicable) with the offence/s currently recorded on the Incident Report, to ensure they match. The offence outcome status code should be an accurate description of the outcome and must be recorded alongside each offence listed within the Incident Report. For the correct offence outcome status code, refer to Annexure Five. Potential score: 1 mark (for compliance and accuracy) 14. IMS Incident Write Off Resolution of all investigations must be conducted according to The5KIS and each strategy must be considered during the investigation. This aspect of the doctrine (write off) does not seek to implement duplication of process, rather it requires the IO to document the rationale for the decision. As a minimum the write off should outline: 1. The outcome 2. The number of investigative actions identified within each category; and 3. If an investigative action was not completed, the reason why. The process intends the IO to look within each of the five categories and identify whether or not there is investigative opportunity. Supervisors must not accept file write offs which have recorded ‘The5KIS considered’; this is not the intent of this process. The IHC will assess this component by reviewing IMS reports and assessing whether references to The5KIS have been made at write off stage by the IO. These references should include what strategies have been completed and what are outstanding (if any). Any strategies not completed should be subject to decisions recorded within the running sheet34. Potential score: 5 marks (1 for compliance, 1 for addressing each of The5KIS and 3 for quality). 15. Hard Copy CRIME File The WA Police Force has an obligation to retain documents associated with the investigation of offences and utilises the printed hard copy CRIME File (HCCF) folder as a means of managing investigation documents35. A HCCF is to be commenced in all circumstances where an investigation results in the creation or collection of documents or items which are not retained in recognised WA Police Force repositories36. The IHC will assess this component by reviewing the IMS report to determine whether physical documentation/evidence has been collected, such as hand-written statements, notes, documentary evidence etc., and should be held within a HCCF. 34 Western Australia Police Force, as above n2. 35 Western Australia Police Force, Police Manual CF-01.00 Using IMS to Conduct Case and File Management, (Perth: WA Police Force 2014) 36 Western Australia Police Force, Investigation Doctrine (v2.2, Perth: WA Police Force, 2021) 14 Once the IHC reviewer is satisfied that a HCCF should exist then the location must be determined. Once a HCCF is located within the business unit repository it can be reviewed for compliance with agency standards. The collation of material within a CRIME file should reflect The5KIS with all material relating to a particular strategy placed together. It is recognised that there is some material which does not strictly fall within one of The5KIS and this should therefore be collated under ‘Investigative Administration’.37 Potential score: 3 marks (1 for the existence of a HCCF file, when necessary, 1 for the inclusion of all required documents and 1 for the HCCF compilation) 16. Evidence Matrix The Evidence Matrix (EM) is the tool that supports decision-making pertinent to the endorsement to charge (ETC) process. The EM is used to separate an offence into its elements and indicate how each element is to be proved to establish a prima facie case or otherwise.38 An EM also provides for the consideration of defences to the particular offence and the evidence which negates the defence or indicates why a defence does not apply. For simple and either way offences, officers will prepare an EM in the following way: • Prepare an EM with the elements of the offence • Discuss the evidence with the supervisor, and • If satisfied, the supervisor will endorse the EM. Officers are not required to record their evidence in writing on the EM for simple or either way offences, unless directed to do so by a supervisor. A fully written out Evidence Matrix is only mandatory for purely indictable offences39. The IHC assesses this component by reviewing evidence matrices to ensure they are in existence when required and they are correctly completed, identifying the evidence that exists against each element of the offence. Potential score: 2 marks (1 for compliance and 1 for quality) Note. EMs requiring verbal endorsement only are to be scored out of one for compliance (ensuring each offence element is listed), as the quality component cannot be assessed. 17. Endorsement to Charge (ETC) ‘Within the context of an investigation, the WA Police Force uses the ETC process to comply with the legal framework. The ETC acts as a validation process to ensure prima facie evidence exists prior to a charge being preferred’.40 37 Western Australia Police Force, Crime File Compilation and Management, (v2.1, Perth: WA Police Force
rop|inve-heal-chec-2023-8-15: 38 Western Australia Police Force, Integrated Staged Brief Process (v4.9, Perth, WA Police Force, 2024) 36. 39 Western Australia Police Force Endorsement to Charge (v1.4, Perth, WA Police Force, 2020) 6. 40 Western Australia Police Force, Investigation Doctrine (v2.1 Perth: WA Police Force 2020) 14. To assist with the accurate and correct charging of a person, there is a requirement for an endorsement to charge in all circumstances where a prosecution is to be commenced. The endorsement involves independent assessment of the available evidence and determining whether a prima facie case exists. The elements of the offence and corresponding evidence are presented for endorsement through an EM.41 This criterion generally applies where a brief exists and the evidence matrix/endorsement to charge process can be viewed via the Prosecution System. On occasion EMs have been completed as a write off tool illustrating the lack of evidence as it relates to a particular element, this should also be reviewed, commented on and endorsed accordingly during the IHC. The completion of an EM as a write-off tool is not common but considered best practice in certain circumstances. The IHC will assess this component of the IHC by reviewing endorsements to charge to ensure they are ‘Endorsed’ or ‘Not Endorsed’ appropriately (bearing in mind that it is not mandated to have the evidence detailed/described for simple and either way offences). Whilst compliance with the ETC process accounts for one mark, a second mark applies to the quality of the endorsing officer’s comments or records, relating to the justification of a decision. Potential score: 2 marks (1 for compliance and 1 for quality) 18. Statement of Material Facts It is important to recognise the significance of the Statement of Material Facts (SMF) in the initial phases of any prosecution, but particularly that of an indictable charge. It is the document which sets out the case against the accused, as it is known at the time of arrest and charge. If the accused elects to plead guilty without proceeding to a District Court hearing, it describes the factual basis upon which the accused is to be sentenced42. It is essential that the SMF is a comprehensive statement of the criminal culpability which, on the basis of the evidence, can be reasonably proved against the accused43. Plain English and short, clear sentences should be used, ensuring the SMF is accurate, adequate in content, professional and without any errors. The SMF needs to embrace the elements of the offence as thoroughly as possible and must adequately reflect the seriousness of the offence. Where confessional evidence has been obtained, this is to be noted at the bottom of the statement of material facts together with the type of evidence which will be adduced (i.e., partial/full admissions, AVROI, CCTV, BWC footage, admissions on search video etc). If additional evidence which is materially relevant to sentence becomes available before an accused pleads guilty, the SMF should be amended to include the new material information and served on the accused as soon as practicable44. 41 Western Australia Police Force, Integrated Staged Brief Process (v4.9, Perth: WA Police Force 2024) 55. 42 Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, Statement of Material Facts Guidelines (2017). 43 Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, as above n54. 44 Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, as above n54. The IHC will examine SMFs, particularly where there has been a plea of guilty, to ensure that it complies with the standard as detailed within the Statement of Material Facts guide located on the Investigative Standards Unit website45. The SMF should be read with the aim of the reader understanding the elements of the alleged offence, the accused’s culpability and the summary of evidence. The score will directly depend on how well the SMF explains the above in a concise and professional manner. This criterion is relevant where a brief exists and the SMF can be viewed via the Prosecution System. Potential score: 5 marks (for compliance with SMF guidelines and overall quality) 19. Unified Witness List (UWL) The Unified Witness List (UWL) is the standard document for recording all witnesses identified during an investigation, irrespective of whether they are required to give evidence at any subsequent trial. The UWL exists within the Prosecution System and assists investigators comply with disclosure obligations. The UWL provides a consolidated, point in time, summary of witnesses, their contact particulars, unavailability and the evidence they may provide associated with an investigation. This assists the investigator and prosecutor to assess the evidence or likely evidence to be given by each witness and to manage information concerning that witness within a single location.46 The UWL is mandated for investigations into purely indictable offences. In relation to simple offences or either-way matters heard in a Magistrate’s court, a UWL is also required where there is a plea of not guilty or disclosure is ordered by the Magistrate (either way offences)47. The IHC will assess this component by determining the jurisdiction of the offence under investigation and if mandatory as described in the paragraphs above, ensure that a UWL exists, is up to date, detailed and able to be used as a disclosure tool. This is a criterion that only applies where a brief exists and is either subject to disclosure or a plea of not guilty has been entered. Potential score: 2 marks (1 for compliance and 1 for quality) 20. Unified Physical Material List (UPML) The Unified Physical Material List (UPML) is the standardised method of recording all physical material that has been collected during an investigation, irrespective of whether it is to be led as evidence at any subsequent trial. Physical material includes any item whether tangible or electronic, such as physical items, forensic material, documents or electronic data recordings. The UPML exists within the Prosecution System and assists investigators comply with disclosure obligations. 45 Western Australia Police Force, Statement of Material Facts (v1.3 Perth: WA Police Force 2019). 46 Western Australia Police Force, Integrated Staged Brief Process (v4.9, Perth: WA Police Force 2024) 47 Western Australia Police Force, as above note. The UPML must be completed for investigations into purely indictable offences, or when an investigation results in a plea of not guilty or ‘full disclosure’ being necessary (Disclosure/Committal Hearing, 19B Hearing etc). The IHC will assess this component by determining the jurisdiction of the offence under investigation and if mandatory as described in the paragraph above, ensure that a UPML exists, is up to date, detailed and able to be used as a disclosure tool. This is a criterion that only applies where a brief exists and is either subject to disclosure or a plea of not guilty has been entered. Potential score: 2 marks (1 for compliance and 1 for quality) How to Score (in Percentage) - optional IHC have traditionally been scored as a percentage. The process and calculation will be explained within this section and the reader is referred to Annexure Four – Health Check Assessment Key. Within the key, on the right-hand side, are two columns under the headings P and A. P is the potential maximum score of a particular criterion either 1,2,3 5 or 10. A is the actual score given by the reviewer. Not applicable criteria: where a particular criterion does not apply, for example the brief related criteria where there is no brief associated with the investigation under review, then no actual score can be given. It is imperative that the potential score is recorded as ‘not applicable’ as well. Not making this adjustment will cause the overall percentage to be incorrect. Example: Criteria 16 – Evidence Matrix cannot be measured where there is no brief associated with the particular CRIME file under review and the actual score should be marked on the assessment key as ‘not applicable’. Since the actual score is not applicable, the potential score is also not applicable and not to be included within the total of the relevant potential scores. Calculating the percentage is a matter of adding the relevant P scores and A scores into their respective totals. Percentage can then be calculated by multiplying the total A score by 100 and dividing the product by the total P score. Example: Total A score = 65 Total P score = 85 Percentage = (A x 100)/P i.e. (65 x 100)/85 = 6500/85 = 76.47% rounded to 76% ANNEXURE ONE – INVESTIGATION HEALTH
