rop|inve-plan-v-INTRODUCTION: This should be a succinct summary of the situation identifying key areas relevant to the area of command. It should include pertinent points such as: time, date, location and nature of the investigation victim details suspect details (if known). The introduction should state briefly what it is that the plan intends to achieve and who is responsible for the plan.
rop|inve-plan-v-BACKGROUND: The background should be a detailed account of what has occurred and what investigations have been conducted to date. It should also be reflective on any intelligence gathered. The background is the most detailed component of the plan, but it typically requires little work as the information is already captured electronically in systems such as IMS, IDM or Viper. The background is dictated by the events that have transpired, it is a factual account, and should not include personal comment or any form of narration.
rop|inve-plan-v-OBJECTIVES: The plan needs to have clear objectives. This will ensure the investigation remains focused and the scope of the investigation is more effectively defined. It is important the objectives are achievable, realistic and measurable. It is usually beneficial to have a small number of objectives which are central to what you are trying to achieve. The objectives of the investigation must be in line with the objectives of the organisation. The optimal way to create objectives is to apply the S.M.A.R.T. principles which are regarded worldwide as the foundation for the construction of quality ‘goals and objectives’. The investigator should ensure that each objective is: Specific; Measurable; Achievable; Relevant; and Timely If all of the above criteria are fulfilled then the objective is realistic. Specific objectives are clear and well-defined. This helps both the IO and the supervisor, as the IO knows what is expected of them and the supervisor is able to monitor and assess actual performance against the specific objectives. Specific objectives may on occasion, include a ‘scope’ description, which includes details of what is ‘not’ included. Measurable objectives allow the progression towards the objectives to be monitored whilst the investigation is under way. It is also required to know when that work has been done and the objectives are completed. A measurable objective achieves this end. Achievable objectives are essential as the investigation may not be able to achieve it for various reasons, including a lack of skill, not having enough resources, not having access to key people and not having management support. Achievable objectives are set within the availability of resources, knowledge and time. Relevant objectives should also add useful value within the context of where they are being set. Relevant objectives are created by ensuring alignment with strategies and higher goals. Timely objectives should also include timescales of what is required by when. This may also include details of partial completion of deliverables, stating when components of an objective are to be completed. Giving a time scale adds appropriate sense of urgency and ensures that the objectives do not extend out over an unreasonably long timescale. The objectives of the investigation are broad and easily understood. The objectives are the ‘this is what I want to achieve’ component of the investigation plan.
rop|inve-plan-v-STRATEGIES: When formulating an investigation plan it is essential the strategies that are going to be used to achieve the objectives are included. Officers must realise it is their investigation and how they choose to conduct it is completely up to them, however the investigative strategies need to be realistic and achievable. Strategies are generated from ‘The5KIS’, Officers must consider all ‘The5KIS’ to ensure a thorough investigation plan has been compiled. The strategies should provide the reader with an overview of how the investigation will be conducted to achieve the objectives. This should include the types of investigative methods and intelligence processes that are intended to be used. The strategies do not need to be overly descriptive and specific tasks should not be detailed. Strategies will vary depending on the type of investigation and available resources. Additionally, different officers will utilise different strategies for the same investigation, this will be based on prior investigative experience. ‘No strategies are wrong if they are supportive of the objectives, there will only be situations when the strategy is not the most effective or efficient way of conducting the investigation’.
rop|inve-plan-v-IMPLEMENTATION: Every investigation plan should have a finite timeframe; this does not mean that if the investigation is not complete within this timeframe that it is discontinued, it is simply a way of managing the investigation and the way it is progressing, both from an IO and supervisory level. At this point the specifics of each strategy are identified; each strategy should be broken down into the individual components that are required to complete it, these components are referred to as the investigative actions associated with the investigation. Some strategies will be all encompassing and will not require reduction to separate components, in these cases the strategy will in itself be an investigative action. Once the investigative actions are identified, the IO needs to group them into areas that can be implemented during specific phases. Simply put, these phases will consist of investigative actions that form a chronology of how the investigation will unfold. The individual phases then need to be time framed. Time framing allows for the IO to monitor the progress of the investigation. The Timeframe can take the form of a date or date range, or the form of a milestone. Therefore the phase can commence on a specific date or at the completion of another investigative action.
rop|inve-plan-v-RESOURCES: When planning an investigation it is important to establish what resources will be required to implement the strategies and ultimately achieve the objectives within the given timeframes outlined during the plans implementation stage. There are four key areas within resource management that need to be addressed in most circumstances: Human; Physical; Financial; and Information management. When planning an investigation it is imperative that there is a balance between cost, quality and time, and this can be achieved through proper resource allocation. The phases of the implementation will associate directly with the resource management. Officers must make a critical assessment as to what resources are required at what phase of the investigation and reflect this within the investigation plan. The resource requirements for individual investigations will vary greatly and it will be the responsibility of the IO to accurately identify what resources are required at what stage and for how long.
rop|inve-plan-v-PERFORMANCE-INDICATORS: Performance indicators are tangible methods of determining if the investigation has achieved its objectives. They are direct reflection of the success of the investigation and as such are linked explicitly to the objectives of the investigation plan. Performance indicators measure in a qualitative or quantitative way whether the investigation or parts of the investigation have been successful.
rop|inve-plan-v-RISK-MANAGEMENT: Risk management has a dual purpose within the investigation plan. It has the traditional implications in regards to risk to personnel, the greater community and possibly property, but in addition it also encompasses risk to the investigation itself. With regard to traditional risk management, officers will be guided by existing ‘standard operating procedures’ and ‘occupational health and safety’. Investigative risk is somewhat less tangible in that it requires the IO to review the investigation plan and analyse what components of the plan are potentially open to compromise. This is the part where the IO must critically analyse what can go wrong with the plan and identify possible contingencies. Investigative risk may be an issue of unwanted media attention, a compromise of any covert methodology or an operational impasse. Therefore, when planning the investigation, ensure that any foreseeable risks are identified. Risk management maximises the investigations integrity. Risk management will be unfamiliar to a number of officers as it requires the IO to identify possible issues with the investigation. It is not the, what will go wrong, it is the, what may go wrong, and requires some lateral thinking on behalf of the IO to achieve.
rop|inve-plan-v-Example-of-Risk-Manageme: The above Risk Management Plan is provided as an example only and is not exhaustive. The IO should consider all risks relevant to the investigation at hand.
rop|inve-plan-v-REVIEW-PROCESS: The review component of the investigation plan addresses when, how and by who the plan shall be reviewed. The review process is vital to ensure the effectiveness of the investigation is assessed and that any errors identified are not repeated in subsequent investigations. For example, you may assess the issues that arose such as resources usage, occupational health and safety issues, management systems, investigative practices and strategies used. This component of the investigation plan is essential to identify what has gone well during the plan and what has been unsuccessful. Review is essential for the identification of best practice.
rop|inve-plan-v-CONCLUSION: A conclusion should be included in the investigation plan to tie all of the components together and give it context within the organisation’s strategic direction District/Division TCG This operation investigation plan has been reviewed by the District/Division TCG process and is approved.

rop|medi-cann-fact-FREQUENTLY-ASKED-QUES: February 2024 OOFFFFIICCIIAALL This document answers some common questions about medicinal cannabis including: • What is medicinal cannabis? • Who can prescribe medicinal cannabis? • What happens if a prescription is from another state or territory? • Who can possess medicinal cannabis? • What if a person with a prescription is supplying or selling their medicinal cannabis? • Can people cultivate their own medicinal cannabis? • Is there a test I can do to determine if the cannabis is medicinal or illicit? • Is there a way to verify the legitimacy of a medicinal cannabis prescription? • Is there an offence for improper storage of medicinal cannabis? • Is there an offence for smoking medicinal cannabis through ‘bongs’, pipes etc? • Can a person carry and smoke medicinal cannabis in public? • Is a person who has consumed medicinal cannabis permitted to drive? Please read in conjunction with PS-03.00 Medicinal Cannabis and the relevant legislation. Q: What is medicinal cannabis? A: Medicinal cannabis refers to legal, pharmaceutical grade, standardised cannabis preparations intended for therapeutic use, including: • Pharmaceutical cannabis preparations, such as oils, tinctures and other extracts • Cannabis resin (hashish), natural and synthetic cannabinoids • Untreated cannabis (raw and dried cannabis) In relation to dried herb products, these are available in containers of 5g, 7g, 9g, 10g or 15g, depending on the brand. See examples in Appendix A. The cannabis plant contains cannabinoids and the two most common cannabinoids are cannabidiol (CBD) and delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). Many medicinal cannabis products contain CBD and/or THC. CBD and THC have different effects. THC is the main psychoactive compound in cannabis and there are concerns around driving, cognitive impairment, and drug dependence when products containing THC are used. Cannabidiol-only products pose fewer risks. Medicinal Cannabis – Frequently Asked Questions OOFFFFIICCIIAALL Q: Who can prescribe medicinal cannabis? A: In Western Australia any medical practitioner can prescribe medicinal cannabis if they believe it is clinically appropriate and they have the necessary Commonwealth and State approvals. Because medicinal cannabis products are classified as ‘unapproved therapeutic goods’, medical practitioners must be authorised to prescribe under the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA)’s alternative pathways, such as the Special Access Scheme (SAS) or the Authorised Prescriber (AP) scheme The Medicines and Poisons Act 2014 adopts the schedules and a number of other parts of the Poisons Standard by reference. Medicinal cannabis products are classified as either Schedule 8 medicines (controlled drugs) if they contain THC or as Schedule 4 (prescription only) medicines if they only contain CBD. Prescribers in WA must comply with criteria in the S8 Medicines Prescribing Code when prescribing medicinal cannabis in WA. Refer to the current TGA Poisons Standard, also known as the ‘Standard for the Uniform Scheduling of Medicines and Poisons’ (SUSMP), for the latest information.1 Q: What happens if a prescription is from another state or territory? Every State has different legislation and policy surrounding the acceptance, or rejection, of interstate prescriptions. In WA, Schedule 4 and 8 poisons can be supplied on the provision of an interstate prescription. Currently, prescriptions for S8 medicinal cannabis products written by an interstate doctor for patients located in WA cannot be dispensed by a WA pharmacy. This means patients in WA may have medicinal cannabis with a label from an interstate pharmacy. Q: Who can possess medicinal cannabis? A: Whilst cannabis is a prohibited drug under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1981 (MDA), possession of cannabis can be lawful for persons who are prescribed medicinal cannabis from an authorised medical practitioner. The MDA specifies in s7(3)(a) that an exception to an offence of possession of cannabis is created where ‘[a person] was 1 Note: the SUSMP is regularly updated, on average around four times per calendar year. Medicinal Cannabis – Frequently Asked Questions OOFFFFIICCIIAALL authorised by or under this Act or the Medicines and Poisons Act 2014 (WA) to have possession of a prohibited drug obtainable from the plant.’ Any cannabis possessed outside of the regulatory framework is considered a prohibited drug. The MDA criminalises the unlawful possession, manufacture, sale or supply prohibited dangerous drugs including cannabis. Cannabis is classified under s4(2)(b) of the MDA (refer item 3 of Schedule II to the MDA) as a prohibited plant and (under item 5 of Schedule I) also a prohibited drug. Q: What if a person with a prescription is supplying or selling their medicinal cannabis? A: If there is evidence that a person prescribed medicinal cannabis is selling or supplying their medication, then they may have committed an offence contrary to either: • s14(1) of the Medicines and Poisons Act 2014 (WA) for supply of a Schedule 4 or 8 poison. The maximum penalty is a fine of $45,000 and imprisonment for 3 years; s 115(1)(a)(i) MPA; or • s6(1) or s 7(1) of the MDA for the sale or supply of a prohibited drug. Q: Can people cultivate their own medicinal cannabis? A: No. Home grown cannabis cannot be used as medicinal cannabis. Licensing of cultivation and manufacture is through the Narcotic Drugs Act 1967 (Commonwealth) and this legislation is administered by the Commonwealth’s Office of Drug Control (ODC). A list of licensed manufacturers and importers is available on the ODC website and includes suppliers. Q: Is there a test I can do to determine if the cannabis is medicinal or illicit? A: No. Although medicinal cannabis is cultivated under strict scientific conditions, there is no forensic testing that enables differentiation of medicinal cannabis from illicit cannabis, as they are both derived from the same genus of plants (cannabis) and may contain various quantities of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). The legal difference is based on how a person comes to possess the cannabis. There are some features which may indicate the cannabis is medicinal cannabis but these are indicators only and not to be relied on. As a general indication medicinal cannabis flower and bud products tend to: Medicinal Cannabis – Frequently Asked Questions OOFFFFIICCIIAALL • have less leaves attached because they are trimmed in the manufacturing process. • are less green in colour because the product must be cured to comply with Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP). • have less moisture because the product is sterilised and the moisture content must be less than 10%. Please see Appendices A and B for images of dried herb medicinal cannabis products. Q: Is there a way to verify the legitimacy of a medicinal cannabis prescription? Pharmacies are required to label medicinal cannabis products when dispensed to the patient. These labels must include the following: • the words “Keep Out of Reach of Children” in red on a white background at the top of the label • the name of the patient • the name and strength and form of the medicine (for example Cannabis Flower THC 20%), can contain the brand name of the product as well • the total quantity of the medicine in the container when dispensed (for example 15 g, 50 mL or 20 capsules) • adequate directions for use (usually both amount per dose and number of doses to be taken per day) • the name, address and telephone number of the pharmacy that dispensed the medicine • the name of the prescriber • prescription reference number (this number will correspond with the dispensing record at the pharmacy). • the date the medicine was dispensed An example of a dispensing label is below. Example of dispensing label

Maximum TOTAL combined daily dose of flower to be ONE gram per day. John SMITH Dr Steven Peters 20/06/2023 One repeat Medicinal Cannabis – Frequently Asked Questions OOFFFFIICCIIAALL The Compounding Pharmacy, 1 Street, Perth 9123 4567 The pharmacy can be contacted to verify they dispensed the medicinal cannabis product for the person. When a prescription for medicinal cannabis in S8 is dispensed in WA, pharmacies are required to retain these records for at least 5 years. The details of the dispensing are also transmitted to ScriptCheckWA, WA’s real time prescription monitoring system. The WA Department of Health’s Medicines and Poisons Regulation Branch can only provide information about a specific patient to the WA Police Force as required by law (an ‘order to produce’ will be required). Note: Details of prescriptions dispensed in other states and territories are not available via ScriptCheckWA. Q: Is there an offence for improper storage of medicinal cannabis? A: No. Packaging and labelling legislation is targeted at manufactures and not the end consumer. Consider this in the context of people who remove their medication from the packaging and place it into the week-day pill boxes as an example. A person is permitted to remove and repackage their medication. Q: Is there an offence for smoking medicinal cannabis through ‘bongs’, pipes etc? A: No. If the cannabis being smoked in the thing (bong) is lawfully possessed under a prescription, then we are unable to prove the “unlawful” element in regard to possession under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1981. There is no offence for taking/administering medication against the prescribed or recommended method. Q: Can a person carry and smoke medicinal cannabis in public? A: Yes (mostly) So long as it is lawfully prescribed – smoking medicinal cannabis can be treated as a smoking product and must be used in accordance with tobacco legislation - they are governed by the same no-smoking rules as cigarettes/vaporisers. Q: Is a person who has consumed medicinal cannabis permitted to drive? A: It is an offence to drive while a relevant drug (Cannabis/THC), is present in blood or saliva. There is no differentiation between illicit or prescribed detection. Medicinal Cannabis – Frequently Asked Questions OOFFFFIICCIIAALL A person who has legally obtained and used medicinal cannabis and who tests positive for driving whilst THC is present in their saliva commits an offence under the Road Traffic Act 1974: s64AC Driving with prescribed illicit drug in oral fluid or blood (1) A person who drives or attempts to drive a motor vehicle while a prescribed illicit drug is present in the person’s oral fluid or blood commits an offence. For the purposes of section 65 of the Road Traffic Act 1974, the Road Traffic (Drug Driving) Regulations 200,7 tetrahydrocannabionol is declared to be a “prescribed illicit drug”. It provides guidance and assistance to all members of the Western Australia Police Force (WA Police Force). INTRODUCTION In a criminal prosecution it is incumbent upon the prosecution to articulate facts which address all elements of the offence, there is also a need to give context regarding that articulation. The Statement of Material Facts (SMF) is used to satisfy both of the aforementioned. Accordingly, the SMF has enormous power to influence the accused’s plea at an early stage. The more information it contains, the more the accused will understand about the case against them and, importantly, the more their defence counsel will be in a position to give them sound legal advice as to the strength of the case against them at the earliest stage1. This guide provides information on: 1. The compilation of the SMF; and 2. The benefits of a well-compiled SMF. This guide applies to all prosecutions commenced by the WA Police Force. WHY IS THE ‘SMF’ IMPORTANT The SMF is intended to inform the accused of all of the material facts upon which the accused is to be sentenced2. If sufficiently comprehensive, with a ‘fast track plea of guilty’ the SMF may be the only information a court will require as to the facts of the case for sentencing purposes, this has substantial benefits, including:  Reduced need for police witness statements  Early resolution for victims. As a result, it is essential that the SMF is a comprehensive statement of the criminal culpability which, on the basis of the evidence, can be reasonably proved against the accused3. See Section ‘A Well-Drafted ‘SMF’ Can Benefit You’ 1 Office of the Director Public Prosecutions (ODPP), Statement of Material Facts Guidelines, 6 September 2017. 2 ODPP, as above n1. 3 ODPP, as above n1.

The type of information which should be included in SMF’s varies by the type of charges to which the facts relate. However, there are a number of general requirements4. Use plain English and short, clear sentences. Ensure the SMF is accurate, adequate in content, and professional without any errors. The presentation of the SMF will reflect the author’s professionalism. The SMF needs to embrace the elements of the offence as comprehensively as possible, which must adequately cover the degree of seriousness of the offence. Tell the whole story of criminal culpability which the evidence, from the investigation, has uncovered. Include the features that set out what really happened5. Where confessional evidence has been obtained, this is to be noted at the bottom of the statement of material facts and the type of evidence which will be adduced, i.e. partial/full admissions VROI, CCTV, body worn camera footage, admission on search video etc. Language The SMF concerns events that occurred in the past, therefore use past and not present tense. The problem of incorrect use of present tense often arises when describing a scene, or relationship between things, system, practice, or state of affairs. The use of present tense disguises the true evidence about the state of affairs at the relevant time. The language used in the SMF should be plain and not a legalistic equivalent. People ‘see’ rather than ‘observe’ things. They ‘say’ rather than ‘inform’ or ‘advise’. They ‘read’ and do not ‘peruse’ and they ‘send’, ‘post’, ‘fax’ or ‘email’ rather than ‘forward’ documents. The witness ‘went’ rather than ‘proceeded’ somewhere6. Do not use abbreviations within the SMF, the use of abbreviations can lead to confusion which could completely change the context of the SMF from the reader’s perspective. Unless the abbreviation is universally recognised, i.e. AM/PM, do not use it. Passive expressions that simply describe an event without identifying the individuals concerned should be avoided. For example, ‘The side of the house was where the man came from’. Unless it is clear from the context, the form should be ‘I saw the man walk from the side of the house’7. 4 ODPP, as above n1. 5 ODPP, as above n1. 6 Paper was presented on 11 September 2002 at an advocacy course conducted by the Supreme Court of Western Australia and Murdoch University 7 Supreme Court, as above n6. Content Include details as to the relationships between the parties (including the length and closeness of the relationship, any estrangements, restraining orders, custody arrangements, where pertinent to the offending)8. Include any aggravating or pertinent features of the conduct such as the possession/use of weapons, threats or demands made, vulnerability of a victim, proximity of children or intoxication of the accused9. Include details of any injuries suffered by the complainant and, if known, their seriousness and permanence10. If the accused is one of a number of offenders, state, if possible, the acts of each and the manner in which the accused is said to be liable for the offence (e.g. as a principal offender, or an aider11). It will not be necessary, in a group assault scenario, to specify the injury caused by individuals or individual blows (all participants will generally be liable for all injuries caused in a group assault)12. Admissions/Interviews Ensure that the summary of the accused’s admissions is accurate and sufficient to convey the full effect of the accused’s record of interview (or unrecorded admissions, if made). Assume the accused and/or their defence counsel may not have been able to view the record of interview at this early stage13. ‘Full admissions’, is not an adequate phrase to summarise a record of interview in which an accused admits committing an act but makes a claim to a defence (such as an assault done in self-defence)14. Similarly, for example: 1. In a case where possession with intent to sell/supply is alleged, ‘full admissions’ does not accurately summarise a record of interview in which an accused admits possession of drugs but denies an intention to sell or supply them to another15. 2. A sexual assault is not admitted if the accused admits the touching/penetration but denies a lack of consent16. Stating that an accused made ‘partial admissions’ does not assist the prosecution or a defence lawyer (or the accused) to assess the strength of the case against the accused. 8 ODPP, as above n1. 9 ODPP, as above n1. 10 ODPP, as above n1. 11 Criminal Code Compilation Act 1913 (WA) s 7. 12 ODPP, as above n1. 13 ODPP, as above n1. 14 ODPP, as above n1. 15 ODPP, as above n1. 16 ODPP, as above n1. Similarly, stating that an accused ‘denied the offence’ when they admitted a number of the elements is of limited assistance17. Other Evidence Refer to any compelling piece of evidence, such as good quality CCTV of the offence, phone downloads, an audio recording of admissions (e.g. a 000 call), evidence of threats before an act of violence, post offence conduct (such as disposing of evidence or significant lies)18. There is no reason not to include all important allegations in the SMF, if there is a foundation for them. Provided that, if the facts were to be challenged, the person compiling the SMF properly believes that admissible evidence would be available to prove them, either directly or circumstantially, they should be included in the SMF. A Word of Caution As important as it is to comprehensively state the material facts about the particular charge against an accused, it is equally important not to overstate the case against the accused. Overstatement will only increase the prospect that a plea of not guilty will be maintained until after all evidentiary material (the committal brief) has been served19. If the case has been overstated, there is a strong likelihood that, later in proceedings, the prosecution will be required to make concessions as to the overstated features and a plea of guilty will then be entered. In such circumstances, the need for the investigating officer to comply with the disclosure obligations of the Criminal Procedures Act (CPA)20 by way of serving the evidentiary material (committal brief) would have been wholly unnecessary had the facts not been overstated at the outset21. Offence Specific SMF Drug Matters22 A prosecutor should not have to seek a copy of the exhibits log or the EVR log/video to determine where items relevant to a drug prosecution were located. The SMF should include: 1. Details and location of the prohibited drugs, and any paraphernalia found with the prohibited drugs, such as money, scales (and whether if they have any apparent drug traces on them), clip seal bags, firearms or other weapons, smoking implements or needles or tick lists. 2. How the drugs were packaged/stored on seizure. 17 ODPP, as above n1. 18 ODPP, as above n1. 19 ODPP, as above n1. 20 Criminal Procedures Act 2004 (WA) 21 ODPP, as above n1. 22 ODPP, as above n1. 3. The nature of the intention allegedly held by the accused in relation to prohibited drugs (for example, that the accused was carrying on a commercial drug dealing business, was a user/dealer dealing to support an addiction, or supply (only) to friends/acquaintances). Information which might have enabled the investigating officer to form a view in this regard might come from intelligence or surveillance, the product of telephone downloads or inspection of an accused’s mobile phone, the extent of paraphernalia or money seized at the same time as the drugs, admissions made by the accused, information from witnesses, the quantity of the drugs, or a combination of all of these matters. 4. Even if the basis for the allegation as to intention is admissions of the accused, the allegation should still be made as part of the main part of the SMF, not simply as part of the summary of the record of interview. This is because it is important to distinguish the facts alleged from a mere summary of the accused’s admissions in their record of interview. 5. Conversely, there may be evidence to support a more serious allegation than that admitted. For example, if the surveillance and phone downloads support an allegation of commercial dealing, whilst the accused only admits an intention to supply friends. If the allegation of commerciality is omitted, a statement that the accused ‘admitted intending to supply friends’ is liable to be misread as an acceptance by the investigator that that was the accused’s actual intention, thus creating confusion as to what the accused has accepted by their plea of guilty. 6. The approximate value of the drugs seized, if possible. See Section ‘Demonstrated Example of Linkage’ Sex Offences23 The SMF should include: 1. If a complainant did not consent to sexual conduct on the part of the accused, a statement to that effect (even if lack of consent is not an element of the offence, it can be an aggravating feature on sentence). Generally, ‘consent’ by a child will not be a mitigating feature in the case of a charge where consent is not an element of the offence. 2. Any grooming behaviour in relation to children or cognitively impaired complainants (such as giving of gifts/money, text messaging, instant messaging or other online or personal contact or infiltrating the complainant’s social or family circle) prior to the offending conduct. 3. Any allegations as to ongoing sexual conduct made by the complainant but which cannot be sufficiently particularised to form the basis for a charge. 4. Any threats or demands made to the complainant or weapons held/used. 5. The circumstances in which the initial disclosure was made and how the prosecution came about. 6. Information as to the context of any pre-text call. 23 ODPP, as above n1. Child Exploitation Material24 SMF should include: 1. Details of the number of videos/images in each category. 2. For each category, a brief factual summary of the content of representative images/videos. 3. The approximate age/age range of the children depicted. Property/Damage/Stealing Offences25 The SMF should include details of the quantity or value of the property affected. Demonstrated Example of Linkage Consider the following generic scenario: A Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA) search warrant is executed at a residential address with the suspect in attendance. During the course of the search 10 grams of methylamphetamine is located in a single bag. Additionally a set of digital scales is located along with a number of small clip seal bags. A search of the suspect results in a clip seal bag containing a small amount of methylamphetamine and a syringe located in their jeans pocket. During the interview the suspects tells you that all of the items are theirs’ and it is all for personal use. As a collective, the above seized items amount to a reasonable suspicion that the suspect was selling or supplying a prohibited drug. However if tendered in isolation the court may not choose to draw the desired inference. In that case the prosecution is relying purely upon the presumption within the Misuse of Drugs Act26. The SMF should clearly articulate the linkage between the drugs, implements and other physical material. The following example of an SMF does not sufficiently define that link: At about 11.30 a.m. Wednesday 19 April 2017, police executed a Misuse of Drugs Act search warrant………………..During the execution of the search warrant police located 10 grams of methylamphetamine, 20 clip seal bags and a set of digital scales. Police also found on the accused’s person a clip seal bag containing a small amount of methylamphetamine. The above articulates the seizure of a number of items, several of which are not illegal to possess. The following SMF is an example of how to link the items into evidence early: 24 ODPP, as above n1. 25 ODPP, as above n1. 26 Misuse of Drugs Act 1981 (WA) During the search police located 10 grams of methylamphetamine. 10 grams is in excess of the presumption to sell and supply pursuant to schedule 5 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1981 Located on the accused was a syringe and a small clip seal bag which contained a small amount of methylamphetamine. Police also located a set of digital scales which presumptively tested positive to methylamphetamine the same drug type as the 10 grams. Located near to the digital scales was 20 small clip seal bags, these bags were of the same type and size as the one located on the accused which contained methylamphetamine. This SMF highlights the linkage and details the assertions of the charging officers. Drawing a conclusion to the inference is the responsibility of the court, but in presenting evidence in this manner the SMF is outlining the evidentiary link. A WELL-DRAFTED ‘SMF’ CAN BENEFIT YOU As soon as practicable, after the service of a Prosecution Notice containing one or more indictable charges, the CPA27 requires a written SMF of each charge to be served on the accused28. The SMF forms the foundation for the proceedings which follow. In the case of an accused who enters a plea of guilty to an indictable charge before committal, the SMF has an extremely important status. In those circumstances, the SMF is intended to inform the accused of all of the material facts upon which the accused is to be sentenced29. Except in rare circumstances an accused, committed for sentence, cannot change their plea to one of not guilty when they appear for sentence, provided the facts stated at the time of their sentencing do not differ materially from the material facts disclosed to the accused before they entered their plea in the summary jurisdiction30. As a result, it is essential that the SMF is a comprehensive statement of the criminal culpability which, on the basis of the evidence, can be reasonably proved against the accused. Further, if additional evidence which is materially relevant to sentence becomes available before an accused pleads guilty, the SMF should be amended to include the new, material information, and served on the accused as soon as practicable31. 27 Criminal Procedures Act 2004 (WA) s 35(4)(a) 28 ODPP, as above n1. 29 ODPP, as above n1. 30 ODPP, as above n1. 31 ODPP, as above n1. This process by which an accused is committed for sentence pursuant to the CPA32 (also known as a ‘fast track plea’) is one in which the ODPP has no involvement, occurring as it does at a stage before the ODPP takes over the conduct of indictable matters. Accordingly, the sole responsibility for ensuring the accuracy and proper formulation of the SMF in fast track pleas necessarily rests upon the investigating officer33. If an accused enters a fast track plea pursuant to the CPA34, there will be no requirement upon the investigating officer to obtain and serve evidentiary material in accordance with the CPA35. That is, there will be no obligation to compile a committal brief36. Other benefits to the criminal justice system of a fast track plea are37: 1. WA Police Force officers who are witnesses will not have to provide witness statements as to their involvement in the matter. 2. Any victim/s of the offence/s will have the comfort of an early resolution of the matter, with no appeal open on the conviction (except in very rare cases). 3. There are less appearances in court, thus saving the resources of the Magistrates Court, and all associated costs with an appearance, such as the time of Police Prosecutors, court security, prisoner transport or appearance (if an accused is in custody). 4. An accused in custody will be on remand for less time, thus enabling them to have access to rehabilitation programs and to be moved to appropriate custodial programs. 5. An accused on bail will be on bail for less time, saving costs to WA Police Force in monitoring reporting, curfews, and compliance with other bail conditions, particularly protective bail conditions, which are frequently imposed for indictable offences. Prior to the service of a committal brief, all an accused person will have is the SMF and, perhaps, a copy of their record of interview (which will not have been transcribed). If the accused is in custody, it is unlikely they will even have access to their record of interview38. Accordingly, the SMF has enormous power to influence the accused’s plea at an early stage. The more information it contains, the more the accused will understand about the case against them and, importantly, the more their defence counsel will be in a position to give them sound legal advice as to the strength of the case against them at the earliest stage39. Where Additional Evidence is Necessary or Appropriate There are some matters, where in addition to the SMF, some additional evidence is very likely to be required to enable the proper sentencing of the offender, even in a fast track plea. In particular, those are40: 32 Criminal Procedures Act 2004 (WA) s 41(3) 33 ODPP, as above n1. 34 Criminal Procedures Act 2004 (WA) s 41(3) 35 Criminal Procedures Act 2004 (WA) s 42 36 ODPP, as above n1. 37 ODPP, as above n1. 38 ODPP, as above n1. 39 ODPP, as above n1. 40 ODPP, as above n1. 1. Drug offences, where the Certificate(s) of Analysis is/are required. 2. Cases involving injury to a complainant, where it may be necessary to produce a medical report or updated medical report (depending on the seriousness of the injury) and where photographs of the injury will be extremely useful at sentencing. 3. Sex offences and domestic violence offences, where the statement of the complainant and any eye witnesses may be of assistance (if already taken at the time of the plea). 4. Damage/arson cases where photographs of the damage would be of utility. As a general rule, however, if material is stated within the Statement of Material Facts, it will not be necessary to seek statements to support it, unless a matter is contested. The likelihood of matters being in issue is greatly reduced if the relevant points and elements have been clearly set out in the SMF. rop|susp-mana-cons-INITIAL-CONSIDERATION: What is their description: Physical Clothing Marks/tattoos Vehicle being driven The above will aid in the timely creation of BOLOs and radio broadcasts. Attend known addresses: Known address of the suspect Workplace Relatives Linked addresses from intel searches When attending the above, consider the questions, you will ask those in attendance. Don't rely solely on one question like "is………..here?" Some planning in this area could gain valuable information to progress the search and ultimately, the investigation. Consider the following: How often do they attend this address? When was the last time you saw them? What clothing worn, last time you saw them? What were they driving last time you saw them? rop|vict-repo-v-AIM-OF-THE-VICTIMOLOGY-R: A high quality Victimology Report will create substantial investigative opportunities. The completion of this form should not be considered a process, it should be considered a crucial part of any investigation in which the primary victim cannot be spoken to. A victimology is a living document and all information relating to the victim’s lifestyle should be recorded in the report. Consideration should be given to collecting supporting documentation that may assist the investigation. Family Liaison Officers (FLO) should be inquisitive and tenacious when completing the document. FLO should seek to validate information supplied, because it is not unusual for family members to not know everything about their loved ones lives. Significant investment is required in the completion of this report as it paints a complete picture of the victim’s lifestyle and may identify significant lines of inquiry. Listed below are prompts for each section to assist completing this form, however, FLO should not limit their questioning to these suggestions. 1. LAST KNOWN CLOTHING/APPEARANCE/EFFECTS: Last known clothing or usual style of dress, effects worn (jewellery, watch, optical/hearing aids, earrings), footwear, head dress or any other identifiable items. 2. LIFESTYLE: Habits, secrets, sexual preferences, unusual characteristics or mannerisms, risk taking behaviour or political views. Victim’s daily routines, usual places visited. Likes/dislikes. 3. EDUCATION: Education history – primary/secondary/tertiary. 4. EMPLOYMENT: Occupation, trade, skills, qualifications, current employer and previous employers 5. INCOME: Include debts, recurring payments 6. ASSETS: Houses, contents, vehicles, Bank Accounts, shares and General Assets. Significant personal possessions, mobiles, laptops, tablets. 7. FAMILY BACKGROUND: Parents/siblings and type of relationship with them. 8. MARITAL STATUS/RELATIONSHIPS: Current marital status and background on any significant current or past relationships. 9. PERSONALITY: Describe the victim’s personality (shy, aggressive, pretentious or friendly etc.). How did the victim react to strangers/being confronted? Was the victim ever concerned about personal security or safety? 10. FRIENDS/ASSOCIATES: Friends, associates, and work colleagues. Include close and extended friends. Consider friendship circles and previous partners. New people in their life, immaterial of how long. 11. LEISURE-ACTIVITIES-HOBBIES: Did the victim have any hobbies or belong to any group or organisations? 12. ALCOHOL-DRUG USE OR ABUSE: This may requires consultation with numerous people, close family may not be aware of the depth of usage. 13. MEDICAL HISTORY: Physical and mental history (any known attempt suicide/self- harm, sexual abuse, drug or alcohol history/usage, prescription medication). Any known physical impairments or disabilities. Hospital admissions/psychiatric/psychological treatment. If possible, obtain doctor and dentist contact details. 14. TRANSPORTATION: Preferred mode of transport/ownership or access to vehicles. 15. RELIGIOUS BELIEFS: Type of religion and any regular attendance at faith disciplines. 16. SIGNIFICANT EVENTS PRIOR TO CRIME/DISAPPEARANCE: Create a timeline of movements including any activities prior to the crime. 17. DIGITAL PROFILING: Social media usage and accounts, all email addresses, cloud storage, web sites frequented and ensure as many passwords as possible are obtained. 18. OTHER: Was the victim afraid of, or specifically avoiding anyone? Are you aware of anyone who had a motive to kill or harm the victim? Who would benefit financially or otherwise from the victims death? What do you think happened? How do you think the victim would like to be remembered? Is there anything else you would like to add that has not already been covered? Interviewee: Date interviewed:

rro|rwa-indu-inve-FOETAL-ALCOHOL-SPECTRU: CONCLUSION ................................................................................................................ 11 INTRODUCTION There is an inherent complexity when interviewing Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people that are the focus of the Anunga Guidelines. Therefore, an interviewing officer must remain flexible in their approach when conducting interviews. When an officer is considering interviewing an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, they must understand the possible vulnerabilities and the impact those vulnerabilities have on admissibility (voluntariness and fairness). The information outlined in this package is equally applicable when interviewing witnesses, including children. An interviewee who does not comprehend what is being asked of them or feels they must answer in a particular way to please the interviewer, may give a flawed account. Flawed information could impact the direction of the investigation or ultimately result in a miscarriage of justice. A vulnerable person for the purpose of a police interview, be that suspect or witness, is defined as someone that falls within one or more of the following categories: • A child is always a vulnerable person; and • People with impaired intellectual function are always vulnerable. Or; • People who have impaired physical functioning; • People who are Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islanders; • People who are from non-English speaking background; or • People that have suffered an emotional or traumatic incident. Which as a result, may: • Predispose them to suggestibility. • Impact on voluntariness. • Complicate communications between the police and the interviewee. Any of the above circumstances may result in flawed information being captured during the interview. Persons fitting this definition must be afforded enhanced services to ensure fairness to the person and accuracy of the information obtained during an interview. There are many Aboriginal languages and dialects recognised throughout Western Australia, some of which are only spoken by a small group of people. It is imperative to plan your interview to ensure you are making good quality assessments of the interviewee, incident and legal requirements. Fairness and voluntariness are judicial requirements of any interview. If communication difficulties are apparent in the interview then there is a very real possibility that these requirements have been breached and deem your interview inadmissible. Witnesses and suspects need to be assessed in accordance with how they present to police; deal with them as if it was the first time you have met them. Even if they are well known to you, never presume to know their individual circumstances or situation and always ask questions to ascertain their level of vulnerability. If in doubt, treat them as a vulnerable person to ensure fairness. There will be occasions where a vulnerable person will not be able to be interviewed due to the lack of cognitive understanding of their rights. If the interviewee does not understand their rights, then, in consultation with your supervisor, a decision not to interview may be made. All decisions of this nature must be recorded. Evaluating the level of vulnerability of the person at first point of contact is particularly relevant for officers working in the Mid-West Gascoyne, Pilbara and Kimberley Police Districts. The percentage of interviewees suffering from a vulnerability is significantly higher in these districts. Police must consider the varied vulnerabilities that may be present and act accordingly to ensure judicial requirements are met. In every instance interviewing officers will plan for the interview they are going to conduct in accordance with the Suspect and Witness Investigative Interviewing manuals. These can be located on the Investigative Standards website. All suspect interviews must be conducted utilising the Investigative Interviewing, Conversation Management model. Interviewers must endeavour to use open questions. In order to achieve this TEDS and 5W&H type questions should be used. Interviewers should only ask one question at a time and use simple language.
rro|rwa-indu-inve-ANUNGA-GUIDELINES: On 30 April 1979, Mr. Justice FORSTER handed down his reasons for rejecting typewritten records of conversations in the matter of QUEEN v Angus ANUNGA, Sandy AJAX, Clancy AJAX, TJINGUNYA, Nari WHEELER and Frankie Miller JAGAMARA in the Northern Territory Supreme Court in August 1975. (R v Anunga (1976) 11 ALR 412) Inter alia Mr. Justice FORSTER said: "It seems to me now, however, to be important that the Court should put on record general guidelines for the conduct of Police Officers when interrogating Aboriginal persons. I preface this statement of guidelines by pointing out that Aboriginal people often do not understand English very well and that, even if they do understand the words, they may not understand the concepts which English phrases and sentences express. Even with the use of interpreters this problem is by no means solved. Police and legal English sometimes is not translatable into the Aboriginal language at all and there are no separate Aboriginal words for some simple words like "in", "at", "on", "by", "with", or "over'', these being suffixes added to the word they qualify. Some words may translate literally into Aboriginal language but mean something different. "Did you go into his house?" means to an English-speaking person, "did you go into the building?", but to an Aboriginal it may also mean, "did you go within the fence surrounding the house?" English concepts of time, number and distance are imperfectly understood if at all by Aboriginal people, many of the more primitive of whom cannot tell the time by a clock. One frequently hears the answer "long time", which depending on the context may be minutes, hours, days, weeks, or years. In case I may be misunderstood, I should also emphasise that I am not expressing the view that Aboriginal people are any less intelligent than white people but simply that their concepts of certain things and the terms in which they are expressed may be wholly different to those of white people. Another matter which needs to be understood is that most Aboriginal people are basically courteous and polite and will answer questions by white people in the way in which they think the questioner wants. Even if they are not courteous and polite there is the same reaction when they are dealing with an authority figure such as a policeman. Indeed their action is probably a combination of natural politeness and their attitude to someone in authority. Some Aboriginal people find the standard caution quite bewildering, even if they understand that they do not have to answer questions, because if they do not have to answer questions, then why are the questions being asked? Guidelines to be Followed when Interviewing Aboriginals Bearing in mind these preliminary observations which are based partly upon my own knowledge and partly by evidence I have heard in numerous cases I lay down the following guidelines. They apply, of course, to persons who are being questioned as suspects.1 Based on the above recommendations by Mr. Justice FORSTER, the Anunga rules were formulated as interviewing considerations for Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islanders. It is important to understand that not all Aboriginals or Torres Strait Islander descent people are vulnerable, however interviewing officers must always consider the Anunga Guidelines. Sound judgement should be applied when applying the Anunga Guidelines, for instance; it may not be necessary to provide the interviewee every Anunga rule on every occasion. A scaled approach reduces the likelihood of appearing condescending and thus increases rapport. Remember, Anunga Guidelines are about fairness and voluntariness. It is your responsibility to ensure that their application achieves those two requirements. There are nine Anunga rules (in Italics), each followed with some explanatory notes. 1 R v Anunga (1976) 11 ALR 412 Unless fluent in English provide an interpreter 1. When an Aboriginal person is being interrogated as a suspect, unless he is as fluent in English as the average white man of English descent, an interpreter able to interpret in and from the Aboriginal person's language should be present, and his assistance should be utilised whenever necessary to ensure complete and mutual understanding. If the suspect is communicating with a basic level of understanding of the English language, it is likely they may not fully comprehend instructions or questions asked of them. In all instances, you must use the services of a qualified interpreter. Further, it may become apparent the suspect’s cognitive understanding is still questionable, despite having the assistance of an interpreter. In this instance; consult with your supervisor and decide whether to continue with the interview. During the interview speak directly to the suspect or witness using short simple phrases. This improves the interpreter’s ability to interpret the exact words. Give the option of an 'Interview Friend' 2. When an Aboriginal is being interrogated it is desirable where practicable that a "prisoner's friend"2 (who may also be the interpreter) be present. The "prisoner's friend', should be someone in whom the Aboriginal has apparent confidence. He may be a mission or settlement superintendent or a member of the staff of one of these institutions who knows and is known to the Aboriginal. He may be a station owner, manager or overseer or an officer from the Department of Aboriginal Affairs. The combinations of persons and situations are variable and the categories of persons I have mentioned are not exclusive. The important thing is that the "prisoner's friend', be someone in whom the Aboriginal has confidence, by whom he will feel supported. An interview friend is a person who is present at the request of the suspect. They must be someone known to the suspect, independent of the police, able to speak the suspect's principal language and be someone the interviewee has confidence in. The interview friend must also be impartial to the matter under investigation. If you cannot locate an interview friend, you should consider using the services of an independent person or decide not to proceed with the interview. Even though there is no statutory obligation to provide a witness with an interview friend, an interview friend may be present for the purposes of assisting in the interview process. Ensure Caution is given and all elements are understood 3. Great care should be taken in administering the caution when it is appropriate to do so. It is simply not adequate to administer it in the usual terms and say, "Do you understand that?" or "Do you understand you do not have to answer questions?" Interrogating Police Officers, having explained the caution in simple terms, should ask the Aboriginal to tell 2 Western Australia Police Force use the term Interview Friend them what is meant by the caution, phrase by phrase, and should not proceed with the interrogation until it is clear the Aboriginal has apparent understanding of his right to remain silent. Most experienced police officers in the Territory already do this. The problem of the caution is a difficult one but the presence of a "prisoner's friend" or interpreter and adequate and simple questioning about the caution should go a long way towards solving it. The caution may need to be broken down into manageable sections. The police caution consists of three key parts. It is the interviewing officer’s responsibility to ensure the suspect’s explanation of all parts demonstrates their full understanding of the caution. A simple yes or no answer from the suspect does not demonstrate their understanding If, after this process, you do not feel the suspect understands the caution you should stop the interview and seek advice from a supervisor. Formulation of questions 4. Great care should be taken in formulating questions so that so far as possible the answer which is wanted or expected is not suggested in any way. Anything in the nature of cross-examination should be scrupulously avoided as answers to it have no probative value. It should be borne in mind that it is not only the wording of the question, which may suggest the answer, but also the manner and tone of voice which are used. Officers should use TEDS (Tell, Explain, Describe, Show) and 5W&H (Who, What, When, Where, Why and How) style questions to obtain open responses from the suspect. Take time to formulate questions during the interview and don’t rush. Keep your questions short and simple, be patient and allow sufficient time to answer. If the suspect does not understand your question, re-phrase it. Corroborate any admissions from other sources 5. Even when an apparent frank and free confession has been obtained relating to the commission of an offence, police should continue to investigate the matter in an endeavour to obtain proof of the commission of the offence from other sources. Failure to do this, among other things, led to the rejection of confessional records of interview in the cases of Nari WHEELER and Frank JAGAMARA. Always seek to clarify any admissions made by gathering further evidence to support the information given by the suspect. Due to their culture, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander suspects may want to please the interviewer and inadvertently admit to something they have little or no knowledge of. Offer meals, drinks, have toilets available to use 6. Because Aboriginal people are often nervous and ill at ease in the presence of white authority figures like policemen, it is particularly important that they be offered a meal, if they are being interviewed in a Police Station, or in the company of Police or in custody when a meal time arrives. They should always be offered a drink of water. They should be asked if they wish to use the lavatory if they are in the company of Police or under arrest. A meal, drink and an offer to use the toilet should be offered to the suspect. The offer of a meal and drink is not necessarily about sustenance but about making the interviewee feel comfortable. As stated earlier, the Anunga Guidelines are applied in a scaled approach, for example, if an interviewee has only just had a meal it may not be necessary to offer one, however that should be addressed during the introduction phase of the interview. Should not interview anyone who is ill, intoxicated or tired 7. It is particularly important that Aboriginal and other people are not interrogated when they are disabled by illness or drunkenness or tiredness. Admissions so gained will probably be rejected by a Court. Interrogation should not continue for an unreasonably long time. If a suspect indicates or you believe they are tired, then the interview will be delayed until they are rested. If the suspect says they are tired and wishes to rest you must facilitate this. If a suspect presents or indicates as being intoxicated, drug affected or ill you will not interview them. You will allow them to rest/sleep and only interview them once they are in a fit state. Section 141(k) Criminal Investigation Act gives the power to detain a suspect for this purpose. If the interview is lengthy, the suspect requests it or you believe the suspect would benefit from a break, then a break should be considered. Legal assistance is offered and reasonable steps taken to obtain it 8. Should an Aboriginal seek legal assistance reasonable steps should be taken to obtain such assistance. If an Aboriginal states he does not wish to answer further questions or any questions the interrogation should not continue. If a suspect requests to speak with a legal practitioner, this is to be allowed either in person or on the telephone. This right is usually exercised before the interview, however, the right may be exercised during or after the interview. Talking with a legal practitioner is an ongoing right of a suspect and if during the interview they request to speak with a legal practitioner you must stop the interview and facilitate the request. If the suspect indicates they do not want to answer any questions the interview should be stopped immediately, however, the interviewer needs to be mindful of whether the interviewee is merely uncomfortable with that particular topic or whether they are declining to answer any questions. If clothing is seized/removed, provide substitute clothing 9. When it is necessary to remove clothing for forensic examination or for the purposes of medical examination, steps must be taken forthwith to supply substitute clothing." Be mindful that wearing the standard forensic overalls police provide to suspects when there clothing has been seized may be perceived as prejudicial to the suspect if your AVROI is viewed by a magistrate, jury or judge. If practicable, provide them with everyday replacement clothing.
rro|rwa-indu-inve-FOETAL-ALCOHOL-SPECTRU: FASD3 is a mental impairment and will effect individuals differently depending on the severity of the condition. The neurological effects of FASD can have some cognitive and behavioral consequences such as; learning disabilities, poor memory, hyperactivity and in some cases, low IQ. These neurological effects may increase the likelihood of suggestibility in individuals with FASD; a term referring to the ability for an individual to be easily persuaded to take another’s position. This increased vulnerability of suggestibility for individuals with FASD requires careful consideration when interviewing a suspect with FASD, to ensure the interview is conducted with the principles of fairness and voluntariness. In addition to applying the tips outlined below, all suspect interviews will be conducted using the Investigative Interviewing and Conversation Management model. Individuals with suspected or confirmed FASD, function highest in structured and predictable environments. At the beginning of the interview, it may be helpful to explain the format of the interview and the type of questions that will be asked in detail, to decrease the likelihood of adverse emotional and behavioural reactions. In addition to this, individuals with FASD may have sensory processing disturbances that make crowds, noise, or bright lights difficult to manage. These conditions can cause agitation and difficulty to focus. Therefore, it may be helpful to conduct the interview in a quiet and softly lit environment with limited persons present in the room. An adult with FASD frequently presents with the same development and functioning capabilities of half their chronological age (dysmaturity). This factor should be taken into account and reflected in the simple language used by the interviewer. This is especially important when ascertaining if the individual can display a level of understanding of their legislative rights and the caution. In accordance with the Investigative Interviewing and Conversational Management model, interviewers should provide the individual with an opportunity to tell their version of the story, uninterrupted at the outset of the interview session. Interviewers should rely on open questions (TEDS, 5W&H) and check often for a level of understanding. Interviewers should also only ask one question at a time and use simple language, as those with FASD have 3 Mental Health Act 2014 s 6(1) significant difficulty understanding abstract concepts and making inferences from context. Multiple questions asked in the one sentence should be avoided. Interviewers should refrain from using judgmental or accusatory tones or phrases because this can heighten anxiety and limit information processing in individuals with FASD. Similarly, using overly complimentary language may encourage the individual to falsely answer questions, in order to please authority. In all instances, seek corroborative evidence to confirm the suspect’s version of events. If individuals with FASD are struggling to give verbal responses, allow them to communicate in a different way. If appropriate, consider allowing them to act it out or draw pictures to assist their response. Alternatively, consider writing out the questions and allow them to write out their response. Suggestibility coupled with memory deficiencies may lead to confabulation. Confabulation is an unintentional effort to fill in gaps of memory, without the intention to be untruthful or mislead others4. Suggestion and confabulation are particularly likely in situations where interviewers ask leading questions or pressure interviewees. Interviewers should only challenge a suspect’s version of events in the ‘Challenge Phase’ of an interview, in line with the Conversation Management model. If reading is required in the interview, allow adequate reading time for individuals with FASD and offer the option of reading the material aloud. Be sure to verify comprehension as some individuals with FASD develop strategies such as displaying strong emotional reactions, to avoid detection of their poor reading skills, even if they agreed to read the material. Individuals with FASD generally work harder to focus on social interactions, so they may only be able to handle a few minutes of an interview at a time. If pushed too hard, they may become withdrawn (shut down or not speak at all) or volatile (overly emotional, crying, screaming or violent towards self and others). In this emotional state, there is risk the individual may provide false or inaccurate information as a strategy to cope with the inability to handle the anxious situation. In line with Investigative Interviewing principles, taking breaks in the case of interviewing someone with FASD, may increase the likelihood of gaining more accurate information. A break could include suspending the interview and allowing the individual to leave the room for a period of time, if practicable. Many people with FASD find their brains work better when their bodies are engaged in some form of movement. It may be helpful if the individual engages in some form of physical activity such as; pacing about the room, doodling, fidgeting with a stress ball or other small benign item during the interview, if safe to do so. FASD and suggestibility may increase the likelihood of false confessions during police interviews. This increases the risk of interviews deemed inadmissible if vulnerabilities are not adequately identified and addressed. By following these tips outlined above and increasing awareness about FASD, these risks may be decreased.5 4 Foetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder and Suggestibility/Brown et al. British Journal of Clinical Psychology (1993) 5 Foetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder and Suggestibility/Brown et al. British Journal of Clinical Psychology (1993) CONCLUSION All interviews will be conducted using the Investigative Interviewing Model which is the Western Australia Police Force standard. This document includes information to assist officers when interviewing people with vulnerabilities, specifically Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander people in the Mid-West Gascoyne, Kimberley and Pilbara districts. Any officer who fails to adhere to the guidance in this document risks their interview or statement being ruled inadmissible, miscarriages of justice, poor service delivery to the community and substantial embarrassment to the Western Australia Police Force. Further information can be located on the Investigative Interviewing page on the Investigative Standards website.

rsd|sda-comm-comm-Overview: This form is to be completed by any Investigating Officer who wishes to communicate protected information, as defined by section 45 of the Surveillance Devices Act 2004 (Cth) (the Act), to any officer of a law enforcement agency other than Western Australia Police. It is the policy of Special Operations Application Unit (SOAU) not to permit communication of protected information obtained through the use of surveillance devices with other law enforcement agencies without the permission of the Officer-in-Charge of SOAU. The use, communication and publication of protected information is restricted under the Act and is subject to record keeping requirements if communication of the protected information is approved by the OIC SOAU. The Investigating Officer is to complete the below form and submit to SOAU for approval.

rsd|sda-comm-emai-Overview: Commonwealth SDA (Warrant approved/issued) Your application for a Commonwealth SDA warrant(s)/or extension to warrant XX of 202X, has gone to court and a warrant(s) was issued/or extension granted by [TITLE – Justice] XXXXX for a period of XX days. Please note the EXPIRY DATE of XX/XX/202X. It is your responsibility to submit a supplementary TRF to the State Intelligence and command Portfolio, Covert Coordinator 14 days prior to the expiry date if you believe that you are going to require an extension/further extension. Please liaise with the Police Technical Unit, Operations Manager on 08 9315 4409 (all hours) to arrange the installation or retrieval of surveillance devices pursuant to your warrant (s). As the applicant for a Commonwealth SDA you must be aware and abide by the following legislation compliance matters: For assistance on Commonwealth SDA procedures seek further information: Blue Book | State Crime | Crime Support and Services | Special Operations Application Unit | Surveillance Devices – PROCEDURES Execution of Warrant: Should you as the applicant cease for any reason to have responsibility for the execution of the warrant, the Chief Officer of the agency in writing, must nominate another person as the law enforcement officer. If this is unable to be done, the warrant should be revoked and another warrant sought. (e.g. transfer to another business unit, extended leave etc.) See s6(3) Surveillance Devices Act 2004 (Commonwealth) Storage of Protected Information: Section 46(1)(a) of the Act requires the chief officer to ensure that every record comprising protected information is kept in a secure place that is not accessible to people who are not entitled to deal with the information. The definition of 'protected information' under s 44(1) of the Act includes information obtained from the use of a surveillance device. PLEASE ENSURE THAT ANY STORAGE OF PRODUCT ON USB’s, HARD DRIVES OR DISCS ARE ENCRYPTED AND ONLY AVAILABLE TO THOSE PERSON ENTITLED TO DEAL WITH IT. Keeping Records of Each use: Under s 45 of the Act, the use, recording, communication, or publication of protected information is prohibited unless it is for a permitted purpose detailed under s 45(4) of the Act. Section 45(5) of the Act further provides permitted purposes to use, record, communicate or publish, or admit in evidence protected information. Under s 52(1)(e) of the Act, the chief officer of a law enforcement agency must keep 'details of each use' by the agency, or by a law enforcement officer of the agency, of information obtained using a surveillance device or access to data held in a computer. Section 52(1)(f) of the Act requires the same for ‘details of each communication' by a law enforcement officer of the agency to a person other than a law enforcement officer of the agency. PLEASE ENSURE RECORDS ARE KEPT ON EACH USE AND THE RECORD KEEPING REQUIREMENTS SURROUNDING EACH USE. PLEASE KEEP DETAILED RUNNING SHEETS ON EACH USE OF THE SDA AND SUPPLY WITH THE COMPLETE UCL WITH A COPY OF THESE RUNNING SHEETS TO BE KEPT ON FILE FOR INSPECTION BY THE COMMONWEALTH OMBUDSMAN. Revocation of Warrants: The chief officer must revoke a surveillance device warrant, by instrument in writing, if the prescribed circumstances in s 21 of the Act apply. This includes where the chief officer is satisfied that the use of a surveillance device under the warrant is no longer necessary for the purpose of enabling evidence to be obtained of the commission of a relevant offence or the identity or location of an offender. PLEASE NOTIFY SOAU IMMEDIATELY IF THE WAARANT IS NO LONGER NECESSARY FOR ITS ORIGINAL PURPOSE. SOAU WILL THEN ARRANGE REVOCATION WITH THE CHIEF OFFICER. Final Investigators Report: Section 49(1) of the Act states that the chief officer must as soon as practicable after a warrant or authority ceases to be in force, make a report to the Minister. PLEASE REFERENCE RECORDS KEPT FOR THE USE OF THE SDA INCLUDING ANY RUNNING SHEETS WHEN COMPILING THE INVESTIGATOR REPORT. Please ensure all appropriate details are included within the Final Investigators Report addressing all matters as per section 49(2)(b) of the Act. The report must include details of any premises on which the device was installed or any place at which the device was used. For assistance in completing this report please refer to example report situated at: Blue Book | State Crime | Crime Support and Services | Special Operations Application Unit | Surveillance Devices | (SDA) – Commonwealth Procedures Forms NOTE - If you are making an application for any covert services, either for a telecommunication intercept, surveillance devices, physical surveillance or undercover officers you are required to complete a 'WAPOL Tasking Request Form’ Please contact the SOAU Covert Applications Supervisor on 9223 3521 (ext 13521) if you have any queries or concerns. Destruction of Protected Information: Destruction of Protected Information and/or data obtained through the execution of surveillance device warrant will be undertaken in accordance to a destruction regime pursuant to section 46(1)(b) of the Act. Only upon issue of a Destruction Order is Protected Information to be destroyed. Inquiries regarding the destruction of Protected Information should be directed to SOAU. Any Protected Information obtained through execution of a surveillance warrant held by another law enforcement or government agency shall be subject to the WA Police Force Destruction Process with evidence of the destruction required to be recorded within the warrant file. SOAU will manage and coordinate the destruction of all protected information on behalf of the WA Police Force.

Essential checklist for Emergency Use of Surveillance Devices. Annexure 2. Application for Emergency Authorisation Annexure 3. Emergency Authorisation Annexure 4. Section 21 Surveillance Device Act 1998 ✅ Essential Checklist for Emergency Use of Surveillance Devices 1. Imminent Threat or Serious Offence Is there an imminent threat of serious violence to a person or substantial damage to property? 2. Drug Offence Criteria (if applicable) Has an indictable drug offence (or external indictable drug offence) been, or is likely to be, committed? Is the immediate use of a surveillance device necessary to: Deal with the threat or investigate the offence? Obtain evidence of the offence? Identify or locate the offender? Are the circumstances so serious and urgent that use of the device is warranted? Is it not practicable to apply under section 15 or 16? 3. General Serious Offence Criteria (if applicable) Has an offence punishable by 2 or more years’ imprisonment been, or is likely to be, committed? Is the immediate use of a surveillance device necessary to: Deal with the threat or investigate the offence? Obtain evidence of the offence? Identify or locate the offender? Are the circumstances so serious and urgent that use of the device is warranted? Is it not practicable to apply under section 15 or 16?
