rsd|surv-devi-emer-21-Emergency-authoris: (1) An authorised person may issue an emergency authorisation under this section if satisfied by an application made in that behalf that there are reasonable grounds for believing — (a) that an imminent threat of serious violence to a person or of substantial damage to property exists; (b) that — (i) an indictable drug offence or an external indictable drug offence has been or may have been, is being or is about to be, or is likely to be, committed; (ii) the use of a listening device, an optical surveillance device, or a tracking device is immediately necessary for the purpose of dealing with that threat or investigating that offence or suspected offence, or of enabling evidence to be obtained of the commission of that offence, or the identity or location of the offender; (iii) the circumstances are so serious and the matter is of such urgency that the use of the device in the course of the duty of the applicant is warranted; and (iv) an application under section 15 or 16 is not practicable; or (c) that — [(i) deleted] (ia) an offence punishable by 2 or more year’s imprisonment has been or may have been, is being or is about to be, or is likely to be, committed; (ii) the use of a listening device, an optical surveillance device, or a tracking device is immediately necessary for the purpose of dealing with that threat or investigating that offence or suspected offence, or of enabling evidence to be obtained of the commission of that offence, or the identity or location of the offender; (iii) the circumstances are so serious and the matter is of such urgency that the use of the device in the course of the duty of the applicant is warranted; and (iv) an application under section 15 or 16 is not practicable. (2) An authorised person may issue an emergency authorisation under this section if satisfied by an application made in that behalf that there are reasonable grounds for believing that — (a) retrieval of a listening device, an optical surveillance device, or a tracking device is immediately necessary in order that an investigation into an indictable drug offence or an external indictable drug offence is not jeopardized; (b) the circumstances are so serious and the matter is of such urgency that the retrieval of the device in the course of the duty of the applicant is warranted; and (c) an application under section 22 is not practicable. (3) An application under subsection (1) or (2) may be made either orally or in writing or by means of a radio, telephone, video recording, facsimile transmission or any other communication device. (4) A person to whom an emergency authorisation has been issued under subsection (1) must deliver without delay a written report to a judge — (a) stating whether a surveillance device was used under the authorisation; (b) if a surveillance device was so used — (i) giving particulars of the use and the period during which it was used; (ii) specifying the name, if known, of any person whose private conversation was monitored, recorded or listened to or whose private activity was observed or recorded; (iii) specifying the name, if known, of any person whose geographical location was monitored by use of a tracking device; (iv) containing particulars of any premises where the device was installed or any place at which the device was used; (v) containing particulars of any specified object in or on which the device was installed or any premises where the object was located when the device was installed; (vi) containing particulars of the general use made or to be made of any evidence or information obtained by use of the device; and (vii) containing particulars of any previous use of a surveillance device in connection with the matter or offence or suspected offence in respect of which the emergency authorisation was granted. (5) A person to whom an emergency authorisation has been issued under subsection (2) must deliver without delay a written report to a judge — (a) stating whether a surveillance device was retrieved under the authorisation; and (b) if a surveillance device was so retrieved, giving particulars of the retrieval. (6) Subject to necessary modifications, the provisions of section 13(8)(f), (g), (i) and (j), (9), (11) and (12) apply to emergency authorisations in the same manner as they apply to warrants. (7) An authorised person may issue one composite emergency authorisation having effect in accordance with its terms in respect of the attachment, installation, use or maintenance of more than one kind of surveillance device or a surveillance device that has more than one kind of function. (8) Where a report is given to a judge under subsection (4), the judge may direct that any record of evidence or information obtained by the use of the surveillance device to which the report relates be brought before the judge. (9) A record of evidence or information brought before a judge under subsection (8) must be kept in the custody of the Supreme Court and the judge may order that it be returned, or made available to any person, or destroyed. (10) On consideration of a report under this section, a judge may direct that use of the surveillance device cease immediately. [Section 21 amended: No. 78 of 2003 s. 74.]

rsd|surv-devi-cth-INTRODUCTION: The following procedures are provided for use by all Western Australia Police Force personnel exercising powers provided under the Surveillance Devices Act 2004 (Commonwealth) (the Act). The procedures relate to the application processes, storage, use and communication, destruction and other considerations when using the Act. The procedures also contain information and guidance provided to the WA Police Force by the Commonwealth Ombudsman. These procedures should be read in conjunction with the Act and are provided to maintain and ensure legislative compliance with the Act, by the WA Police Force.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-ROLES-RESPONSIBILITIES: Various positions and personnel within the WA Police Force are required to undertake certain roles and maintain specific responsibilities within the Act. Following is a brief outline of these positions and roles.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-CHIEF-OFFICER: The Chief Officer has numerous powers and functions afforded to him/her under the Act. These include: Section 20(2) Warrant revocation; Section 46(1)(b) Destruction of records; Section 49(1) Warrant and authorisation reporting; and Section 50(1) Annual report to the Minister. The powers and functions afforded to the Chief Officer under the Act may be delegated pursuant to section 63 of the Act to a suitable approving officer within the WA Police Force. Currently, the Commissioners functions are delegated to the Assistant Commissioner (State Crime) and Commander (State Crime). The Officer-in-Charge (OIC) Special Operations Applications Unit (SOAU) holds copies of delegations, and they are also available from the Corporate Knowledge Base under “Legislative Instruments.”
rsd|surv-devi-cth-INVESTIGATING-OFFICER-: The applicant will be ultimately responsible for a warrant or power exercised under the provisions of the Act. The applicant based upon his or her knowledge initially seeks approval for a warrant to be obtained under the provisions of the Act. An applicant is encouraged to consult with the SOAU Operations Manager or SOAU Covert Applications Team Manager, prior to seeking a warrant under the Act. The applicant will be responsible for providing all evidence and intelligence to support the application for the warrant. The applicant will be required to swear or affirm the affidavit before a Justice of the Peace once completed and approved. A SOAU Covert Applications Team member will attend The Family Court of Western Australia or Administrative Appeals Tribunal (AAT) on behalf of the applicant. The applicant should be contactable via telephone, should the Judge/AAT Member require any clarification, or ancillary information, or require the applicant to provide additional sworn evidence on the application. The applicant must ensure appropriate records are made of the disclosure/communication and use of all ‘Protected Information’ obtained through the execution of a warrant under the Act. If the applicant to whom a warrant is issued believes that the use of a surveillance device under the warrant is no longer necessary for the purpose of enabling evidence to be obtained of the commission of the relevant offence, or the identity or location of the offender, (or if in relation to a recovery order, for the purpose of enabling the location and safe recovery of the child to whom the order relates) the applicant MUST, pursuant to section 21(5) of the Act, apply for the warrant to be revoked. The applicant is required to complete and submit a Destruction Advice Report to the OIC of SOAU with a recommendation as to whether the records and reports are to be destroyed or retained. Where responsibility ceases to exist for the applicant for reasons such as extended leave or departure from the business unit, it is the responsibility of the applicant to nominate another person as the new law enforcement officer primarily responsible for executing the warrant or authorisation by contacting the SOAU Manager. All Tasking Request Forms (TRF) submitted by an applicant for use of warrants under the Act must be approved by their relevant supervisor and OIC and be in accordance with an approved Investigation Strategy.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-LEGAL-ADVICE: Legal advice and guidance for applicants in respect to the obtaining of warrants and the exercising of powers under the Act are available via Legal Services Branch, or the State Solicitor’s Office as required.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-SPECIAL-OPERATIONS-APP: The SOAU Covert Application Supervisor is available to provide investigators or applicants guidance in the preparation of documentation under the Act. Following an approved IDM TRF, SOAU Covert Application Team members (upon receipt of an Assessment Form) will prepare affidavits from the applicant and prepare the warrant and all other associated documentation required for presentation to the relevant Judge or AAT Member. On a warrant being issued, a SOAU Covert Application Team member will provide information outlining the responsibilities of the applicant for the warrant in accordance with the Act. SOAU will maintain security and storage of warrant documents in accordance with legislative requirements and advice provided by the oversight bodies (Commonwealth Ombudsman and Compliance Unit). SOAU are responsible for the collation, preparation and presentation of Chief Officer Reports pursuant to sections 49(1) and 50(1) of the Act. The OIC of SOAU will ensure these reports are prepared and presented to the Chief Officer, or his authorised delegate in accordance with the legislative timeframes provided. SOAU are responsible for the preparation and presentation of Warrant Revocations and Destruction Requests pursuant to sections 20(2) and 46(1)(b) of the Act to the Chief Officer (or delegate). SOAU are responsible for maintaining a General Register pursuant to section 53 of the Act. SOAU will maintain responsibility for the retention and destruction of all Protected Information, ensuring destruction is undertaken in accordance with section 46 of the Act.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-OIC-SPECIAL-OPERATIONS: The OIC of SOAU maintains overall responsibility for ensuring WA Police Force policies and procedures regarding the Act are up to date and contemporary. The OIC shall ensure advice/suggestions provided by the oversight bodies are considered and take all required action to implement changes to procedures and processes to ensure compliance. The OIC may change processes and procedures as required if it is identified a current practice or procedure will result in non-compliance. It is the responsibility of the OIC to ensure all legislative reporting obligations of the Chief Officer are undertaken within the allocated timeframes. The OIC will maintain and ensure any delegation instrument pursuant to section 63 of the Act is contemporary and reflective of ranks and positions for which Chief Officer powers or functions have been delegated. The OIC of SOAU will be required to facilitate inspections performed by the Commonwealth Ombudsman as required.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-OIC-POLICE-TECHNICAL-U: The OIC PTU is responsible for the technical execution of warrants obtained pursuant to the Act. It will be the responsibility of the OIC PTU to ensure all internal processes and guidelines are in accordance with the WA Police Force Procedures (this document) and the Act. Guidelines in regard to the collection, storage, security, and destruction of Protected Information are to be regularly reviewed to ensure best practice and agency compliance is maintained. The OIC PTU will be required to participate in Ombudsman inspections as requested and will be responsible for the implementation of suggestions and guidance provided in respect to the technical deployment of resources pursuant to the Act.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-COMPLIANCE-UNIT: The WA Police Force Ethical Standards Division Compliance Unit will undertake independent inspections to ensure compliance with legislative and policy requirements are being maintained, pursuant to the Act and Ombudsman recommendations. Findings from the inspections will be reported to the business area’s Superintendent, Commander State Crime and the Commonwealth Ombudsman. The Compliance Unit will work closely with the OIC SOAU, SOAU members and OIC PTU to ensure ongoing review of practices, processes and procedures, suggesting and implementing changes as required to maintain legislative compliance.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-APPLICATION-PROCESS: All applications for warrants, extensions or variations made under the Act will be prepared by SOAU on behalf of WA Police Force to ensure all record keeping, reporting and destruction is accurate and performed in accordance with legislation. All applications for warrants pursuant to the Act will commence with the application of a TRF submitted via the Operations Coordinator. Upon approval of a TRF the applicant will be provided guidance and assistance in the application and court processes. All additional applications (extensions, variations etc.) will require submission of a supplementary TRF to the Operations Coordinator.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-MAKING-APPLICATIONS-FO: SOAU Covert Application Team members will assist an Investigator/applicant to obtain a warrant pursuant to the Act. All formal requests for warrants under the Act are to be commenced via the submission of a TRF. It is recommended the investigator/applicant communicate with the SOAU Operations Coordinator prior to submission of the TRF to ensure the request is appropriate. The provisions of the Act allow the use of surveillance devices as a tool to assist in the investigation of a relevant offence. Applications for warrants, emergency authorisations and tracking device authorisations under the provisions of the Act must comply with the legislation. The provisions of the Act regulate: there are different types of surveillance devices, including a data surveillance device, a listening device, an optical surveillance device and a tracking device; types of warrant, including a surveillance device warrant, retrieval warrant, computer access warrant, data disruption warrant and network activity warrant; and three different locations whereby surveillance devices, subject to a warrant, can be installed, including in a specified premise, a specified object and with respect to a specified person. An application for a surveillance device warrant can be made either in writing or orally (usually by telephone) in accordance with Section 14, ss6 and ss7 and Section 15 of the Act. The nature and circumstances that require the use of the surveillance device will determine how the application is made.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-FORM-OF-APPLICATION: Upon advice from the Operations Coordinator to proceed, the investigator/applicant will complete an approved Assessment Form, by electronic means to SOAU containing the facts and other grounds on which the application for the surveillance device warrant is based. The affidavit will be prepared by a SOAU Covert Application Team member. Where possible, the affidavit will be sworn/affirmed by the Investigator/applicant in charge of the investigation, however another officer of the WA Police Force may make an application on that person’s behalf. SOAU will be responsible for making applications on behalf of members located in regional Western Australia. The Covert Application Team Supervisor is responsible for checking the entire application to ensure that it complies with the legislation and that the documentation is of an appropriate standard to be submitted to an eligible Judge or nominated AAT member. When complete and ready for signature, the investigating officer is to perform a final check of the application for accuracy and content and sign the affidavit before a Justice of the Peace. SOAU will collate the documents required to proceed to Court, which includes: the affidavit, sworn by the member in charge of the investigation; the application cover sheet, appropriately endorsed with the relevant information and signed by the applicant; the warrant form, appropriately endorsed with the relevant information; and an expiry date indicator. PLEASE NOTE: Affidavits should include specific details about the privacy impacts on any person, and the existence of alternative means (and/or more traditional forms of surveillance) of obtaining evidence. When using particularly intrusive technologies, WA Police must provide sufficient detail in affidavits to enable the issuing authority to have regard to the use and capability of the technology, and the extent to which the privacy of any person is likely to be affected.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-MAKING-APPLICATIONS-FO: An officer of WA Police Force may apply for an extension to the period a warrant is in force, up to a maximum of 90 days after the day the warrant would have otherwise expired, or for a variation of any of the other terms of the warrant. Should an Investigator/applicant seek to extend or vary a warrant issued pursuant to the Act, an Investigator/applicant should first contact SOAU and a supplementary TRF is required to be submitted through the SOAU Operations Coordinator. Following TRF approval and receipt of a completed Assessment Form containing the additional information, a SOAU Covert Application Team member will prepare the required affidavit/s and accompanying documents to obtain the required extension or variation from an eligible Judge or nominated AAT member. SOAU are responsible for making applications for extensions or variations on behalf of regional Western Australia. As per the original application, the application to extend or vary the warrant will be reviewed by the SOAU Covert Application Team Supervisor. Upon review, the Investigator/applicant will check the application for accuracy and content and sign the affidavit before a Justice of the Peace. SOAU will collate the documents required to proceed to court and will arrange for the warrant application to be heard by an eligible Judge or nominated AAT member as per the process outlined in the ATTENDING THE FAMILY COURT OF AUSTRALIA OR ADMINISTRATIVE APPEALS TRIBUNAL, section of this document.

The Act provides for an officer of WA Police Force to apply for a retrieval warrant in respect of a surveillance device that was lawfully installed under a surveillance device warrant or a tracking device authorisation. A supplementary TRF is required to be considered by the SOAU Operations Coordination Supervisor. The application must be made to an eligible Judge or a nominated AAT member and must be accompanied by an affidavit setting out the grounds on which the retrieval warrant is sought. A SOAU Covert Applications Team member will prepare the required affidavit/s and accompanying documents to obtain the required retrieval warrant from an eligible Judge or nominated AAT member. The process for obtaining a Retrieval Warrant is the same as the process for obtaining the initial warrant with an affidavit prepared and signed, and reviewed by the SOAU Covert Application Team Supervisor. SOAU will arrange for the application to be heard by an eligible Judge or nominated AAT member as per the process outlined at ATTENDING THE FAMILY COURT OF AUSTRALIA OR ADMINISTRATIVE APPEALS TRIBUNAL.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-ATTENDING-THE-FAMILY-C: SOAU staff will contact the court officer at the Family Court of Australia or the AAT and advise the court officer that WA Police Force wish to proceed with the matter and request that an eligible Judge or nominated AAT member be made available to consider the warrant. A SOAU Covert Applications Team member will attend the Family Court of Australia or the AAT with the relevant documentation on behalf of the Investigator/applicant. The Investigator/applicant will be available via telephone at the request of the eligible Judge or nominated AAT member to clarify or provide further sworn evidence if required.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-DETERMINATION-OF-APPLI: Once a warrant is issued, the surveillance device warrant and all documentation is to be conveyed by a SOAU member to the SOAU Warrant Administration Team for the purposes of recording and compliance. SOAU will provide a copy of the warrant to the Investigator/applicant and PTU. On the warrant being issued, the SOAU Covert Applications Team member will provide the Investigator/applicant information via email pertaining to their responsibilities during the period of the warrant. Should the eligible Judge or nominated AAT member refuse to grant a warrant, this information must be reported on the General Register, along with the reason for the refusal. The OIC of SOAU is to be advised, who in turn will liaise with the investigating officer and determine whether or not to make an amended application in relation to the warrant sought. All application documents must be kept and retained by SOAU.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-EMERGENCY-AUTHORISATIO: Under certain urgent circumstances, an appropriate authorising officer may consider applications for an emergency authorisation for the use of a surveillance device which would otherwise require a warrant. Before making an application to an appropriate authorising officer for an emergency authorisation, the applicant must reasonably suspect that: in relation to an investigation of a relevant offence: an imminent risk of serious violence to a person or substantial damage to property exists; the use of a surveillance device is immediately necessary for the purpose of dealing with that risk; the circumstances are so serious and the matter is of such urgency that the use of a surveillance device is warranted; and it is not practicable in the circumstances to apply for a surveillance device warrant; or in relation to a recovery order that is in force: the circumstances are so urgent as to warrant the immediate use of a surveillance device; and it is not practicable in the circumstances to apply for a surveillance device warrant.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-APPROPRIATE-AUTHORISIN: Section 6 of the Act defines an Appropriate Authorising officer as: (a) of a law enforcement agency—has the meaning given by subsection 6A(4); or (b) in relation to a law enforcement officer belonging to or seconded to a law enforcement agency—means an appropriate authorising officer of the law enforcement agency. Section 6A(4) provides a table defining the ranks or classifications of an Appropriate Authorising Officer, which for WA Police Force are: the Chief Officer or the person holding equivalent rank; or an Assistant Commissioner (State Crime) or a person acting in the position; or a Commander (State Crime) or a person acting in the position. WA Police Force will seek emergency authorisations from a person holding the rank of (or equivalent rank) an Assistant Commissioner (State Crime). Upon application for an Emergency Authorisation SOAU will coordinate, obtain access to and assist the applicant and relevant Authorising Officer.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-EMERGENCY-AUTHORISATIO: An application for an Emergency Authorisation may be made orally, in writing or by telephone, fax, email or any other means of communication. The appropriate authorising officer may give the emergency authorisation if satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for the suspicion founding the application. Should an appropriate authorising officer give an emergency authorisation, that officer must, as soon as practicable, make a written record of the giving of that authorisation, including in the record: the name of the applicant for the authorisation; the date and time the authorisation was given; and the nature of the authorisation given. This original written record made by the appropriate authorising officer is to be provided to the OIC of SOAU, who will cause the record to be filed with the appropriate documentation and ensure the details of the emergency authorisation are entered into the General Register. Within 48 hours after giving an emergency authorisation the appropriate authorising officer who gave the authorisation, or another person on the appropriate authorising officer’s behalf, must apply to an eligible Judge or nominated AAT member for approval of the giving of the emergency authorisation. It is possible during the same application to apply for a warrant authorising the ongoing use of the surveillance device, providing all the normal legislative requirements are met as per a standard warrant application under the Act. The application: must specify: the name of the applicant for the approval; and the kind or kinds of surveillance device to which the emergency authorisation relates and, if a warrant is sought, the nature and duration of the warrant; must be supported by an affidavit setting out the grounds on which the approval (and warrant, if any) is sought; and must be accompanied by a copy of the written record made after the giving of the emergency authorisation. A copy of this application must be kept in the relevant Codafile by the responsible SOAU officer. SOAU will assist the appropriate authorising officer, or the officer acting on the appropriate authorising officer’s behalf, in relation to this application, in a manner substantially similar to the process followed in the normal application for a surveillance device warrant outlined by the Form of Application.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-MAKING-APPLICATIONS-FO: Under certain circumstances, an appropriate authorising officer may give a tracking device authorisation to an officer of WA Police Force, authorising the use of a tracking device without a warrant in the investigation of a relevant offence, or in the location and safe recovery of a child to whom a recovery order relates. The appropriate authorising officer may also authorise the retrieval, without a warrant, of a tracking device to which a tracking device authorisation relates. An appropriate authorising officer must not give permission under the Act for the use, installation or retrieval of a tracking device if the installation of the device, or its retrieval, involves entry onto premises without permission or an interference with the interior of a vehicle without permission. The applicant, being an officer of WA Police Force, must apply orally or in writing to the appropriate authorising officer and must address in that application the matters that would be required to be addressed as if the officer were making an application for a surveillance device warrant or a retrieval warrant, as the case requires. Should an appropriate authorising officer give a tracking device authorisation, that officer must, as soon as practicable, make a written record of the giving of that authorisation, including in the record: the name of the applicant for the authorisation; the date and time the authorisation was given; the nature of the authorisation given, including where applicable: the alleged offence or offences in respect of which the authorisation is given; if in relation to a recovery order, the date the order was made and the name of the child to whom the order relates; the object or class of object in or on which the use of the tracking device is authorised; the vehicle or class of vehicle on which the use of the tracking device is authorised; the name of the specified person of which the use of the tracking device is authorised; and the premises or object from which the tracking device is to be retrieved, if authorising the retrieval of a tracking device; the name of the officer of WA Police Force who is primarily responsible for executing the authorisation; and any conditions subject to which a tracking device may be used, under the authorisation. This original written record made by the appropriate authorising officer is to be provided to the OIC of SOAU, who will cause the record to be filed with the appropriate documentation and ensure the details of the tracking device authorisation are entered into the General Register.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-COMPUTER-ACCESS-WARRAN: Computer access warrants, which allows law enforcement: to covertly access devices to investigate serious crimes; to search devices such as laptops, mobile phones, USBs, and collect information; and to conceal the fact that a device has been accessed. Law enforcement computer access warrants must be issued by an independent authority (a Judge or AAT member) and cannot authorise interference with, or material loss or damage to, a computer. Computer access warrants can be sought only for serious offences (offences that attract a penalty of three years or more). Division 4, section 27A of the Act (Computer Access Warrants) provides for the use of Computer Access Warrants.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-MAKING-APPLICATIONS-FO: An Investigator/applicant seeking to obtain a Computer Access Warrant shall contact SOAU to discuss the application prior to submission of a formal TRF. An Investigator/applicant will complete an Assessment Form and accompanying documentation and submit it to the SOAU Covert Applications Team for preparation of an affidavit to obtain a Computer Access Warrant. Procedures for the obtaining the Computer Access Warrant via an eligible a Judge or AAT member and Investigator/applicant responsibilities remain consistent with the same processes of obtaining a Surveillance Device Warrant.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-DATA-SURVEILLANCE: Data Surveillance is only possible under the provisions of the Act with deployment of any data surveillance devices undertaken by the PTU and with the existence of a data surveillance warrant. Applications for a Surveillance Devices Act Warrant are made under section 14 of the Act, for a surveillance device warrant to be issued under section 16 of the Act. Section 18(1)(c) of the Act provides for use of a surveillance device in respect of the conversations, activities or location of a specified person or person whose identity is unknown. Each deployment of a data surveillance device will be undertaken in accordance with the Act in respect to collection, storage, communication, use and destruction of Protected Information obtained through the execution of the warrant. In all instances a data surveillance device warrant is executed under the provisions of the Act, the following procedures must be adhered to and complied with.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-DATA-SURVEILLANCE-DEVI: WA Police PTU will utilise only an approved device for the collection of data under the provisions of a warrant issued pursuant to the Act. An approved device is defined as a device authorised for use by the Commander, State Crime. The device may be provided by another law enforcement or government agency whereby an appropriate Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between the WA Police Force and other agency exists. PTU staff with the required training and qualifications operate data surveillance devices.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-STORAGE-OF-DATA-OBTAIN: All data obtained through the execution of a data surveillance device warrant issued pursuant to the Act, will be uploaded and stored upon the WA Police Force Digital Evidence Management System (PDEMS) with access to this data restricted only to persons requiring authorised access. Protected information obtained through execution of a warrant and provided to an investigator will be provided to the investigator via the Intelligence Data Management (IDM) platform.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-DATA-VETTING: As the collection of data through use of a data surveillance device will likely result in a large volume of data NOT relevant to the investigation, PTU will, upon upload to the PDEMS platform, review and undertake a vetting process to identify only the data which is relevant to the investigation for which the warrant was obtained. Once the relevant information has been identified it is to be provided to the investigator via the IDM platform. The investigator will be provided the relevant IDM reference and communication of the Protected Information is to be recorded within the relevant Use and Communication Register and PTU running sheets. The remaining Protected Information will be secured within the PDEMS platform with access restricted as required until destroyed in accordance to a destruction regime pursuant to section 46(1)(b) of the Act (please refer to DESTRUCTION AND RETENTION OF PROTECTED INFORMATION).
rsd|surv-devi-cth-DESTRUCTION-OF-PROTECT: Destruction of data obtained through the execution of data surveillance device warrant will be undertaken in accordance to a destruction regime pursuant to section 46(1)(b) of the Act. Only upon issue of a Destruction Order is Protected Information stored within PDEMS and IDM to be destroyed. Inquiries regarding the destruction of Protected Information should be directed to SOAU. Any Protected Information obtained through execution of a data surveillance warrant held by another law enforcement or government agency shall be subject to the WA Police Force Destruction Process with evidence of the destruction required to be recorded within the warrant file. SOAU will manage and coordinate the destruction of all protected information on behalf of the WA Police Force.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-MAKING-APPLICATIONS-FO: An Investigator/applicant seeking to obtain a Data Disruption or Network Activity Warrant shall contact SOAU to discuss the application prior to submission of a formal TRF. An Investigator/applicant will complete an Assessment Form and accompanying documentation and submit it to the SOAU Covert Applications Team for preparation of an affidavit to obtain a Data Disruption or Network Activity Warrant. Procedures for the obtaining the Data Disruption or Network Activity Warrant via an eligible a Judge or AAT member and Investigator/applicant responsibilities remain consistent with the same processes of obtaining a Surveillance Device Warrant.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-REVOCATION-PROCESS: There are a number of situations that may occur where a surveillance device warrant may, or must, be revoked. A surveillance device warrant may, by instrument in writing, be revoked by an eligible Judge or nominated AAT member on his or her own initiative at any time before the expiration of the period of validity specified in the warrant. The eligible Judge or nominated AAT member must give a copy of the instrument of revocation to the Chief Officer, who in turn will forward the copy of the instrument of revocation to the OIC SOAU, who will cause the copy of the instrument of revocation to be filed in the relevant Codafile and ensure the necessary updates in the General Register are made. Pursuant to section 21(5) of the Act, if the investigating officer to whom a warrant is issued believes that the use of a surveillance device under the warrant is no longer necessary for the purpose of enabling evidence to be obtained of the commission of the relevant offence, or the identity or location of the offender, (or if in relation to a recovery order, for the purpose of enabling the location and safe recovery of the child to whom the order relates) the investigating officer must immediately inform the Chief Officer (via the OIC SOAU) of that belief. If the Chief Officer is satisfied that the use of a surveillance device under the warrant sought is no longer necessary for the purpose of enabling evidence to be obtained of the commission of the relevant offence, or the identity or location of the offender, (or if in relation to a recovery order, for the purpose of enabling the location and safe recovery of the child to whom the order relates) the Chief Officer must: by instrument in writing, revoke the warrant; and take the steps necessary to ensure that use of the surveillance device authorised by the warrant is discontinued. This instrument of revocation is to be forwarded to the OIC of SOAU who will cause the instrument of revocation to be filed in the relevant Codafile and ensure the necessary updates in the General Register are made.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-INVESTIGATOR-REQUIREME: On issue of a Commonwealth SDA warrant, investigators will be advised about revocation requirements. This includes the requirement for law enforcement officers to notify the Chief Officer immediately upon forming the belief that use of a surveillance device under the warrant is no longer necessary for its original purpose. SOAU will provide a prompt to investigators each month after the issue of a Commonwealth SDA warrant, to ascertain if the warrant is still required. If the warrant is no longer required SOAU will seek a revocation in writing from the Chief Officer as soon as practicable on notification that the warrant is no longer required and in any event within two weeks of that notification. Records of the correspondence, including the prompts will be kept on file.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-ELECTRONIC-STORAGE-OF-: Upon receipt of an approved TRF for a warrant, an emergency authorisation or a tracking device authorisation, the responsible SOAU officer will cause any documentation to be saved electronically on the SOAU secure network drive in the appropriate folder. Any further documentation concerning the warrant, emergency authorisation or tracking device authorisation that is created during the application process, including supporting affidavits, is also to be saved in the appropriate folder. Requests for access to the SOAU secure network drive will be considered by the OIC of SOAU.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-HARD-COPY-STORAGE-OF-D: All hard copy applications, affidavits, warrants, emergency authorisations, tracking device authorisations and associated documentation will be stored at SOAU. Once the warrant, emergency authorisation or tracking device authorisation application is approved by the eligible Judge or nominated AAT member, or authorising officer, the SOAU officer will convey the hard copy applications, affidavit, signed warrant, emergency authorisation or tracking device authorisation and associated documentation to the Warrant Administration section of SOAU for storage, reporting and record keeping. All hard copy documents will be stored in a restricted-access secure area at SOAU in a Codafile specific to that warrant, emergency authorisation or tracking device authorisation. Requests for access to SOAU restricted-access secure area will be considered by the OIC of SOAU.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-CREATION-OF-A-CODAFILE: The responsible SOAU officer is to cause a Codafile to be created for each warrant, emergency authorisation and tracking device authorisation that is applied for by WA Police Force. Codafile creation materials are to be located in the stationery area of SOAU and can be re-ordered through the administration officer of SOAU. The Codafile is to be appropriately labelled with the designator of the warrant, emergency authorisation or tracking device authorisation and will include a print-out of the cover sheet document on red card immediately inside. Any person updating documentation within the Codafile is to ensure the checklist component of the cover sheet document is updated accordingly.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-DOCUMENTS-REQUIRED-TO-: SOAU will ensure the following documents are kept in the relevant Codafile for each warrant, emergency authorisation and tracking device authorisation applied for by WA Police Force under the Act: Warrants: each warrant issued; each instrument of revocation, if applicable; a copy of each application made for a warrant, or for an extension or variation of a warrant; a copy of the completed Investigator Report document; a copy of any relevant Communication of Protected Information forms; a copy of any relevant Destruction Advice Reports; and a copy of any evidentiary certificates issued pursuant to section 62 of the Act. Emergency authorisations: each written record made by the authorising officer after giving an emergency authorisation, pursuant to section 31 of the Act; each written application for an emergency authorisation; a copy of each application made pursuant to section 33 of the Act, in relation to approval of an emergency authorisation issued by an authorising officer; a copy of the completed Investigator Report document; a copy of any relevant Communication of Protected Information forms; a copy of any relevant Destruction Advice Reports; and a copy of any evidentiary certificates issued pursuant to section 62 of the Act. Tracking device authorisations: each written record made by the authorising officer after giving a tracking device authorisation, pursuant to section 40 of the Act; each written application for a tracking device authorisation; a copy of the completed Investigator Report document; a copy of any relevant Communication of Protected Information forms; a copy of any relevant Destruction Advice Reports; and a copy of any evidentiary certificates issued pursuant to section 62 of the Act.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-OTHER-DOCUMENTS-REQUIR: The responsible SOAU officer is to cause the following documents to be kept in an appropriate location: a copy of each report made to the Minister pursuant to section 49 of the Act; a statement as to whether each application made for a warrant, or for the extension or variation of a warrant, was granted, refused or withdrawn; a statement as to whether each application made by an officer of Western Australia Police Force for an emergency authorisation was granted, refused or withdrawn; a statement as to whether each application made by an appropriate authorising officer for approval of the giving of an emergency authorisation to an officer of Western Australia Police Force was granted, refused or withdrawn; a statement as to whether each application made for a tracking device authorisation was granted, refused or withdrawn; and details of the destruction of records or reports, pursuant to section 46(1)(b) of the Act. See DESTRUCTION AND RETENTION OF PROTECTED INFORMATION.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-GENERAL-REGISTER: The responsible SOAU officer is to maintain a General Register of warrants, emergency authorisations and tracking device authorisations applied for by WA Police Force, pursuant to section 53 of the Act.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-COMPLETION-OF-INVESTIG: Upon a warrant, emergency authorisation or tracking device authorisation ceasing to be in force, either through expiration or revocation, the responsible SOAU officer is to forward the investigating officer a copy of the Investigator Report document. This report will form the basis for the Chief Officer’s report to the Minister, pursuant to section 49 of the Act. The investigator is to complete this document as soon as practicable by entering the required details and return it via email to SOAU. The report is to be filed by the responsible SOAU officer in the relevant Codafile for the warrant, emergency authorisation or tracking device authorisation.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-COMPLETION-OF-REPORT-T: Upon a warrant, emergency authorisation or tracking device authorisation ceasing to be in force, either through expiration or revocation, the Chief Officer is required to, as soon as practicable, make a report to the Minister, pursuant to section 49 of the Act. Utilising the completed Investigator Report, SOAU will prepare the relevant documentation in order for the Chief Officer to make his or her report. This will be forwarded to Chief Officer’s authorised delegate through the OIC of SOAU. The prepared documentation is to include: a draft cover letter for consideration by the Chief Officer authorised delegate; a copy of the relevant warrants, emergency authorisations or tracking device authorisations; a copy of any instrument revoking, extending or varying the relevant warrants, emergency authorisations or tracking device authorisations; and a copy of the completed Investigator Report document for the relevant warrants, emergency authorisations or tracking device authorisations. SOAU is required to keep a copy of this report. The office of the Chief Officer will arrange for a final copy of the report sent from the Chief Officer to the Minister to be provided to SOAU for this purpose.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-ANNUAL-REPORT-TO-MINIS: The Chief Officer is required to, as soon as practicable after the end of each financial year, and in any event within 3 months after the end of the financial year, submit a report to the Minister in respect of the use of the Act by WA Police Force during that financial year. On behalf of the Chief Officer, SOAU will prepare the relevant documentation required and forward to the office of the Chief Officer through the OIC of SOAU. The information is to be presented in such a way as to identify the number of warrants issued, emergency authorisations given and tracking device authorisations given in respect of each different kind of surveillance device.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-PROTECTED-INFORMATION: Protected information is defined as: any information obtained from the use of a surveillance device under a warrant, an emergency authorisation or a tracking device authorisation, any information relating to an application for, the issue of, the existence of, or the expiration of, a warrant, an emergency authorisation or a tracking device authorisation; any information relating to an application for approval of powers exercised under an emergency authorisation; any information that is likely to enable the identification of a person, object or premises specified in a warrant, an emergency authorisation or a tracking device authorisation; and any information obtained by an officer of WA Police Force without the authority of a warrant, a tracking device authorisation or an emergency authorisation that was subsequently approved, in contravention of the requirement for such a warrant, tracking device authorisation or emergency authorisation.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-USE-OF-PROTECTED-INFOR: Any use, recording, communication or publication of protected information must be in compliance with the Act. Protected information may be used, recorded, communicated or published, or may be admitted in evidence, if it is necessary to do so for any of the following purposes: the investigation of a relevant offence (as defined by the Act); the making of a decision whether or not to bring a prosecution for a relevant offence; a relevant proceeding; an investigation of a complaint against, or into the conduct of, a public officer (as defined by the Act); and inspection, compliance and reporting purposes required under the Act. The above list is not exhaustive and investigators and other officers concerned should direct any enquiries to the OIC of SOAU.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-COMMUNICATING-PROTECTE: The Act contains provisions for the communication of protected information obtained through the use of surveillance devices with other law enforcement agencies. Details of this communication must be entered onto a Register maintained by SOAU, which is subject to inspection by oversight bodies. Therefore, it is the policy of SOAU not to permit communication of protected information obtained through the use of surveillance devices with other law enforcement agencies without the permission of the OIC of SOAU. Investigating officers and other officers concerned who wish to communicate protected information to any officer of a law enforcement agency other than WA Police Force are required to complete and submit a Communication of Protected Information form to the OIC of SOAU for consideration. This Communication of Protected Information form is to filed in the relevant Codafile, once granted or refused by the OIC of SOAU.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-RECORD-KEEPING-OF-THE-: Pursuant to section 52(1)(e) to (h) of the Act, the Chief Officer is required to record the following details concerning the use of protected information: details of each use by WA Police Force, or by an officer of WA Police Force, of information obtained by the use of a surveillance device by an officer of WA Police Force; details of each communication by an officer of WA Police Force to a person other than an officer of WA Police Force of information obtained by the use of a surveillance device by an officer of WA Police Force; details of each occasion when information obtained by the use of a surveillance device by an officer of WA Police Force was given in evidence in a relevant proceeding; and details of each occasion when information obtained by the use of a surveillance device by an officer of WA Police Force was used in the location and safe recovery of a child to whom a recovery order related.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-ACCESS-TO-PROTECTED-IN: All access to electronic documentation that relates to protected information is only to be made available to those people entitled to deal with the protected information. Access to the protected information must be in accordance with WA Police Force policy LO-01.06 Restricted Access to Information on the Police Computer System, in addition to compliance with Part 6 Division 1 of the Act, concerning restrictions on use, communication and publication of information. All access to hard copy documentation that relates to protected information is only to be made available to those people entitled to deal with the protected information. Most hard copy records in relation to protected information will be stored in the secure environment of SOAU, however investigators and other officers concerned must ensure any hard copy documentation that relates to protected information, regardless of its location, is stored in a secure-access area and access is restricted to those people entitled to deal with the protected information.
rsd|surv-devi-cth-DESTRUCTION: Any record or report that comprises protected information is to be subject to a destruction regime pursuant to section 46(1)(b) of the Act. The Chief Officer must cause to be destroyed any record or report that comprises protected information: as soon as practicable after the making of the record or report, if the Chief Officer is satisfied that no civil or criminal proceeding to which the material contained in the record or report relates has been, or is likely to be, commenced, and that the material contained in the record or report is not likely to be required in connection with any activity or purpose referred to in sections 45(4), 45(5) or 45A(1) of the Act; and within the period of 5 years after the making of the record or report, and within each period of 5 years thereafter, unless, before the end of that period, the Chief Officer is satisfied in relation to the material contained in the record or report of a matter referred to in the paragraph above and certifies to that effect [i.e. that the matter is ongoing]. Those records or reports that are consistent with the WA Police Force Serious Crime Exhibit Retention Management (SCERM) policy (CR-15.2 Serious Crime Exhibit Retention and Management) will be dealt with under those provisions. This is to ensure WA Police Force remains compliant under the Act, as well as consistent with the objectives of the policy, being to ensure all serious crime exhibits are managed in such a way as to protect any future loss of evidence, even in circumstances where it is thought a trial (guilty verdict) has brought a conclusion to a crime. SOAU will maintain a Destruction Register concerning all records and reports comprising protected information and will continually reconcile the storage of records and reports comprising protected information against the requirement for destruction. The Destructions Register is to include the following information in relation to the relevant warrant, emergency authorisation or tracking device authorisation: the warrant or authorisation designator; the date of application; whether the application was granted, refused or withdrawn; the period in force; the date of revocation or expiration; the name of the investigating officer; the unit the investigating officer is attached to; the destruction review date (to be adjusted as required); whether or not a Destruction Advice Report has been received; details of the use of protected information; whether the records and reports are to be destroyed or retained; whether the records and reports are subject to the Criminal Organisation Control Act 2012 (WA); whether the records and reports are subject to the WA Police Force SCERM policy; whether the records and reports have been inspected by the Commonwealth Ombudsman; whether destruction of the records and reports has been authorised by the Chief Officer; the location of all records and reports; and whether the records and reports have been destroyed. The investigating officer is required to complete and submit a Destruction Advice Report concerning the above information to the OIC of SOAU with a recommendation as to whether the records and reports are to be destroyed or retained. Once the decision to destroy records and reports comprising protected information has been approved, the destruction of said records and reports is to occur in accordance with WA Police Force policy RM 10 Records Retention and Disposal Guidelines and in consultation with the Records Management Centre, Office of Information Management. SOAU has a dedicated destructions officer to ensure no destructions are carried out in contravention of section 46 of the Act. Any information or records required for destruction by the investigator are now forwarded to SOAU to facilitate. All investigators are now provided with a copy of these Standard Operating Procedures which refers to the destruction process and retention of records for longer than 5 years.

(xii) give details of the compliance with the conditions (if any) to which the warrant or authorisation was subject; GIVE DETAILS IF APPLICABLE (c) if the warrant or authorisation was extended or varied, state: (i) the number of extensions or variations; SE (ii) the reasons for them. rsd|surv-devi-cth-EMAIL-INVESTIGATOR-REQ: Commonwealth SDA (Warrant approved/issued) Your application for a Commonwealth SDA warrant(s)/or extension to warrant XX of 202X, has gone to court and a warrant(s) was issued/or extension granted by [TITLE – Justice] XXXXX for a period of XX days. Please note the EXPIRY DATE of XX/XX/202X. It is your responsibility to submit a supplementary TRF to the State Intelligence and command Portfolio, Covert Coordinator 14 days prior to the expiry date if you believe that you are going to require an extension/further extension. Please liaise with the Police Technical Unit, Operations Manager on 08 9315 4409 (all hours) to arrange the installation or retrieval of surveillance devices pursuant to your warrant (s). As the applicant for a Commonwealth SDA warrant you must be aware and abide by the following legislation compliance matters: For assistance on Commonwealth SDA procedures seek further information Blue Book / State Crime / Crime Services and Services / Special Operations Application Unit (SOAU) / Surveillance Devices Storage of Protected Information: Section 46(1)(a) of the Act requires the chief officer to ensure that every record comprising protected information is kept in a secure place that is not accessible to people who are not entitled to deal with the information. The definition of 'protected information' under s 44(1) of the Act includes information obtained from the use of a surveillance device. PLEASE ENSURE THAT ANY STORAGE OF PRODUCT ON USB’s, HARD DRIVES OR DISCS ARE ENCRYPTED AND ONLY AVAILABLE TO THOSE PERSON ENTITLED TO DEAL WITH IT. Keeping Records of Each use: Under s 45 of the Act, the use, recording, communication, or publication of protected information is prohibited unless it is for a permitted purpose detailed under s 45(4) of the Act. Section 45(5) of the Act further provides permitted purposes to use, record, communicate or publish, or admit in evidence protected information. Under s 52(1)(e) of the Act, the chief officer of a law enforcement agency must keep 'details of each use' by the agency, or by a law enforcement officer of the agency, of information obtained using a surveillance device or access to data held in a computer. Section 52(1)(f) of the Act requires the same for ‘details of each communication' by a law enforcement officer of the agency to a person other than a law enforcement officer of the agency. PLEASE ENSURE RECORDS ARE KEPT ON EACH USE AND THE RECORD KEEPING REQUIREMENTS SURROUNDING EACH USE. PLEASE KEEP DETAILED RUNNING SHEETS ON EACH USE OF THE SDA AND SUPPLY A COPY OF THESE RUNNING SHEETS TO BE KEPT ON FILE. Revocation of Warrants: The chief officer must revoke a surveillance device warrant, by instrument in writing, if the prescribed circumstances in s 21 of the Act apply. This includes where the chief officer is satisfied that the use of a surveillance device under the warrant is no longer necessary for the purpose of enabling evidence to be obtained of the commission of a relevant offence or the identity or location of an offender. PLEASE NOTIFY SOAU IMMEDIATELY IF THE WAARANT IS NO LONGER NECESSARY FOR ITS ORIGINAL PURPOSE. SOAU WILL THEN ARRANGE REVOCATION WITH THE CHIEF OFFICER. Final Investigators Report: Section 49(1) of the Act states that the chief officer must as soon as practicable after a warrant or authority ceases to be in force, make a report to the Minister. PLEASE REFERENCE RECORDS KEPT FOR THE USE OF THE SDA INCLUDING ANY RUNNING SHEETS WHEN COMPILING THE INVESTIGATOR REPORT. For assistance in completing this report please refer to example report situated at Blue Book / State Crime / Crime Support and Services / Special Operations Application Unit / Commonwealth SDA Procedures NOTE - If you are making an application for any covert services, either for a telecommunication intercept, surveillance devices, physical surveillance or undercover officers you are required to complete a 'WAPOL Tasking Request Form’ Please contact the SOAU Covert Applications Supervisor on 9223522 if you have any queries or concerns. Destruction of Protected Information: Destruction of Protected Information and/or data obtained through the execution of surveillance device warrant will be undertaken in accordance to a destruction regime pursuant to section 46(1)(b) of the Act. Only upon issue of a Destruction Order is Protected Information to be destroyed. Inquiries regarding the destruction of Protected Information should be directed to SOAU. Any Protected Information obtained through execution of a surveillance warrant held by another law enforcement or government agency shall be subject to the WA Police Force Destruction Process with evidence of the destruction required to be recorded within the warrant file. SOAU will manage and coordinate the destruction of all protected information on behalf of the WA Police Force. rst|stat-prep-v-DECLARATIONS-ON-WITNESS-: Adoption .................................................................................................................... 17 Handwritten Statements ............................................................................................ 18 Versions of Statements ............................................................................................. 19 Hostile Witnesses ..................................................................................................... 20 Negative Witness Statements ................................................................................... 21 SUMMARY ............................................................................................................... 21 BIBLIOGRAPHY ....................................................................................................... 22 PURPOSE The Investigation Training Précis are maintained by the Investigative Standards Unit. The précis have been written to offer guidance and assistance to all members of the Western Australian Police Force (WA Police Force) in relation to police investigations. The précis are written to highlight the theory and methodology underpinning ‘Criminal Investigations’ and are not intended to be referenced as Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs). Should information regarding SOPs be sought then readers should refer to the ‘Investigation Standards’ link located on the WA Police Force computer desktop. The précis are an ‘all of agency’ resource but readers should be aware they are specifically written for Investigator Training. INTRODUCTION A statement is the product of the interview process. Investigators should remember when interviewing a witness the primary objective is to obtain a comprehensive account with the secondary objective being to record the account in a statement. A good statement will only ever be possible by conducting a quality interview utilising recognised ‘Investigative Interviewing’1 techniques. Conversely, a poor interview will result in a poor quality statement. For further information, refer to the ‘Investigative Standards’ website under the ‘Investigative Interviewing’ tab. Additionally a witness statement can be used by the investigation team to better inform investigators to plan and strategise investigative actions. This subject addresses the methodology that should be utilised by investigators to prepare, formulate and structure quality statements to best reflect the potential evidence to be provided by a witness. Statements are a key method of recording the information and evidence obtained as a result of witness related investigative actions under the Five Key Investigative Strategies (The5KIS)2.
rst|stat-prep-v-WITNESS-STATEMENT: A statement is a guide for the prosecution and defence detailing the oral testimony a witness may give. It captures all of the potentially relevant oral testimony that a witness will give at trial. The purpose of the witness statement is to set out the evidence of the witness prior to the trial commencing so that all parties involved in the trial have an appreciation of the situation. Therefore the statement must fully reflect all the potential evidence that the witness can (or cannot) provide to the court. This will ensure any decision to conduct the trial or to enter a plea of guilty will be fully informed and based on the totality of the available evidence. 1 Western Australia Police Force, Investigative Interviewing, Witness Manual (Perth: WaPol 2018) 2 Western Australia Police Force, WA Police, Investigation Doctrine (Perth: WaPol 2017) The construction of a witness statement is a relatively simple process but there are many nuances that need to be adhered to, in order for the finished product to form a professional document that may be presented before the court. The WA Police Investigation Doctrine identifies five categories of witnesses (see below). Witnesses come in many forms and each is as important as the other during the trial process. It is the testimony of all witnesses as a collective that reconstruct the offence and subsequent investigation within the confines of the court. Therefore, investigators should maintain professional standards for all statements prepared from all witnesses. It is possible a witness may fall into a number of categories dependent on the circumstances of the offence and this includes police officers. Where this occurs investigators should ensure the statement meets the expectations of each respective category. Victim The content of the victim’s statement will depend on the circumstances of the offence(s) and may include proof of facts such as legal entity, age, legal status, consent and/or all of the elements. Investigators should ensure they are fully conversant with the elements of the offence(s) under investigation and where required are addressed in the statement accordingly. Eye Witnesses Eyewitness testimony is generally presumed to be the best type of evidence. This is typically because the witness can give evidence of what they saw, heard, smelt, touched or tasted whilst the offence was actually occurring. There have been numerous studies into witnesses. One study involved an experiment in which subjects acted as jurors in a criminal case. Jurors heard a description of a robbery- murder, then a prosecution argument, then an argument for the defence. Some jurors heard only circumstantial evidence, others heard from a clerk who claimed to identify the defendant. In the first case, 18% percent found the defendant guilty, but in the second, 72% found the defendant guilty3. Although studies indicate that eye witness testimony carries a lot of weight with jurors, eye witness testimony is often flawed, this can occur because of a person's faulty observation and recollection, a person's bias or due to the witness lying. If several people witness a crime it is probative to look for similarities in their collective descriptions to substantiate the facts of an event, keeping in mind the contrasts of individual descriptions. This illustrates the point that investigators should not stop the search for witnesses just because they have identified one eye witness. 3 Bell, B.E., & Loftus, E.F. Degree of detail of eyewitness testimony and mock juror judgements. Journal of Applied Social Psychology, (1988). 18(14), 1171-1192 The above illustrates the importance of Corroboration in a Statement ensuring an eye witness account is accurately A statement, where possible, should include recorded in statement form and clearly points that can corroborate the witnesses articulates how and what they actually were account. able to observe (by one or more of the five senses) in relation to the offence(s). Potential If the witness saw an offence and then acted in sources of corroboration should also be a particular way i.e. phoned the police, then the calling of the police should be detailed in the recorded in the statement, this could include statement. The telephone records will provide ‘who they were with at the time’ or possibly independent support of their evidence regarding documentary evidence e.g. phone records. the time of the offence. This corroboration will increase the witness’s credibility. Other Significant Witnesses ‘Other Significant Witness’ is a person who has observed (by one or more of the five senses) events which are relevant before or after the actual offence. Examples include the clothing worn by a suspect, observing the suspect to leave a house after they have committed an offence, observing a suspect to play with a knife before the offence, police officer interviewing the suspect etc. Therefore it is important the witness statement reflects how they observed these events but also articulates that they did not see the actual offence. Expert Witnesses Opinions, inferences and beliefs of ordinary individuals are irrelevant in a court of law. The opinions of experts are admissible if it is based on their area of expertise. An expert witness or professional witness is a person who, by virtue of their education, training, skill, or experience, is believed to have knowledge in a particular subject beyond that of the average person. It is considered this knowledge is sufficient that others may legally rely upon the witness's specialised opinion about evidence or a fact in issue within the scope of their expertise and this is referred to as expert opinion. Typically, experts are relied upon for opinions on cause of death, severity of injury, degree of insanity, comparisons of items, scientific experiments and the like. The expert has a heavy responsibility, especially in trials. The use of expert witnesses is sometimes Junk science is a term used in U.S. political criticised because they are often used by both and legal disputes that brands an advocate's sides to advocate differing positions, and it is left claims about scientific data, research, or up to a jury or laymen to decide which expert analyses as spurious. The term may convey witness to believe. Sometimes one side will a pejorative connotation that the advocate is driven by political, ideological, financial, or utilise an expert witness to provide junk science other unscientific motives. testimony in order to convince a jury. It is for these reasons that investigators should ensure that the expert witness’s statement clearly details: 1. The qualifications and experience of the person making the statement. 2. The relevance of the person’s qualification or experience to the fact in issue. 3. The processes used to establish the findings. 4. What the person’s expert opinion is in relation to the fact in issue. General Witnesses ‘General Witness’ is a person who provides relevant evidence with regard to continuity and/or procedure. They may also give evidence of background information which assists with building a context for the offence(s). It is important the witness statement clearly reflects the role of the witness or articulates they are providing background information only. This type of evidence is often admissible under ‘Res Gestae’ the principle of completeness. An example of a general witness is a bank manager simply providing documents to police to support the commission of an offence.

The statement should contain all of the witness’s relevant knowledge of the event. Any variation between a statement and the testimony given by the witness will invariably result in cross-examination by the defence and it may, in some circumstances, affect the witness’s credibility. The statement should read in a chronological order, this is because the testimony of the witness will in most cases be chronological. A jury will also be able to follow a chronological story better than one that jumps from event to event and back again. Descriptions play a big part in the identification of an accused or other persons involved in an offence. All descriptions in a statement need to be as detailed as the witness can recall. This will make any subsequent formal identification more credible, reduce faulty identifications and subject the evidence to less scrutiny by the court. Description is not restricted to physical description, but includes the clothing described by the witness. Investigators are reminded that in the case of a sexual offence, a detailed description of the victims clothing is essential. A witness statement must contain truthful and reliable evidence, according to the clear recollection and personal experience of the witness. Its contents should tell the prosecutor and defence what the witness recalls detailed in distinguishable topic areas (paragraphs). The topic areas will assist the court to explore these topic areas in a logical manner and avoid confusing the witness evidence. A witness statement is a story told by the witness about a series of events that the witness experienced in the past. For the most part these events can be described in the words of the witness by using reference to time, place and the experience. Each event is part of the witness's personal experience. The description of the event should be what the witness saw, said, heard or did. When another person forms part of the experience of the witness then the description of the event should refer to what that other was heard to say or seen to do6. The rules of hearsay need to be considered when the conversation is relayed. A witness statement that is prepared in this way becomes a written version of what otherwise might be the script for a film of the described events. If an event cannot be imagined as image or sound then it is likely that the witness statement is not in the correct form. The witness should be told by the interviewer to only include in their statement what they recollect and know to be true. That knowledge comes from recollection of personal experience of events and the witness should be confident about that recollection. The witness should not speculate or guess. If they are not confident about whether an event occurred then this should be detailed in the statement i.e. “John came over Friday night. I’m not sure what time it was or if he came with anyone, but I know it was Friday night because I was watching Friday Night Football”. Correct Tense Most evidence concerns events that occurred in the past. Witness statements should therefore use past and not present tense. The problem of incorrect use of present tense often arises when a witness describes a scene, or talks about a relationship between things, 6 Paper was presented on 11 September 2002 at an advocacy course conducted by the Supreme Court of Western Australia and Murdoch University system, practice, or state of affairs. The use of present tense disguises the true evidence about the state of affairs at the relevant time. Usually it is a conclusion about or evaluation of personal experience that has not been set out in the statement. The specified substance of the words spoken constitutes the evidence. Use Active Voice Most sentences should identify the witness and if another person is involved should identify that person. The sentence should then say what the relevant individuals saw, said, heard or did. The witness may however be revealed by the context provided by the statement8. Avoid Passive Voice Passive expressions that simply describe an event without identifying the individuals concerned should be avoided. For example "The side of the house was where the man came from" does not reveal anything about what the witness experienced. The sentence should reveal that the witness saw the man come from the side of the house. Unless it is clear from the context the form should be "I saw the man walk from the side of the house"9. Avoid Collective Expressions The individual experience of the witness is usually relevant and not some form of collective or corporate experience. The witness should talk about what ‘I’ saw, did, said or heard rather than what ‘we’ or some corporate entity saw, did, said or heard10. Likewise where another individual said or did something the individual should be identified and not ‘they’ or the name of some corporate or collective entity. Corporations do not talk or act, only people do and hence they must be identified. A sentence that links conduct to a corporation is a conclusion about whom the individual represented rather than a statement about what happened11. 8 Supreme Court, as above n3. 9 Supreme Court, as above n3. 10 Supreme Court, as above n3. 11 Supreme Court, as above n3. It is rarely helpful or admissible to state in a witness statement what ‘we agreed’ or what ‘we discussed’. These are expressions of conclusions from words spoken that have not been stated12. Avoid the State of Mind In most cases the state of mind of the witness is not relevant. It may be relevant where an allegation is made that there was a common intention in a contractual context that was not correctly recorded in the final written contract and a claim is made for rectification. It might also be relevant in the context of foreseeability and the actual knowledge of the defendant when an allegation of negligence is made. In most cases however the state of mind of the witness is not relevant. It is not a description of the personal experience of the witness. It is not what the witness saw, said, did or heard13. There are numerous expressions that reveal an irrelevant state of mind and should not be included in witness statements. They include ‘I understood’, ‘I thought’ or ‘I intended’. Avoid Interpreting Documents A related problem is interpretation of a document. In most cases what the words used in a document mean is an issue to be decided by the court. The author’s interpretation is not admissible. A sentence in the form ‘When I wrote this letter I meant in paragraph 2 ...’ is not likely to be admissible. The same applies to conversations. ‘When I said to her [words spoken] I meant ...’ and like forms should not be used. Again, interpretation usually is not a description of what the witness saw, said, heard or did14. Avoid Repeating Contents of Documents In most cases, it is not necessary to repeat the contents of a document identified by the witness. It is sufficient for the witness to say that a document was prepared and what was done with it or that a document was Examples When Referencing Documents received and read and then acted on Exhibits Log and to describe the action.
