rst|stat-prep-v-STATEMENT-FORMAT: The WA Police Force have a standard format for the construction of statements16. All statements must be prepared on the approved template. Statements are to be compiled using the right half of the page only, as this allows space for the prosecutor to enter extensive notes on the left half. Computer generated statements must be constructed using 12 point ‘ARIAL’ font, line spacing should be formatted at 1.5 and each paragraph is to be numbered. Margins at the top and bottom of the document are to 3 centimetres. Pages are to be numbered. The name of the witness should be at the top of each page, the first page should read: (Witnesses’ Name) States. Subsequent pages should read: Statement of (Witnesses’ Name) continued. Statement Introduction The first paragraph of the witness’s statement should include a brief introduction. This introduction should contain the witness’s age, their occupation and the suburb they live in. The witness’s actual address should not be included on the statement, unless the address is an evidentiary factor such as in the case of a burglary where an element of the offence is ‘enters a place of another’17 and as such the address becomes a fact that must be proved. A police statement will also include an introduction. Traditionally police statements only included rank and work location, however with the introduction of educational qualifications and in line with the professionalising of investigators it is appropriate to include the investigators’ qualifications in the introductions. Police statements should also include the Example Statement Introductions Witness Statement investigator’s role within the investigation. These I am 30 years of age, employed as a roles will vary but may include such things as shop assistant and currently live in the investigating officer, exhibits officer, video operator. metropolitan area. Complex investigation roles will include Senior Police Statement Investigating Officer, Forensic Liaison Officer and I am a Detective Constable currently Family Liaison Officer. attached to the Cannington Detectives Office. I have been a Detective for four years and am a level five investigator. I The introduction of the statement sets the scene for currently hold an Advanced Diploma in the jury or judge for the testimony which will follow Public Safety (Police Investigations). in the body of the statement. 16 Criminal Code Act, Compilation Act 1913 (WA). Body of the Statement The statement should always be written in the first-person. First-person is a narrative mode in which a story is narrated by only one character that explicitly refers to him or herself using words and phrases involving ‘I’ (referred to as the first-person singular). This style of writing ensures that the witness only indicates the things that they have experienced with one of their five senses. The statement should be constructed using concise paragraphs to detail the points which are relevant to the matter under investigation. The use of concise paragraphs does not mean a reduction in the detail, it simply means that long expansive pieces of information should be structured clear sub-events. Paragraphs should not be split over two pages, this makes the statement look unprofessional and in some circumstances could lead to allegations that part of the paragraph had been changed to alter the context. Most statements will at some point refer to a time and this should be formatted in the 12 hour clock. The 24 hour clock format should not be used. Juries comprise members of the public and as such many will not be familiar with the 24 hour clock format. Confusion on behalf of the jury regarding times may have a monumental impact on the trial.
rst|stat-prep-v-MARGINAL-NOTES: Throughout many statements there will be a need to include marginal notes to notify the prosecutor of the introduction of an exhibit or the identification of the accused. Exhibit If the witness makes reference to any ‘real evidence’18 in their statement the word ‘EXHIBIT’ is to be placed on the left-hand side of the page opposite the place or places in the statement where a reference is made to the exhibit. This does not only occur when the witness is tendering an exhibit but should occur at any point the first time an exhibit is referred to, for each individual item. This will prompt the prosecutor to show the exhibit to the witness and have it either tendered or marked for identification. Marked for identification is a process where an exhibit is shown to witnesses involved in the trial and the witness indicates that is the exhibit to which they are referring, the exhibit is not tendered in evidence until the chain of custody is complete and the witness that had last possession of the exhibit gives evidence. The statement should include a detailed description of the exhibit including, if applicable serial numbers and model numbers. A minimal description of the exhibit could lead to confusion or legal challenge during the trial. The most detailed description a witness can give for every exhibit is important. 18 See Investigation Precis, Physical Material Management.(Perth: WaPol 2017) The statement must also address what interaction the witness had with the exhibit, such as how the witness came to be in possession of the exhibit and what was done with it at the completion of dealing with it. This information will assist in constructing the chain of custody. A document that is to be tendered through a witness should be explained by reference to the personal experience of the witness. The relevance of the document needs to be explained to ensure that’s it importance is conveyed to the jury. Identify Insert ‘IDENTIFY’on the left-hand side of the page opposite the place or places in the statement where a reference is made to an offender that has been categorically identified by name. This does not include when a witness that sees an offender and the offender is subsequently identified. Example of Extract from Exhibits Officer Statement Role Description …The role of the Exhibits Officer is to receive and number each exhibit seized, record a description of the item, the details of the locating officer and where the item was located. Property Example During the search I was handed a black handled knife, the details of which were recorded onto Exhibit Log B12345 as item BWJ1. … later I conveyed the item to the office and recorded it onto the police IMS system. …The item was then secured in the property store. Drug Example During the search I was handed a clear plastic bag which contained a crystal like substance. I placed it into security movement envelope W0012345 and recorded it onto Exhibit Log number B12345 as item BWJ1. …I later attended the office where I recorded it onto the police Information Management System (IMS). I also opened Security Movement Envelope W0012345 and weighed the contents. I replaced the contents into Security Movement Envelope W0012346. I placed the Security Movement Envelope into the Secure Drug Storage Area. …On the 01/01/2010 I conveyed Security Movement Envelope W0012346 to the Drug Receival Unit and handed it to Senior Constable Smith. 1. During the In a police statement the ‘IDENTIFY’ marginal note should again be when the offender is categorically identified by name and not by description. This does not include the first instance the police associate the name with an offence. Once the suspect has been identified by name in the police statement he/she is to then be referred to as the accused thereafter. Statement Conclusion The conclusion of the statement should outline the final piece of information that witness has to offer the court. A witness statement may include the circumstances that caused the witness to supply a statement i.e. I then attend at the Wanneroo Police Station and gave this statement. A Police Statement in which the investigator prefers a charge may need to state the final dealings they had with the accused i.e. At the conclusion of the interview, the present charge was preferred and whether the accused was arrested, charged and bailed, or was charged by summons. It is not necessary to state that the accused was lodged at the lock-up. Investigators should be cautious as to how they conclude the statement and avoid terminology such as ‘the accused refused to participate in a video record of interview’. This type of statement has been deemed to be prejudicial to the accused as the jury may infer some guilt as to why an innocent person would refuse to talk to police.
rst|stat-prep-v-DECLARATIONS-ON-WITNESS-: The Criminal Procedures Act19 mandates that a declaration must be placed at the end of every statement that is made by a person who is twelve years of age or over. The Criminal Procedures Act outlines that the declaration complies with the act if it contains words to the effect of: This statement is true to the best of my knowledge and belief. I have made this statement knowing that, if it is tendered in evidence, I will be guilty of a crime if I have wilfully included in the statement anything that I know to be false or that I do not believe is true20. To comply with this schedule of the act the WA Police have adopted the following as the standard jurat to be contained within a witness statement: This statement is true to the best of my knowledge and belief. I have made this statement knowing that, if it is tendered in evidence, I will be guilty of a crime if I have wilfully included in the statement anything that I know to be false or that I do not believe is true. Where the maker of a statement is a child of less than twelve years of age then the following declaration should be contained within the statement: I know what the truth is and what lies are. Everything I have said today is the truth and is what happened to me. I have not told any lies. I know it is wrong to tell lies. Where the statement is made by a person who cannot read, it should be read aloud to them by a person whom the witness nominates (not the interviewing officer), before they sign it. It is accompanied by a declaration of the person who read the statement to the effect that it was so read. The following declaration should be included after the official declaration: I declare that this statement was read aloud to me whereupon I agree that its contents are true and correct and that the statement is in compliance with the above mentioned declaration. 19 Criminal Procedure Act 2004 (WA). 20 Criminal Procedure Act 2004 (WA), Schedule 3, s 4. It is the accepted practice in Western Australia that the declaration forms the last paragraph of the statement. Ensure the declaration is presented in its entirety and not as a split paragraph. Immediately following the declaration the maker of the statement and a witness must adopt the statement. Adoption Adoption is crucial for the legal admissibility of the statement and care in this area will ensure that the witness statement is not the subject of legal argument during the court case. The investigator must ensure that the person making the statement adopts it as being a true and accurate record of events. Prior to the statement being adopted, the witness must be given the opportunity to read the statement and cause any amendment they wish to be made. Every witness statement must be adopted by the maker and witnessed: • For handwritten and typed hard copy statements the maker must sign and date the bottom of every page observed by the witness, who then signs and dates the bottom of every page. On the last page further witness details such as where, time, date and who need to be completed. • An electronic statement via the Statement Generator App can be completed with electronic signatures appearing on the last page only. Example of Required Details Witness signature Police signature & No. Time 12.30 pm Time 12.30 pm Date 1st July 2004 Date 1st July 2004 Both comply with the Schedule 3 provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act 2004. The difference in adoption is due to the electronic statement initial pages are subject to PDF and cannot be changed whereas the hand written or typed hard copy initial pages can be amended and substituted if unsigned. The final page of all statements must also include the suburb the statement was taken. If the witnessing officer’s name is not clearly evident from their signature, then they should legibly write their name along with their signature. Final Page of Statement Completed by interviewee Signed__________________________ Date________________Time________ Completed by person witnessing signature Witnessed at______________________ On_____________at_______________ By______________________________ Rank________________Reg_________ _________________________________ Police Witness signature Police Witness signature It is most important that the officer taking a witness statement can identify the statement in court using their signature as a verification method. It is important an officer can demonstrate the witness was fully aware of the requirement to tell the truth during the interview and that the statement accurately represents their knowledge of the event(s). The correct adoption procedure and inclusion of the jurat are key methods of demonstrating the above. Police statements are adopted in the same way as other witness statements and reinforce that a police witness is treated equally before the law. At the completion of the statement the witness should be offered a copy of the statement as a matter of courtesy and professional conduct. All copies of the statement including handwritten statements shall reflect the above mentioned adoption process. Handwritten Statements It is acceptable to take a handwritten statement from a witness. Handwritten statements are commonly taken at scenes of incidents. One common example is a victim's statement at the scene of an assault. The statement must be clearly legible. Handwritten statements must comply with the Criminal Procedures Act to be considered acceptable in court21 and compliance with the details stated earlier in this subject will accomplish that. 21 Criminal Procedures Act 2004 (WA). Do not use any type of correction fluid on handwritten statements, any mistakes or changes should have a neat line ruled through mistakes and initialed by the witness. Where circumstances are such that only a handwritten statement can be obtained it should be retyped at the earliest possible opportunity and signed by the witness, remembering at all times retain the original handwritten statement, as it will form part of your case file and will be subject to disclosure. All handwritten statements must also be copied onto the statement template for inclusion on a trial brief. The typed copy is to be attached to the handwritten statement. Even though there is no legal need to have the typed copy signed by the witness, as a matter of professionalism it is recommended that investigators get all handwritten statements typed and signed, this will enhance the professionalism of the brief. The typed copy must be an exact copy of the handwritten statement in every detail, including any grammatical errors. The details of the countersigning officer are also to be endorsed on the last page of the typed copy. It is of utmost importance that witness statements are obtained as soon after the event as possible, the human memory is fallible and erodes with the passage of time22. The timely taking of a statement will aid in capturing the best evidence. Versions of Statements Planning an interview23 and gathering all the evidence a witness has to offer at the earliest opportunity is imperative. Poorly written first statements which omit salient points will necessitate additional work to capture the required information. This will then inevitably become a point of cross examination as to why such important information was not included in the first statement. Where a witness makes a new statement, the original statement is to be attached to the rear of the new one. In most cases the contents of the first statement is generally repeated in the new one. However, by attaching the original statement to the new statement, the original statement date is still effective in relation to that evidence. Where a witness is re-interviewed to clarify a matter, or provide further information relating to an event, the second statement should commence with: ‘Further to my statement made on (Date) I wish to provide further information that was not detailed in my previous statement’. The statement should then detail what the additional information (observation) is and also explain why this was not included in the original statement. Where additional information is supplied by a witness i.e. something they have done post the arrest, such as convey an item to Pathwest, then the additional or addendum statement is to be attached to the rear of the original statement. 22 See Investigative Interviewing Manual, Investigative Interviewing Philosophy and Theory. (Perth: WaPol 2017). 23 As above note 1. Every subsequent or new statement is to be signed and dated when it was done, do not back date to the original statement date. Where the subsequent or new statement conflicts with the original, the reason why should be stated by the witness in the subsequent or new statement. Witnesses are also on occasion known to change their recollection of events, there can be a number of reasons for this to occur, but there is always the possibility that a witness may become hostile. Hostile Witnesses The Evidence Act deals with hostile witnesses and stipulates that the party producing the witness is not be allowed to impeach his credit by general evidence of bad character, but may contradict him by other evidence, if in the opinion of the judge he is hostile to the party producing him24. The Judge may allow a previous inconsistent statement to be produced to the witness under certain circumstances25. A detailed statement taken at the time of the event can assist the prosecution in discrediting a hostile witness. 24 Evidence Act 1906 (WA), Section 20. 25 Evidence Act 1906 (WA), Section 22. Negative Witness Statements Occasions arise from time to time where the police interview a person who claims to have seen and heard nothing, knows nothing and will say nothing about an event , even though other evidence at hand may indicate otherwise. There are various reasons why the witness may adopt this attitude. It may be because the witness entertains prejudices against the police generally, or it may be because the witness is aligned towards the suspect under investigation. A statement should be obtained from the witness under these circumstances to the effect that the witness saw nothing, heard nothing, etc. Statements of this nature are referred to as ‘negative statements’, however this is a police term only and a negative statement should only ever be referred to as a statement. In the event that the witness is called by defence counsel at a subsequent hearing, and offers evidence which is favourable to the accused, or in any way inconsistent with the previous statements made to the police investigator, the negative statement can be used by the prosecution to negate the credibility of the witness. The taking of negative statements can be an integral part of the investigative process and should be considered at all times when a witness claims to know nothing but evidence suggests otherwise. SUMMARY Investigators should remember that witnesses are individuals, each may entertain a specific point of view, perception, bias or prejudice and from time to time a witness may even try to influence the course of an investigation by providing misleading information. Some witnesses may be cooperative and others reluctant, some may be experts in a given field and others not, some witnesses may require special considerations to be afforded them either by law, established procedure or by circumstance e.g.: children, victims of sexual assaults, people who cannot speak or understand the English language. The compilation of a witness statement is a crucial part of any investigation as it commences building a picture of what has happened. Attention to detail and thoroughness is essential when obtaining a witness statement, they should not be seen as mundane or insignificant, and a detailed witness statement has the potential to direct the investigation to its desired conclusion. Witness statements also form an important part of the court process and a quality witness statement will reflect the professionalism of the investigator taking it and the professionalism of the investigation as a whole. rsw|sear-warr-draf-DISPOSING-OF-PROPERTY: INTRODUCTION A search warrant is a judicial document, which authorises police and in some cases persons assisting to enter various properties and places to search for and seize specified items, which would be admissible as evidence relating to an offence. The primary function of a search warrant is the power to enter premises. The power to search is incidental to the power of entry. ‘A man’s home is his castle’ is still a valid maxim and the law regards a person’s home as their private domain in which they can do what they like with their own, without interference from anybody. It also regards their capacity to deny admission to anyone and provides measures for them to take action against trespassers and the like. Search warrants may be obtained only in accordance with the various statutes, which authorise their issue. Likewise, there are a number of statutes controlling the manner in which police may execute such warrants. The coverage in this drafting guide is mainly based on the law and the procedure for gaining an application. It will therefore be necessary to make such adjustments as are required by the specific Act you intend to operate under. Whilst the following procedures relate specifically to the execution of search warrants, the principles, where practicable, may be applied to all searches including searches of persons, vehicles and premises with or without warrant. Principally this document will relate to the physical execution of searches however for the sake of thoroughness, it will on occasion reference topics outside of that area. Section 13 CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION ACT 2006 (WA) – APPLYING FOR A SEARCH WARRANT In Western Australia, the right to enter and search places, as well as search persons, is dependent upon: • Statutory powers of search; and • Very limited common law powers of search. An application for a search warrant must be made to a Justice of the Peace (JP) in accordance with Section 13 Criminal Investigation Act (CIA). The application must be made on oath, unless the application is made by remote communication. Since the JP must make a ‘decision’ based on the material in the application, in much the same manner as they would when determining if a defendant is guilty or not guilty, there must be sufficient factual evidence before the JP to justify the issuance of a search warrant. It is a prerequisite to the issuance of a valid search warrant that the JP must be satisfied on the sworn evidence before them; firstly, that there are reasonable grounds for suspecting the presence of the things sought in the place, the object of the search, and secondly, that there are reasonable grounds for believing the same will afford evidence of the commission of the offence per Morse & Thompson v Harlock [1977] WAR. 65. Therefore, it is not sufficient to just say “I reasonably suspect...” or “I reasonably believe...” in the application. Whilst the facts relied upon to establish reasonable cause must be set out in the written application, it is not necessary to repeat them on the face of the warrant. The issue of a search warrant is not something that should be undertaken lightly as it makes lawful what would otherwise be a trespass, entry upon a person’s premises without their consent. Issue of a Search Warrant is a ‘Decision’ When an application for the issue of a search warrant is properly made to a Magistrate or JP who has jurisdiction to issue the warrant, this person must decide upon the basis of the application made before them on oath, whether they will issue a search warrant or not. In other words, the Magistrate or JP must exercise their own judgement, not just rely on the oath of the police officer, but proceed judicially according to legal principles. When issuing a Section 42 Search Warrant under the CIA the JP must follow Section 42(4) CIA. If a JP refuses to issue a search warrant, the JP must record on the application the fact of, the date and time of, and the reasons for, the refusal. Only one JP is required to make a decision to issue a search warrant. Should the JP consider they have issued a search warrant improperly or by a mistake in a matter of fact reached the wrong decision, the JP may withdraw the warrant at any time per Barons v Luscombe [1933] 3 A.D. and B. 589.
rsw|sear-warr-draf-APPLICATION-FOR-A-SEA: It is recommended that all search warrants are prepared using the ‘Search Warrant’ section via the Investigative Standards Portal. All applications for a search warrant must show the full name and official details of the person swearing the application. In order to provide sufficient grounds for a JP to issue a search warrant, the party seeking the warrant must give evidence on oath before the JP. When applying for a CIA search warrant the applicant must comply with Section 13 CIA. (Warrants & orders, applying for) The CIA search warrant application must be made in person before the judicial officer unless the warrant or order is needed urgently; and the applicant reasonably suspects that a judicial officer is not available within a reasonable distance of the applicant, in which case it may be made to a judicial officer by remote communication; and the judicial officer must not grant it unless satisfied. Remote communication means any way of communicating at a distance including by telephone, fax, email and radio. The application must be made in writing unless the application is made by remote communication; and it is not practicable to send the judicial officer written material, in which case it may be made orally; and the judicial officer must make a written record of the application and any information given in support of it. The application must be made on oath unless the application is made by remote communication; and it is not practicable for the judicial officer to administer an oath to the applicant, in which case it may be made in an unsworn form; and if the judicial officer issues a warrant or order, the applicant must as soon as practicable send the judicial officer an affidavit verifying the application and any information given in support of it. If on an application made by remote communication a judicial officer issues a warrant or order, the judicial officer must, if practicable, send a copy of the original warrant or order to the applicant by remote communication, but otherwise — the judicial officer must give the applicant by remote communication any information that must be set out in the warrant or order; the applicant must complete a form of a warrant or order with the information received and give the judicial officer a copy of the form as soon as practicable after doing so; and the judicial officer must attach the copy of the form to the original warrant or order and any affidavit received from the applicant and make them available for collection by the applicant. For a warrant or an order to be made by remote communication there are two considerations that must be taken into account; • The warrant or order is needed urgently • The applicant reasonably suspects that a judicial officer is not available within a reasonable distance of the applicant. Therefore, the reasonable distance referred to will be relative to the urgency of the warrant or order. Applying for warrants and orders are relatively straight forward under the CIA, however there are certain aspects of this section which officers need to be made aware of to ensure they are acting lawfully. Officers must comply with subsection (6)(d) and (7)(b) of Section 13 or any evidence obtained can be deemed inadmissible and require prosecutors to argue for the inclusion of that evidence under Section 155 of the Act. The copy of the original warrant or order sent, or the form of the warrant or order completed, as the case may be, has the same force and effect as the original warrant or order.
rsw|sear-warr-draf-COMPILING-AN-APPLICAT: When applying for a search warrant under any statute it is necessary to show sufficient particularity in relation to: • the offence under investigation • the place to be searched • the item/s to be searched for. Where there is a lack of specific information about any of these matters, some explanation for the lack of it should be included in the application. When making application for a search warrant under Section 41 CIA, the application must particularise the following:
rsw|sear-warr-draf-OFFENCE-UNDER-INVESTI: A search warrant can only be issued where a criminal offence is involved, however, whilst there is some variation from statute to statute, warrants can be obtained where: • An offence has been committed. • An offence is suspected/believed to have been committed. • It is suspected/believed an offence is being committed. • It is suspected/believed an offence will be committed. Applications to ground search warrants must clearly show one of the above categories in accordance with the provisions of the particular statute. The offence for which the warrant is sought should also be described with sufficient particularity so as to leave the occupier of the premises in no doubt as to the reason for the search. Whilst the description will depend on what information is available at the time of applying for the warrant, it can be said that to simply insert terms such as ‘Stealing’ or ‘Burglary’ will not be sufficient. Section 41(3)(c) CIA requires the Police Officer or Public officer to state ‘the grounds on which the applicant suspects that the offence has been or may be committed’. Grounds on which the applicant On Monday 1 April 2019, Craig SMITH of 123 South suspects that the offence has Coastal Highway, Denmark WA reported to Police the been or may have been offence of Stealing, pursuant to section 378 Criminal committed s41 (3)(c) Code was committed on his place of business. Incident Report 010496 1000 7911 refers. I have inquired into this information and believe it to be true. This may be as simple as stating that a telephone call has been received from a complainant advising that an offence has been committed and an Incident Report submitted or that police have attended a scene and made observations which lead them to suspect an offence has been or may be committed. To satisfy particularity it is necessary to state the offence in full and the incident report number which relates.
rsw|sear-warr-draf-PLACE-TO-BE-SEARCHED: A clear description of the place to be searched is essential. This should include the nature and situation, e.g., a house, giving the number, street, suburb or town. Where this cannot be done, it is advisable to mention the nearest cross street in suburban areas; or other fixed feature, such as kilometre post, where it is a country road. If possible, the place to be searched should be observed before applying for a search warrant and, if practicable, a photograph taken so as to ensure an accurate description and/or a map can be produced to pinpoint its location. In large buildings such as office blocks and hotels, the room or floor numbers may have to be included. Bear in mind some firms have a reception area on the ground floor, and offices or storerooms, on other floors. Other tenants may occupy intervening rooms or floors. Where such details are not specific, such as a shanty in the bush, as clear a description as possible should be stated as to the location and type of building, e.g.: Room 546, Hyatt Hotel 56 St Georges Terrace Perth, Western Australia 6000 Remember that an incorrect address will invalidate a warrant and cause a police officer to become classed as a trespasser. These principals are well enumerated in the case of (State v Deowraj Buddhu (2002) SC 1665).
rsw|sear-warr-draf-ITEM-S-TO-BE-SEARCHED: Most search warrants are available for specific enactments to search for particular types of articles, e.g. Section 26 Firearms Act for firearms; Section 24 Misuse of Drugs Act for drugs, and those search warrants should be used accordingly. Section 42 CIA grants wider powers of search in many respects, in that this type of search warrant is to look for ‘things relevant to an offence’ or to search the place for a ‘target person’ as distinct from certain items. However, it is advisable, wherever possible, to specify the property or evidence for which a search is desired per Jones v German [1896] 2 Q.B. 418. Example (1): Should information be received that a certain person had entered a shop by forcing a window with a crow bar and stole a quantity of cigarettes (Section 401 Criminal Code), it would be sufficient to describe the property on a search warrant as: A crow bar and a quantity of cigarettes (naming the various brands, if known). Example (2): Where a search warrant is required to look for evidence relative to obtaining property by fraud (Section 409[1] Criminal Code), the property could be nominated as: • One chequebook on (Bank and branch) containing cheques numbered from (first number) to (last number) inclusive. • Letter dated (specify if possible) from manager (or accountant) of (bank and branch) advising account of (offender's name) is overdrawn. • Receipt dated (specify) from (e.g. Myers Ltd.) for (specify amount). • Gents suit, brown colour, size 105, ‘Parini’ make. You will have noticed examples (1) and (2) relate to ‘things relevant to an offence’ which are likely to be located at the suspect’s premises. The ‘things relevant to an offence’ include property either stolen or obtained from both the complainants as well as articles used by the offender(s) to commit the offences. Item 2 in example (2) is a ‘thing relevant to an offence’ which will afford real evidence.
rsw|sear-warr-draf-REASONABLE-GROUNDS-FO: BELIEF While reading the statutes you will notice a variety of terms in different sections indicating the state of mind a police officer must have before he or she can arrest any person, for example: • Just cause to suspect • Reasonable and probable cause for believing or suspecting • Reasonable and probable cause for believing • Reason to suspect • Reasonably suspected • Believes, on reasonable grounds • Reasonable grounds for believing. The same provisions apply to ‘Search and Seizure’. In fact, they apply on any occasion required by statute. These can be separated into two categories: 1. Reasonable suspicion 2. Reasonable belief. ‘Reasonable’ means sound of judgement, sensible, moderate, not absurd, tolerable, fair. ‘Suspect’ means have an impression of the existence or presence of (something). ‘Suspicion’ means partial or unconfirmed belief (especially) that something is wrong or someone is guilty. ‘Belief’ means trust or confidence (in), acceptance as true or existing (of any fact, statement). ‘Believe’ means have faith in, put trust in truth of statement. ‘Faith’ means reliance, trust, belief founded on authority. Therefore, ‘suspect’ is of a lower standard than ‘believe’ per Seven Seas Publishing Pty Ltd v Sullivan [1968] N.Z.L.R. 663. The case of Hughes v Dempsey 17 W.A.L.R. 81, held that: “Reasonable suspicion means that there must be something more than imagination or conjecture. It must be the suspicion of a reasonable man warranted by facts from which inference can be drawn, but it is something which falls short of legal proof.” In other words, a police officer’s suspicion may be right, but then again, it may be wrong. Provided such suspicion is reasonable it can be expected to be supported. This applies to exercising powers of search as much as to powers of arrest. When applying for a CIA search warrant a police officer must have a reasonable suspicion. Section 4 of the Act provides a definition of Reasonable Suspicion. s.4 Criminal Investigation Act 2016, “Reasonably suspects”, meaning of: For the purposes of this Act, a person reasonably suspects something at a relevant time if he or she personally has grounds at the time for suspecting the thing and those grounds (even if they are subsequently found to be false or non-existent), when judged objectively, are reasonable. A good practical approach is to consider three general factors: TIME: • Would certain acts done in the night time be more suspicious than during the day (and vice versa)? • Was there only a short time between the offence and the cause for suspicion? PLACE: • How innocent is the person or place? • Where is the person or place in relation to the offence committed? CIRCUMSTANCES • Were there furtive activities? • Was the person/place/car of similar description? • Did the person have the motive, means and opportunity? Reasonable suspicion may be based on a police officer’s own observations, but evidence of independent witnesses is just as valid, and, as often as not, is better. Suspicion can arise sometime after the offence is committed, but must be before effecting an arrest or search, as the case may be. Hearsay evidence can be used as part of the grounds of reasonable suspicion, provided it is of ‘high reliability’ per Inglewood Servicemen's Club [INC.] v Mauriri [1981] N.Z.L.R. 882. Documents such as incident reports or witness statements, which are sometimes hearsay evidence, may be incorporated as part of the written application to assist in establishing the required standard, i.e., reasonable suspicion or reasonable belief. Damages may be awarded against police if suspicion is too easily aroused per Dumbell v Roberts [1944] 1 All E.R. 326 and McArdle v Egan [1933] 98 J.P. 103. In other words if a search is conducted, or an arrest is made, whether on warrant or not, and there were not sufficient grounds for reasonable suspicion (or belief), police could be liable civilly even though any charge laid following the search or arrest was successfully proved.
rsw|sear-warr-draf-APPROVAL-REQUIRED-BEF: Prior to approaching a JP, a police officer must consult a Senior Officer (Sergeant or above, including Acting) independent of the inquiry to review the application for the issue of the warrant. This addition to procedure has been implemented to ensure that a suitable system of supervision and managerial accountability exists and to ensure that members are aware of their obligations in relation to search warrants (refer to Police Manual SZ-01.03 Search Warrants) When permission is granted by the reviewing police officer, the application for a search warrant can be presented to a JP.
rsw|sear-warr-draf-VALIDITY-OF-SEARCH-WA: The Australian courts will construe strictly the statutory authority for the issue of a search warrant, so as to provide safeguards for the rights of the individual. In this respect, the propositions expounded by Fox J. in R v Tillett; ex parte Newton (1969) 14 F.L.R. 101 emphasise the attitude in Australia of strict statutory compliance so as to save the search warrant from invalidity: 1. The JP when approached to issue a warrant must act as an independent authority, exercising their own judgement and not automatically accepting the informant’s claim. 2. The JP has a discretion, which they must exercise judicially pursuant to rules laid down by the judges. To enable this discretion to be properly exercised, the informant must place before the JP adequate and sworn evidence. 3. The warrant itself must clearly state the findings of the JP, as these findings will not otherwise be assumed. 4. As a necessary corollary to the power of seizure, a particular offence must be selected and specified both in the application and the warrant. This is so even where the statute simply uses the words ‘any offence’ and makes no clear reference to a need to specify the particular offence. 5. The warrant must not authorise the seizure of things in general or things, which are related to offences in general. Thus, the warrant in referring to a particular offence should authorise seizure by reference to that offence. 6. The warrant may be struck down for going beyond the requirements of the occasion in the authority to search. 7. The time for execution of the warrant must be strictly adhered to. The above propositions relate to the validity of a search warrant. If the warrant is invalid then a superior court can take cognisance of the invalidity and quash the warrant by means of the prerogative writs of Certiorari (where the proceedings have been completed) or Prohibition (where it is sought to prevent the proceedings continuing). The following passage, which is equally applicable in Western Australia, is an extract from the Australian Federal Police ‘Search Warrant Manual’ by Detective Inspector A.J. SING (November 1981): “In recent years there have been many challenges against the validity of search warrants and the Courts will not hesitate to quash search warrants based on insufficient information, or because they are deficient for want of a particularity, failure to comply with the relevant statutory provision, lack of jurisdiction or failure to specify the offence alleged. As a result, the framing of complaints and search warrants has become an art form, which demands a considerable amount of knowledge, skill and attention to detail. Generally, when a challenge is mounted against a search warrant the defence (law enforcement agency) will be limited to the written details on the complaint and warrant itself. Consequently, it is essential that all the information relied upon to support the issue of the warrant be included in the written complaint and the warrant itself is properly drawn.”
rsw|sear-warr-draf-PROCEDURE-WHEN-APPROA: Whilst there are a number of legal points involved in the obtaining of a search warrant, there are five fundamental steps to be observed after initial introductions and informing the JP a search warrant is desired. 1. Police officer (complainant) takes the oath or affirmation. 2. Police officer (complainant) states or reads the application for requiring the search warrant. 3. Police officer (complainant) signs the complaint. 4. JP signs the complaint indicating that the matters contained therein were sworn or affirmed before them. 5. If satisfied with the application, JP signs the warrant. The police officer completes both the ‘application for a search warrant’ and the ‘search warrant’ in full. Taking the oath or affirmation entails the police officer holding up their right hand and saying: I swear by Almighty God / Sincerely declare and affirm that the contents of this application are true and correct. After taking the oath or affirmation, the police officer gives evidence on the grounds of suspicion in the complaint and accompanying statement. The JP signs the complaint to signify it has been correctly laid before them. The JP can make notes on the complaint of any other grounds sought, or the reasons for their decision. If the JP decides to issue the search warrant and agrees with its contents, they sign it. Again the JP can add to the warrant any conditions or restrictions he or she feels should apply: • In the case of a CIA search warrant the JP should nominate the period, not exceeding 30 days, during which it may be executed; and • If a JP refuses to issue a CIA search warrant, the JP must record on the application the fact of, the date and time of, and the reason for refusal. Where the search warrant requires an endorsement by the JP to authorise the search in the ‘night-time’ this should be added and signed by the JP. The application for the search warrant should be placed in the case file.
rsw|sear-warr-draf-GENERAL-PROVISIONS: Once a search warrant has been executed, a second search cannot be made using the old warrant. A fresh complaint must be sworn and a further warrant obtained. When a warrant is directed to a particular person for execution, that person must execute it and has no power to delegate the authority conferred upon them per Symonds v Kurtz [1898] 53 J.P. 727. Normally they can use such assistance as is necessary for the purpose, e.g. Section 14 Misuse of Drugs Act. Should a search warrant be addressed to ‘all police officers in the State...’ it means that any officer can execute it. In both instances, any police officer can swear the complaint to ground and obtain the warrant, but the police officer executing it should have it with them at the time.
rsw|sear-warr-draf-SEARCH-WARRANT: When property is seized under the provisions of the Firearms Act it is to be taken forthwith before a JP, it need not be the JP who issued the warrant. When property is seized under the provisions of the CIA it is to be dealt with in accordance with Part 13 of the CIA and the Criminal and Found Property Act 2006. Before property is returned to the owner, members should be aware that the best evidence is the production of the original item where possible.
rsw|sear-warr-guid-COMMENCEMENT-OF-SEARC: Knock and Announce Tactical Forced Entry • Activate BWC on approach. • Conduct Forced Entry Risk Assessment during • Identify yourself and advise occupier of planning phase prior to entry. BWC. • Consider Senior Officer Orders for neighbouring • Inform the occupier of intent to enter the properties. place. • Activate BWC on approach. • Give occupier copy of warrant and • Enter premises as per OSSTU Method of Entry inform the occupier of the reason and the procedures. statutory authority for the entry. • Detain all parties and assemble in a suitable area. • Give the occupier an opportunity to give consent to the place being entered. As soon as practicable after the place is entered: • Secure the premises and assemble those present in a suitable area. • Identify yourself • Give occupier a copy of search warrant • If the entry was under some other statutory authority, inform the occupier of the reason, and the statutory authority, for the entry. Provide Caution and CIA Rights to all occupants and advise each person of their status. Searching Persons for Security Risk Items • Basic search with camera on, or • Strip search all parties one at a time whilst camera is still on (not in the view of the camera). The other officers and I are here to execute a Search Warrant pursuant to the Act. rsw|sear-warr-guid-CAUTION-ALL-PERSONS-P: “You are not obliged to say anything unless you wish to do so. Anything you do say or do will be recorded and may be given in evidence.” Ensure each occupant adequately details their understanding of the caution and their knowledge; • They do not have to answer any questions; • If they do respond to questions their answers will be recorded; and • The recording may be used as evidence in court.
