rsw|sear-warr-proc-OTHER-SEARCH-WARRANT-: Unoccupied Premises and Independent Person Considerations .............................. 16 Independent Person Guide ....................................................................................... 16 Investigative Interviewing .......................................................................................... 17 Clandestine Drug Laboratories ................................................................................. 17 Proceeds of Crime Considerations ........................................................................... 17 High Risk/Terrorist Incident ....................................................................................... 18 Undisclosed Search Warrant – s.24 Misuse of Drugs Act......................................... 18 Use of Detection Dogs .............................................................................................. 19 CIA Search Warrant Ancillary Powers ...................................................................... 19 Adjacent Premises – Senior Officer Order ................................................................ 19 Annexure One – SEARCH WARRANT GUIDE ........................................................ 20 Annexure Two - SEARCH WARRANT QUICK GUIDE ............................................. 23 INTRODUCTION This manual contains the overarching principles relating to the execution of search warrants by the WA Police Force. Any police officer can execute a search warrant, whether it was applied for by them or another officer1. Every member in charge of a warrant and every member involved in a warrant is individually responsible for their actions. This manual is an informing document that provides guidance for members in charge of a search warrant, supervisors and staff at all stages of development who seek to learn about search warrants. Reference material relating to WA Police Force search warrants is located in the following areas: • Criminal Investigation Act 2006 (WA) (CIA) s.41-45. • Misuse of Drugs Act 1981 (WA) - (MDA) s.24. • Firearms Act 1973 (WA) - (FA) s. 26. • Weapons Act 1999 (WA) – (W/Act) s.14. • Police Manual SZ-01.03 Search Warrants. • Body Worn Camera (BWC) SOPs 8.2 Use of BWC During Search Warrants. This document principally refers to the procedures required to comply with the CIA. Where specific legislation relates to MDA, FA or W/Act warrants, reference is made to the different procedures and relevant statute. Although many similarities exist when executing all types of warrants, members must know the legislative differences that apply in the relevant acts. Warrant templates can be located: • The WA Police Force CIA Forms intranet page, located here. • The Investigative Standards intranet page under the heading, Search Warrants. • Relevant legislation.
rsw|sear-warr-proc-SEARCH-WARRANT: Obtaining the Warrant Application for search warrants must meet legal requirements for the valid issue of the warrant. The Search Warrant Drafting Guide provides instructions that align with the legal requirements. For approval relating to warrants for unoccupied premises and conditions for an independent person, refer to the unoccupied premises section, within this document. 1 s.43(5) CIA For approval relating to planned covert execution under the provisions of the MDA refer to undisclosed search warrants within this document. Planning and Responsibilities Operational Order In every case where members execute a search warrant, the member in charge shall ensure that an investigative operational order is prepared. The order will contain: • A risk assessment of the premises and occupants. • A statement of the roles and responsibilities for the: ▪ Member-in-charge of search ▪ Interviewing officer ▪ Physical material officer ▪ Video camera operator ▪ Searching officer ▪ Security officer • A record of the briefing provided by the member in charge of the warrant or senior investigating officer. Member in Charge of Search The member in charge of the search will ensure: • The warrant is reviewed for correctness and is signed by a Justice of the Peace (JP). • They are in possession of the warrant at the time of execution, unless the warrant is obtained by remote communication. • All members of the search warrant have reviewed the operational order, are aware of their responsibilities and are aware of potential risks. Physical Material Officer The physical material officer will ensure a forensic exhibits kit2 is provided at each warrant. Video Camera Officer The video camera operator will ensure an approved electronic device used to audio-visually record the planned search warrant is charged and in working order. Minimum Number of Officers Six officers is the recommended minimum to conduct a safe, efficient and effective search.3 2 Refer to Forensic exhibit handling and packaging guidelines. 3 This does not preclude an officer in charge of a search from deploying fewer officers; for example, when executing a low risk search warrant to seize CCTV footage etc. The member in charge of the warrant will continually assess the risk, ensuring sufficient staff are provided to mitigate the risk. Planned Time of Execution The warrant is to be executed at a time appropriate to the legislation. Under s.43(6) CIA, a search warrant is to be executed between 6:00am and 9:00pm, unless the officer executing it reasonably suspects that if it were, the safety of any person, including the officer, may be endangered or the effectiveness of the proposed search may be jeopardised. Under s.24(1) MDA, a search warrant can be executed at any time, however it is recommended all search warrants are executed between 6:00am and 9:00pm unless for the reasons above.
rsw|sear-warr-proc-ENTRY-PROCEDURE: The execution of all search warrants and searches will be audio visually recorded4. All members are to ensure searches are conducted in a thorough and professional manner and the integrity of the search is maintained at all times. In general, search warrants may be executed by: • Knocking and announcing. Planned lower risk warrant where it is planned to approach the target place, and seek occupiers consent to enter by knocking on the door and talking to an occupant5. • Tactical forced entry. Planned higher risk warrant where rapid tactical entry is reasonably believed to be necessary, and occupiers rights are given to the occupant after an initial security search of the target place is complete. The policy for tactical forced entry is located at FR-01.08 Forced Entry to Premises. A third type of warrant, a covert entry warrant is discussed later in this manual. Body Worn Cameras - Entry BWCs are to be turned on and recording prior to entering a target place6, until after occupier’s rights7 are given and the target place is secured. After police enter and secure the target place, the member in charge of the search will coordinate the turning on of the audiovisual recording device and switching BWC to buffering mode.8 4 s.45(2) CIA and Police Manual SZ-01.03.2. 5 s.31 CIA 6 SOP 8.2 Use of BWC in Search Warrants
rsw|sear-warr-proc-7-S-31-CIA: 8 SOP 8.2 Use of BWC in Search Warrants Occupier’s Rights s.31(2) CIA CIA occupier’s rights are an essential consideration of any warrant. The officer in charge must consider the requirements of the legislation under which the warrant was issued. For example: • ‘Occupier’s Rights’, s.31 CIA are to be provided to all occupants in CIA search warrants. Rights will generally be given before entry unless the member in charge of the search reasonably suspects that to do so will endanger any person, including the officer, or jeopardise the purpose of the proposed entry and or the effectiveness of any search of the place9. • In MDA Warrants there is no legislative requirement to provide occupiers rights found at s.31 CIA. It is recommended that where practicable, the same rights outlined in s.31 CIA are given to occupiers where an MDA warrant is executed. This recommendation does not apply to MDA warrants where covert entry is made. The decision and rationale to provide or not to provide occupier’s rights rests with the member in charge of the MDA warrant. Knock and Announce Entry BWC is to remain activated until occupier’s consent is obtained and the premises is secured10. Officers will11: • Identify themselves to the occupier. If in plain clothes, produce police identification. • Inform the occupier that it is intended to enter the place. • If the place is to be entered under a search warrant, give the occupier a copy of the warrant. • If the place is to be entered under some other statutory authority, inform the occupier of the reason, and the statutory authority, for the entry • Give the occupier an opportunity to give informed consent to the place being entered. Occupier’s consent only extends to allowing police to enter the premises. The CIA search warrant gives police the power to both enter and search the premises. Regardless of occupier’s consent, police will execute the search warrant. Use of Force If entry is refused, reasonable force may be used to gain entry12. Security Once entry is made, secure the target premises and assemble those present in a suitable area. Safety and security of police, suspects, witnesses and members of the public is to be a primary consideration at all times. 9 s.31(2) CIA 10 SOP 8.2 Use of BWC in Search Warrants 11 s.31 CIA 12 s.16 CIA Tactical Forced Entry A tactical forced entry may be necessary when an officer reasonably suspects that if they were to enter in compliance with s.31(2) CIA (Occupier's Rights), such entry will endanger any person and or may jeopardise the proposed entry or effectiveness of the search. Where an officer intends to conduct a tactical entry, they must be justified in doing so. For all search warrants, officers are encouraged to consult their supervisor or an independent senior officer prior to executing a tactical entry. A “Forced Entry Risk Assessment” form must be completed where it is known a forced entry will occur. Before consideration of forced entry is made to premises, the member in charge shall ensure: • The correct target address is confirmed. • The necessity to use force is considered. • The amount of planned force is reasonable. • The vulnerabilities and age (especially children) of all occupants is considered. • All members are dressed in contemporary personal protective equipment as prescribed by Operational Safety & Tactics Training Unit (OSTTU). • Damage is kept to the minimum required to affect the entry. • The necessity for Senior Officer Orders for adjacent premises is considered. In cases of high risk, officers may request the Tactical Response Group (TRG) to assist in the entry. Refer to High Risk Entry and SS-7.2.2 TRG Call-Out and Deployment Procedures. • Upon arrival operate BWC in accordance with BWC SOP 8.2. • Enter the premises in accordance with Method of Entry procedures available from OSTTU, using approved method of entry equipment available on RMIS. • Once entry is made, secure the premises and assemble those present in a suitable area. • As soon as possible after police have entered and secured the target place, provide occupiers rights to the occupant.
rsw|sear-warr-proc-PERSONS-RIGHTS: After entry is made and the target place is secured, occupier’s rights are given and occupants are secured in a suitable area, the legal status of all occupants must now be considered. Obtain personal details from each occupant and decide their status. Arrested Suspect – s.128 CIA Ensure the Arrested Suspect is provided their CIA s.137 and s.138 rights. Record the time and place the rights were given. Ensure the arrested suspect is cautioned and has a full understanding of each section of the police caution and their rights. Accompanying Person – s.28 CIA People accompanying officers to be informed of their rights – s.28 CIA. This applies to all search warrants regardless of the legislative power. Record the time and place the rights were given. Ensure the accompanying person is cautioned and has a full understanding of each section of the police caution and their rights. If there is any uncertainty whether the accompanying person may become a suspect, provide all of their rights at s.137 and s.138 CIA, with the exception of telling them they are under arrest. This will safeguard any subsequent confessional evidence. Detain and Search Persons Present s.43(8)(b)(ii) CIA authorises an officer to conduct a basic or strip search of a person who is in the target place when the warrant is being executed for the target thing. s.24(1) MDA specifies that any person present can be detained and searched during a search warrant, using such force as necessary. If necessary to search an occupant of the premises the video camera is to remain on during the course of the body search. In the case of a strip search the camera is to be pointed away so as not to visually record the body search. The officer conducting the search is to provide an audio commentary of what is occurring so as to allow the audio to be recorded. If any items of interest are located they may be photographed in the position they are found on the body.13
rsw|sear-warr-proc-SEARCHING-PROCEDURES-: Member in Charge of Search The member in charge of the warrant is expected to have sufficient experience or supervision to lead a search warrant. The member in charge of the search should oversee the search and not involve themselves in physically searching the target place. They will exercise overarching control of the search, delegating tasks where appropriate and ensuring the lawful collection of evidence. The member in charge of the search will take all necessary steps to minimise the risk of harm to all people present. After entry the member in charge will consider: • Inviting the occupant to declare any prohibited or dangerous items, or those items prescribed in the warrant. • Ensure where possible that the occupant views the search14. 13 s.65(4) CIA 14 s.31 CIA • If the occupant is not present or declines to accompany police, the member in charge of the search will stop the search and comply with the process outlined in the unoccupied premises and independent person section. • Do not place the occupant or independent person in a position where they must observe police search more than one room (or area) at a time15. • Conduct a systematic (room to room, one room at a time) search of the target place. • Where a room or area is locked, or access is made difficult because the occupant has secured a room, request the occupier’s assistance to access the room (keys, code) before using force to gain entry. • Prior to stopping an audiovisual recording ensure a time and date is announced. • When an audiovisual recording is recommenced, ensure a time and date is announced, and provide a short commentary on what occurred whilst the camera was switched off. Invite the occupier to comment. Remind the occupier of their rights and the police caution. • Sign and date the execution of the search warrant on both the occupiers copy and the original. • File the endorsed warrant with the application on the CRIME file. • Ensure you retain possession of the original warrant so it can be produced in court if required. • Ensure that forced entry repairs or damage to any property is dealt with appropriately. Audiovisual Recording of Search Warrants s.45(2) CIA states that if reasonably practicable, an audiovisual recording must be made of the execution of the search warrant. Officers will audio visually record all search warrants, unless exceptional circumstances exist. Where a recording is not made, officers must be prepared to justify the absence of that recording to the court. Generally, it is not practical to video record an entire search warrant, therefore intermittent recording should be adopted. Where intermittent video recording is utilised, on each occasion recording is re-commenced, the officer in charge will give a short commentary on what occurred whilst the camera was switched off and invite the occupier to comment. Where a search is not audio visually recorded, the officer entering the execution of a search warrant on IMS will briefly outline the reasons for the absence of any audiovisual recording of the search in the free form text area of that system. All members participating in the search are to be mindful of inappropriate language or comments made during search warrants. Poor language, comments or behaviour by police can unnecessarily prejudice the admissibility of evidence. Officers are to take great care and remain professional at all times. All search warrant recordings are copied to disc and placed onto IMS property as a Search Warrant Recording, including search warrants recorded on One Force mobile phones. This 15 If there is more than one occupant, this would not preclude arranging for sufficient staff to conduct more than one room search simultaneously, observed by individual occupants. disc is sent to the Video Interview Suspects Unit as a master for storage, in the same manner as a suspect interview16. Video Camera Operator The nominated camera operator will record the warrant. The camera operator's duties include: • Ensuring the audiovisual equipment is functional before deploying to the search location. • Ensuring the time and date showing on the video camera is correct. • Ensuring the time and date is recorded. If the time and date is not correct or is not functioning, consider changing the video camera. If this is not a viable option explanation of the incorrect date and time should be stated on the recording at the earliest opportunity. • The camera operator will record the current condition of the target premises by conducting a pan of the premises before searching commences, and at the conclusion of the search, in company with the occupier and security officer. These procedures outline the minimum requirement for the recording of searches. Where deemed appropriate and practicable, additional parts of the search or the entire search may be recorded. The audiovisual recording of the search shall include: • An introduction of all members assisting during the search warrant to the occupier. • A commentary of all occupier’s rights and introductions provided. • The police caution and check of understanding. • The production of the search warrant. • A request to declare any prohibited items such as prohibited drugs. • A request to declare any dangerous items secured or unsecured that pose a potential occupational health and safety risk to occupiers or police involved such as hypodermic syringes. • A request to declare any weapons secured or unsecured such as firearms. • A request to declare any large sums of money or items of value such as jewellery or gold. • A request to declare any items particularised in the warrant. • An explanation to the occupier of the procedure to be adopted during the search. • Any items located during the search, which are to be seized. • The counting of any money located during the search. • The sealing into Security Movement Envelopes (SMEs) of any money, items of value or drugs. • Any comment made by the occupier relating to items located during the search. • The process where the physical material officer identifies and shows the items seized to the occupant, providing them with an Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log (Copy), including the return of any items to the occupier. • Any damage caused during the entry to the premises or the subsequent search. • Any complaint made by the occupier. • While recording, if a recording is interrupted for any technical reason (battery, fault), upon resumption of recording an explanation is to be recorded. 16 Police Manual SZ-01.03 and ER-01.01 Searching Officer Great care is to be taken when searching for evidence. Experience has shown when searches are rushed or not systematic, evidence can be overlooked. Personal safety is to be exercised when searching and members should take every opportunity to use appropriate personal protective equipment. Searchers will employ a mindset that considers the protection of all forensic evidence in accordance with forensic exhibit handling procedures. If physical material is located and a video recording device is not on, if the officer is wearing BWC they should immediately activate their BWC, back capturing the previous 30 seconds, including the moments when they discovered the item. The member in charge of the search will coordinate the switching of BWC to buffering mode once the video camera operator recommences recording. Physical Material Officer • Direct the video camera operator to video or photograph seized property in situ prior to moving the item. This is particularly important if the weight or nature of an exhibit is likely to make production in court impractical. • Packaging of seized items will comply with Forensic Exhibit Handling and Packaging Guidelines. • Every item seized is to be recorded on the Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log, noting the location of where it was found. Where possible use the description of the room as specified by the occupant in the initial pan of the premises. • Where no property or drugs are seized the Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log shall be endorsed “Nil Seized”. • Ensure that seized money, items of value or drugs are recorded. • SMEs are used to secure seized money, items of value or drugs. • At completion of the search, the physical material officer will: ▪ Review the Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log. ▪ Identify items located during the search which are to be seized. ▪ Return any items not to be seized to the occupier. • A copy of the Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log is to be provided to the occupier. Invite the occupier to sign the log as a true and accurate record of the items seized. Securing the Premises After the Search At the completion of a search, where no person is to remain at the premises, the member in charge shall ensure the premises are left secure. If the premises are unable to be secured, arrangements shall be made for a contractor to attend and affect the necessary repairs prior to police departure. Where damage has occurred effecting entry or during the search, such damage shall be photographed or audio visually recorded. Forced Entry Repairs At the completion of a forced entry search, where no person remains at the premises, the member in charge of the search must ensure that the premises are left secured. The following procedure will assist officers when securing premises: • If the premises are unable to be secured, arrangements should be made in the metropolitan area through the District Operational Supervisor (DOS) or in Regional WA (RWA), the relevant District Office for a service provider to attend and affect the necessary repairs prior to police departure. • Upon receiving the following information, DOS or RWA equivalent will arrange for the service provider to attend. The requesting officer will provide: ▪ Name, rank and regimental number. ▪ Station/unit. ▪ CAD incident job number. ▪ Nature of the damage. • Payment by WA Police for forced entry repairs shall only be authorised where: ▪ Temporary repairs are required in order to secure premises. ▪ Unnecessary or unreasonable force was used to gain entry. ▪ No offender or evidence was found and no charges result from the search. ▪ An innocent third party is financially disadvantaged as result of damage caused on entry or during the search.
rsw|sear-warr-proc-PROPERTY-GENERALLY: Seizure of Property • All seized property is to be recorded onto an Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log. • The original Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log (white copy) is to be retained with the CRIME file/brief, the duplicate copy (pink) is to be given to the occupier and the triplicate copy (yellow) is to remain in the book for Good Governance. • Property details recorded on the Property Receipt/Physical Material Log are to be entered onto IMS as soon as practicable17. • All seized property shall be correctly labelled and include the IMS number and IMS barcode. • All seized property shall be stored securely and correctly prior to transfer to the Exhibit Management Unit (EMU). Seized property is not to be stored in desks, filing cabinets or the general office areas of your working area. • All movements of seized property shall be recorded on IMS. • At the completion of the court hearing, all seized property shall be dealt with in accordance with the court order. • All receipts for the return of property shall be filed with the officer-in-charge. 17 PR-1.1.3 Recording and Entering Property in Police Possession Seizure of Drugs • All drug seizures shall be sealed in SMEs or a vented bag and secured with a security tag. • The securing of the prohibited drugs into the SME is to be audio visually recorded. • The SME shall be marked with a description of the seizure and the signature and regimental number of the exhibit officer and correctly recorded onto the Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log. • The occupier or an independent person shall be requested to sign the SME. • Subsequent weighing of drugs at a police station will be done in accordance PR-01.02. All seized drug (and paraphernalia) property shall be correctly entered on IMS. ‘Clan Lab’ responses are located in the Clandestine Drug Laboratories section of this document. Seizure of Money • Audio visually record and photograph in situ any money located. • In the presence of the occupier, count the money and place it into an SME. • If the volume of money is substantial, package the money into an SME and use the ‘money serial recorder’ located at the Drug & Firearm Squad. • If the volume of money presents a handling problem, additional envelopes shall be obtained or a commissioned officer may arrange for another secure method of transport. • The occupier shall be requested to read aloud the envelope numbers. • All seized money shall be correctly entered onto IMS. • All SMEs containing money shall be stored in a safe or another secure location designated for that purpose. • All seized money shall be banked in the Police Suspense Account unless it is required for some legitimate forensic purpose. The receipt shall be filed with the officer-in-charge. • Prior to banking any seized money or dealing with it in any way it shall be photographed in a manner to record type, denominations and consideration should be given to recording individual serial numbers. • When any money is banked, IMS shall be updated. Opening Security Movement Envelopes (SMEs) • When SMEs containing drugs or other items seized are opened for any reason, the whole procedure shall be audiovisually recorded in the presence of two officers. • The SME shall be cut open at the bottom, so that the seals are left intact. The member cutting open the SME shall endorse the time, date and location of opening the envelope and sign it. A witnessing member shall also sign the envelope. The reason for the opening the envelope should be audio visually recorded. • Upon re-sealing the contents into a new SME, the opened envelope shall also be sealed in the new envelope in a manner so that the serial number is clearly visible. • Both officers are to sign the new SME. • Record the number of the second SME on the item record within the IMS, together with the date and time of opening, the reasons for opening, and the names of the authorising supervisor, the officer opening the SME, and the witnessing officer. • Audiovisual recordings used to record the opening of SMEs and the processing of physical material shall be stored at the recording office/station. • For further information, refer PR-01.02.1.1.
rsw|sear-warr-proc-OTHER-SEARCH-WARRANT-: Unoccupied Premises and Independent Person Considerations When entry is affected and the premises are found to be unoccupied, the member in charge shall: • Immediately withdraw all staff from the premises. • Advise a commissioned officer who may nominate an independent person (sergeant or above) to be present during the search. • Ensure no search is conducted until the arrival the nominated independent person. • No approval shall be granted unless it is shown that it is necessary to conduct the search in the absence of the occupier or owner. • Where the premises are unoccupied the member in charge must leave the following in a prominent position: ▪ A notice stating the officer’s official details and that the place has been entered. ▪ If entry was gained by search warrant, a copy of that warrant. ▪ A copy of the Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log. ▪ If entry was obtained by the use of another statutory authority, the reason, and the statutory authority, for the entry. Independent Person Guide Independent persons are appointed to ensure and observe compliance with search warrant procedures. They are to ensure impartiality. They will not make operational decisions or have specific involvement in the search or seizure. Should a situation arise that requires intervention from the independent person, they shall bring this matter to the attention of the member in charge of the search. Independent persons must: • Be nominated by an authorising commissioned officer. • Hold the rank of sergeant or above (includes a member officially acting in that position or rank). • Where practicable, not be from the case officer’s organisational unit. • Ensure the search warrant is sighted and correct. • Be present throughout the entirety of the search. • Monitor compliance and ensure the search is conducted in a professional manner. Upon arrival, and at commencement of their role, the following statements should be used as a guide, and is to be audiovisually recorded before recommencement of the search: “I am a nominated Supervisor, from [business unit], appointed by [Name of Authorised Commissioned Officer], as the independent person for the execution of this search warrant. My role is to monitor compliance with regards to Legislation, WA Police Force Policy and Standard Operating Procedures. I have sighted the search warrant which has been approved by a Justice of the Peace, and will ensure any physical material seized during the execution of the search warrant is recorded onto an Interim Property Receipt/Physical Material Log.” Investigative Interviewing All interviews, whether recorded at the search warrant location, police station or other location are to be conducted in accordance with the WA Police Force investigative interviewing model. A preliminary interview of a suspect at the location does not negate the need for an audiovisual record of interview upon return to the police station. Clandestine Drug Laboratories In the event of discovery of a clandestine drug laboratory, the member in charge of the warrant will cease all activity and withdraw all personnel to a safe distance18. Initial action includes: • All Police personnel and suspects depart the site and remain at a safe distance in case of fire, explosion and/or chemical contamination. • No ignition sources are taken into the site. • The scene will be preserved and Drug & Firearm Squad are to be notified immediately. • No attempt is made to shut down any on-going chemical process or remove a power source to the premises without the advice of a Forensic Chemist. • Where possible provide the Forensic Chemist with a description of the laboratory set-up, including whether the laboratory appears to be operating at the time. • Do not re-enter a laboratory for any of the above purposes. • After the Forensic Chemist has rendered the site safe, photographs and audiovisual recordings of the scene may be made, where appropriate. Proceeds of Crime Considerations The Proceeds of Crime Squad (PCS) conduct investigations into matters pursuant to the Criminal Property Confiscation Act 2000 (WA) (CPCA) and may commence confiscation proceedings where: 18 CR-07.05 Clandestine Drug Laboratories • A person has been charged with a serious drug offence and has the potential to be declared a drug trafficker pursuant to s.32A(1) of the MDA. • A person has property directly or indirectly used in or derived from a confiscable offence (i.e. punishable by two or more years imprisonment) including being in possession of large amounts of unexplained cash. • The apparent wealth of individuals or criminal organisations cannot be adequately explained. PCS can assist during the planning stage of a search warrant by compiling or providing financial / asset profiles of the target and should be contacted in all instances at the earliest opportunity if there is any potential the target person may be charged with: • A serious drug offence likely to render them a drug trafficker under the MDA; or • In any other Act, where property is crime used (i.e. a house used for cannabis cultivation or a vehicle used in a sex assault) or crime derived (i.e. paid for with the proceeds of crime). If, during a search warrant, large amounts of cash or assets reasonably suspected to be crime used or crime derived are located, contact PCS. PCS will provide advice and may attend the location. The powers under the CPCA are “here and now” powers and must be executed while the target is in possession of the property, during the search warrant. Charging the suspect prior to PCS conducting a compulsive interview will likely prevent a compulsive interview being conducted and result in potential loss of evidence. For more information on PCS guidelines refer to the Proceeds of Crime Investigation Manual located on the Investigative Standards intranet site. High Risk/Terrorist Incident The deployment of TRG for all other incidents should fall within the roles and responsibilities of the TRG as outlined in SS-07.02 and will be at the discretion of the OIC TRG or the Police Tactical Group (PTG) Commander. All personnel requesting the TRG for planned operations shall submit a Tasking Request Form and Investigators Target Summary as located in the WAPOL Intranet under the SID T&CG Process. Requests must be approved at District Inspector or Divisional Inspector level prior to being forwarded to the TRG. The TRG will respond to all incidents classified high-risk as determined by the provisions of SS-07.02 Tactical Response Group (TRG). Undisclosed Search Warrant – s.24 Misuse of Drugs Act s.24 MDA Undisclosed Search Warrants should only be considered under exceptional circumstances and where operationally necessary. Where it is necessary to conduct a planned search covertly on a premises pursuant to s.24 MDA, the Drug & Firearm Squad is to be notified. Use of Detection Dogs • The Canine Section is able to provide the following specialist resources: ▪ Narcotic detection dogs (NDDs) for the searching of premises, vehicles, vessels etc. ▪ Passive alert drug detection dogs (PADs) for the mass screening of passengers on public transport, patrons in entertainment districts and at special events. • Where practical, a Tasking Request Form (TRF) is to be submitted to the Canine Operations Deployment Supervisor. Dynamic requests will be accepted by telephone or by Station Mail email. • The Canine Section can be contacted 24/7 via 9370 7368 and all out of hours requests must be submitted to SOCC. • Under no circumstances are WA Police Force members to approach other agencies such as the Australian Border Force (ABF), Australian Federal Police (AFP) or the Department of Justice (DOJ). Protocols have been established between these external agencies to utilise all resources appropriately. These agencies will only consider the use of their dog resources at the request of the OIC Canine Section. • After entry has been effected, and before searching commences, the dog handler shall instruct the occupier of the procedure to be adopted during the search. • Before searching commences the handler and the dog may examine the premises in the presence of the occupier or independent person and a nominated member of the search team. • Any positive reaction shown by the dog shall be brought to the attention of the member in charge of the search before the actual search is conducted. • The area or object of positive reaction shall be searched in the presence of the occupier or an independent person in accordance with these procedures. CIA Search Warrant Ancillary Powers A search warrant issued under the provisions of the CIA also authorises the officer executing it to exercise any or all of the ancillary powers found at s.44 CIA. Officers are required to be fully conversant with the powers conferred under a search warrant within the relevant Act prior to executing the search warrant. Adjacent Premises – Senior Officer Order s.44(2) CIA search warrant ancillary powers makes provision for police to enter but not search a place near the target place if an officer reasonably suspects it is necessary to do so in order to prevent a thing from being concealed or disturbed, prevent a person fleeing a target place, or to protect the safety of any person, including the officer, who is near the target place. s.44(3) CIA states that this power cannot be exercised without senior officer approval. Senior Officer orders are located here. ANNEXURE ONE – SEARCH WARRANT GUIDE This guide is not comprehensive and is intended as a ready reckoner for Members in Charge (MIC) of search warrants to prompt their memories relating to key processes during a search warrant. Officers using this guide are to refer to the Investigative Standards Unit Search Warrant Procedures manual for further information. Thoroughly brief all officers on all aspects of the search warrant to be conducted, point and type of entry, known suspects, items of interest, roles and responsibilities. See Operational Order. Check correct address and particulars and ensure MIC is in possession of signed warrant.

INTRODUCTION “I advise you the camera is now recording everything we say and do. The time is_________, the date is __________, and we are at “ “ “I am [Member in Charge] from the [ Business Unit ]. The other officers and I are here to execute a Search Warrant pursuant to the Act. Arrested Suspects Rights s.137/138 CIA Notified Of Afforded • Inform of the offence for which they have • Any necessary medical treatment been arrested. • Reasonable degree of privacy from mass media • Caution before interviewing. • If they are unable to understand spoken English • Reasonable opportunity to communicate with sufficiently, not to be interviewed until the services of an a lawyer. interpreter are available. • Reasonable opportunity to communicate with a friend or family member to advise them of their whereabouts. rsw|sear-warr-proc-CAUTION-ALL-PERSONS-P: “You are not obliged to say anything unless you wish to do so. Anything you do say or do will be recorded and may be given in evidence.” Ensure each occupant adequately details their understanding of the caution and their knowledge; • They do not have to answer any questions; • If they do respond to questions their answers will be recorded; and • The recording may be used as evidence in court.
rsw|sear-warr-proc-CONDUCT-A-PAN-OF-THE-: “We will now conduct a pan of the house to show the condition it is in. Please follow the camera operator to identify each room.” Security Officer to accompany. Record any damage made on entry. “Before we start searching are there any large amounts of money or valuables you wish to secure?” “Are there any items that may be a risk to officers conducing the search such as syringes, weapons, chemicals or anything else?” “Are there any drugs or items listed on the search warrant you wish to declare?” “We are going to commence our search and the camera will be turned off. If anything of interest is found the camera will be turned back on and you may be asked questions in relation to anything found.” “The time is _____ and we’re going to turn off the camera.” Ensure the occupant can clearly view each area being searched.
rsw|sear-warr-proc-RECOMMENCING-SEARCH-W: “The time is the date is and we are still at . “ Provide a short commentary on what occurred whilst the camera was switched off and invite the occupier to comment. “I remind you that you are still under caution and don’t have to say anything unless you wish to do so. Your rights given to you earlier are ongoing and can be exercised at any time”
rsw|sear-warr-proc-CONCLUSION-OF-SEARCH-: “The time is ___________, The date is______________ and we are at______________________. We have completed the search. I’ll hand you over to the physical material officer who will go through the seized items.” PHYSICAL MATERIAL OFFICER (Recorded on Camera) • Go through exhibits log (show exhibit log number to camera), name what items have been seized. • Sign exhibit log and give the occupier the opportunity to sign the exhibit log. • Give the occupier their copy of the exhibit log.

rsw|sear-warr-proc-ANNEXURE-TWO-SEARCH-W: GUIDE Officers using this quick guide are to refer to the Investigative Standards Search Warrant Manual. This guide is not comprehensive and is intended as a ready reckoner for members in charge of searches, to refresh their memories relating to key evidentiary benchmarks during a search warrant. This document omits key considerations found in the manual. Immediately Prior to Entry: • The IO is to have the signed Search Warrant in their physical possession • Check correct address / time / particulars. Occupiers Consent: • BWC activated – occupant advised • Provide CIA occupier’s rights • Give a copy of search warrant to the occupant • Member in charge will coordinate BW activation and deactivation (to buffering mode). Evidence Collection: • Introduction of member in charge. Time, date, location (recorded on camera) • Name, address and DOB of occupants • CIA Arrested Suspect / Accompanying Person Rights • Check of Understanding • Cash or valuables / items posing a risk of harm • Audiovisual pan of premises • Question to Occupant – are the items listed in the warrant here? Search: • Advise occupant of search process • Question to Occupant – do you have any questions? • Systematic search – room by room • Locate item - activate BWC, recording the last 30 secs • Member in charge coordinate camera operator to commence audiovisual recording and deactivation (buffering mode) of searching officer’s BWC • Member in charge to revisit caution, rights and check of understanding when audiovisual device is turned back on • Relevant investigative interviewing questions*. Search Complete: • Physical Material Officer to provide copy of exhibits register • Record and address any complaints • Question to Occupant – any questions? • Pan of premises • Time and date - announce time and completion of warrant. *Note – this does not necessarily negate the need for audiovisual record of interview upon return to police station.

rti|afp-bord-aler-AFP-NOSSC-2: Border Alert Guidelines / State & Territory Police Urgent requests NOSSC manages Border Alerts on behalf of a number of stakeholders and prioritises those requests accordingly and processes all requests as promptly as possible. If your request is urgent because of imminent travel, it is essential that: • Your email clearly articulates the urgency and • the requesting officer telephones to advise that an urgent request has been emailed. Confidential Alerts In some rare circumstances it may be possible for law enforcement agencies to request that a confidential alert be created. These alerts operate in the same way as any other alert, but they are created directly on the AM System, no record of the alert will be on AFP systems, reducing the likely hood of the subject being made aware the Border Alert in place for them. A confidential alert should only be raised if the investigation is of a very sensitive nature and where it would be prudent to limit visibility of the alert. The NOSSC Watchfloor Supervisor can be contacted on the details at the bottom of this guide if you would like to discuss further the option of a confidential alert. Confirmation of the Alert Request When the alert request has successfully been created, NOSSC will send confirmation to the requesting officer via email. The confirmation will provide the alert reference number, which must be quoted in any future correspondence, and the expiry date. If confirmation is not received to the alert request within 48 hours, it is suggested that the requesting officer contact the NOSSC. In the event an alert request is received but doesn’t meet requirements, NOSSC will attempt to contact the requesting officer via telephone to discuss what is required for approval. If the requirements cannot be meet NOSSC will reject the request and provide the reason why the alert request was rejected via email. Where multiple stakeholders have an interest The AM system only allows for one active alert on a subject at a time. It often occurs that another stakeholder has an interest in the same subject. For example, police may have an interest on a subject, but an active alert is in place by a trustee for a Bankrupt. When this occurs, NOSSC may choose to combine these requests into one alert without consulting the stakeholders, the case officer would be advised that another stakeholder has an interest but wouldn’t be advised of who that stakeholder is or the details of their alert. The case officer will only be advised that they are the primary or secondary owner of the alert. Actions that can be requested on an alert A list of actions that can be requested along with a brief explanation of what each action involves is provided below. It is possible to select different actions for inwards and outwards travel. When selecting the actions you want ABF officers to undertake, please keep in mind that some actions are resource intense, it is essential that you only request actions that will assist in your investigation of the subject. The actions requested must be reviewed after every activation, or whenever the Border Alert is being retained to ensure that they are still appropriate and are not utilising Commonwealth resources needlessly.
rti|afp-bord-aler-AFP-NOSSC-3: Border Alert Guidelines / State & Territory Police
rti|afp-bord-aler-ACTION-DESCRIPTION: ADVISE AUTHORITIES - NOSSC will phone alert contact immediately at any time day or night. IMMEDIATELY Must be updated where contact changes. ADVISE AUTHORITIES NOSSC will only notify the contact officer of an activation during business hours or via email. ATTN TO TRAVEL COMPS Attention to travel companions. If identified, travel companions are typically subjected to the same response actions as the alert subject. ATTN TO EXCESS CURRENCY Where intelligence holdings suggest the alert subject may carry excess currency or BNI’s across the border without declaring. For ABF to search for excess currency, they must be satisfied that the investigation complies with Customs Act or ASIO Act or Intelligence Services Act. Can only be undertaken with a baggage exam. ASSESS NEED FOR BODY Assess need for Personal Search (s219L – s219ZJ of the Customs Act). SEARCH (inwards only) Where it is likely prohibited goods will be carried on or in the person. Under s219, it is the detention officer who must form the view that there are reasonable grounds for a personal search. Can only be undertaken with a baggage exam. ASSESS DOCUMENTS Assessment of personal, commercial or travel documents of subject. For ABF to obtain a copy of any documents, they must be satisfied that the investigation complies with Customs Act or ASIO Act or Intelligence Services Act. Can only be undertaken with a baggage exam. ASSESS ELECTRONIC STORAGE Assess any hard drives, electronic storage devices or SIM/IMEI of DEVICE mobile phone, laptop, iPod etc. For ABF to assess items stored on an electronic storage device for potential download, they must be satisfied that the investigation complies with Customs Act or the ASIO Act or Intelligence Services Act. Can only be undertaken with a baggage exam. Due to the size of modern devices these can take a long time to assess DETAIN Detain and deliver alert subject to custody of a police officer as soon as practicable after detention. Can only be actioned with an Order, Warrant or Bail conditions. DO NOT ALERT TO LAW Do not make the alert subject aware of law enforcement interest against ENFORCEMENT INTEREST them. This action will allow the traveller to pass through Smart Gate with the appearance of being undetected. This action cannot be requested with a bag exam or associated action. IMAGE Photograph of subject (traveller), travelling companions (if identified) or persons who meet the alert subject in public area upon arrival – TRAVELLER (greeter). Requests for photos should be removed after a photo has been supplied. – COMPS – GREETER (inwards only) VIDEO SURVELLIANCE Conduct video surveillance of alert subject from time of immigration clearance to the boundary of camera coverage. Requests for video – TRAVELLER surveillance are resource intensive and should be removed after video has been supplied. – COMPS – GREETERS (inwards only)
rti|afp-bord-aler-AFP-NOSSC-4: Border Alert Guidelines / State & Territory Police VIDEO SURVEILLANCE – ATTN ABF will take video footage of the subject and note the subject’s mode TO MOD of departure from an airport (inwards action only) This action is resource intensive and should be removed after video has been supplied. 100% BAGGAGE EXAM Conduct 100% exam of alert subject’s baggage. Or this action can also be used to allow for law enforcement response where ABF has no power to detain, for example. Warrants for state and territory offences not prescribed under s219ZJAA of the Customs Act 1901. Requests to undertake a baggage examination Where a baggage examination is requested, a legislative reference to the specific offence must be provided on the Border Alert Request Form. ABF have provided advice concerning the legislative requirements of baggage exams, and the actions of copying documents and examination of electronic devices. A mobile phone is considered to be a document for the purposes of the Customs Act which defines ‘document’ in section 4 to include ‘any article or material from which sounds, images or writing is capable of being produced with or without the aid of a computer or of some other device’. ABF officers are only permitted to copy documents and/or download electronic devices if the offence relates to a prescribed Act as outlined in Section 118 of the Customs Act 1901. The below table outlines the relevant Commonwealth Acts that are prescribed by ABF that fit within section 186A of the Customs Act. This table can be used by members for reference purposes. Item Relevant Act 1 Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2 Aviation Transport Security Act 2004 3 Bankruptcy Act 1966 4 Biosecurity Act 2015 5 Crimes Act 1914 6 Crimes (Aviation) Act 1991 7 Crimes (Hostages) Act 1989 8 Crimes (Internationally Protect Persons) Act 1976 9 Crimes (Ships and Fixed Platforms) Act 1992 10 Criminal Code Act 1995 11 Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation act 1999 12 Family Law Act 1975 13 Financial Transaction Reports Act 1988 14 Fisheries Management Act 1991 15 Geneva Convention Act 1957
rti|afp-bord-aler-AFP-NOSSC-5: Border Alert Guidelines / State & Territory Police 16 Migration Act 1958 17 Proceeds of Crime Act 1987 18 Torres Strait Fisheries Act 1984 S186 of the Customs Act provides the general power to examine goods subject to customs control at a customs place. Section 186A (1) of the Act gives an officer the power to make a copy or take an extract from a document that has been examined under section 186 if, as a result of that examination, the officer is satisfied that the document may contain information relevant to the following (as per s 186A(1)(b)): i. an importation or exportation, or to a proposed importation or exportation, of prohibited goods; or ii. the commission or attempted commission of any other offence against this Act or any offence against a prescribed Act; or iii. the performance of functions under section 17 of the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Act 1979; or iv. the performance of functions under section 6 of the Intelligence Services Act 2001; or v. security (within the meaning of section 4 of the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Act 1979). The definition of an ‘offence’ under s 183UA of the Customs Act includes an offence against the Customs Act, an offence against the Commerce (Trade Descriptions) Act 1905, an offence against s 72.13 or Division 307 or 361 of the Criminal Code 1995, or an offence against a provision in Subdivision 308-A in Schedule 1 to the Taxation Administration Act 1953. This definition excludes an offence against the Firearms Act or any other state and territory legislation. It is requested that relevant information be provided on the Border Request Form to guide ABF officers in what is required in the baggage examination. For example, if “ASSESS ELECTRONIC STORAGE DEVICE” is selected as an action, an explanation should be provided that specifically details what ABF officers should looking for when assessing the subject’s mobile device (SIM card numbers, contact details, recent calls, stored messages etc.), including the commonwealth legislative reference. Failure to provide a legislative reference may result in ABF not undertaking the requested baggage examination. Subject to Warrant or on Bail If the Arrest Warrant refers to Commonwealth offences, ABF officers will detain the alert subject. If the alert subject is on Bail for Commonwealth offences, and the Bail conditions include the condition that the person is not to depart Australia, ABF officers are also able to detain the subject. A copy of the original Bail Undertaking/Conditions or the Arrest Warrant should be sent with the Border Alert Request Form. The NOSSC will not obtain a copy of any Warrants or Bail documents from any Department or Warrant Bureau (State or Federal) on behalf of police officers for Border Alert requests for subjects of a Warrant or Bail, the police officer will need to have their relevant Department or Bureau forward a copy of the Warrant (a not for execution copy will suffice) or Bail to NOSSC as soon as possible to prevent delay in processing the Alert Request for a subject on a Warrant or Bail. A Border Alert request for a Warrant or Bail cannot be approved without these documents. The legislative reference to the offences under which the person has been charged, or the warrant has been issued must be quoted in the Offence Details field on the Border Alert Request Form. It is essential that information stated within Border Alerts remain current and accurate. The NOSSC must be immediately advised of all changes to the status of Warrants or Bail conditions to prevent unnecessary intervention and action by ABF and AFP officers.
rti|afp-bord-aler-AFP-NOSSC-6: Border Alert Guidelines / State & Territory Police ABF officers will contact the NOSSC who will request AFP officers to attend the customs control point. The case officer will be contacted by a NOSSC member as soon as possible after the Border Alert has triggered to advise that the Border Alert subject has been taken into custody. Permission to travel Except for persons subject to travel restrictions included in bail conditions or court orders, there must be a reasonable expectation of travel to and/or from Australia when requesting a Border Alert. Request for Passenger (PAX) Cards, photos or video surveillance PAX cards Copies of passenger (PAX) cards for subjects including their travelling companions can no-longer be requested as an alert action on a Border Alert. This is in response to ABF moving away from providing physical PAX cards to the AFP for further dissemination and Processing. To obtain a copy of a PAX card, the following Request for Information – Law Enforcement Agencies and other Government Agencies form will need to be submitted directly to ABF. This form can be submitted without a Border Alert being in place. Photos and Video Surveillance Passenger Photos and Video surveillance can be selected as an Alert action, however obtaining video surveillance requires significant ABF resources and should only be requested if the footage will genuinely assist your investigation. It is assumed that only one photo and/or one video of a subject is required, and after an alert has matched against the subject an amendment should be submitted to NOSSC to have these actions removed. Photos and videos are forwarded by ABF to the NOSSC via AFP airport members by internal mail. Currently there are no procedures in place for ABF to obtain these electronically. Therefore, it will be some weeks before these are provided to the case officer. NOSSC will only email photos to a protected email address, therefore the protected email address should be provided within the request form if a photo is required. If no protected email address is provided, NOSSC will forward the photo via secure safe hands delivery. Video surveillance is provided to NOSSC as a DVD, and are subject to a protected security classification, these DVD’s can only be provided to the case officer via safe hands delivery. A postal address that is not a PO Box should be provided within the request form if a photo or video is required. Notification of travel When the alert triggers at an airport or seaport ABF officers will advise the NOSSC of the alert activation. Depending on the notification selected within the alert request, the NOSSC will notify the contact officer either immediately or during business hours advising of the alert activation using the contact details provided. The inability for the NOSSC to contact the contact officer for an ADVISE AUTHORITIES IMMEDIATELY action, will result in unnecessarily delay, and the subject maybe permitted to, or denied travel. The AFP does not accept any liability for incorrect actions taken because of the contact officer being unavailable. For this reason, it is essential that contact details provided are correct and if immediate notification is required, the contact provided is available 24 hours 7 days a week.
rti|afp-bord-aler-AFP-NOSSC-7: Border Alert Guidelines / State & Territory Police Maintenance of alerts Border Alerts will normally remain active for period of 90, 180 or 360 days (depending on the alert type), if it is required to keep the alert active for an extended period, an email will need to be sent to the NOSSC before the expire date indicating your desire to retain the alert for a further 90-, 180- or 360-day period. The alert will cease to remain active if a retention request is not provided before the expire date. A new request form including supporting documentation will need to be submitted if the alert is still required. When an alert triggers at an airport or seaport, the alert goes into a review period of 30 days, if the alert is required for another 90, 180 or 360 day period, an email requesting the retention of the alert must be received with 30 days of that activation, or you can inform the NOSSC member over phone at the time of initial activation that you want the alert to remain active. If a request to retain the alert either via phone or email is not received within that 30-day period the alert will cease to remain active, regardless of if the expiry date provided by the NOSSC is well into the future e.g. 100 days, and a new request form including supporting documentation will need to be submitted if the alert is still required. If the alert is no-longer required, please do not allow the alert to expire, an email must be received advising to delete the alert, this is to ensure alerts are not on the system that shouldn’t be, and that the subjects travel plans are not affected. It is the sole responsibility of the case officer requesting the Border Alert to monitor and maintain that alert. The NOSSC does not send reminders to renew Alerts after the expiry date or after 30 days following an activation. The AFP and ABF rely significantly on the accuracy of the information provided within a border alert. If at any time changes to the contact details, information, or response actions are required to be made to the alert, it is imperative that the NOSSC is advised at the earliest opportunity, so the required changes are made to the alert. Where a request for a retention, amendment or a deletion to an alert is made, the requesting officer should expect confirmation from the NOSSC within 72 hours. If confirmation is not received, the requesting officer must contact the NOSSC to ensure that the request is progressed. Serious Contravention: Defined in s.5E – includes offences ≥ 3 years Issuing Authority Judge, Magistrate, or ART member appointed under s.6DB. Prescribed offence ≥ 3 years imprisonment Secondary Use Must be for a permitted purpose under the Act (e.g. related investigation). Notes: All access must be proportionate and justified. Destruction obligations apply to records no longer required (s.79, s.150). Direct all questions and queries in relation to these products directly to SOAU.

rti|stor-comm-cth-1-INTRODUCTION: This procedure provides comprehensive operational guidance to WA Police Force members for the preservation, access, use, retention and destruction of stored communications in accordance with Chapter 3 of the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979 (Cth) (“the Act”). The Act establishes a general prohibition on accessing stored communications without the knowledge of either party, subject to specific statutory exemptions. This procedure translates those statutory requirements into practical investigative steps to ensure lawful access, proper oversight and compliance with external inspection regimes. This procedure applies to all WA Police Force investigations where stored communications are sought, whether access is obtained: 1. with a stored communications warrant under s116, or 2. without a warrant where the relevant person has knowledge or has been notified. This is covered in more detail is Section 5 and 6 or this document.
rti|stor-comm-cth-2-STORED-COMMUNICATION: Definitions in this procedure adopt the meanings set out in s5 and s6EB of the Act, unless otherwise stated. Stored Communication A communication that:  Has passed over a telecommunications system,  Is held on equipment operated by, and in the possession of, a telecommunications carrier; and  Cannot be accessed without the assistance of the carrier (s5 – definition of “stored communication”). Stored Communications Warrant A warrant issued under Part 3-3, Division 2 of the Act authorising covert access to stored communications. Preservation Notice A notice issued under Part 3-1A, Division 2 requiring a carrier to preserve stored communications to prevent deletion. Serious Contravention A contravention meeting the threshold set out in s5E of the Act (generally offences punishable by at least three years imprisonment or equivalent penalty).

rti|stor-comm-cth-3-LAWFUL-ACCESS-TO-STO: The following information is intended to assist an investigator or applicant who is investigating an offence and, as part of that investigation, seeks access to stored communications held by a telecommunications carrier (Telco). Depending on the circumstances, there are two lawful methods by which access to stored communications may be obtained: a) The Act permits access to stored communications without the knowledge of the relevant person using a stored communications warrant (s 116 of the Act); or b) Access to stored communications may be obtained with the knowledge of the relevant person. In these circumstances, a stored communications warrant is not required; however, alternative procedures apply.
rti|stor-comm-cth-COMMUNICATIONS-WARRANT: The following outlines the step-by-step process for applying for a Stored Communications Warrant. Each step is explained in further detail later in this Procedural Guide.
rti|stor-comm-cth-STEP-1: Request for Information (RFI) – IPND/SUBSCRIBER To ensure a Stored Communications Warrant is served on the correct Telco, an IPND request via Information Data Management (IDM) is required before the process of applying for a warrant can commence.
rti|stor-comm-cth-STEP-2: Preservation Notice (PN) The purpose of the preservation is to prevent the communications held by a Telco from being destroyed before they can be accessed under warrant.
rti|stor-comm-cth-STEP-3: PN served on Telecommunications Carrier (Telco) SOAU Warrant Administration Team will organise for the Preservation Order to be sent to the telecommunications carrier requiring them to isolate and hold the stored communications.

rti|stor-comm-cth-5-PRESERVATION-NOTICES: To prevent communications held by a Telco from being destroyed before they can be accessed under warrant, certain agencies can give a preservation notice to a Telco requiring them to preserve all stored communications that they hold. There are two types of domestic preservation notices: a) Historic — covering the period that commences prior to the carrier receiving the notice and ends at the conclusion of the day on which the carrier receives the notice; and b) Ongoing — covering the period that commences at the time the carrier receives the notice and ends at the conclusion of the 29th day after the day the carrier receives the notice. The period for which historic stored communications can be preserved will vary. It is therefore critical that, as part of a criminal investigation, investigators engage with the SOAU Warrant Administration Team as early as possible to coordinate the preservation request. rti|stor-comm-cth-8-ACCESSING-STORED-COM: PERSON WITH THE PERSON’S KNOWLEDGE OR CONSENT The prohibitions contained in the Act do not prevent WA Police Force from having access to stored communications with the consent of, or knowledge of either party to that communication. It is therefore necessary to inform the person of an intention to access his or her communications. The person could be a suspect, a victim or a witness to an offence. The process involves serving a Notice of Intention to Access Data on the person and then execute a CIA Search Warrant on the Telco. A Stored Communication Warrant is not required. rti|stor-comm-cth-11-REVOCATION-STORED-C: WARRANTS Under section 122 of the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979, a Stored Communications Warrant must be revoked when it is no longer required, or may be revoked at any time by the Chief Officer or an authorised delegate. (See annexure) If the reasons for issuing the warrant no longer exist, the Chief Officer or delegate must:  Promptly inform any other law-enforcement agency’s Chief Officer using the warrant that it will be revoked; and  Revoke the warrant in writing. Warrants that have already expired cannot be revoked. Process Once it is determined that access to stored communications is no longer required, the Investigator/Applicant must immediately notify SOAU via email. SOAU will:  Contact the relevant Telco to arrange revocation; and  Complete the Stored Communications Warrant Revocation template.  Request Effectiveness Report and Destruction Advice Report from the investigator. Note: Revocation of an ongoing preservation order must be signed by Inspector in charge of SOAU. After revocation In accordance with section 123 of the Act, SOAU will:  Complete all required statutory notifications; and  Provide the Telco with a certified copy of the revocation instrument.

OFFICIAL - Sensitive Part 3-4 of the Act explains the rules for dealing with accessed information. Under section 133, it is an offence for a person to do any of the following unless authorised:  share the information with someone else.  use the information.  make a record of the information, or  give the information as evidence in a legal proceeding, where the information is: o lawfully accessed information. o information obtained by unlawfully accessing a stored communication. o information obtained under a preservation notice; or o information obtained under a stored communications warrant. Penalty: Imprisonment for 2 years or 120 penalty units, or both. These exemptions are set out in section 134 and apply where the information is dealt with for the purposes of Parts 3-1A, 3-2, 3-3, 3-5, 3-6 or Chapter 4A of the Act. Stored Communications Information given in evidence Stored communications information can be given in evidence only in limited types of proceedings and for no other purpose. Under section 139(4), this information may be used in:  A criminal prosecution for a relevant offence.  Proceedings to confiscate or forfeit property, or to impose a financial penalty linked to that offence.  Proceedings under the Spam Act 2003.  Proceedings to take evidence under section 43 of the Extradition Act 1988, where they relate to the offence.  Extradition proceedings between States or Territories relating to the offence.  Proceedings to recover a financial penalty for a relevant contravention; or  Police disciplinary proceedings. Stored communications information must only be used for one or more of these purposes and must not be used for any other reason.

Destruction Destruction of Section 151 Records Once the statutory retention requirement has been satisfied, WA Police Force may lawfully destroy records retained under section 151. The destruction must be:  Authorised by the Chief Officer or a delegate; and  Documented to demonstrate compliance and accountability. Destruction of Stored Communications Information Information or records obtained by accessing stored communications:  Are not subject to mandatory retention under section 151, and  Must be destroyed once they are no longer required for a permitted purpose under the Act. Destruction may only occur where the Chief Officer is satisfied the information is no longer required for any lawful investigative, evidentiary, or regulatory purpose. Oversight and Accountability WA Police Force ensures that:  Retention and destruction decisions are lawful and proportionate.  Destruction occurs in a way that prevents reconstruction of information; and  Sufficient records are kept demonstrating compliance with legislative requirements and external oversight. These obligations apply regardless of internal administrative arrangements and support transparency, privacy protection, and independent review by the Commonwealth Ombudsman. Destruction of stored communications information and records When stored communications information or records are authorised for destruction, the destruction must be carried out by an authorised officer and witnessed by another officer. The destruction process must ensure that:  Any stored communications information held on physical media (including compact discs or other electronic storage) is securely destroyed so it cannot be recovered.  All electronic copies of stored communications information are permanently deleted from police systems where the information was stored or processed; and  Any stored communications information held on external systems is formally closed to prevent further access. All destruction must be undertaken in accordance with s150 and ensure the information is destroyed. Any destruction activity completed is to be recorded on the relevant destruction certificate and filed in the relevant Warrant Codafile and then archived and the Warrant Management System updated. Communications Recording WA Police Force investigators and applicants must keep clear records to show that stored communications information is used and shared only as permitted by section 139 of the Act. A record must be made each time stored communications information is shared, whether verbally or in writing, when it is:  Shared outside the investigation team; or  Shared with another agency. These records demonstrate that the use or communication of stored communications information was lawful, necessary, and authorised. Any sharing of stored communications information, whether within WA Police Force or with an external agency, must be approved by the OIC of SOAU, and recorded on a Restricted Record Register. SOAU is responsible for preparing the necessary documents for communication to outside agencies. rti|stor-comm-cth-15-COMMONWEALTH-OMBUDS: INSPECTIONS The Commonwealth Ombudsman perform inspections and provide guidance to the WA Police Force in respect to Chapter 3 - Stored Communications. SOAU will facilitate inspections and provide assistance, making records available as required for the duration of the inspection. Inspections by the Ombudsman (Commonwealth) The inspection will be conducted, and the subsequent report to an agency will be prepared, based on the focus areas listed below. The Ombudsman will place particular emphasis on whether WA Police Force has appropriate policies, procedures and controls in place to ensure that:  Access to Stored Communications is lawful, authorised and supported by a valid warrant or statutory authority.  Stored Communications are only accessed, used and communicated for permitted purposes under the Act.  Records relating to Stored Communications (including applications, warrants, preservation notices, use and communication logs, and destruction records) are complete, accurate and properly maintained.  Stored Communications and related records are stored securely and protected from unauthorised access, use or disclosure.  Access to Stored Communications is limited to authorised personnel with a legitimate operational need.  Stored Communications and records are destroyed in accordance with the Act once retention is no longer permitted or required.  Internal oversight, governance and audit mechanisms exist to monitor compliance with Chapter 3 of the Act.  The Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) have been made accessible to all members of staff through the WA Police internal intranet site.
